body.translated_text: #<s>Bhāmatī</s>#

children.translated_text: Of Him who is the source, endowed with the pair [of powers] — ineffable <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), whose transformations (<s>vivarta</s>) are these — space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
From whom this universe arose — moving and unmoving, high and low — we bow to that <s>Brahman</s>, of limitless bliss, knowledge, and immortality.
The <s>Veda</s>s are his exhalation; the five elements are his glance;
This world of moving and non-moving beings is his smile; and the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>) is his sleep.
Endowed with six limbs (<s>aṅga</s>s), and with various imperishable [auxiliaries],

children.text: śāśvatāya namaskurmo vedāya ca bhavāya ca //3 //
children.translated_text: We bow to the eternal <s>Veda</s> and to <s>Bhava</s> (<s>Śiva</s>).
We salute <s>Mārtaṇḍa</s> (the Sun), <s>Tilaka</s>, <s>Svāmī</s>, and <s>Mahāgaṇapati</s> —
Who are revered by the universe and who bestow all <s>siddhi</s>s (perfections).
To him, the author of the <s>Brahmasūtra</s>s, to <s>Vyāsa</s>, the other <s>Vedhas</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>),
Who is the descent of the power of knowledge of the Lord <s>Hari</s> — homage!
Having bowed to <s>Śaṅkara</s>, the treasury of compassion, of purified knowledge,
His commentary (<s>bhāṣya</s>), lucid and profound, is here analyzed.
Even words of people such as ourselves, which have entered into the teacher's composition,
Purify — just as gutter-water falling into the stream of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> [becomes purifying].

body.text:
atha yadasaṃdigdhamapirayojanaṃ ca na tatprekṣāvatpratipitsāgocaraḥ, yathā samanaskendriya- saṃnikṛṣṭaḥ sphītālokamadhyavartī ghaṭaḥ, karaṭadantā vā ; tathā cedaṃ brabmeti vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiḥ /
tathā hi-- bṛhattvādbṛṃhaṇatvādvātmaiva brahmeti gīyate /
sa cāyam ākīṭapataṅgebhya ā ca devarṣibhyaḥ prāṇabhṛnmātrasyedaṅkārāspadebhyo dehendriyamanobuddhiviṣayebhyo vivekena 'aham' ityasaṃdigdhāviparyastāparokṣānubhavasiddha iti na jijñāsārapadam /
na hi jātu kaścidatra saṃdigdhe 'ahaṃ vā nāhaṃ vā' iti /
na ca viparyasyati 'nāhameva' iti /
na ca 'ahaṃ kṛśaḥ, sthūlaḥ, gacchāmi' ityādidehadharmasāmānādhikaraṇyadarśanāddehālamno 'yamahaṅkāra iti sāṃpratam /
tadālambanatve hi 'yo 'haṃ bālye pitarāvanvabhūvaṃ sa eva sthāvire praṇaptṝnanubhavāmi' iti pratisaṃdhānaṃ na bhavet /
na hi bālasthavirayoḥ śarīrayorasti manāgapi pratyabhijñānagandho yenaikatvaṃ adhyavasīyeta /
tasmādyeṣu vyāvartamāneṣu yadanuvartate tattebhyo bhinnaṃ yathā kusumebhyaḥ sūtram /
tathā ca bālādiśarīreṣu vyāvartamāneṣvapi parasparamahaṅkārāspadamanuvartamānaṃ tebhyo bhidyate /
api ca svapnānte divyaṃ śarīrabhedamāsthāya taducitānbhogānbhuñjāna eva pratibuddho manuṣyaśarīramātmānaṃ paśyan 'nāhaṃ devo manuṣya eva' iti devaṣaśarīre bādhyamāne 'pyahamāspadamabādhyamānaṃ śarīrādbhinnaṃ pratipadyate /
api ca yogavyāghraḥ śarīrabhede 'pyātmānamabhinnamanubhavatīti nāhaṅkārālambanaṃ dehaḥ /
ata eva nendriyāṇyapyasyālambanam, indriyabhede 'pi 'yo 'hamadrākṣaṃ sa evaitarhi spṛśāmi' ityahamā-lambanasya pratyabhijñānāt /
viṣayebhyastvasya vivekaḥ sthavīyāneva /
body.translated_text:
Now, that which is neither doubtful nor purposeless is not an object of inquiry for the discerning — just as a pot that is in the proximity of a person with healthy senses, situated in the midst of ample light, or the tusks of an elephant. If so, [the proposition] 'this is <s>Brahman</s>' would be an instance of the fallacy of contradiction with something universally established.
For indeed — because of its greatness (<s>bṛhattva</s>) and because of its capacity to expand (<s>bṛṃhaṇatva</s>), the Self (<s>Ātman</s>) itself is celebrated as <s>Brahman</s>.
And this very [Self], from insects and moths up to divine sages — the abode of the sense of 'this' (<s>idaṅkāra</s>) for every breathing being — is established through the indubitable, non-erroneous, immediate experience of 'I,' as distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects. Therefore it is not a fit subject for inquiry.
For never does anyone entertain the doubt: 'Am I, or am I not?'
Nor does anyone erroneously conclude: 'I am not at all.'
Nor is it correct [to say] that this ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) takes the body as its object, on the grounds that one observes co-referentiality of bodily properties in [statements like] 'I am thin,' 'I am fat,' 'I am walking.'
For if it had the body as its object, the recognition 'I who as a child had parents am the very same who in old age experience my grandchildren' would not occur. For between the bodies of childhood and old age, there is not the slightest trace of recognition by which identity could be determined.
Therefore, that which persists when [other things] change is different from them — like a thread from flowers.
And so, even as the bodies of childhood and the like change, the abode of ego-sense that persists through [them all] is different from them.
Moreover, at the end of a dream, having assumed a divine bodily form and enjoying pleasures appropriate to it, upon awakening, seeing himself as a human body, [one thinks] 'I am not a god, I am indeed a human' — even though the divine body is sublated, the abode of 'I' remains unsublated, and one ascertains it as different from the body.
Moreover, the tiger among <s>yogī</s>s experiences the Self as unchanged even when the body changes — therefore the body is not the object of ego-sense.
For the same reason, the senses too are not its object, since even when the senses change, there is recognition: 'I who saw am the very one who now touches' — confirming the continuity of the 'I'-referent.
And the distinction of [the Self] from objects is even more firmly [established].

body.text: buddhimanasośca karaṇayoḥ 'aham' iti kartṛpratibhāsaprakhyānālambanatvāyogaḥ /
body.translated_text: And as for intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) and mind (<s>manas</s>), which are instruments (<s>karaṇa</s>), they cannot be the object [of ego-sense], because [ego-sense] manifests as the agent 'I' [rather than as an instrument].

body.text:
'kṛśo 'ham' 'andho 'ham' ityādayastu prayogā asatyapyabhede kathañcit 'mañcāḥ krośanti' ityādivadaupacārikā iti yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ /
tasmādidaṅkārāspadebhyo dehendriyamanobuddhiviṣayebhyo vyāvṛttaḥ sphuṭatarāhamanubhavagamya ātmā saṃśayābhāvādajijñāsya iti siddham /
body.translated_text:
And such usages as 'I am thin,' 'I am blind,' and the like — even in the absence of [actual] identity — are, like 'the cots are crying,' figurative (<s>aupacārika</s>). This we consider reasonable.
Therefore it is established that the Self, distinguished from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects — which are the abodes of 'this'-sense (<s>idaṅkāra</s>) — and apprehended through the most vivid experience of 'I,' is not a subject of inquiry, due to the absence of doubt.

body.text:
aprayojanatvācca /
tathā hi- saṃsāranivṛttirapavarga iha prayojanaṃ vivakṣitam /
body.translated_text:
And because it is purposeless.
For indeed, the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), which is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), is the purpose intended here.

body.text: saṃsāraśca ātmayāthātmyānanubhavanimitta ātmayāthātmyajñānena nivartanīyaḥ /
body.translated_text: <s>Saṃsāra</s>, which is caused by the non-experience of the true nature of the Self, is to be removed by the knowledge of the true nature of the Self.

body.text:
sa cedayamanādiranādinā ātmayāthātmyajñānena sahānuvartate, kuto 'sya nivṛttiḥ avirodhāt ? kutaścātmayāthātmyānanubhavaḥ ? na hi 'aham' ityanubhavādanyadātmayāthātmyajñānamasti /
na ca 'aham' iti sarvajanīnasphuṭatarānubhavasamarthita ātmā dehendriyādivyatiriktaḥ śakya upaniṣadāṃ sahasrairapyanyathayitum, anubhavavirodhāt /
na hyāgamāḥ sahasramapi ghaṭaṃ paṭayitumīśate /
tasmādanubhavavirodhādupacaritārthā evopaniṣada iti yuktamutpaśyāma ityāśayavānāśaṅkya pariharati- yuṣmadasmatpratyayagocarayoḥ iti /
body.translated_text:
But if this [<s>saṃsāra</s>] is beginningless and has persisted together with the beginningless knowledge of the Self's true nature, whence its cessation — since there is no contradiction? And whence the non-experience of the Self's true nature? For there is no knowledge of the Self's true nature other than the experience of 'I.'
And the Self, confirmed by the most vivid experience universal to all people as 'I,' as distinct from the body, senses, and the like, cannot be made otherwise even by a thousand <s>Upaniṣad</s>s — because that would contradict experience. For not even a thousand scriptures are capable of making a pot into a cloth.
Therefore, since [the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s] contradict experience, we consider it reasonable that the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s have a figurative meaning — anticipating this objection, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes it: 'of the spheres of the you-concept and the I-concept' (<s>yuṣmad-asmat-pratyaya-gocarayoḥ</s>).

body.text:
atra ca yuṣmadasmat ityādiḥ mithyeti bhavituṃ yuktaṃ ityantaḥ śaṅkāgranthaḥ /
tathāpi ityādiḥ parihāragranthaḥ /
tathāpi ityabhisaṃbandhācchaṅkāyāṃ yadyapīti paṭhitavyam /
idamasmatpratyayagocarayoriti vaktavye yuṣmadgrahaṇamatyantabhedopalakṣaṇārtham /
yathā hyahaṅkārapratiyogī tvaṅkāro naivamidaṅkāraḥ, 'ete vayam, ime vayam, āsmahe' iti bahulaṃ prayogadarśanāditi /
citsvabhāva ātmā viṣayī, jaḍasvabhāvā buddhīndriyadehaviṣayā viṣayāḥ /
ete hi cidātmānaṃ visinvanti avabadhnanti ; svena rūpeṇa nirūpaṇīyaṃ kurvantīti yāvat /
parasparānadhyāsahetau atyantavailakṣaṇye dṛṣṭāntaḥ - tamaḥ prakāśavat iti /
na hi jātu kaścitsamudācāradvṛttinī prakāśatamasī parasparātmatayā pratipattumarhati /
tadidamuktam - itaretarabhāvānupapattau iti /
itaretarabhāvaḥ itaretaratvam, tādātmyamiti yāvat ; tasyānupapattāviti /
body.translated_text:
Here, the objection-passage begins with 'you (<s>yuṣmad</s>) and I (<s>asmat</s>)' and ends with 'it is fitting [to say] that [this] is false.' The refutation-passage begins with 'even so' (<s>tathāpi</s>). Because of the syntactic connection with 'even so,' in the objection, '<s>yadyapi</s>' (although) should be read. The mention of '<s>yuṣmad</s>' (you), where '<s>idam</s>' (this) and '<s>asmat</s>' (I) would have sufficed, is for the purpose of indicating the utmost distinction [between subject and object]. For the 'you'-sense (<s>tvaṅkāra</s>) is the exact counterpart of the 'I'-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), while the 'this'-sense (<s>idaṅkāra</s>) is not [its exact counterpart], because the usage 'we are these, we are those' is seen abundantly.
The Self, whose nature is consciousness (<s>cit</s>), is the subject (<s>viṣayī</s>); the intellect, senses, body, and objects, whose nature is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), are the objects (<s>viṣaya</s>). For these latter bind, entangle, the conscious Self — that is, they cause it to be defined by their own forms.
The example for the mutual non-superimposition when there is utter dissimilarity is: 'like darkness and light.' For never can anyone, even in ordinary usage, apprehend darkness and light, which are mutually opposed, as being each other's self.
This is what is stated — 'when the mutual identity (<s>itaretarabhāva</s>) is impossible.' <s>Itaretarabhāva</s> means becoming one another, i.e., identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) — its impossibility.

body.text:
syādetat /
mā bhūddharmiṇoḥ parasparabhāvaḥ ; taddharmāṇāṃ tu jāḍyacaitanyanityatvānityatvādīnāṃ itaretarādhyāso bhaviṣyati /
dṛśyate hi dharmiṇorvivekagrahaṇe 'pi taddharmāṇāmadhyāsaḥ, yathā kusumādbhedena gṛhyamāṇe 'pi sphaṭikamaṇāvatisvacchatayā japākusumapratibimbodgrāhiṇi 'aruṇaḥ sphaṭikaḥ' ityāruṇyavibhrama ityata idamuktam - taddharmāṇāmapi iti /
itaretaratra dharmiṇi dharmāṇāṃ bhāvo vinimayaḥ, tasyānupapattiḥ /
ayamabhisaṃdhiḥ - rūpavaddhi dravyamatisvacchatayā rūpavato dravyāntarasya tadvivekena gṛhyamāṇasyāpi cchāyāṃ gṛhṇīyāt, cidātmā tu nīrūpo viṣayī na viṣayacchāyāmudgrāhayitumarhati /
yathāhuḥ-
body.translated_text:
One might say: let there be no mutual identity of the two substrata (<s>dharmin</s>s); but there may be mutual superimposition of their properties (<s>dharma</s>s) — such as inertness, consciousness, permanence, impermanence, and the like.
For even when the distinction of the two substrata is grasped, superimposition of their properties is observed — just as a crystal gem, even though distinguished from a <s>japā</s> flower, due to its extreme transparency captures the reflection of the red <s>japā</s> flower, [resulting in] the erroneous perception 'the crystal is red.' Therefore [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'of their properties also' (<s>taddharmāṇām api</s>).
The exchange (<s>vinimaya</s>) of properties of one substratum upon the other — its impossibility.
The purport is this: a substance that has form, due to its extreme transparency, may capture the reflection of another substance that has form — even when the latter is apprehended as distinct. But the subject (<s>viṣayī</s>), which is the conscious Self, is formless (<s>nīrūpa</s>) and cannot be made to display the reflection of an object.
As they say:

body.text:
'śabdagandharasādīnāṃ kīdṛśī pratibimbatā' iti /
tadiha pāriśeṣyādviṣayaviṣayiṇoranyonyātmasaṃbhedenaiva taddharmāṇāmapi parasparasaṃbhedena vinimayātmanā bhavitavyam , tau ceddharmiṇau atyantavivekena gṛhyamāṇāvasaṃbhinnau, asaṃbhinnāḥ sutarāṃ tayordharmāḥ, svāśrayābhyāṃ vyavadhānena dūrāpetatvāt /
tadidamuktam - sutarāṃ iti /
tadviparyayeṇa iti /
viṣayaviparyayeṇetyarthaḥ /
mithyāśabdaḥ apahnavavacanaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati - adhyāso bhedāgraheṇa vyāptaḥ, tadviruddhaścehāsti bhedagrahaḥ, sa bhedāgrahaṃ nivartayaṃstadvyāptamadhyāsamapi nivartayatīti /
mithyeti bhavituṃ yuktaṃ yadyapi tathāpīti yojanā /
body.translated_text:
'How can there be a reflection of sound, smell, taste, and the like?'
Therefore, here, by elimination, the exchange of properties must be through the mutual confusion of the identities of the object and the subject themselves. But if these two substrata are apprehended with utter distinction as unconfused, their properties are even more unconfused — because they are more remote, being separated by their own substrata.
This is what is stated: 'all the more so' (<s>sutarām</s>).
'By the contrary thereof' means: by the contrary of the object — this is the meaning.
The word 'false' (<s>mithyā</s>) means denial.
What is stated amounts to this: superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) is invariably concomitant with the non-apprehension of difference; and here, its opposite — the apprehension of difference — is present, which, by removing the non-apprehension of difference, removes the superimposition that it invariably accompanies.
The syntactic connection is: 'although it is fitting [to say] that it is false, even so...'

body.text:
idamatrākūcam - bhavedetadevaṃ yadi 'aham' ityanubhave ātmatatvaṃ prakāśeta /
na tvetadasti /
tath hi samastopādhyanavacchinnānantānandacaitanyaikarasamudāsīnamkamadvitīyamātmatattvaṃ śrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇeṣu gīyate /
na caitānyupakramaparāmarśopasaṃhāraiḥ kriyāsamabhihāreṇedṛgātmatattvamabhidadhati tatparāṇi santi śakyāni śakreṇāpyupacaritārthāni kartum /
abhyāse hi bhūyastvamarthasya bhavati yathā 'aho darśanīyā aho darśanīyā' iti, nālpatvamapi prāgevopacaritatvamiti /
ahamanubhavastu prādeśikamanekavidhaśokaduḥkhādiprapañcopaplutamātmānamādarśayan kathamātmatattvagocaraḥ kathaṃ vānupaplavaḥ ? na ca jyeṣṭhapramāṇapratyakṣavirodhādāmnāyasyaiva tadapekṣasyāprāmāṇyamupacaritārthatvaṃ veti yuktam, tasyāpauruṣeyatayā nirastasamastadoṣāśaṅkasya, bodhakatayā ca svataḥsiddhapramāṇabhāvasya svakārye pramitāvanapekṣatvāt /
pramitāvanapekṣatve 'pyutpatau pratyakṣāpekṣatvāttadvirodhādanutpattilakṣaṇamasyāprāmāṇyamiti cet, na, utpādakāpratidvandvitvāt /
na hyāgamajñānaṃ sāṃvyavahārikaṃ pratyakṣasya prāmāṇyamupahanti yena kāraṇābhāvānna bhavet ; api tu tāttvikam /
na ca tāttvikamasyotpādakam, atāttvikapramāṇabhāvebhyo 'pi sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇebhyastattvajñānotpattidarśanāt /
tathā ca varṇe hrasvatvadīrghatvādayo 'nyadharmā api samāropitāḥ tattvapratipattihetavaḥ /
na hi laukikāḥ 'nāgaḥ' iti vā"nagaḥ"iti vā padātkuñcaraṃ vā taruṃ vā pratipadyamānā bhavanti bhrāntāḥ /
na cānanyaparaṃ vākyaṃ svārtha upacaritārthaṃ yuktam /
uktaṃ hi - 'na vidhau paraḥ śabdārthaḥ' iti /
jyeṣṭhatvaṃ ca anapekṣitasya bādhyatve hetuḥ na tu bādhakatve, rajatajñānasya jyāyasaḥ śuktijñānena kanīyasā bādhadarśanāt /
tadamapabādhane tadapabādhātmanaḥ tasyotpatteranupapatteḥ /
darśitaṃ ca tāttvikapramāṇabhāvasyānapekṣitatvam /
tathā ca pāramarṣaṃ sūtram - 'paurvāparye pūrvadaurbalyaṃ prakṛtivat' iti /
tathā ca -
body.translated_text:
This is the intended meaning: this would indeed be so if the true nature of the Self were revealed in the experience of 'I.' But this is not the case.
For the true nature of the Self — infinite, blissful consciousness of a single essence (<s>ekarasa</s>), undivided by any limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>), detached, non-dual (<s>advitīya</s>) — is celebrated in the <s>Śruti</s>s, <s>Smṛti</s>s, <s>Itihāsa</s>s, and <s>Purāṇa</s>s.
And those [texts], which through their opening, reference, and conclusion (<s>upakrama-parāmarśa-upasaṃhāra</s>), and through the accumulation of statements, teach such a nature of the Self — being devoted to it — cannot be rendered figurative even by <s>Indra</s> himself.
For in repetition, the emphasis (<s>bhūyastva</s>) of meaning increases — as in 'Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful!' — it does not diminish, let alone become figurative.
But the 'I'-experience, displaying a limited Self beset by manifold elaborations of grief, suffering, and the like — how can it pertain to the true nature of the Self? And how can it be free from error?
Nor is it reasonable [to argue] that because of the contradiction with perception, the superior means of knowledge, it is scripture that is non-authoritative or figurative — for [scripture], being impersonal (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), is free from all suspicion of defect, and being a means of knowledge (<s>bodhakatā</s>), its status as a means of knowledge is self-established and independent of any other means of knowledge for generating valid cognition.
[Objection:] Even if it is independent in generating cognition, it depends on perception for its origin, and since it contradicts [perception], its non-validity takes the form of non-origination. [Reply:] No, because it is not opposed by its cause of origination. For scriptural knowledge does not undermine the conventional (<s>sāṃvyavahārika</s>) validity of perception — so that it would not arise due to the absence of [its] cause. Rather, [it undermines] the ultimate (<s>tāttvika</s>) [validity]. And the ultimate [validity] is not its cause of origination, since the arising of knowledge of reality is seen even from non-ultimate, conventional means of knowledge.
And so, even properties superimposed on a syllable — such as shortness, length, and the like — are causes of apprehending reality. For ordinary people comprehending 'elephant' or 'tree' from the word '<s>nāga</s>' are not deluded.
Nor is it reasonable for a sentence that has no other purpose to be taken figuratively in its own meaning. For it has been said: 'There is no other meaning of a word beyond [what it conveys in] an injunction.'
And the superiority [of perception] is a reason for something being sublated when it is independent, but not for sublation [by it] — since the sublation of the stronger silver-cognition by the weaker nacre-cognition is observed.
That [perception] cannot sublate [scripture], because the arising of [something] whose own nature is the sublation of that [perception] would be impossible.
And the independence of the ultimate status as a means of knowledge has been demonstrated.
And thus the aphoristic <s>sūtra</s> of [<s>Jaimini</s>] regarding sequential priority states: 'In [cases of] prior and posterior, the weakness of the prior — as is natural.'
And thus —

body.text: pūrvātparabalīyastvaṃ tatra nāma pratīyatām /
body.translated_text: Let it be accepted that the later [means of knowledge] is stronger than the earlier;

body.text: anyonyanirapekṣāṇāṃ yatra janma dhiyāṃ bhavet //
body.translated_text: Where the cognitions arise independently of each other.

body.text: - iti //
body.translated_text: — thus.

body.text:
api ca ye 'pyahaṅkārāspadamātmānamāsthiṣata tairapyasya na tāttvikatvamabhyupetavyam, 'ahamihaivāsmi sadane jānānaḥ' iti sarvavyāpinaḥ prādeśikatvena grahaṇāt uccataragiriśikharavartiṣu mahātaruṣu bhūmiṣṭhasya dūrvāpravālanirbhāsapratyayavat /
na cedaṃ dehasya prādeśikatvamanubhūyate na tvātmana iti sāṃpratam /
na hi tadaivaṃ bhavati 'aham' iti, gauṇatve vā na 'jānānaḥ' iti /
api ca paraśabdaḥ paratra lakṣyamāṇaguṇayogena vartata iti yatra prayoktṛpratipattroḥ saṃpratipattiḥ sa gauṇaḥ /
sa ca bhedapratyayapuraḥsaraḥ /
tadyathā, naiyamikāgnihotravacane 'gnihotraśabdaḥ prakaraṇāntarāvadhṛtabhede kuṇḍapāyināmayanagate karmaṇi 'māsamagmihotraṃ juhoti' ityatra sādhyasādṛśyena gauṇaḥ, māṇavake cānubhavasiddhabhede siṃhātsiṃhaśabdaḥ /
na tvahaṅkārasya mukhyor'tho nirluṭhitagarbhatayā dehādibhyo bhinno 'nubhūyate, yena paraśabdaḥ śarīrādau gauṇo bhavet /
na cātyantanirūṭhatayā gauṇe 'pi na gauṇatvābhimānaḥ sārṣapādiṣu tailaśabdavaditi veditavyam /
tatrāpi snehāttilabhavādbhede siddha eva sārṣapādīnāṃ tailaśabdavācyatvābhimānaḥ, na tvarthayostailasārṣapayorabhedādhyavasāyaḥ /
tatsiddhaṃ gauṇatvamubhayadarśino gauṇamukhyavivekavijñānena vyāptam, tadiha vyāpakaṃ vivekavijñānaṃ nivartamānaṃ gauṇatāmapi nivartayatīti /
body.translated_text:
Moreover, even by those who hold that the self is the substrate of the ego-sense (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>), its ultimate reality need not be accepted, since the all-pervading [self] is apprehended as spatially limited in [the cognition] 'I am here in the house, knowing' — like the perception of green sprouts by one standing on the ground in relation to great trees standing on the peaks of higher mountains.
Nor is it tenable [to say] that it is the spatial limitation of the body that is experienced, not of the self.
For it is not the case that [the cognition] arises as merely 'I' — or if it were figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>), then [the qualification] 'knowing' would not [apply].
Moreover, a figurative expression (<s>para-śabda</s>) operates by connection with a quality observed [to belong] to another; therefore, where there is mutual agreement between the speaker and the hearer, that [usage] is figurative.
And that [figurative usage] is preceded by the cognition of difference.
For example, the word '<s>agnihotra</s>' in the context of the regular fire-sacrifice, when the difference [of meaning] has been ascertained in another context, is figurative by similarity with the primary meaning, as applied to the rite of the <s>kuṇḍapāyin</s>s during the sacrificial session, in [the statement] 'he offers the monthly <s>agnihotra</s>'; and [similarly] the word 'lion' [applied] to a boy, where the difference is established through experience.
But the primary meaning of the ego-sense is not experienced as different from the body etc., as though its core had been extracted, such that the word [for 'self'] would be figurative when [applied to] the body etc.
Nor should it be supposed that, due to extreme conventionalization, even in figurative usage there is no awareness of figurativeness, as with the word 'oil' (<s>taila</s>) in [expressions like] 'mustard oil' etc.
Even there, the awareness that mustard etc. are denoted by the word '<s>taila</s>' [arises] only when the difference — based on the unctuous quality from sesame, from which [<s>taila</s>] is derived — is already established; it is not that there is a determination of non-difference between the [two] referents, [true] sesame-oil and mustard-[oil].
Thus it is established that figurativeness is invariably accompanied (<s>vyāpta</s>) by the discernment of the distinction between figurative and primary [meanings] on the part of one who perceives both. Here, this pervading factor — the discernment of distinction — being absent, negates figurativeness as well.

body.text:
na ca bālasthaviraśarīrabhede 'pi 'so 'ham' ityekasyātmanaḥ pratisaṃdhānadehādibhyo bhedenāstyātmānubhava iti vācyam /
parīkṣakāṇāṃ khalviyaṃ kathā, na laukikānām /
parīkṣakā api hi vyavahārasamaye na lokasāmāmyamativartante /
vakṣyatyanantarameva hi bhagavānbhāṣyakāraḥ -'paśvādibhiścāviśeṣāt' iti /
bāhyā apyāhuḥ -'śāstracintakāḥ khalvevaṃ vivecayanti na pratipattāraḥ' iti /
tatpāriśeṣyāccidātmagocaramahaṅkāram 'ahamihāsmi sadane' iti prayuñjāno laukikaḥ śarīrādyabhedagrahādātmanaḥ prādeśikatvamabhimanyate nabhasa iva ghaṭamaṇikamallikādyupādhyavacchedāditi yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Nor should it be said that even though there is a difference in the bodies of childhood and old age, the experience of a single self in 'I am that same [person]' — through the reconnection (<s>pratisaṃdhāna</s>) [of memory] — proves that there is an experience of the self as different from the body etc.
This discussion belongs to critical investigators (<s>parīkṣaka</s>s), not to ordinary people.
Even critical investigators, at the time of practical activity, do not transgress the common [understanding] of the world.
For the revered commentator [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] will say immediately after: 'And because there is no distinction from animals etc.' (<s>paśvādibhiś cāviśeṣāt</s>).
The <s>Bauddha</s>s also say: 'Theoreticians (<s>śāstra-cintaka</s>s) indeed discriminate in this way, not [ordinary] cognizers.'
Therefore, by elimination, the ordinary person who employs the ego-sense — whose object is the conscious self (<s>cid-ātman</s>) — in [the statement] 'I am here in the house,' entertains the notion of the self's spatial limitation due to the non-apprehension of the difference [of the self] from the body etc. — just as [infinite] space [appears limited] due to the limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>s) of a pot, a jewel, a jasmine flower, etc. — this we consider reasonable.

body.text:
na cāhaṅkāraprāmāṇyāya dehādivadātmāpi prādeśika iti yuktam /
tadā khalvayamaṇuparimāṇo vā syāddehaparimāṇo vā /

children.text: aṇupariṃmāṇatve 'sthūlo 'ham, dīrghaḥ' iti ca na syāt /
children.translated_text: If of atomic dimension, then [the cognition] 'I am stout, I am tall' etc. would not arise.
If of the dimension of the body, then since [the self] would have parts, the unwanted consequence of impermanence — like the body — would follow.

children.text: kiñca asminpakṣe avayavasamudāyo vā cetayet, pratyekaṃ vāvayavāḥ /
children.translated_text: Furthermore, in this view, either the aggregate of parts would be conscious, or each individual part [would be conscious].

children.text: pratyekaṃ cetanatvapakṣe bahūnāṃ cetanānāṃ svatantrāṇāmekavākyatābhāvādaparyāyaṃ viruddhadikkriyatayā śarīramunmathyeta, akriyaṃ vā prasajyeta //
children.translated_text: In the case where each [part] is individually conscious, since many independent conscious [entities] cannot form a single coordinated [action], the body would be torn apart by contradictory directional activities, or alternatively, inaction would result. //

body.translated_text:
Nor is it reasonable [to argue] that, to validate the ego-sense, the self too is spatially limited like the body etc.
For then it would be either of atomic dimension or of the dimension of the body.

body.text:
samudāyasya tu caitanyayoge vṛkṇa ekasminnavayave cidātmano 'pyavayavo vṛkṇa iti na cetayet /
na ca bahūnāmavayavānāṃ parasparāvinābhāvaniyamo dṛṣṭaḥ /
ya evāvayavo yadā viśīrṇastadā tadabhāve na cetayet /
body.translated_text:
But if consciousness belonged to the aggregate, then when one part is cut, a part of the conscious self too would be cut, and so [the aggregate] would not be conscious.
Nor is there any observed rule that many parts are invariably concomitant with one another.
Whatever part is destroyed at whatever time — in the absence of that, [the aggregate] would not be conscious.

body.text:
vijñānālambanatve 'pi ahaṃpratyayasya bhrāntatvaṃ tadavasthameva, tasya sthiravastunirbhāsatvādasthiratvācca vijñānānām /
etena 'sthūlo 'ham andho 'ham gacchāmi' ityādayo 'pi adhyāsatayā vyākhyātāḥ /
body.translated_text:
Even if [one holds] that consciousness is the object of cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>), the erroneousness of the ego-cognition (<s>ahaṃ-pratyaya</s>) remains just the same, since it has the appearance of a stable entity whereas cognitions are unstable.
By this, [cognitions like] 'I am stout,' 'I am blind,' 'I go,' etc. are also explained as being [instances of] superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>).

body.text:
tadevamuktena krameṇa ahaṃpratyaye pūtikūṣmāṇḍīkṛte bhagavatī śrutiḥ apratyūhaṃ kartṛtvabhoktṛtvasukhaduḥkhaśokādyātmatvamahamanubhavaprasañjitamātmano niṣeddhumarhatīti /
tadevaṃ sarvapravādaśrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇaprathitamithyābhāvasyāhaṃpratyayasya svarūpanimittaphalairupavyākhyānam - anyonyasmin ityādi /
anyonyasmindharmiṇyātmaśarīrādau anyonyātmakatāmadhyasya - ahamidaṃ śarīrāditi /
'idam' iti ca vastutaḥ, na pratītitaḥ /
lokavyavahāraḥ lokānāṃ vyavahāraḥ /
sa ca 'ayamaham' iti vyapadeśaḥ /
iti śabdasūcitaśca śarīrādyanukūlaṃ pratikūlaṃ ca prameyajātaṃ pramāṇena pramāya tadupādānaparivarjanādiḥ /
body.translated_text:
Thus, by the method stated — the ego-cognition having been reduced to a rotten gourd, as it were — the revered <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) is entitled to negate without obstruction the selfhood of agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>), enjoyership (<s>bhoktṛtva</s>), happiness, suffering, grief, etc., which is foisted [on the self] by the ego-experience.
Thus, the explanation — by way of its nature (<s>svarūpa</s>), cause (<s>nimitta</s>), and effect (<s>phala</s>) — of the ego-cognition, whose false existence is renowned in all philosophical schools, <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, <s>Itihāsa</s>, and <s>Purāṇa</s>, [is given in the words] 'in one another' (<s>anyonyasmin</s>) etc.
'Having superimposed upon each other' — that is, upon the two substrates (<s>dharmin</s>), the self and the body etc., the mutual identity — [the cognition] 'I am this body etc.'
And 'this' (<s>idam</s>) [refers to what is real] in truth, not in appearance.
'Worldly transaction' (<s>loka-vyavahāra</s>) is the conduct of people.
And that [consists of] the designation 'I am this [body].'
And [the transaction] indicated by the word '<s>iti</s>' [includes]: having ascertained by a means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) the entire range of knowable objects that are favorable or unfavorable to the body etc., the adoption [of the favorable] and avoidance [of the unfavorable] etc.

body.text:
anyonyadharmāṃścādhyasya anyonyasmindharmiṇi dehādidharmān janmamaraṇajarāvyādhyādīnātmani dharmiṇi adhyastadehādibhāve samāropya, tathā caitanyādīnātmadharmān dehādāvadhyastātmabhāve samāropya 'mamedaṃ jarāmaraṇaputrapaśusvāmyādi' iti vyavahāro vyapadeśaḥ /
itiśabdasūcitaśca tadanurūpaḥ pravṛttyādiḥ /
atra ca adhyāsavyavahārakriyābhyāṃ yaḥ kartā unnītaḥ sa samāna iti samānakartṛkatvena 'adhyasya vyavahāraḥ' ityupapannam /
pūrvakālatvasūcitamadhyāsasya vyavahārakāraṇatvaṃ sphuṭayati - mithyājñānanimittaḥ vyavahāraḥ iti /
mithyājñānamadhyāsaḥ, tannimittaḥ, tadbhāvābhāvānuvidhānādvyavahārabhāvābhāvayorityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
'And having superimposed the properties of each upon the other' — upon the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) [which is the self], having superimposed the properties of the body etc. — birth, death, old age, disease, etc. — upon the self as substrate, through the [prior] superimposition of the body etc. [upon the self]; and likewise, having superimposed the properties of the self — consciousness etc. — upon the body etc. through the [prior] superimposition of the self [upon the body] — [the transaction is:] 'This is mine — old age, death, sons, cattle, lordship, etc.,' such designation.
And [the transaction] indicated by the word '<s>iti</s>' is the corresponding activity etc.
Here, the agent who is inferred from the two — the superimposition and the [resulting] worldly transaction — is the same; thus, through the identity of the agent, [the expression] 'having superimposed, [there is] worldly transaction' is appropriate.
The causal relation of superimposition to worldly transaction, indicated by the earlier temporal position [of superimposition], is clarified [in the phrase] 'worldly transaction caused by false knowledge' (<s>mithyā-jñāna-nimittaḥ</s>).
<s>Mithyā-jñāna</s> (false knowledge) is superimposition; 'caused by that' means that the existence and non-existence of worldly transaction conforms to the existence and non-existence of that [superimposition] — this is the meaning.

body.text:
tadevamadhyāsasvarūpaṃ phalaṃ ca vyavahāramuktvā tasya nimittamāha - itaretarāvivekena iti /
vivekagrahaṇenetyarthaḥ /
atha aviveka eva kasmānna bhavati, tathā ca nādhyāsa ityata āha - atyantaviviktayordharmadharmiṇoḥ /
paramārthato dharmiṇoratādātmyaṃ vivekaḥ dharmāṇāṃ cāsaṃkīrṇatā vivekaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Thus, having stated the nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) and the effect (<s>phala</s>), namely worldly transaction, of superimposition, [the text] states its cause — 'through the non-discrimination of one from the other' (<s>itaretarāvivekena</s>).
[This means:] 'through the non-apprehension of discrimination' — this is the meaning.
Now, [one may ask,] why should there not be simply non-discrimination, and consequently no superimposition? To this [the text] says — 'of properties and substrates that are absolutely distinct' (<s>atyanta-viviktayoḥ dharma-dharmiṇoḥ</s>).
In ultimate reality, the non-identity of the two substrates is their discrimination (<s>viveka</s>); and the non-intermingling of the properties is their discrimination.

body.text:
syādetat /
viviktayorvastusatorbhedāgrahanibandhanastādātmyavibhramo yujyate śukteriva rajatādbhedāgrahe rajatatādātmyavibhramaḥ /
iha tu paramārthasataḥ cidātmano 'nyanna dehādyasti vastusat, tatkutaḥ cidātmano bhedāgrahaḥ kutaśca tādātmyavibhramaḥ ityata āha - satyānṛte mithunīkṛtya iti /
vivekāgrahādadhyasyeti yojanā /
satyaṃ cidātmā, anṛtaṃ buddhīndriyadehādiḥ ; te dve dharmiṇī mithunīkṛtya yugalīkṛtyetyarthaḥ /
na ca saṃvṛtiparamārthasatoḥ pāramārthakaṃ mithunamastītyabhūtatadbhāvārthasya cveḥ prayogaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati - apratītasyāropāyogādāropyasya pratītirupayujyate na vastusatteti /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
A delusion of identity due to non-apprehension of difference is possible between two really existing things — just as a delusion of identity with silver [arises] from non-apprehension of the difference of mother-of-pearl from silver.
But here, apart from the ultimately real conscious self (<s>cid-ātman</s>), no other thing — body etc. — really exists. So how can there be non-apprehension of difference from the conscious self, and how can there be a delusion of identity?
To this [the text] says — 'having coupled the real and the unreal' (<s>satyānṛte mithunīkṛtya</s>).
The construction is: [the superimposition occurs] through non-apprehension of discrimination.
The 'real' (<s>satya</s>) is the conscious self; the 'unreal' (<s>anṛta</s>) is the intellect, senses, body, etc. These two substrates are 'coupled' — made into a pair — this is the meaning.
Nor does there exist an ultimately real pairing of the conventionally real and the ultimately real; hence the use of the suffix '<s>cvi</s>' in the sense of 'becoming what it was not before.'
What is meant is this: since superimposition is not possible of what is not cognized, the cognition (<s>pratīti</s>) of what is to be superimposed is required — but not its real existence (<s>vastu-sattā</s>).

body.text:
syādetat /
āropyasya pratītau satyāṃ pūrvadṛṣṭasya samāropaḥ samāropanibandhanā ca pratītiriti durvāraṃ parasparāśrayatvamityata āha - naisargika iti /
śvābhāvikaḥ anādirayaṃ vyavahāraḥ /
vyavahārānāditayā tatkāraṇasyādhyāsasya, anāditoktā, tataśca pūrvapūrvamithyājñānopadarśitasya buddhīndriyaśarīrādeḥ uttarottarādhyāsopayoga ityanāditvāt bījāṅkuravanna parasparāśrayatvamityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
If the cognition of what is to be superimposed is granted, then there is the superimposition of what was previously seen; and the cognition [of the superimposed] is based on the superimposition — thus the inescapable defect of mutual dependence (<s>parasparāśrayatva</s>) [arises].
To this [the text] says — '<s>naisargika</s>' (innate).
'Natural' (<s>svābhāvika</s>) — this transaction is beginningless (<s>anādi</s>).
Due to the beginninglessness of the transaction, its cause — superimposition — is also beginningless, as stated. Therefore, the intellect, senses, body, etc. that are presented by each preceding false cognition serve as the basis for each succeeding superimposition; and since this is beginningless — like the seed and sprout — there is no mutual dependence. This is the meaning.

body.text:
syādetat /
advā pūrvapratītimātramupayujyate ārope, na tu pratīyamānasya paramārthasattā /
pratītireva tu atyantāsato gaganakamalinīkalpasya dehendriyādeḥ nopapadyate /
prakāśamānatvameva hi cidātmano 'pi sattvaṃ na tu tadatiriktaṃ sattāsāmānyasamavāyor'thakriyākāritā vā dvaitāpatteḥ /
sattāyāścārthakriyākāritāyāśca sattāntarārthakriyākāritāntarakalpane anavasthāpātāt prakāśamānataiva sattā abhyupetavyā /
tathā ca dehādayaḥ prakāśamānatvānnāsantaḥ cidātmavat, asattve vā na prakāśamānāḥ ; tatkathaṃ satyānṛtayormithunībhāvaḥ ?
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
Alternatively, mere prior cognition (<s>pūrva-pratīti-mātra</s>) is required for superimposition, not the ultimate existence of what is cognized.
But the very cognition of something absolutely non-existent — like a sky-lotus — such as the body, senses, etc., is not possible.
For indeed, even in the case of the conscious self, existence (<s>sattva</s>) is nothing but being manifest (<s>prakāśamānatva</s>), and not something over and above that — such as the universal of existence (<s>sattā-sāmānya</s>), the relation of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), or causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā-kāritā</s>) — since [accepting any of] these would entail duality.
And if for existence and causal efficacy one postulates yet another existence and another causal efficacy, the defect of infinite regress arises; therefore, being-manifest alone must be accepted as existence.
Accordingly, the body etc. are not non-existent, since they are manifest — just like the conscious self; or, if they were non-existent, they would not be manifest. Then how can there be a coupling of the real and the unreal?

body.text:
tadabhāve vā kasya kuto bhedāgrahaḥ ? tadasaṃbhave kuto 'dhyāsaḥ ? ityāśayavān āha ākṣeptā- ko 'yamadhyāso nāma iti /
ka ityākṣepe /
samādhātā lokasiddhamadhyāsalakṣaṇamācakṣāṇa evākṣepaṃ pratikṣipati- ucyate- smṛtirūpaḥ paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa iti /
avasannaḥ avamato vā bhāsaḥ avabhāsaḥ /
pratyayāntarabādhaścāsya avasādo 'vamāno vā /
etāvatā mithyājñānamityuktaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text:
Or, in the absence of that [coupling], whose non-apprehension of difference from what? And if that is impossible, how can there be superimposition?
With this intent, the objector raises [the question] — 'What is this so-called superimposition?' (<s>ko 'yam adhyāso nāma</s>).
'<s>Ka</s>' [is used] in the sense of objection.
The answerer, in the very act of stating the definition of superimposition as commonly established, rebuts the objection — 'It is said: it has the form of memory (<s>smṛti-rūpa</s>), the appearance of something previously seen in something else' (<s>paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa</s>).
'<s>Avabhāsa</s>' (appearance) means a <s>bhāsa</s> (cognition) that is <s>avasanna</s> (subdued) or <s>avamata</s> (disregarded).
And its being subdued or disregarded [consists in its being] sublated by another cognition.
By this much, it is effectively stated that [superimposition] is false knowledge (<s>mithyā-jñāna</s>).

body.text:
tasyedamupavyākhyānam 'pūrvadṛṣṭa-' ityādi /
pūrvadṛṣṭasyāvabhāsaḥ pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsaḥ /
mithyāpratyayaśca āropaviṣayāropaṇīyamithunamantareṇa na bhavatīti pūrvadṛṣṭagrahaṇenānṛtamāropaṇīyamupasthāpayati /
tasya ca dṛṣṭatvamātramupayujyate na vastusatteti dṛṣṭagrahaṇam /
tathāpi vartamānaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ darśanaṃ nāropopayogīti pūrva- ityuktam /
tacca pūrvadṛṣṭaṃ svarūpeṇa sadapyāropaṇīyatayā anirvācyamityanṛtam /
āropaviṣayaṃ satyamāha- paratra iti /
paratra śuktikādau paramārthasati /
tadanena satyānṛtamithunamuktam /
body.translated_text:
The explanation of that is [given in the phrase] 'previously seen' etc.
'The appearance of the previously seen' — <s>pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa</s> — is a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> compound.
False cognition does not occur without the pair of the locus of superimposition and the object to be superimposed; therefore, by the [qualifying] word 'previously seen,' the unreal — the object to be superimposed — is brought forward.
And only its having-been-seen is required, not its real existence — hence the word 'seen' (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>).
Even so, what is presently seen — present perception — is not useful for superimposition; therefore, '<s>pūrva</s>' (previously) is said.
And that 'previously seen,' though existent in its own form, is indescribable (<s>anirvācya</s>) insofar as it is the object of superimposition — hence it is 'unreal' (<s>anṛta</s>).
The 'real,' which is the locus of superimposition, is stated by '<s>paratra</s>' (in something else).
'<s>Paratra</s>' — in mother-of-pearl etc. — that which is ultimately real.
By this, the 'coupling of the real and unreal' has been stated.

body.text:
syādetat /
paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa ityalakṣaṇam , ativyāpakatvāt /
asti hi svastimatyāṃ gavi pūrvadṛṣṭasya gotvasya paratra kālākṣyāmavabhāsaḥ /
asti ca pāṭaliputre pūrvadṛṣṭasya devadattasya paratra māhiṣmatyāmavabhāsaḥ samīcīnaḥ /
avabhāsapadaṃ ca samīcīne 'pi pratyaye prasiddham, yathā nīlasyāvabhāsaḥ pītasyāvabhāsa iti /
ata āha- smṛtirūpa iti /
smṛteḥ rūpamiva rūpamasyeti smṛtirūpaḥ /
asaṃnihitaviṣayatvaṃ ca smṛtirūpatvam /
saṃnihitaviṣayaṃ ca pratyabhijñānaṃ samīcīnamiti nātivyāptiḥ /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
'The appearance of something previously seen in something else' is a faulty definition (<s>alakṣaṇa</s>), because of over-extension (<s>ativyāpti</s>).
For there is the appearance, in a cow with an auspicious mark, of cow-ness previously seen — [and this is] in something else, namely a dark-eyed [cow] — [yet this is valid, not erroneous].
And there is the appearance of <s>Devadatta</s> previously seen in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>, in something else — namely in <s>Māhiṣmatī</s> — and this is a correct [recognition].
Moreover, the word '<s>avabhāsa</s>' (appearance) is well established even in correct cognition, as in 'the appearance of blue,' 'the appearance of yellow.'
To this [the text] says — '<s>smṛti-rūpa</s>' (having the form of memory).
'<s>Smṛti-rūpa</s>' means: its form is like (<s>iva</s>) the form of memory.
And 'having the form of memory' means having an absent object [as its content].
Recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>), which has a present object, is correct — thus there is no over-extension.

body.text:
nāpyavyāptiḥ, svapnajñānasyāpi snṛtivibhramarūpasyaivaṃrūpatvāt /
tatrāpi hi smaryamāṇe pitrādau nidropaplavavaśādasaṃnidhānāparāmarśe, tatra tatra pūrvadṛṣṭasyaiva saṃnihitadeśakālatvasya samāropaḥ /
evam 'pītaḥ śaṅkhaḥ' 'tikto guḍaḥ' ityatrāpyetallakṣaṇaṃ yojanīyam /
tathā hi- bahirvinirgacchajatyacchanayanaraśmisaṃpṛktapittadravyavartinīṃ pītatāṃ pittarahitāmanubhavan, śaṅkhaṃ ca doṣācchāditaśuklimānamanubhavan, pītatāyāśca śaṅkhāsaṃbandhamananubhavan, asaṃbandhāgrahaṇasārūpye 'pītaṃ tapanīyapiṇḍaṃ' 'pītaṃ bilvaphalaṃ' ityādau pūrvadṛṣṭaṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ pītatvaśaṅkhatvayorāropyāha 'pītaḥ śaṅkhaḥ' iti /
etena 'tikto guḍaḥ' iti pratyayo vyākhyātaḥ /
evaṃ vijñātṛpuruṣābhimukheṣvādarśodakādiṣu svaccheṣu cākṣuṣaṃ tejo lagnamapi balīyasā saureṇa tejasā pratisrotaḥ pravartitaṃ mukhasaṃyuktaṃ mukhaṃ grāhayet, doṣavaśāttaddeśatāmanabhimukhatāṃ ca mukhyasyāgrāhayat, pūrvadṛṣṭābhimukhādarśodakadeśatāmābhimukhyaṃ ca mukhasyāropayatīti pratibimbavibhramo 'pi lakṣito bhavati /
etena dvicandradiṅmohālātacakragandharvanagaravaṃśoragādivibhrameṣvapi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ yojanīyam /
body.translated_text: Nor is there under-extension [of the definition], since even dream-cognition, which is itself of the nature of erroneous memory, has this very form. For therein too, when the father and the like are being remembered, due to the disturbance of sleep there is no apprehension of their non-presence [at the current location], and there is superimposition of being-present-in-the-current-place-and-time upon what was previously seen elsewhere. Similarly, in cases like 'the conch is yellow' or 'the jaggery is bitter,' this same definition should be applied. For instance: experiencing the yellowness residing in the bile-substance mixed with the transparent rays of vision issuing outward, without the whiteness of the conch which is concealed by the defect, and not experiencing the non-connection of yellowness with the conch — due to the similarity of non-apprehension-of-non-connection to [cases like] 'a yellow lump of gold' or 'a yellow wood-apple fruit' where co-referentiality of yellowness and conch-ness was previously seen — one superimposes and says 'the conch is yellow.' By this, the cognition 'the jaggery is bitter' is explained. Similarly, in mirrors, water, and other clear [surfaces] facing the cognizing person, the visual radiance, though attached [to them], is propelled counter-current by the more powerful solar radiance and, being connected with the face, causes the face to be apprehended; but due to the defect, it does not cause apprehension of the face's actual location and its non-facing-ness, and superimposes upon the face the location-in-the-mirror-or-water and the facing-ness that were previously seen. Thus the illusion of reflection is also covered [by the definition]. By this, the definition should be applied, as appropriate, to illusions such as the double moon, directional confusion, the circle of a firebrand, the celestial city (<s>gandharva-nagara</s>), the bamboo-snake, and the like.

body.text:
etaduktaṃ bhavati- na prakāśamānatāmātraṃ sattvam, yena dehendriyādeḥ prakāśamānatayā sadbhāvo bhavet /
na hi sarpātadabhāvena rajjvādayo vā sphaṭikādayo vā raktādiguṇayogino na pratibhāsante, pratibhāsamānā vā bhavanti tadātmānastaddharmāṇo vā /
tathā sati maruṣu marīcikānicayam 'uccāvacamuccalattuṅgataraṅgabhaṅgamāleyamabhyarṇabhavatīrṇā mandākinī' ityabhisaṃdhāya pravṛttaḥ tattoyamāpīya pipāsāmupaśamayet /
tasmādakāmenāpi prakāśamānasyāpyāropitasya na vastusattvamabhyupagamanīyam /
body.translated_text: What has been said amounts to this: mere being-manifest is not existence (<s>sattva</s>), such that the body, senses, and the like would have real existence by virtue of being manifest. For it is not the case that ropes and the like, or crystals and the like, do not appear as possessing qualities such as redness merely because the snake and the like are absent [from them], or that when appearing [thus] they actually become of that nature or possess those properties. If that were so, a person who has set out toward the mirages in a desert, thinking 'the <s>Mandākinī</s>, with its undulating waves of varying height, cresting and breaking in garlands, has come near and can be crossed,' would drink that water and quench his thirst. Therefore, even unwillingly, one must not accept that what is superimposed, even though manifest, has the reality of a real thing.

body.text: na ca marīcirūpeṇa salilamavastusat svarūpeṇa tu paramārthasadeva dehendriyādayastu svarūpeṇāpyasanta ityanubhavāgocaratvātkathamāropyanta iti sāṃpratam ; yato yadyasanto nānubhavagocarāḥ kathaṃ tarhi marīcyādīnāmasatāṃ toyādyātmatayānubhavagocaratvam ? na ca svarūpasattvena toyādyātmanāpi santo bhavanti /
body.translated_text: Nor is the following objection sound: 'Water is unreal in the form of a mirage but is ultimately real in its own nature; while the body, senses, and the like are unreal even in their own nature — hence, being beyond the range of experience, how can they be superimposed?' For if non-existents are not objects of experience, then how do mirages and the like, which are non-existent, become objects of experience in the form of water and the like? Nor do they become existent — possessing the nature of water — by virtue of their own inherent reality.

body.text:
yadyucyeta- nābhāvo nāma bhāvādanyaḥ kaścidasti, api tu bhāva eva bhāvāntarātmanā abhāvaḥ svena rūpeṇa tu bhāvaḥ /
yathāhuḥ-
body.translated_text: If it be said: 'There is no such thing as non-existence separate from existence; rather, existence itself, in the form of some other entity, is non-existence, while in its own form it is existence.' As they say —

body.text:
'bhāvāntaramabhāvo hi kayācittu vyapekṣayā' /
iti /
tataśca bhāvātmanopākhyeyatayā asya yujyeta anubhavagocaratā /
prapañcasya punaratyantāsato nirastasamastasāmarthyasya nistattvasya kuto 'nubhavaviṣayabhāvaḥ, kuto vā cidātmanyāropaḥ ? na ca viṣayasya samastasāmarthyavirahe 'pi vijñānameva tattādṛśaṃ svapratyayasāmarthyādadṛṣṭāntasiddhasvabhāvabhedamupajātamasataḥ prakāśanam, tasmādasatprakāśanaśaktirevāsyāvidyeti sāṃpratam /
yato yeyamasatprakāśanaśaktirvijñānasya kiṃ punarasyāḥ śakyam ? asaditi cet, kimetatkāryam, āhosvidasyā jñāpyam ? na tāvatkāryam, asatastattvānupapatteḥ /
nāpi jñāpyam, jñānāntarānupalabdheḥ, anavasthāpātācca /
vijñānasvarūpameva asataḥ prakāśa iti cet. kaḥ punareṣa sadasatoḥ saṃbandhaḥ ? asadadhīnanirūpaṇatvaṃ sato jñānasya asatā saṃbandha iti cet, aho batāyamatinirvṛtaḥ pratyayatapasvī yadasya asatyapi nirūpaṇamāyatate /
na ca pratyayastatrādhatte kiñcit, asata ādhāratvāyogāt /
asadantareṇa pratyayo na prathata iti pratyayasyaivaiṣa svabhāvaḥ na tvasadadhīnamasya kiñciditi cet, aho batāsya asatpakṣapātaḥ yadayamatadutpattiḥ atadātmā ca tadavinābhāvaniyataḥ pratyaya iti /
tasmādatyantāsantaḥ śarīrendriyādayo nistattvā nānubhavaviṣayā bhavitumarhantīti /
body.translated_text: 'Non-existence is indeed another entity, but only from a certain perspective.' Thus, since [non-existence] is describable as having the nature of an entity, its being an object of experience would be justified. But as for the phenomenal world (<s>prapañca</s>), which is absolutely non-existent, devoid of all capacity, and without any real essence — how could it become an object of experience, and how could it be superimposed upon the consciousness-self (<s>cidātman</s>)? Nor is the following position tenable: 'Even in the absence of all capacity in the object, consciousness itself, of such a nature, through the power of its own causes, with intrinsic differentiation established by analogy, arises as the manifestation of the non-existent; therefore, the power of manifesting the non-existent is itself its <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).' For regarding this power of consciousness to manifest the non-existent — what further can this power do? If it is said 'the non-existent,' then is this its effect or its object of knowledge? It is not an effect, since the production of the non-existent is impossible. Nor is it an object of knowledge, since no other cognition is apprehended [of it], and because of the fallacy of infinite regress. If it be said that the very nature of consciousness is the manifestation of the non-existent — then what kind of relation is this between the existent and the non-existent? If it be said that the relation of the existent cognition with the non-existent consists in the cognition's being dependent on the non-existent for its characterization — oh, what an excessively contented ascetic of cognition this is, that his characterization extends even to the non-existent! Nor does the cognition place anything there [in the non-existent], since the non-existent cannot serve as a substratum. If it be said that the cognition does not manifest without the non-existent, and this is simply the nature of cognition, not that anything of it depends on the non-existent — oh, what partiality for the non-existent this is, that this cognition, which does not arise from it and is not of its nature, is nevertheless invariably connected with it! Therefore, the body, senses, and the like, being absolutely non-existent and devoid of any real essence, cannot possibly be objects of experience.

body.text:
atra brūmaḥ- nistattvaṃ cennānubhavagocaraḥ, tatkimidānīṃ marīcayo 'pi toyātmanā satattvāḥ yadanubhavagocarāḥ syuḥ /
na satattvāḥ, tadātmanā marīcīnāmasattvāt /
dvividhaṃ ca vastūnāṃ tattvam- sattvamasattvaṃ ca tatra pūrvaṃ svataḥ, paraṃ tu parataḥ /
yathāhuḥ-
body.translated_text: To this we reply: If what is devoid of real essence cannot be an object of experience, then are mirages also possessed of real essence in the form of water, that they should be objects of experience? They are not possessed of real essence, since mirages do not exist with that nature [of water]. And the reality of things is twofold — existence and non-existence; the former is intrinsic, the latter is extrinsic. As they say:

body.text: 'svarūpapararūpābhyāṃ nityaṃ sadasadātmake /
body.translated_text: 'In a thing that is always of the nature of both existent and non-existent, by its own form and by another's form,

body.text: vastuni jñāyate kiñcidrūpaṃ kaiścitkadācana //
body.translated_text: some particular form is known by some persons at some time.' //

body.text:
-iti /
tatkiṃ marīciṣu toyanirbhāsapratyayastattvagocaraḥ ? tathā ca samīcīna iti na bhrānto nāpi bādhyeta /
addhā ! na bādhyeta yadi marīcīnayaṃ atoyātmatattvānatoyātmanā gṛhṇīyāt /
toyātmanā tu gṛhṇan kathama bhrāntaḥ, kathaṃ vā abādhyaḥ ? hanta ! toyābhāvātmanāṃ marīcināṃ toyabhāvātmatvaṃ tāvanna sat, teṣāṃ toyābhāvādabhedena toyabhāvātmatānupapatteḥ /
nāpyasat ; vastvantarameva hi vastvantarasyāsattvamāsthīyate /
body.translated_text: Then is the cognition of water-appearance in mirages directed toward their real essence? And if so, it would be correct, not erroneous, and would not be sublated. Indeed! It would not be sublated if one were to cognize the non-water essence of the mirages as having a non-water nature. But when cognizing [them] as having a water-nature, how is one not erroneous, and how is one not sublated? Now then: the mirages, whose nature is the absence of water, do not truly possess the nature of the presence of water, since from the absence of water in them, their having the nature of the presence of water is impossible as non-different [from them]. Nor is it [simply] non-existent; for what is accepted as the non-existence of one entity is simply another entity.

body.text:
'bhāvāntaramabhāvo 'nyo na kaścidanirūpaṇāt' iti vadadbhiḥ /
na cāropitaṃ rūpaṃ vastvantaram ; taddhi marīcayo vā bhavet, gaṅgādigataṃ toyaṃ vā /
pūrvasminkalpe 'marīcayaḥ' iti pratyayaḥ syāt, na 'toyam' iti /
uttarasmiṃstu 'gaṅgāyāṃ toyam' iti syāt, na punaḥ 'iha' iti /
deśabhedāsmaraṇe 'toyam' iti syāt, na pula 'iha' iti /
na cedamatyantamasat nirastasamastasvarūpamalīkamevāstu iti sāṃpratam, tasyānubhavagocaratvānupapatteḥ, ityuktamadhastāt /
tasmānna sat, nāsat, nāpi sadasat parasparavirodhāt, ityanirvācyamevāropaṇīyaṃ marīciṣu toyamāstheyam ; tadanena krameṇādhyastaṃ toyaṃ paramārthatoyamiva, ata eva pūrvadṛṣṭamiva ; tattvatastu na toyam, na ca pūrvadṛṣṭam ; kiṃ tu anṛtam anirvācyam /
evaṃ ca dehendriyādiprapañco 'pi anirvācyaḥ ; apūrvo 'pi pūrvamithyāpratyayopadarśita iva paratra cidātmanyadhyasyata iti upapannam, adhyāsalakṣaṇayogāt /
dehendriyādiprapañcabādhanaṃ ca upapādayiṣyate /
cidātmā tu śrutismṛtītihāsapurāmagocaraḥ tanmūlatadaviruddhanyāyanirṇītaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaḥ sattvenaiva nirvācyaḥ /
abādhitā svayaṃprakāśataiva asya sattā, sā ca svarūpameva cidātmanaḥ, na tu tadatiriktaṃ sattāsāmānyasamavāyaḥ arthakriyākāritā vā iti sarvamavadātam /
body.translated_text: As those who say: 'Non-existence is another entity; there is no other uncharacterizable [non-existence].' But the superimposed form is not another entity; for it would either be the mirages themselves or the water in the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and the like. In the first case, the cognition would be 'these are mirages,' not 'this is water.' In the second case, it would be 'water in the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' not 'here.' When the difference of place is not remembered, it would be 'water,' but not 'here.' Nor is it tenable that this is absolutely non-existent, a completely void non-entity devoid of all intrinsic nature, since its being an object of experience would be impossible — as has been stated above. Therefore, not existent, not non-existent, and not both existent and non-existent due to mutual contradiction — what is to be superimposed upon the mirages as water must be accepted as indescribable (<s>anirvācya</s>); and by this process, the superimposed water, like real water, and therefore as if previously seen; but in truth it is neither water nor previously seen — rather, it is unreal (<s>anṛta</s>) and indescribable (<s>anirvācya</s>). And thus the phenomenal world of body, senses, and the like is also indescribable; though unprecedented, it is as if shown by prior erroneous cognition, and is superimposed upon the consciousness-self (<s>cidātman</s>) elsewhere — this is well-established, since it fits the definition of <s>adhyāsa</s> (superimposition). The sublation of the phenomenal world of body, senses, and the like will also be demonstrated. The consciousness-self (<s>cidātman</s>), however, is the domain of <s>Śruti</s> (scripture), <s>Smṛti</s> (tradition), <s>Itihāsa</s> (epic), and <s>Purāṇa</s> (ancient lore); its nature as pure, awakened, and liberated is ascertained by reasoning rooted in and not contradicting these [sources]; it is describable only as existent (<s>sattva</s>). Its unsublated, self-luminous nature is its existence, and that is the very nature of the consciousness-self — not something additional like the co-inherence of universal existence, or the capacity to produce effects. Thus everything is clarified.

body.text: sa cāyamevaṃlakṣaṇako 'dhyāsaḥ anirvacanīyaḥ sarveṣāmeva saṃmataḥ parīkṣakāṇām ; tadbhede paraṃ vipratipattirityanirvacanīyatāṃ draḍhayitumāha- taṃ kecit iti /
body.translated_text: This <s>adhyāsa</s> (superimposition) of such characteristics, being indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>), is accepted by all critical thinkers; the disagreement among them concerns its varieties. To consolidate its indescribability, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '<s>taṃ kecit</s>' (some [regard] it...) and so forth.

body.text:
anyadharmasya jñānadharmasya rajatasya ; jñānākārasyeti yāvat /
adhyāsaḥ anyatra bāhye /
sautrāntikanaye tāvadbāhyamasti vastusat ; tatra jñānākārasyāropaḥ /
vijñānavādināmapi, yadyapi na bāhyaṃ vastusat tathāpyanādyavidyāvāsanāropitamalīkaṃ bāhyam ; tatra jñānākārasyāropaḥ /
upapattiśca- yadyādṛśamanubhavasiddhaṃ rūpaṃ tattādṛśameva abhyupetavyamityutsargaḥ ; anyathātvaṃ punarasya balavadbādhakapratyayavaśāt ; 'nedaṃ rajatam' iti bādhakasya idantāmātrabādhenāpyupapattau na rajatagocaratocitā /
rajatasya dharmiṇo bhādhe hi rajataṃ ca tasya dharma idantā ca bādhite bhavetām ; tadvaramidantaivāsya dharmo bādhyatām, na punā rajatamapi dharmi ; tathā ca rajataṃ bahirbādhitamarthādāntare jñāne vyavatiṣṭhata iti jñānākārasya bahiradhyāsaḥ sidhyati /
body.translated_text: The property of another — of the cognized object, namely silver — the property of cognition, that is, the form of cognition — <s>adhyāsa</s> (superimposition) is upon something else, the external [object]. In the <s>Sautrāntika</s> system, there does indeed exist an external object that is substantially real; upon that, the form of cognition is superimposed. Even for the <s>Vijñānavādin</s>s (Consciousness-only school), although no external object is substantially real, nevertheless there is a false external [appearance] superimposed by beginningless <s>avidyā</s>-impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>); upon that, the form of cognition is superimposed. And the justification is: as a general rule, whatever form is established through experience, that very form must be accepted as such; its being otherwise is only due to the force of a powerful sublating cognition. With the sublation 'this is not silver,' since it is possible to explain [the sublation] as sublating only the 'this-ness,' the cognition need not be directed toward silver. For if the property — silver — were sublated along with the possessor of the property — the 'this-ness' — then both silver and its property 'this-ness' would be sublated; it is better that only the property 'this-ness' be sublated, and not silver as the property-possessor. And thus silver, sublated externally, implicitly remains in the internal cognition — and so the superimposition of the form of cognition upon the external [object] is established.

body.text:
kecittu- jñānākārakhyātāvaparituṣyanto vadanti- yatra yadadhyāsaḥ tadvivekāgrahanibandhano bhrama iti /
aparitoṣakāraṇaṃ cāhuḥ- vijñānakāratā rajatāderanubhavādvā vyavasthāpyeta, anumānādvā /
tatrānumānamupariṣṭānnirākariṣyate /
anubhavo 'pi rajatapratyayo vā syāt, bādhakapratyayo vā /
na tāvadrajatānubhavaḥ /
body.translated_text: But some, not satisfied with the theory of the appearance of the form of cognition, say: 'Wherever there is superimposition of something, that error is rooted in the non-apprehension of the distinction [between the two].' And they state the reason for dissatisfaction: 'The silver-nature of cognition (<s>vijñānakāratā</s>) would be established either from experience or from inference.' Therein, inference will be refuted later. Experience too would be either the cognition of silver or the sublating cognition. The experience of silver, at least, does not [establish it] —

body.text:
sa hi idaṅkārāspadaṃ rajatamāvedayati na tvāntaram /
'aham' iti hi tadā syāt, pratipattuḥ pratyayādavyatirekāt /
bhrāntaṃ vijñānaṃ svākārameva bāhyatayādhyavasyati, tathā ca nāhaṅkārāspadamasya gocaraḥ, jñānākāratā punasya bādhakapratyayamālocayatvāyuṣmān /
sa kiṃ purovarti dravyaṃ rajatādvivecayati āho jñānākāratāmapyasya darśayati ? tatra jñānākāratopadarśanavyāpāraṃ bādhakapratyayasya bruvāṇaḥ ślāghanīyaprajño devānāṃ priyaḥ /
purovartitvapratiṣedhādarthādasya jñānākārateti cet, na /
asaṃnidhānāgrahaniṣedhādasaṃnihito bhavati /
pratipatturatyantasaṃnidhānaṃ tvasya pratipatrātmakaṃ kutastyam ? na caiṣa rajatasya niṣedhaḥ, na ca idantāyāḥ, kiṃ tu vivekāgrahaprasañjitasya rajatavyavahārasya /
na ca rajatameva śuktikāyāṃ prasañjitaṃ rajatajñānena /
na hi rajatanirbhāsasya śuktikālambanaṃ yuktam, anubhavavirodhāt /
na khalu sattāmātreṇālambanam, atiprasaṅgāt /
sarveṣāmarthānāṃ sattvāviśeṣādālambanatvaprasaṅgāt /
nāpi kāraṇatvena, indriyādīnāmapi kāraṇatvāt /
tathā ca bhāsamānataivālambanārthaḥ /
na ca rajatajñāne śuktikā bhāsate, iti kathamālambanam ? bhāsamānatābhyupagame vā kathaṃ nānubhavavirodhaḥ ? api cendriyādīnāṃ samīcīnajñānopajanane sāmarthyamupalabdhamiti kathamebhyo mithyājñānasaṃbhavaḥ ? doṣasahitānāṃ teṣāṃ mithyāpratyaye 'pi sāmarthyamiti cet, na, doṣāṇāṃ kāryopajananasāmarthyavidhātamātre hetutvāt ; anyathā pluṣṭādapi kuṭajabījādvaṭāṅkurotpattiprasaṅgāt /
api ca svagocaravyabhicāre vijñānānāṃ sarvatrānāśvāsaprasaṅgaḥ /
tasmātsarvaṃ jñānaṃ samīcīnamāstheyam /
tathā ca 'rajatam','idam' iti ca dve vijñāne smṛtyanubhavarūpe /
tatra 'idaṃ' iti purovartidravyamātragrahaṇam, doṣavaśāttadgataśuktitvasāmānyaviśeṣasyāgrahāt tanmātraṃ ca gṛhītaṃ sadṛśatayā saṃskārodbodhakrameṇa rajate smṛtiṃ janayati /
sā ca gṛhītagrahaṇasvabhāvāpi doṣavaśādgṛhītatvāṃśapramoṣāc grahaṇamātramavatiṣṭhate /
tathā ca rajatasamṛteḥ purovartidravyamātragrahaṇasya ca mithaḥ svarūpato viṣayataśca bhedāgrahaṇāt, saṃnihitarajatagocarajñānasārūpyeṇa 'idam',
body.translated_text:
For it [the 'this'-sense] presents the silver as an object of 'this'-apprehension, but not the inner [consciousness].
'I' would [be the appropriate word] in that case, because the cognizer is not distinct from his cognition.
A deluded cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) apprehends its own form alone as external — and so the object of ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) is not its content. As for its being a form of cognition, let the venerable one consider the sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka-pratyaya</s>).
Does it [the sublating cognition] discriminate the object before one as distinct from silver, or does it also reveal that the latter is merely a form of cognition? In that case, one who declares the sublating cognition to have the function of revealing [something's nature as] a mere form of cognition is praiseworthy in intelligence and dear to the gods.
[Objection:] Since the sublating cognition negates [the silver's] being before one, by implication its being a form of cognition [is also established]. [Reply:] No. From the negation of the non-presence being a negation of non-proximity, it becomes merely non-proximate.
But whence the absolute proximity of this [silver] to the cognizer, which would make it of the nature of the cognizer? Nor is this a negation of silver, nor of 'this'-ness, but rather of the silver-usage that was brought about by the non-apprehension of distinction.
Nor was silver itself superimposed on the nacre by the silver-cognition.
For it is not reasonable that a cognition appearing as silver should have nacre as its object (<s>ālambana</s>), since this would contradict experience.
Indeed, something is not an object merely by virtue of its existence — for that would lead to an over-extension.
Since all things are equally existent, all would have to be objects — which is absurd.
Nor is something an object by virtue of being a cause, since the sense-organs etc. are also causes.
Therefore, being manifest [in awareness] alone constitutes the meaning of 'object.'
But in the silver-cognition, the nacre does not appear — so how can it be the object? Or if its appearance is conceded, how is there no contradiction with experience?
Moreover, since the capacity of the sense-organs etc. to produce correct cognition is observed, how can erroneous cognition arise from them?
[Objection:] When they are accompanied by defects, they have the capacity even for erroneous cognition. [Reply:] No — because defects serve merely to determine the capacity to produce a [particular] effect; otherwise, even from a burnt <s>kuṭaja</s>-seed, a banyan sprout would have to arise.
Moreover, if cognitions deviate from their proper objects, there would be a loss of confidence in all [cognitions] everywhere.
Therefore, all cognition should be accepted as correct.
Accordingly, 'silver' and 'this' are two cognitions — of the nature of memory and experience respectively.
There, 'this' is the apprehension of merely the object-as-present; due to a defect, there is non-apprehension of the generic and specific properties of nacre-ness belonging to it — and what is apprehended in its mere form, by virtue of similarity, through the process of arousing latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), generates a memory of silver.
And that [memory], though by nature an apprehension of what was [previously] apprehended, due to the defect loses the aspect of 'having been apprehended' and remains as mere apprehension.
Thus, because of the non-apprehension of the mutual distinction — both in their own natures and in their objects — between the memory of silver and the apprehension of the mere present object, by virtue of the resemblance to a cognition of silver actually present, [the two cognitions with regard to] 'this,'

body.text:
ṭarajatam', iti dve ete api grahaṇasmaraṇe abhedavyavahāraṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaṃ ca pravartayataḥ /
kvacitpunargrahaṇe e mithaḥ agṛhītabhede, yathā 'pītaḥ śaṅkhaḥ' iti /
atra hi vinirgacchannayanaraśmivartinaḥ pittadravyasya kācasyeva svacchasya pītatvaṃ gṛhyate pittaṃ tu na gṛhyate /
śaṅkho 'pi doṣavaśācchuklaguṇarahitaḥ svarūpamātreṇa gṛhyate /
tadanayorguṇaguṇinorasaṃsargāgrahasārūpyāt pītatapanīyapiṇḍapratyayāviśeṣeṇābhedavyavahāraḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaśca /
bhedāgrahaprasañjitābhedavyavahārabādhanācca 'nedam' iti vivekapratyayasya bādhakatvamapyupapadyate ; tadupapattau ca prāktanasya pratyayasya bhrāntatvamapi lokasiddhaṃ siddhaṃ bhavati /
tasmādyathārthāḥ sarve vipratipannāḥ saṃdehavibhramāḥ, pratyayatvāt, ghaṭādipratyayavat /
tadidamuktam- yatra yadadhyāsa iti /
yasmin śuktikādau yasya rajatāderadhyāsa iti lokaprasiddhiḥ nāsāvanyathākhyātinibandhanā, kiṃ tu gṛhītasya rajatādestatsmaraṇasya ca gṛhītatāṃśapramoṣeṇa gṛhītamātrasya yaḥ 'idam' iti puro 'vasthitāddravyamātrāttatprajñānācca vivekaḥ, tadagrahaṇanibandhano bhramaḥ /
bhrāntatvaṃ ca grahaṇasmaraṇayoritaretarasāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśo rajatādivyavahāraśceti /
body.translated_text:
'silver' — these two, namely apprehension and memory, produce the usage of non-difference and the predication of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>).
Sometimes, however, in apprehension alone, when the mutual difference is not grasped — as in 'the conch is yellow.' For here, the yellowness of the bile-substance situated in the outgoing eye-rays — which is transparent like glass — is grasped, but the bile itself is not grasped.
The conch too, due to the defect, is grasped in its mere form, devoid of its whiteness.
Thus, due to the resemblance arising from non-apprehension of the connection of these two — quality and qualified — the usage of non-difference and the predication of co-referentiality proceed without distinction from the cognition of a lump of yellow gold.
And from the sublation of the usage of non-difference that had been brought about by non-apprehension of difference, the fitness of the discriminating cognition 'this is not [silver]' as a sublating cognition is also established. And upon the establishment of that [sublation], the erroneousness of the prior cognition too becomes an established fact well-known in the world.
Therefore, all cognitions are veridical — those of disagreement, doubt, and confusion alike — because they are cognitions, like the cognition of a pot and the like.
This is what was stated [by <s>Śaṅkara</s>]: 'wherever there is superimposition of what upon what.' That upon the nacre and the like there is superimposition of silver and the like — this is the well-known [position]. It is not based on the <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (theory of error as 'cognition of something other'). Rather, the confusion (<s>bhrama</s>) has its basis in the non-apprehension of the distinction between: (1) the silver etc. which was [previously] apprehended and the memory thereof — whose aspect of 'having-been-apprehended' is lost through the defect, leaving only the bare apprehension; and (2) the mere present object apprehended as 'this' and the cognition thereof.
The erroneousness consists in the mutual predication of co-referentiality of the apprehension and the memory, and the silver-usage and the like.

body.text:
anye tu- atrāpyaparituṣyantaḥ- yatra yadadhyāsastasyaiva viparītadharmakalpanāmācakṣate /
atredamākūtam- asti tāvadrajatārthinaḥ 'rajatamidam' iti pratyayātputovartini dravye pravṛttiḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśaśceti sarvajanīnām /
tadetanna tāvadgrahaṇasmaraṇayostadgocarayośca mitho bhedāgrahamātrādbhavitumarhati /
grahaṇanibandhanau hi cetanasya vyavahāravyapadeśau kathamagrahaṇamātrādbhavetām ? nanūktaṃ nāgrahaṇamātrāt, kiṃ tu grahaṇasmaraṇe eva mithaḥ svarūpato viṣayataścāgṛhītabhede, samīcīnapuraḥsthitarajatavijñānasādṛśyenābhedavyavahāraṃ sāmānādhikaṇyavyapadeśaṃ ca pravartayataḥ /
atha samīcīnajñānasārūpyamanayorgṛhyamāṇaṃ vā vyavahārapravṛttihetuḥ, agṛhyamāṇaṃ vā sattāmātreṇa /
gṛhyamāṇe 'pi 'samīcīnajñānasārūpyamanayoridamiti rajatamiti ca jñānayoḥ' iti grahaṇam, atha vā 'tayoreva svarūpato viṣayataśca mitho bhedāgrahaḥ' iti grahaṇam /
tatra na tāvatsamīcīnajñānasadṛśī iti jñānaṃ samīcīnajñānavadvyavahārapravartakam /
na hi 'gosadṛśo gavayaḥ' iti jñānaṃ gavārthinaṃ gavaye pravartayati /
'anayoreva bhedāgrahaḥ' iti tu jñānaṃ parāhatam ; na hi bhedāgrahe anayoriti bhavati, anayoriti grahe bhedāgrahaṇamiti na bhavati /
tasmātsattāmātreṇa bhedāgrahaḥ agṛhīta eva vyavahāraheturiti vaktavyam /
tatra kimayamāropotpādakrameṇa vyavahārahetuḥ, āho anutpāditāropa eva svata iti ? vayaṃ tu paśyāmaḥ- cetanavyavahārasya ajñānapūrvakatvānupapatteḥ āropajñānotpādakrameṇaiva- iti /
nanu satyaṃ cetanavyavahāro nājñānapūrvakaḥ, kiṃ tu aviditavivekagrahaṇasmaraṇapūrvaka iti /
maivam /
na hi rajataprātipadikārthamātrasmaraṇaṃ pravṛttāvupayujyate /
idaṅkārāspadābhimukhī khalu rajatārthināṃ pravṛttirityavivādam /
kathaṃ cāyamidaṅkārāspade pravarteta yadi tu na tadicchet ? anyadicchatyanyatkarotīti vyāhatam /
na cedidaṅkārāspadaṃ rajatamiti jānīyāt kathaṃ rajatārthī tadicchet ? yadi atathātvenāgrahaṇāt iti brūyāt, sa ca prativaktavyaḥ, atha tathātvenāgrahaṇāt kasmānnopekṣeteti /
so 'yamupādānopekṣābhyāmubhayata ākṛṣyamāṇaścecanaḥ avyavasthitaḥ idaṅkārāspade rajatasamāropeṇopādāna eva vyavasthāpyate, iti bhedāgrahaḥ samāropotpādakrameṇa cetanapravṛttihetuḥ /
tathā hi - bhedāgrahādidaṅkārāspade rajatatvaṃ samāropya, tajjātīyasyopakārahetubhāvamanucintya, tajjātīyatayedaṅkārāspade rajate tamanumāya, tadarthī pravartate ityānupūrvyaṃ siddham /
na ca taṭastharajatasmṛtiḥ idaṅkārāspadasyopakārahetubhāvamanumāpayitumarhati, rajatatvasya hetorapakṣadharmatvāt /
ekadeśadarśanaṃ khalvanumāpakaṃ na tvanekadeśadarśanam /
yadāhuḥ-"jñātasaṃbandhasyaikadeśadareśanāt"iti /
samārope tvekadeśadarśanamasti /
tatsiddham- etadvivādādhyāsitaṃ rajatādijñānaṃ purovartivastuviṣayam, rajatādyarthinastatra niyamena pravartakatvāt, yadyadarthinaṃ yatra niyamena pravartakatvāt ; yadyadarthinaṃ yatra niyamena pravartayati tajjñānaṃ tadviṣayaṃ yathobhayasiddhasamīcīnarajatajñānam ; tathā cedam ; tasmāttathā- iti /
yaccoktam anavabhāsamānatayā na śuktirālambanamiti, tatra bhavān pṛṣṭo vyācaṣṭām- kiṃ śuktikātvasya 'idaṃ rajatam' iti jñānaṃ pratyanālambanatvam āhosvit dravyamātrasya puraḥsthitasya sitabhāsvarasya ? yadi śuktikātvasya anālambanatvam, addhā ! uttarasyānālambanatvaṃ bruvāṇasya tavaivānubhavavirodhaḥ /
tathā hi-'rajatamidam' ityanubhavannanubhavitā purovarti vastu aṅgulyādinā nirdiśati /
dṛṣṭaṃ ca duṣṭānāṃ kāraṇānāmautsargikakāryapratibandhena kāryāntaropajananasāmarthyam, yathā dāvāgnidagdhānāṃ vetrabījānāṃ kadalīkāṇḍajanakatvam, bhasmakaduṣṭasya caudaryasya tejaso bahvannapacanamiti /
pratyakṣabādhāpahṛtaviṣayaṃ ca vibhramāṇāṃ yathārthatvānumānamābhāsaḥ, hutavahānuṣṇatvānumānavat /
yaccoktaṃ mithyāpratyayasya vyabhicāre sarvapramāṇeṣvanāśvāsa iti, tat bodhakatvena svataḥprāmāṇyaṃ nāvyabhicāreṇeti vyutpādayadbhirasmābhiḥ parihṛtaṃ nyāyakaṇikāyāmiti neha pratanyate /
diṅmātraṃ cāsya smṛtipramoṣabhaṅgasyoktam ; vistarastu brahmatattvasamīkṣāyāmavagantavya iti /
tadidamuktam- anye tu yatra yadadhyāsastasyaiva viparītadharmakalpanāmācakṣate iti /
yatra śuktikādau yasya rajatāderadhyāsastasyaiva śuktikāderviparītadharmakalpanāṃ rajatatvadharmakalpanāmiti yojanā /
body.translated_text:
Others, however — not being satisfied even with this — describe the superimposition 'wherever there is superimposition of what' as the attribution of contrary properties to the very thing itself.
The intention here is as follows: It is universally accepted that from the cognition 'this is silver,' one who desires silver has an activity toward the object before him, and there is the predication of co-referentiality.
This cannot be accounted for merely by the non-apprehension of the mutual difference between the apprehension and the memory and their respective objects.
For how could the usage and predication — which are founded upon apprehension — of a conscious being, arise from mere non-apprehension?
[Objection:] Was it not said that [it arises] not from mere non-apprehension, but from the very apprehension and memory themselves — when their mutual difference, both in their own natures and in their objects, is not grasped — producing the usage of non-difference and the predication of co-referentiality by virtue of resemblance to correct cognition of actually present silver?
[Reply:] Well then, is this resemblance to correct cognition of theirs [the apprehension and memory] apprehended as the cause of the behavioral activity, or [operative] merely by virtue of its existence, without being apprehended?
Even if apprehended, [the question arises]: is the apprehension 'the resemblance to correct cognition of these two cognitions — the this-cognition and the silver-cognition'? Or is it 'the non-apprehension of the mutual difference of those very two, in their own natures and in their objects'?
Among these, the cognition 'this is similar to correct cognition' does not cause behavioral activity in the manner of correct cognition — for the cognition 'a <s>gavaya</s> is similar to a cow' does not impel one who desires a cow toward a <s>gavaya</s>.
But the cognition 'there is non-apprehension of the difference of these two' is self-defeating (<s>parāhata</s>); for in the non-apprehension of difference, 'of these two' [as a reference] is not possible, and in the apprehension of 'these two,' the non-apprehension of difference does not obtain.
Therefore, it must be said that the non-apprehension of difference, merely by virtue of its existence, unapprehended, is the cause of behavioral activity.
In that case, is this [non-apprehension] the cause of behavioral activity through the process of generating a superimposition (<s>āropa</s>), or does it by itself, without generating a superimposition, [serve as the cause]?
We, however, see it [thus]: since a conscious being's behavioral activity cannot be established without being preceded by cognition, it must be through the process of generating a superimposition-cognition.
[Objection:] True, a conscious being's behavioral activity is not preceded by ignorance, but it is preceded by an apprehension and memory whose distinction is not known. [Reply:] Not so. For a bare memory of the mere denotation of the word 'silver' is not useful for behavioral activity. The activity of those who desire silver is certainly directed toward the object of 'this'-apprehension — this is undisputed. How would one be directed toward an object of 'this'-apprehension if one did not desire it? 'He desires one thing and does another' — that would be contradictory. And if he does not cognize the object of 'this'-apprehension as silver, how would one who desires silver desire it? If one were to say 'because it is not apprehended as being otherwise,' then he is to be answered: 'Well then, since it is not apprehended as being that [i.e., silver] either, why does he not simply disregard it?'
Thus, this conscious being, pulled in both directions by acquisition and disregard, unstable — he is firmly established in acquisition alone through the superimposition of silver upon the object of 'this'-apprehension. Therefore the non-apprehension of difference, through the process of generating superimposition, is the cause of the conscious being's behavioral activity.
For it is thus: from the non-apprehension of difference, superimposing silver-ness upon the object of 'this'-apprehension, reflecting on the instrumentality for benefit of things of that class, inferring through the class-membership [that] the object of 'this'-apprehension is silver, one who desires that [silver] is impelled to act — this sequence is established.
But a memory of silver standing apart cannot serve to make one infer the instrumentality for benefit of the object of 'this'-apprehension — because 'silver-ness,' which is the inferential reason, does not belong to the subject (<s>pakṣa</s>).
Indeed, the observation of one part [of a thing in a substrate where it is actually present] is what enables inference, not the observation of [that part] elsewhere.
As they say: 'From the observation of one part of that whose relation is known.'
But in superimposition, there is the observation of one part [in the substrate].
Thus it is established: this cognition of silver etc. that is the subject of dispute pertains to the object actually before one (<s>purovartī-vastu</s>), because it invariably impels one who desires silver etc. to act toward it.
