Whatever invariably impels one who desires X toward Y, that cognition pertains to Y — like the well-established correct cognition of [actual] silver. And so this [cognition] is likewise. Therefore it is so.
As for the objection that nacre cannot be the object because it does not appear [in the cognition], let the venerable one please explain: is it the nacre-ness that is not the object of the cognition 'this is silver,' or is it the mere present substance — white and gleaming? If it is nacre-ness that is not the object, certainly! But then it is you yourself who has the contradiction with experience, in asserting that the latter [i.e., the substance] is also not the object.
For one who experiences 'this is silver' points to the object before him with a finger and the like.
And it is observed that defective causes have the capacity to produce a different effect by obstructing their normal effect — just as <s>vētra</s>-seeds burnt in a forest fire can produce banana-stalks, and the radiance of the digestive fire, when afflicted by the <s>bhasmaka</s> disease, can digest large quantities of food.
And the inference that delusions are veridical, on the ground that their objects are un-sublated by direct perception — that is a mere semblance of inference, like an inference that fire is not hot.
As for the objection that if erroneous cognition deviates, there would be no confidence in any means of knowledge — that has been addressed by us in the <s>Nyāyakaṇikā</s>, where we demonstrate that self-validity of a means of knowledge consists in its power to generate cognition, not in its non-deviation — so it is not elaborated here.
And only the outline of this refutation of the memory-loss theory has been stated; the details should be understood from the <s>Brahmatattvasamīkṣā</s>.
This is what was stated [by <s>Śaṅkara</s>]: 'Others, however, describe the superimposition wherever there is superimposition of what as the attribution of contrary properties to the very thing itself.' The construction is: wherever upon nacre etc. there is superimposition of silver etc. — of that very nacre etc., the attribution of the contrary property of silver-ness.

body.text:
nanu santu nāma parīkṣakāṇāṃ vipratipattayaḥ, prakṛte tu kimāyātamityata āha- sarvathāpi iti /
anyasyānyadharmakalpanā anṛtatā, sā ca anirvacanīyatetyadhastādupapādayitum /
tena sarveṣāmeva parīkṣakāṇāṃ mate anyasyānyadharmakalpanānirvacanīyāvaśyaṃbhāvinītyanirvacanīyatā sarvatantrasiddhānta ityarthaḥ /
akhyātivādibhirakāmairapi sāmānādhikaraṇyavyapadeśapravṛttiniyamasnehādidamabhyupeyamiti bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Now, let there indeed be disagreements among the examiners; but what bearing does this have on the present topic? To this he [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'In every case' (<s>sarvathā api</s>).
The attribution of the properties of one thing to another is falsity (<s>anṛtatā</s>), and that [falsity] is indeterminable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) — this will be established below.
Thus, in the view of all examiners alike, the attribution of the properties of one thing to another — being indeterminable and inevitable — [the concept of] indeterminability (<s>anirvacanīyatā</s>) is a universally accepted principle (<s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s>) — this is the meaning.
The import is that even the proponents of <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension theory of error) must, despite themselves, accept this — because of the invariable concomitance of the predication of co-referentiality, behavioral activity, and affection (<s>sneha</s>).

body.text:
na kevalamiyamanṛtatā parīkṣakāṇāṃ siddhā, api tu laukikānāmapītyāha- tathā ca loke anubavaḥ śuktikā hi rajatavadavabhāsata iti /
na punā rajatamidamiti śeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Not only is this falsity (<s>anṛtatā</s>) established among the examiners [i.e., philosophers], but among ordinary people as well — thus he [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And so in the world, [there is] experience: nacre appears like silver.' The remainder is: 'but it is not actually silver.'

body.text:
syādetat /
anyasyānyātmatāvibhramo lokasiddhaḥ, ekasya tvabhinnasya bhedabhramo na dṛṣṭa iti kutaḥ cidātmano 'bhinnānāṃ jīvānāṃ bhedavibhrama ityata āha- ekaścandraḥ sadvitīyavat iti /
body.translated_text: It might be said: the confusion (<s>vibhrama</s>) of one thing appearing as another is well-established in the world, but the confusion of difference (<s>bhedabhrama</s>) in a single, undivided entity has not been observed — so whence the confusion of difference among the <s>jīva</s>s (individual souls), who are non-different from the one <s>Ātman</s> (Self)? To this he [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And the one moon [appears] as if with a second.'

body.text:
punarapi cidātmanyadhyāsamākṣipati- kathaṃ punaḥ iti /
ayamarthaḥ- cidātmā prakāśate na vā ? na cet prakāśate, kathamasminnadhyāso viṣayataddharmāṇām ? na khalvapratibhāsamāne purovartini dravye rajatasya vā taddharmāṇāṃ vā samāropaḥ saṃbhavati /
pratibhāsamāne vā na tāvadayamātmā jaḍo ghaṭādivatparādhīnaprakāśa iti yuktam /
na khalu sa eva kartā ca karma ca bhavati, virodhāt /
parasamavetakriyāphalaśāli hi karma, na ca jñānakriyā parasamavāyinīti kathamasyāḥ karma ? na ca tadeva svaṃ ca paraṃ ca, virodhāt /
ātmāntarasamavāyābhyupagame tu jñeyasyātmanaḥ anātmatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
evaṃ tasya tasyetyanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Again, he raises an objection regarding superimposition on the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) — "How again?" The meaning is this: Does the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) manifest or not? If it does not manifest, how can there be superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) of objects and their properties upon it? For surely, superimposition of silver or its properties is not possible upon a substance standing before one that does not appear at all. But if it does manifest, then it is not proper to say that this self (<s>Ātman</s>) is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>) like a pot, having its manifestation dependent on another. For surely the same thing cannot be both the agent and the object of action, due to contradiction. For that which is an object is one that bears the result of an action inhering in another, and the act of knowing does not inhere in another — so how can it be the object of that act? Nor can the same thing be both itself and another, due to contradiction. But if one accepts inherence in another self, there arises the absurd consequence that the self to be known would be a non-self. Thus, there would be the absurd consequence of infinite regress with respect to each successive self.

body.text:
syādetat /
ātmā jaḍo 'pi sarvārthajñāneṣu bhāsamāno 'pi kartaiva na karma, parasamavetakriyāphalaśālitvābhāvāt, caitravat /
yathā hi caitrasamavetakriyayā caitranagaraprāptāvubayasamavetāyāmapi kriyamāṇāyāṃ nagarasyaiva karmatā, parasamavetakriyāphalaśālitvāt, na tu caitrasya kriyāphalaśālino 'pi, caitrasamavāyādgamanakrīyāyā iti /
body.translated_text: One might say this: The self (<s>Ātman</s>), even though inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), even though appearing in all cognitions of objects, is only the agent and not the object, because it does not bear the result of an action inhering in another — like <s>Caitra</s>. For just as when <s>Caitra</s> reaches a city through an action inhering in <s>Caitra</s>, even though the action being performed inheres in both, it is the city alone that is the object, because it bears the result of an action inhering in another, but not <s>Caitra</s>, even though he bears the result of the action, because the action of going inheres in <s>Caitra</s> himself.

body.text:
tanna, śrutivirodhāt /
śrūyate hi 'satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma' iti /
body.translated_text: That is not so, because it contradicts scripture (<s>śruti</s>). For it is heard: "<s>Brahman</s> is truth, knowledge, infinite" (<s>satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma</s>).

body.text:
upapadyate ca /
tathā hi- yo 'yamarthaprakāśaḥ phalaṃ yasminnarthaśca ātmā ca prathete sa kiṃ jaḍaḥ svayaṃprakāśo vā ? jaḍaścet viṣayātmāvapi jaḍāviti kasmin kiṃ prakāśeta aviśeṣāt, iti prāptamāndhyamaśeṣasya jagataḥ /
tathā cābhāṇakaḥ -
body.translated_text: And it is logically established as well. For consider: this illumination of objects, the cognition (<s>phala</s>) in which both the object and the self shine forth — is it inert (<s>jaḍa</s>) or self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>)? If it is inert, then since both the object and the self would be inert, what would be illuminated in what? There being no distinction, the result would be the blindness of the entire universe. And thus there is a saying —

body.text: 'andhasyevāndhalagnasya vinipātaḥ pade pade'
body.translated_text: "Like a blind man following a blind man, there is a fall at every step."

body.text:
iti /
na ca nilīnameva vijñānamarthātmānau jñāpayati cakṣurādivaditi vācyam /
jñāpanaṃ hi jñānajananam, janitaṃ ca jñānaṃ jaḍaṃ sannoktadūṣaṇamativarteteti /
evamuttarottarāṇyapi jñānāni jaḍānītyanavasthā /
tasmādaparādhīnaprakāśā saṃvidupetavyā /
body.translated_text: Nor should it be said that consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), while itself remaining hidden, makes known the object and the self, like the eye and other sense organs. For 'making known' means generating cognition, and the cognition so generated, being inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), would not escape the objection already stated. Thus there would be an infinite regress, as each successive cognition would also be inert. Therefore, consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) must be understood as having a luminosity not dependent on anything else.

body.text:
tathāpi kimāyātaṃ viṣayātmanoḥ svabhāvajaḍayoḥ ? etadāyātaṃ yattayoḥ saṃvidajaḍeti /
tatkiṃ putraḥ paṇḍita iti pitāpi paṇḍito 'stu ? svabhāva eṣa saṃvidaḥ svayaṃprakāśāyā yadarthātmasaṃbandhiteti cet, hanta putrasyāpi paṇḍitasya svabhāva eṣa yatpitṛsaṃbandhiteti samānam /
sahārthātmaprakāśena saṃvitprakāśo na tvarthātmaprakāśaṃ vineti tasyāḥ svabhāva iti cet, tatkiṃ saṃvido bhinnau saṃvidarthātmaprakāśau /
tathā ca na svayaṃprakāśā saṃvit, na ca saṃvit arthātmaprakāśa iti /
atha saṃvidarthātmaprakāśo na saṃvido bhidyete, saṃvideva tau /
evaṃ cet yāvaduktaṃ bhavati saṃvit
body.translated_text: Even so, what follows for the object and the self, which are by nature inert? This follows: that consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) regarding them is non-inert. But then, just because the son is learned, should the father also be learned? If you say it is the nature of consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>), being self-luminous, that it is connected with the object and the self — well then, equally it is the nature of the learned son to be connected with his father, and the parallel holds. If you say that the manifestation of consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) occurs together with the manifestation of object and self, and not without the manifestation of object and self, and that this is its nature — then are the manifestation of object-and-self different from consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>)? If so, then consciousness is not self-luminous, nor is consciousness the illumination of object and self. But if the illumination of object and self is not different from consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>), and is consciousness itself, then in that case, as much as one says "consciousness

body.text:
ātmārthau saheti tāvaduktaṃ bhavati saṃvidarthātmaprakāśau saheti /
tathā ca na vivakṣitārthasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: is together with self and object," so much one says "the illumination of object-and-self by consciousness is together" — and thus the desired conclusion is not established.

body.text:
na cātītānāgatārthagocarāyāḥ saṃvidor'thasahabhāvo 'pi /
tadviṣayahānopādānopekṣābuddhijananādarthasahabhāva iti cet, na, arthasaṃvida iva hānādibuddhīnāmapi tadviṣayatvānupapatteḥ /
hānādijananāddhānādibuddhīnāmarthaviṣayatvam, arthaviṣayahānādibuddhijananācca arthasaṃvidastadviṣayatvamiti cet, tatkiṃ dehasya prayatnavadātmasaṃyogo dehapravṛttinivṛttiheturartha ityarthaprakāśo 'stu ? jāḍyāddehātmasaṃyogo nārthaprakāśa iti cet, nanvayaṃ svayaṃprakāśo 'pi svātmanyeva khadyotavatprakāśaḥ, arthe tu jaḍa ityupapāditam /
body.translated_text: Moreover, there is no co-existence of objects with consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) that has past and future objects as its domain. If you say that the co-existence with objects is because consciousness generates cognitions of avoidance, acceptance, and indifference regarding those objects — no, because just as with the consciousness of objects, those cognitions of avoidance etc. also cannot logically have those objects as their domain. If you say that the cognitions of avoidance etc. have objects as their domain because they generate avoidance etc., and that consciousness of objects has those objects as its domain because it generates cognitions of avoidance etc. regarding objects — then why not say that the connection of the self with the body, being the cause of the body's activity and cessation like effort, is the illumination of objects? If you say that because of inertness, the connection of body and self is not the illumination of objects — but has it not been established that this self, even though self-luminous, illuminates only itself like a firefly, and is inert with regard to objects?

body.text:
na ca prakāśasyātmāno viṣayāḥ ; te hi vicchinnadīrghasthūlatayānubhūyante ; prakāśaścāyaṃ antaro 'sthūlo 'naṇurahrasvo 'dīrdhaśceti prakāśate ; tasmāccandre 'nubhūyamāne iva dvitīyaścandramāḥ svaprakāśādanyor'thaḥ anirvacanīya eveti yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ /
na ca asya prakāśasyājānataḥ svalakṣaṇabhedo 'nubhūyate /
na ca anirvācyārthabhedaḥ prakāśaṃ nirvācyaṃ bhettumarhati, atiprasaṅgāt /
na ca arthānāmapi parasparaṃ bhedaḥ samīcīnajñānapaddhatimadhyāste ityupariṣṭādupapādayiṣyate /
tadayaṃ prakāśa eva svayaṃprakāśa ekaḥ kūṭastho nityo niraṃśaḥ pratyagātmā aśakyanirvacanīyebhyo dehendriyādibhya ātmānaṃ pratīpaṃ nirvacanīyamañcati jānātīti pratyaṅ, sa cātmeti pratyagātmā /
body.translated_text: And objects are not of the nature of luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>); for they are experienced as delimited, long, and gross; whereas this luminosity shines as "inner, not gross, not subtle, not short, not long"; therefore, just as when the moon is perceived a second moon appears, we rightly perceive that the object other than self-luminosity is indeed indeterminable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>). And no difference in intrinsic character is experienced in this luminosity that does not cognize itself as other. Nor can an indeterminable difference in objects break the determinable luminosity, because of over-extension. And it will be established later that the mutual difference among objects themselves does not occupy the path of valid cognition. Therefore, this luminosity itself, self-luminous, one, immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), eternal, partless, is the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) — it turns toward, i.e., cognizes, itself as opposed to the body, senses, and other things that are indeterminable; being turned inward (<s>pratyañc</s>) and being the self (<s>Ātman</s>), it is the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>).

body.text:
sa cāparādhīnaprakāśāt anaṃśatvācca aviṣayaḥ, tasminnadhyāso viṣayadharmāṇām, dehendriyādidharmāṇām, katham ? kimākṣepe /
ayukto 'yamadhyāsa ityākṣepaḥ /
kasmādayamayukta ityata āha - sarvo hi puro 'vasthite viṣaye viṣayāntaramadhyasyati /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- yatparādhīnaprakāśamaṃśavacca tatsāmānyāṃśagrahe karaṇadoṣavaśācca viśeṣāgrahe anyathā prakāśate /
pratyagātmā tu aparādhīnaprakāśatayā na svajñāne kāraṇānyapekṣate, yena tadāśrayairdeṣairduṣyet /
na cāṃśavān, yena kaścidasyāṃśo gṛhyeta, kaścinna gṛhyeta /
na hi tadeva tadānīmeva tenaiva gṛhītamagṛhītaṃ ca saṃbhavatīti na svayaṃprakāśatāpakṣe adhyāsaḥ /
sadātane 'pyaprakāśe puro 'vasthitatvasya aparokṣatvasyābhāvānnādhyāsaḥ /
na hi śuktau apuraḥsthitāyāṃ rajatamadhyasyati 'idaṃ rajatam' iti /
tasmādatyantagrahe atyantāgrahe ca nādhyāsa iti siddham /
body.translated_text: And since that self has luminosity not dependent on another and is partless, it is non-objectifiable (<s>aviṣaya</s>). How then can there be superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) of the properties of objects — the properties of body, senses, etc. — upon it? This is the objection. The objection is that this superimposition is unjustified. Why is it unjustified? To this he says: "For everyone superimposes another object upon an object that is present before one." What this means is: that which has its luminosity dependent on another and is possessed of parts — when the generic aspect is grasped, due to defects in the instrument of cognition the specific aspect is not grasped, and so it appears otherwise. But the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>), since its luminosity is not dependent on another, does not require other causes for its self-knowledge, by which it could be vitiated by defects residing in them. Nor is it possessed of parts, such that some part of it would be grasped while another would not be grasped. For it is not possible that the very same thing at the very same time by the very same means is both grasped and not grasped — hence, on the view that the self is self-luminous, there is no superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>). Even if it is eternally non-manifest, since being present-before-one, i.e., directness (<s>aparokṣatva</s>), is absent, there is no superimposition. For one does not superimpose silver upon a shell that is not present before one, saying "this is silver." Therefore, it is established that there is no superimposition either in complete apprehension or in complete non-apprehension.

body.text:
syādetat /
aviṣayatve hi cidātmano nādhyāsaḥ, viṣaya eva tu cidātmā asmatpratyayasya, tatkathaṃ nādhyāsa ityata āha- yuṣmatpratyayāpetasya iti /
viṣayatve hi cidātmano 'nyo viṣayī bhavet /
tathā ca yo viṣayī sa eva cidātmā /
viṣayastu tato 'nyo yuṣmatpratyayagocaro 'bhyupeyaḥ /
tasmādanātmatvaprasaṅgādanavasthāparihārāya yuṣmatpratyayāpetatvam ; ata eva aviṣayatvamātmano vaktavyam ; tathā ca nādhyāsa ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: One might say this: If the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) is non-objectifiable, there is no superimposition; but the conscious self is indeed the object of the 'I'-cognition (<s>asmatpratyaya</s>), so how can there be no superimposition? To this he says: "being beyond the 'you'-cognition" (<s>yuṣmatpratyayāpeta</s>). For if the conscious self were an object, there would have to be another subject distinct from it. And that subject would itself be the conscious self. But the object would have to be accepted as something other than that, falling within the scope of the 'you'-cognition. Therefore, to avoid the absurd consequence of the self being a non-self and to avoid infinite regress, it must be said that the self is beyond the 'you'-cognition; and for this very reason the self must be declared non-objectifiable; and thus there is no superimposition — this is the meaning.

body.text:
pariharati- ucyate- na tāvadayamekāntenāviṣayaḥ /
kutaḥ ? asmatpratyayaviṣayatvāt /
ayamarthaḥ- satye pratyagātmā svayaṃprakāśatvādaviṣayo 'naṃśaśca ; tathāpi anirvacanīyānādyavidyāparikalpitabuddhimanaḥ sūkṣmasthūlaśarīrendriyāvacchedakabhedena anavacchinno 'pi vastuto 'vacchinna iva abhinno 'pi bhinna iva akartāpi karteva abhoktāpi bhokteva aviṣayo 'pyasmatpratyayaviṣaya iva jīvabhāvamāpannaḥ avabhāsate, nabha iva ghaṭamaṇikamallikādyupādhyavacchedabhedena bhinnamivānekavidhadharmakamiveti /
na hi cidekarasasyātmanaḥ cidāṃśe gṛhīte agṛhītaṃ kiñcidasti /
na khalu ānandanityatvavibhutvādayaḥ asya cidrūpādvastuto bhidyante, yena tadgrahe na gṛhyeran /
gṛhītā eva tu kalpitena bhedena na vivecitā ityagṛhītā ivābhānti /
na ca ātmano buddhyādibhyo bhedastāttvikaḥ yena cidātmani gṛhyamāṇe so 'pi gṛhīta eva bhavet, buddhyādīnāmanirvācyatvena tadbhedasyāpyanirvacanīyatvāt /
tasmāccidātmanaḥ svayaṃprakāśasyaiva anavacchinnasya avacchinnebhyo buddhyādibhyo bhedāgrahāt tadadhyāsena jīvabhāva iti /
tasya ca anidamidamātmanaḥ asmatpratyayaviṣayatvamupapadyate /
tathā hi- kartā bhoktā cidātmā ahaṃpratyaye pratyavabhāsate /
na ca udāsīnasya tasya kriyāśaktirbhogaśaktirvā saṃbhavati /
yasya ca buddhyādeḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātasya kriyābhogaśaktī na tasya caitanyam /
tasmāccidātmaiva kāryakaraṇasaṃghātena grathito labdhakriyābhogaśaktiḥ svayaṃprakāśo 'pi buddhyādiviṣayavicchuraṇāt kathañcidasmatpratyayaviṣayaḥ ahaṅkārāspadaṃ jīva iti ca janturiti ca kṣetrajña iti ca ākhyāyate /
na khalu jīvaścidātmano bhidyate /
tathā hi śrutiḥ- 'anena jīvenātmanā' iti /
tasmāccidātmano 'vyatirekāt jīvaḥ svayaṃprakāśo 'pi ahaṃpratyayena kartṛbhoktṛtayā vyavahārayogyaḥ kriyata ityahaṃpratyayālambanamucyate /
na ca adhyāse sati viṣayatvaṃ viṣayatve ca adhyāsaḥ ityanyonyāśrayatvamiti sāṃpratam,bījāṅkuravadanāditvāt, pūrvapūrvādhyāsatadvāsanāviṣayīkṛtasya uttarottarādhyāsaviṣayatvāvirodhādityuktam-"naisargiko 'yaṃ lokavyavahāraḥ"iti bhāṣyagranthena /
tasmāt suṣṭhūktam- na tāvadayamekāntenāviṣaya iti /
jīvo hi cidātmatayā svayaṃprakāśatayā aviṣayo 'pi aupādhikena rūpeṇa viṣaya iti bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: He resolves this: "It is said: This self is not absolutely non-objectifiable." Why? "Because it is the object of the 'I'-cognition" (<s>asmatpratyayaviṣaya</s>). The meaning is this: In reality, the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>), being self-luminous, is non-objectifiable and partless. Nevertheless, through the delimitation produced by the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), mind (<s>manas</s>), subtle and gross bodies, and sense organs — all fabricated by beginningless indeterminable ignorance (<s>anirvacanīya anādi avidyā</s>) — although in truth undelimited, it appears as if delimited; although undifferentiated, as if differentiated; although not an agent, as if an agent; although not an experiencer, as if an experiencer; although non-objectifiable, as if an object of the 'I'-cognition — having assumed the state of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>), it appears so, just as space (<s>nabhas</s>), through the delimiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) of a pot, a jewel-case, a jasmine bower, etc., appears as if divided and as if possessing manifold properties. For in the self (<s>Ātman</s>), whose sole essence is consciousness (<s>cit</s>), when the consciousness-aspect is grasped, there is nothing left ungrasped. Surely, bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), eternality, all-pervasiveness, and other such qualities do not in reality differ from its nature as consciousness, such that they would not be grasped when that is grasped. They are indeed grasped, but due to the imagined differentiation, they are not discriminated and thus appear as if ungrasped. Nor is the difference of the self from the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) etc. ultimately real, such that when the conscious self is grasped, that difference too would necessarily be grasped — for since the intellect etc. are indeterminable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>), their difference from the self is also indeterminable. Therefore, it is through the non-apprehension of the difference of the self-luminous conscious self — which is in truth undelimited — from the delimited intellect etc., and through superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) of these upon it, that the state of being a <s>jīva</s> arises. And it is fitting that this self, which is not a 'this' and whose nature is not a 'this,' becomes the object of the 'I'-cognition. For the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) as agent and experiencer appears reflected in the 'I'-cognition. And for one who is detached, there can be neither the power of action nor the power of enjoyment. And that aggregate of effects and instruments (<s>kāryakaraṇasaṃghāta</s>) — namely the intellect etc. — which does possess the powers of action and enjoyment, does not possess consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>). Therefore, it is the conscious self alone, being bound together with the aggregate of effects and instruments, having acquired the powers of action and enjoyment, that — though self-luminous — due to its radiation through the objects of the intellect etc., becomes in some manner the object of the 'I'-cognition and is designated as the locus of ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), as <s>jīva</s>, as creature (<s>jantu</s>), and as the knower of the field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>). The <s>jīva</s> is surely not different from the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>). Thus says the scripture (<s>śruti</s>): "by this <s>jīva</s>-self" (<s>anena jīvenātmanā</s>). Therefore, since the <s>jīva</s> is non-different from the conscious self, though self-luminous, it is made fit for transactional usage as agent and experiencer through the 'I'-cognition, and hence is said to be the basis of the 'I'-cognition. And it is not appropriate to object that there is mutual dependence — superimposition requiring objecthood and objecthood requiring superimposition — for like the seed and sprout, it is beginningless; since there is no contradiction in that which has been made an object by prior superimposition and its latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) becoming the object of subsequent superimposition, this has been stated by the <s>Bhāṣya</s> text: "This is the natural (<s>naisargika</s>) worldly transaction." Therefore, it is well said: "This self is not absolutely non-objectifiable." For the <s>jīva</s>, being the conscious self, is non-objectifiable by virtue of being self-luminous, yet by virtue of its adventitious form due to limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), it is objectifiable — this is the purport.

body.text:
syādetat /
na vayamaparādhīnaprakāśatayā aviṣayatvenādhyāsamapākurmaḥ, kiṃ tu pratyagātmā na svato nāpi
body.translated_text: One might say this: We do not deny superimposition on the ground that the self is non-objectifiable due to its luminosity not being dependent on another; rather, we say that the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) does not manifest either from itself or from

body.text:
parataḥ prathata ityaviṣaya iti brūmaḥ /
tathā ca sarvathāprathamāne pratyagātmani kuto 'dhyāsa ityata āha- aparokṣatvācca pratyagātmaprasiddheḥ iti /
pratīca ātmanaḥ prasiddhiḥ prathā, tasyā aparokṣatvāt /
yadyapi pratyagātmani nānyā prathāsti tathāpi bhedopacāraḥ, yathā 'puruṣasya caitanyam' iti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- avaśyaṃ cidātmā aparokṣo 'bhyupetavyaḥ tadaprathāyāṃ sarvasyāprathanena jagadāndhyaprasaṅgādityuktam /
śrutiścātra bhavati- 'tameva bhāntamanu bhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti' iti /
body.translated_text: another, and hence is non-objectifiable. And thus, when the inner self does not manifest in any way whatsoever, how can there be superimposition? To this he says: "And because the self-evidence of the inner self is direct" (<s>aparokṣatvāt ca pratyagātmaprasiddheḥ</s>). The self-evidence (<s>prasiddhi</s>), i.e., the manifestation (<s>prathā</s>), of the inner self — that is direct (<s>aparokṣa</s>). Although in the inner self there is no manifestation other than itself, nevertheless there is figurative attribution of difference, just as in the expression "the consciousness of a person" (<s>puruṣasya caitanyam</s>). What this means is: The conscious self must necessarily be accepted as direct (<s>aparokṣa</s>), for if it did not manifest, everything would fail to manifest, resulting in the absurd consequence of universal blindness — as has been stated. And the scripture (<s>śruti</s>) here is: "Everything shines after That which shines; by the light of That, all this is illuminated" (<s>tameva bhāntam anubhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti</s>).

body.text:
tadevaṃ paramārthaparihāramuktvā abhyupetyāpi cidātmanaḥ parokṣatāṃ prauḍhavāditayā parihārāntaramāha- na cāyamasti iti /
puro 'vasthita eva, aparokṣa eva /
kasmādayaṃ na niyama ityata āha- apratyakṣe 'pi iti /
hiryasmādarthe /
nabho hi dravyaṃ sat rūpasparśavirahānna bāhyendriyapratyakṣam /
nāpi mānasam, manaso 'sahāyasya bāhye apravṛtteḥ ; tasmādapratyakṣam /
atha ca tatra bālā avivekinaḥ paradarśitadarśinaḥ kadācitpārthivacchāyāṃ śyāmatāmāropya, kadācittaijasaṃ śuklatvamāropya, nīlotpalapalāśaśyāmamiti vā rājahaṃsamālādhavalamiti vā nirvarṇayanti /
tatrāpi pūrvadṛṣṭasya taijasasya vā tāmasasya vā rūpasya paratra nabhasi smṛtirūpo 'vabhāsa iti /
evaṃ tadeva talamadhyasyanti avāṅmukhībhūtamahendranīlamaṇimayamahākaṭāhakalpamityarthaḥ /
upasaṃharati- evam uktena prakāreṇa sarvākṣepaparihārāt, aviruddhaḥ pratyagātmanyapyanātmanām- buddhyādīnām- adhyāsaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Having thus set aside the ultimate refutation, and even conceding the imperceptibility of the conscious Self, he offers another refutation by way of bold argumentation: 'Nor is there this [restriction].' [The Self] is right before [us], it is immediate (<s>aparokṣa</s>). Why is there no such restriction? To this he says: 'Even in the case of the imperceptible.' '<s>Hi</s>' means 'because.' For space (<s>nabhas</s>), being a substance, due to the absence of form and touch, is not perceptible to the external senses. Nor is it perceptible to the mind, since the mind without [sensory] support does not engage with external [objects]; therefore it is imperceptible. And yet, in that [space], the undiscerning — children, who see only what others show them — sometimes superimpose an earthy shadow, seeing darkness, [thinking] 'the sky is dark like blue lotus petals,' and sometimes superimpose the fiery [quality of] whiteness, [thinking] 'the sky is white like a garland of royal swans.' Even there, the appearance of a previously seen fiery or dark form upon the space [which is] elsewhere is in the form of memory.
Thus they superimpose upon that very ground [of space], thinking it to be an inverted great bowl made of deep-blue sapphire — this is the meaning.
He concludes: By the manner described, through the resolution of all objections, superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) of non-self [elements] — the intellect and the like — upon the innermost Self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) is not contradicted.

body.text:
nanu santi ca sahasramadhyāsāḥ, tatkimarthamayamevādhyāsa ākṣepasamādhānābhyāṃ vyutpāditaḥ nādhyāsamātramityata āha- tametamevaṃlakṣaṇamadhyāsaṃ paṇḍitā avidyeti manyante /
avidyā hi sarvānarthabījamiti śrutismṛtītihāsapurāṇādiṣu suprasiddham, taducchedāya ca vedāntāḥ pravṛttā iti vakṣyati /
pratyagātmanyanātmādhyāsa eva sarvānarthahetuḥ na punā rajatādivibhramā iti sa evāvidyā, tatsvarūpaṃ cāvijñātaṃ na śakyamucchettumiti tadeva vyutpādyaṃ nādhyāsamātram /
atra ca"evaṃlakṣaṇam"iti evaṃrūpatayā anarthahetutoktā /
yasmātpratyagātmanyaśanāyādirahite aśanāyādyupetāntaḥkaraṇādyahitāropeṇa pratyagātmānamaduḥkhaṃ duḥkhākaroti, tasmādanarthahetuḥ /
na caivaṃ pṛthagjanā api manyante adhyāsam, yena na vyutpādyetetyata uktam-"paṇḍitā manyante"iti /
body.translated_text:
But there are thousands of superimpositions; why then is this particular superimposition explicated through objection and resolution, and not superimposition in general? To this he says: 'The learned consider this superimposition, of such a character, to be <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).' For it is well-established in <s>Śruti</s>s, <s>Smṛti</s>s, <s>Itihāsa</s>s, <s>Purāṇa</s>s, and the like that <s>avidyā</s> is the seed of all harm (<s>anartha</s>); and it will be stated that the <s>Vedānta</s>s (Upaniṣads) are directed toward its removal. The superimposition of the non-self upon the innermost Self alone is the cause of all harm, not the erroneous cognitions of silver and the like — therefore that alone is <s>avidyā</s>. And since its essential nature, being unknown, cannot be eradicated, that alone must be explicated, not superimposition in general.
Here, 'of such a character' (<s>evaṃlakṣaṇam</s>) indicates that its being the cause of harm has been stated by virtue of its such nature. Since, upon the innermost Self which is free from hunger and the like, through the superimposition of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) endowed with hunger and the like, the innermost Self — which is free from suffering — is made to suffer, therefore it is the cause of harm. And ordinary people do not consider [this] to be superimposition, such that it would not need explication — hence it is said: 'the learned consider.'

body.text:
nanu iyamanādiratinirūḍhanibiḍavāsanānubaddhā avidyā na śakyā niroddhum, upāyābhāvāt, iti yo manyante taṃ prati tannirodhopāyamāha - tadvivekena ca vastusvarūpāvadhāraṇam, nirvicikitsaṃ jñānam, vidyāmāhuḥ paṇḍitāḥ /
pratyagātmani khalu atyantavivikte buddhyādibhyaḥ buddhyādibhedāgrahanimitto buddhyādyātmatvataddharmādhyāsaḥ /
tatra śravaṇamananādibhiryadvivekavijñānaṃ tena vivekāgrahe nivartite, adhyāsāpabādhātmakaṃ vastusvarūpāvadhāraṇaṃ vidyā cidātmarūpaṃ svarūpe vyavatiṣṭhata ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
But this <s>avidyā</s>, bound by beginningless, deeply entrenched, dense impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>s), cannot be arrested, for lack of a means — to one who thinks thus, he states the means of its arrest: 'And by discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) from that [<s>avidyā</s>], the ascertainment of the true nature of reality — knowledge free from doubt — the learned call <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge).'
Upon the innermost Self, which is utterly distinct from the intellect and the like, the superimposition of being the intellect and its properties is caused by the non-apprehension of their distinction. When, through hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and the like, the discriminative knowledge arises and thereby the non-apprehension of distinction is removed, the ascertainment of the true nature of reality — which constitutes the sublation of the superimposition — is <s>vidyā</s>: the conscious Self (<s>cidātman</s>) abides in its own true form — this is the meaning.

body.text:
syādetat /
atinirūḍhanibiḍhavāsanānuvidvā avidyā vidyayā apabādhitāpi svavāsanāvaśātpunarudbhaviṣyati pravartayiṣyati ca vāsanādikāryaṃ svocitamityaya āha - tatraivaṃ sati, evaṃbhūtavastutattvāvadhāraṇe sati, yatra yadadhyāsaḥ
body.translated_text: One might object: <s>avidyā</s>, which has followed along with deeply entrenched, dense impressions, even though sublated by <s>vidyā</s>, will again arise through the force of its own impressions, and will produce its appropriate effects such as impressions and the like. To this he says: 'That being so' — when the ascertainment of the true nature of reality of such a kind is present — 'wherever there is superimposition of whatever upon what,

body.text:
tatkṛtena doṣeṇa guṇena vā aṇumātreṇāpi sa na saṃbadhyate, antaḥkaraṇādidoṣeṇāśanāyādinā cidātmā, cidātmano guṇena caitanyānandādinā antaḥkaraṇādi na saṃbadhyate /
etaduktaṃ bhavati - tattvāvadhāraṇābhyāsasya hi svabhāva eva sa tādṛśaḥ, yadanādimapi nirūḍhanibiḍavāsanamapi mithyāpratyayamapanayati /
tattvapakṣapāto hi svabhāvo dhiyām, yathāhurbāhyā api--
body.translated_text:
that [substrate] is not connected even in the slightest with the defect or quality produced by that [superimposition]' — the conscious Self is not connected with the defects of the inner organ such as hunger and the like, nor is the inner organ connected with the qualities of the conscious Self such as consciousness, bliss, and the like.
What is stated amounts to this: it is the very nature of the practice of ascertaining reality that it removes even the beginningless false cognition that is bound by deeply entrenched, dense impressions. For the natural tendency (<s>svabhāva</s>) of cognitions is toward reality — as even the external [philosophers] say:

body.text: nirupadravabhūtārthasvabhāvasya viparyayaiḥ /
body.translated_text: 'The nature of cognition being [oriented toward] the true reality of objects, free from obstruction,

body.text: na bādho 'yatnavattve 'pi buddhestatpakṣapātataḥ //
body.translated_text: It is not overridden by errors, even effortlessly — due to its tendency (<s>pakṣapāta</s>) toward that [reality].'

body.text:
iti /
viśeṣatastu cidātmasvabhāvasya tattvajñānasya atyantāntaraṅgasya kuto 'nirvācyayā avidyayā bādha iti /
body.translated_text:
Thus.
And especially — how can the ineffable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) <s>avidyā</s> override the knowledge of reality, which is of the nature of the conscious Self (<s>cidātma-svabhāva</s>) and is most intimately one's own (<s>atyantāntaraṅga</s>)?

body.text:
yaduktam"satyānṛte mithunākṛtya, vivekāgrahādadhyasya, 'ahamidam' 'mamedam' iti lokavyavahāraḥ"iti tatra vyapadeśalakṣaṇo vyavahāraḥ kaṇṭhoktaḥ /
itiśabdasūcitaṃ lokavyavahāramādarśayati- tametamavidyākhyam iti /
nigadavyākhyātam /
body.translated_text:
What was stated — 'Having made a coupling of the real and the unreal, and through non-apprehension of their distinction, having superimposed [them], "I am this," "this is mine" — thus is worldly transaction' — therein, worldly transaction characterized by verbal expression is explicitly stated.
The word '<s>iti</s>' indicates [further] worldly transaction — he shows it with: 'This [superimposition] known as <s>avidyā</s>...'
The rest is explained by the gloss (<s>nigada</s>).

body.text:
ākṣipati- kathaṃ punaravidyāvadviṣayīṇi pratyakṣādīni pramāṇāni /
tattvaparicchedo hi pramā vidyā ; tatsādhanāni pramāṇāni kathamavidyāvadviṣayāṇi ? nāvidyāvantaṃ pramāṇānyāśrayanti, tatkāryasya vidyāyā avidyāvirodhitvāt iti bhāvaḥ /
santu vā pratyakṣādīni saṃvṛtyāpi yathā tathā ; śāstrāṇi tu puruṣahitānuśāsanaparāṇi avidyāpratipakṣatayā nāvidyāvadviṣayāṇi bhavitumarhantītyāha - śāstrāṇi ca iti /
samādhatte- ucyate iti /
dehendriyādiṣu ahaṃmamābhimānahīnasya, tādātmyataddharmādhyāsahīnasya, pramātṛtvānupapattau satyāṃ pramāṇapravṛttyanupapatteḥ /
ayamarthaḥ- pramātṛtvaṃ hi pramāṃ prati kartṛtvam /
tacca svātantryam /
svātantryaṃ ca pramāturitarakārakāprayojyasya samastakārakaprayoktṛtvam /
tadanena pramākaraṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ prayojanīyam /
na ca svavyāpāramantareṇa karaṇaṃ prayoktumarhati /
na ca kūṭasthanityaścidātmā apariṇāmī svato vyāpāravān /
tasmāt vyāpāravadbuddhyāditādātmyādhyāsāt vyāpāravattayā pramāṇamadhiṣṭhātumarhatīti bhavatyavidyāvatpuruṣaviṣayatvamavidyāvatpuruṣāśrayatvaṃ pramāṇānāmiti /
body.translated_text:
He raises an objection: 'But how can the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>s) such as perception and the like have as their domain one who possesses <s>avidyā</s>?'
For valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), which is the ascertainment of reality, is <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge); the instruments that produce it are the <s>pramāṇa</s>s — how can they have as their domain one possessed of <s>avidyā</s>? The <s>pramāṇa</s>s do not resort to one possessing <s>avidyā</s>, since their effect — <s>vidyā</s> — is opposed to <s>avidyā</s>. This is the purport.
Or, let there be perception and the like, even conventionally; but the scriptures (<s>śāstra</s>s), which are directed toward the beneficial instruction of persons, being the antidote to <s>avidyā</s>, ought not to have as their domain one possessed of <s>avidyā</s> — thus he says: 'And the scriptures...'
He resolves [the objection]: 'It is said...'
When there is the impossibility of being a knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) for one devoid of the notions 'I' and 'mine' regarding the body, senses, and the like — devoid of the superimposition of identity and properties — there is the impossibility of the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>s.
The meaning is this: being a knower means being the agent with respect to valid cognition. And that is independence. And independence is: the knower, who is not prompted by any other <s>kāraka</s> (grammatical factor), being the prompter of all <s>kāraka</s>s. By him, the instrument of valid cognition — the <s>pramāṇa</s> — must be employed. And one cannot employ an instrument without one's own activity. And the conscious Self, which is eternally immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), unchanging, is not inherently active. Therefore, through the superimposition of identity with the intellect and the like — which are endowed with activity — [the Self], as if endowed with activity, becomes capable of wielding the <s>pramāṇa</s>s. Thus the <s>pramāṇa</s>s have as their domain, and as their locus, a person possessed of <s>avidyā</s>.

body.text:
atha mā pravartiṣata pramāṇāni, kiṃ naśchinnamityata āha- na hīndriyāṇyanupādāya pratyakṣādivyavahāraḥ saṃbhavati /
vyavahriyate aneneti vyavahāraḥ phalam, pratyakṣādīnāṃ pramāṇānāṃ phalamityarthaḥ /
indriyāṇi iti indriyaliṅgādīnīti draṣṭavyam, 'daṇḍino gacchanti' itivat /
evaṃ hi pratyakṣādi ityupapadyate /
vyavahārakriyayā ca vyavahāryākṣepātsamānakartṛkatā /
anupādāya yo vyavahāra iti yojanā /
body.translated_text:
But [one might say:] let the <s>pramāṇa</s>s not operate — what loss is that to us? To this he says: 'For without employing the senses, the transaction of perception and the like is not possible.' That by which one transacts — that transaction is the fruit; it is the fruit of the <s>pramāṇa</s>s such as perception and the like — this is the meaning. 'The senses' should be understood as including the senses, inferential marks, and the like — as in 'those bearing staffs go,' [where the staff-bearing implies the persons]. For thus 'perception and the like' is appropriate. And through the activity of transaction, there is the implied inclusion of the object of transaction, hence a common agency [of knower and instruments].
The syntactic connection is: 'the transaction that [occurs] without employing [the senses].'

body.text:
kimiti punaḥ pramātā upādatte pramāṇāni ? atha svayameva kasmānna pravartante ityata āha- na cādhiṣṭhānamantareṇendriyāṇāṃ vyāpāraḥ, pramāṇānāṃ vyāpāraḥ, saṃbhavati /
na jātu karaṇānyanadhiṣṭhitāni kartrā svakārye vyāpriyante, mā bhūtkuvindarahitebhyo vemādibhyaḥ paṭotpattiriti /
atha deha evādhiṣṭhātā kasmānna bhavati ? kṛtamatrātmādhyāsenetyata āha- na cānadhyastātmabhāvena dehena kaścidvyāpriyate ; suṣupte 'pi vyāpāraprasaṅgāditi bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Why does the knower employ the <s>pramāṇa</s>s? Why do they not operate on their own? To this he says: 'And without a superintendent (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>), the operation of the senses — of the <s>pramāṇa</s>s — is not possible.' For never do instruments, unsupervised by an agent, operate in their own function — otherwise, cloth would be produced from looms without a weaver.
But why cannot the body itself be the superintendent? The superimposition of Self upon it would suffice for that — to this he says: 'And no one operates through the body as one upon which Self-nature has not been superimposed'; for [otherwise,] there would be the unwanted consequence of operation even in deep sleep — this is the purport.

body.text:
syādetat /
yathānadhyastātmabhāvaṃ vemādikaṃ kuvindo vyāpārayanpaṭasya kartā, evamanadhyastātmabhāvaṃ dehendriyādi vyāpārayan bhaviṣyati tadabhijñaḥ pramātā ityata āha- na caitasminsarvasmin, itaretarātmādhyāse itaretarātmādhyāse itaretaradharmādhyāse ca, asati, ātmano 'saṅgasya, sarvathā sarvadā sarvadharmadharmiviyuktasya, pramātṛtvamupapadyate /
vyāpāravanto hi kuvindādayo vemādīnadhiṣṭhāya vyāpārayanti, anadhyastātmabhāvasya tu dehādiṣvātmano na vyāpārayogo 'saṅgatvādityarthaḥ /
ātaścādhyāsāśrayāṇi pramāṇānītyāha- na ca pramātṛtvamantareṇa pramāṇapravṛttirasti /
pramāyāṃ khalu phale svatantraḥ pramātā bhavati /
antaḥkaraṇapariṇāmabhedaśca prameyapravaṇaḥ kartṛsthaścitsvabhāvaḥ pramā /
kathaṃ ca jaḍasyāntaḥkaraṇasya pariṇāmaścidrūpo bhavet,
body.translated_text:
One might object: Just as a weaver, operating the loom upon which Self-nature has not been superimposed, is the agent of cloth, so too will the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>), who is acquainted with [the body], be the agent by operating the body and senses upon which Self-nature has not been superimposed. To this he says: 'And when all this — the mutual superimposition of identity and properties — is absent, the agency of the Self, which is unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>), in every way, at all times, separated from all properties and substrata, is not tenable.' For the weaver and others, being themselves possessed of activity, operate by supervising the loom and the like. But for the Self, upon which Self-nature has not been superimposed regarding the body and the like, there is no possibility of activity — because of its unattachedness. This is the meaning.
Therefore, the <s>pramāṇa</s>s depend upon superimposition — thus he says: 'And without being a knower, there is no operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>s.' In the fruit — valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>) — the knower is independent. And the modification of the inner organ, directed toward the object of cognition, stationed in the agent, and of the nature of consciousness — is valid cognition. How would the modification of the inert inner organ be of the nature of consciousness,

body.text:
yadi cidātmā tatra nādhyasyeta ? kathaṃ caiṣa cidātmakartṛko bhavet, yadyantaḥkaraṇaṃ vyāpāravat cidātmani nādhyasyet ? tasmāditaretarādhyāsāccidātmakartṛsthaṃ pramāphalaṃ sidhyati, tatsiddhau ca pramātṛtvam /
tāmeva ca pramāmurarīkṛtya pramāṇasya pravṛttiḥ /
pramātṛtvena ca pramā upalakṣyate /
pramāyāḥ phalasyābhāve pramāṇaṃ na pravarteta /
tathā ca pramāṇamapramāṇaṃ syādityarthaḥ /
upasaṃharati- tasmādavidyāvadviṣayāṇyeva pratyakṣādīni pramāṇāni /
body.translated_text:
if the conscious Self were not superimposed upon it? And how would this [modification] be one whose agent is the conscious Self, if the inner organ — which is endowed with activity — were not superimposed upon the conscious Self? Therefore, through mutual superimposition, the fruit of valid cognition — stationed in the conscious Self as agent — is established; and with that established, the status of being a knower is established.
And having accepted that very valid cognition, the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> [proceeds]. And through being a knower, valid cognition is implied. In the absence of the fruit — valid cognition — the <s>pramāṇa</s> would not operate. And thus the <s>pramāṇa</s> would be a non-<s>pramāṇa</s> — this is the meaning.
He concludes: 'Therefore, perception and the like — the <s>pramāṇa</s>s — indeed have as their domain one possessed of <s>avidyā</s>.'

body.text:
syādetat /
bhavatu pṛthagjanānāmevam ; āgamopapattipratipannapratyagātmatattvānāṃ vyutpannānāmapi puṃsāṃ pramāṇaprameyavyavahārā dṛśyanta iti kathamavidyāvadviṣayāṇyeva pramāṇānītyata āha- paśvādibhiścāviśeṣāt iti /
vidantu nāma āgamopapattibhyāṃ dehendriyādibhyo bhinnaṃ pratyagātmānam ; pramāṇaprameyavyavahāre tu prāṇabhṛnmātradharmatvaṃ nātivartante /
yādṛśo hi paśuśakuntādīnāmavipratipannamugdhabhāvānāṃ vyavahārastādṛśo vyutpannānāmapi puṃsāṃ dṛśyate /
tena tatsāmānyātteṣāmapi vyavahārasamaye avidyāvattvamanumeyam /
caśabdaḥ samuccaye /
uktaśaṅkānivartanasahitā pūrvoktopapattiḥ avidyāvatpuruṣaviṣayatvaṃ pramāṇānāṃ sādhayatītyarthaḥ /
etadeva vibhajate- yathā hi paśvādaya iti /
body.translated_text:
One might object: Let it be so for ordinary people; but even for those who have ascertained the reality of the innermost Self through scripture and reasoning — even for the learned — the transactions of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) are observed. So how can the <s>pramāṇa</s>s have as their domain only one possessed of <s>avidyā</s>? To this he says: 'And because there is no difference from animals and the like.' Let them know, through scripture and reasoning, the innermost Self as distinct from the body, senses, and the like; but in the transaction of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s>, they do not transcend the common characteristic of all breathing beings. For the transaction observed in animals, birds, and the like — who are in a state of unquestioning dullness — is the same as that observed even in the learned. Therefore, by analogy with them, it is to be inferred that even [the learned], at the time of transaction, are possessed of <s>avidyā</s>.
The word '<s>ca</s>' is for aggregation. The meaning is: the reasoning stated above, together with the removal of the stated objection, establishes that the <s>pramāṇa</s>s have as their domain one possessed of <s>avidyā</s>.
He elaborates this very [point]: 'For just as animals and the like...'

body.text:
atra ca śabdādibhiḥ śrotrādīnāṃ saṃbandhe sati iti pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇaṃ darśitam /
śabdādivijñāne iti tatphalamuktam /
pratikūle iti ca anumānaphalam /
tathā hi- śabdādisvarūpamupalabhya tajjātīyasya pratikūlatāmanusmṛtya tajjātīyatayopalabhyamānasya pratikūlatāmanumimata iti /
udāharati- yathā daṇḍa iti /
śeṣamatirohitārtham /
body.translated_text:
Here, 'when there is the connection of the ears and the like with sound and the like' — thereby perception as a <s>pramāṇa</s> is shown. 'In the cognition of sound and the like' — thereby its fruit is stated. 'That which is adverse' — thereby the fruit of inference [is stated]. For: having perceived the nature of sound and the like, and having recalled the adverseness of that kind [of object], one infers the adverseness of what is being perceived as being of that kind.
He illustrates: 'As, for instance, a staff...'
The rest has a transparent meaning.

body.text:
syādetat /
bhavantu pratyakṣādīnyavidyāvadviṣayāṇi /
śāstraṃ tu 'jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta' ityādi na dehātmādhyāsena pravartitumarhati /
atra hi āmuṣmikaphalopabhogayogyaḥ adhikārī pratīyate /
tathā ca pāramarṣaṃ sūtram- 'śāstraphalaṃ prayoktari tallakṣaṇatvāttasmātsvayaṃ prayoge syāt' iti /
na ca dehādi bhasmībhūtaṃ pāralaukikāya phalāya kalpata iti dehādyatiriktaṃ kañcidātmānamadhikāriṇamākṣipati śāstram ; tadavagamaśca vidyā ; iti kathamavidyāvadviṣayaṃ śāstramityāśaṅkyāha- śāstrīyetu iti /
tu-śabdaḥ pratyakṣādivyavahārādbhinatti śāstrīyam /
adhikāraśāstraṃ hi svargakāmasya puṃsaḥ paralokasaṃbandhaṃ vinā na nirvahatīti tāvanmātramākṣipet, na tvarayāsaṃsāritvamapi ; tasyādhikāre 'nupayogāt ; pratyuta aupaniṣadasya puruṣasya akarturabhokturadhikāravirodhāt /
prayoktā hi karmaṇaḥ karmajanitaphalabhogabhāgī karmaṇyadhikārī svāmī bhavati /
tatra kathamakartā prayoktā ? kathaṃ ca abhoktā karmajanitaphalabhogabhāgī ? tasmādanādyavidyālabdhakartṛtvabhoktṛtvabrāhmaṇatvādyabhimāninaṃ naramadhikṛtya vidhiniṣedhaśāstraṃ pravartate /
evaṃ vedāntā apyavidyāvatpuruṣaviṣayā eva /
na hi pramātrādivibhāgādṛte tadarthādhigamaḥ /
te tvavidyāvantamanuśāsato nirmṛṣṭanikhilāvidyamanuśiṣṭaṃ svarūpo vyavasthāpayantītyetāvāneṣāṃ viśeṣaḥ /
tasmādavidyāvatpuruṣaviṣayāṇyeva śāstrāṇīti siddham /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
Let perception and the other [means of knowledge] have as their domain one who is subject to <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
But scripture (<s>śāstra</s>), such as 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>' etc., ought not to operate on the basis of the superimposition of the self upon the body.
For here, the qualified person (<s>adhikārin</s>) is understood as one fit to enjoy the result in the next world.
And thus the aphoristic <s>sūtra</s> of [<s>Jaimini</s>] states: 'The result of scripture [accrues] to the performer, because it has the characteristics of that; therefore he himself should perform [the sacrifice].'
And since the body etc., having been reduced to ashes, cannot serve for the result in the next world, scripture implies some self other than the body etc. as the qualified person; and the knowledge of that is <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) — so how can scripture have as its domain one who is subject to <s>avidyā</s>? Anticipating this objection, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says — 'But the scriptural [transaction]' (<s>śāstrīye tu</s>).
The word '<s>tu</s>' (but) distinguishes the scriptural [transaction] from the [transactions of] perception etc.
For the scripture of qualification (<s>adhikāra-śāstra</s>) cannot function without the connection of the person who desires heaven with the next world; it may imply just that much, but not also that [the person] is essentially non-<s>saṃsāric</s> — since that is of no use for qualification; indeed, [it would be] contrary to the qualification of the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> person, who is a non-agent and non-enjoyer.
For the performer (<s>prayoktṛ</s>) of ritual action — the one who partakes of the fruit generated by action — is the master (<s>svāmī</s>), the qualified person in regard to the ritual.
Then, how can a non-agent be a performer? And how can a non-enjoyer partake of the fruit generated by action?
Therefore, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions operates with reference to a person who, through beginningless <s>avidyā</s>, identifies himself as an agent, enjoyer, <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, etc.
Thus, the <s>Vedānta</s>s also have as their domain only the person subject to <s>avidyā</s>.
For without the division into knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) etc., there is no comprehension of their meaning.
But [the <s>Vedānta</s>s] instruct the person subject to <s>avidyā</s> and, once instructed, establish the taught [person] in his own true nature (<s>svarūpa</s>), having removed all <s>avidyā</s> — this is their only distinctive feature.
Therefore it is established that all scriptures have as their domain only the person subject to <s>avidyā</s>.

body.text:
syādetat /
yadyapi virodhānupayogābhyāmaupaniṣadaḥ puruṣaḥ adhikāre nāpekṣyate tathāpyupaniṣadbhyo 'vagamyamānaḥ śaknotyadhikāraṃ niroddhum /
tataśca parasparaparāhatārthatvena kṛtsna eva vedaḥ prāmāṇyamapajahyādityata āha- prāk ca tathābhūtātma- iti /
satyamaupaniṣadapuruṣādhigamaḥ adhikāravirodhī ; tasmāttu purastātkarmavidhayaḥ svocitaṃ vyavahāramabhinirvartayanto nānupajātena brahmajñānena śakyā niroddhum /
na ca parasparaparāhatiḥ, vidyāvidyāvatpuruṣabhedena vyavasthopapatteḥ /
yathā-'na hiṃsyātsarvā bhūtāni' iti sādhyāṃśaniṣedhe 'pi 'śyenenābhicaran yajeta' iti śāstraṃ pravartamānaṃ 'na hiṃsyāt' ityanena na virudhyate ; tatkasya hetoḥ ? puruṣabhedāditi /
avajitakrodhārātayaḥ puruṣā niṣedhe adhikriyante, krodhārātivaśīkṛtāstu śyenādiśāstre iti /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
Even if, due to contradiction and uselessness, the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> person is not required for [ritual] qualification, nevertheless, being understood from the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s, he is capable of obstructing that qualification.
Consequently, since [the two parts of the <s>Veda</s>] would have mutually contradictory meanings, the entire <s>Veda</s> would lose its authority.
To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says — 'And prior to such a [realization of the] self' (<s>prāk ca tathābhūtātma-</s>).
True, the realization of the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> person does contradict [ritual] qualification; but before that, the ritual injunctions, accomplishing the worldly transaction appropriate to them, cannot be obstructed by the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, which has not yet arisen.
Nor is there mutual contradiction — because the distinction [between the two domains] can be maintained on the basis of the difference between the person subject to <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and the person subject to <s>avidyā</s>.
Just as, although [the injunction] 'One should not harm any being' prohibits [harm] in a certain respect, the scripture 'One who desires to harm should sacrifice with the <s>Śyena</s> [rite]' — though it operates [positively] — does not contradict the [prohibition] 'One should not harm.' Why? Because of the difference of persons.
Persons who have conquered the enemy of anger are the qualified persons for the prohibition; but those controlled by the enemy of anger [are qualified] for the <s>Śyena</s> etc. scripture.

body.text:
avidyāvatpuruṣaviṣayatvaṃ nātivartata iti yaduktaṃ tadeva sphuṭayati- tathā hi iti /
varṇādhyāsaḥ 'rājā rājasūyena yajeta' ityādiḥ /
āśramādhyāsaḥ 'gṛhasthaḥ sadṛśīṃ bhāryāṃ vindeta' ityādiḥ /
vayo 'dhyāsaḥ 'kṛṣṇakeśo 'gnīnādadhīta' ityādiḥ /
avasthādhyāsaḥ 'apratisamādheyavyādhīnāṃ jalādipraveśena prāṇatyāgaḥ' ityādiḥ /
ādigrahaṇaṃ pātakopapātakasaṃkarīkaraṇāpātrīkaraṇamalinīkaraṇādyadhyāsopasaṃgrahārtham /
body.translated_text:
What was stated — that [scripture] does not transcend having as its domain a person subject to <s>avidyā</s> — that very [point] is made explicit: 'For thus' (<s>tathā hi</s>).
Superimposition of <s>varṇa</s> (social class): 'A king should sacrifice with the <s>Rājasūya</s>' and the like.
Superimposition of <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life): 'A householder should take a wife of equal [status]' and the like.
Superimposition of age: 'One with dark hair should establish the [sacrificial] fires' and the like.
Superimposition of condition: 'For those with incurable diseases, the relinquishing of life by entering water etc.' and the like.
The word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) is for the purpose of including the superimposition of sins, minor sins, mixed offenses, loss of caste-status, contamination, and the like.

body.text:
tadevamātmānātmanoḥ parasparādhyāsamākṣepasamādhānābhyāmupapādya pramāṇaprameyavyavahārapravartanena ca dṛḍhīkṛtya tasyānaharthahetutvamudāharaṇaprapañcena pratipādayan tatsvarupamuktaṃ smārayati- adhyāso nāma atasmiṃstadbuddhirityavocāma /
'smṛtirūpaḥ paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsaḥ' ityasya saṃkṣepābhidhānametat /
tatra 'aham' iti dharmitādātmyādhyāsamātram 'mama' ityanutpāditadharmādhyāsaṃ nānarthaheturiti dharmādhyāsameva mamakāraṃ sākṣādaśeṣānarthasaṃsārakāraṇamudāharaṇaprapañcānāha- tadyathā putrabhāryādiṣu iti /
dehatādātmyamātmanyadhyasya dehamarthaṃ putrakalatrādisvābhyaṃ ca kṛśatvādivat āropyāha- ahameva vikalaḥ, sakalaḥ iti /
svasya khalu sākalyena svābhyasākalyāt svāmīśvaraḥ sakalaḥ saṃpūrṇo bhavati ; tathā svasya vaikalyena svāmyavaikalyāt svāmīśvaro visalo 'saṃpūrṇo bhavati /
bāhyadharmā ye vaikalyādayaḥ svābhyapraṇālikayā saṃcaritāḥ śarīre tānātmanyadhyasyatītyarthaḥ /
yadā ca paropādhyapekṣe dehadharme svāmye iyaṃ gatiḥ, tadā kaiva kathā anaupādhikeṣu dehadharmeṣu kṛśatvādiṣu ityāśayavānāha- tathā dehadharmān iti /
dehādapyantaraṅgāṇāmindriyāṇāmadhyastātmabhāvānāṃ dharmān mūkatvādīn, tato 'pyantaraṅgasyāntaḥkaraṇasya adhyastātmabhāvasya dharmān kāmasaṃkalpādīn ātmanyadhyasyatīti yojanā /
body.translated_text:
Thus, having established the mutual superimposition of the self and the non-self through objection and refutation, and having consolidated [it] by showing how it drives the transactions of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, and while demonstrating through an elaboration of examples that [superimposition] is the cause of all harm, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] recalls its nature as already stated: 'Superimposition, as we have said, is the cognition of one thing as another' (<s>adhyāso nāma atasmiṃs tad buddhir ity avocāma</s>).
This is a condensed statement of [the definition] 'it has the form of memory, the appearance of something previously seen in something else.'
Therein, 'I' involves merely the superimposition of substrate-identity (<s>dharmi-tādātmya</s>), while 'mine' (<s>mama</s>), which does not occasion the superimposition of properties (<s>dharma-adhyāsa</s>), is not [by itself] a cause of harm. Therefore, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] elaborates through examples the property-superimposition (<s>dharma-adhyāsa</s>) — the possessive sense (<s>mamakāra</s>) — which is the direct cause of the entire mass of harm constituting <s>saṃsāra</s>: 'For example, with respect to sons, wives, etc.' (<s>tad yathā putra-bhāryādiṣu</s>).
Having superimposed upon the self the identity with the body, and having superimposed the condition of the body as one's own, and [the condition of] sons, wife, etc. as one's own — just like being lean etc. — [one] says: 'I am indeed incomplete (<s>vikala</s>), I am complete (<s>sakala</s>).'
For indeed, through the completeness of one's own [possessions], the owner-lord becomes <s>sakala</s> (complete, prosperous); and through the deficiency of one's own, the owner-lord becomes <s>vikala</s> (incomplete, lacking).
The meaning is that external properties such as deficiency etc., which have traveled through the channel of ownership, [are superimposed] upon the body, and from there upon the self.
And when this is the situation for bodily properties such as ownership that depend on extraneous limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>), what more need be said about non-adventitious bodily properties such as being lean etc.? With this intent, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Likewise, the properties of the body' (<s>tathā deha-dharmān</s>).
The properties of the senses — which are more intimate than the body and upon which selfhood has been superimposed — such as being mute etc.; and the properties of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) — which is even more intimate, and upon which selfhood has been superimposed — such as desire, intention (<s>saṃkalpa</s>), etc. — are superimposed upon the self. This is the construction.

body.text:
tadanena prapañcena dharmādhyāsamuktvā tasya mūlaṃ dharmyadhyāsamāha- evamahaṃpratyayinam /
ahaṃpratyayo vṛttiryasmin antaḥkaraṇādau, so 'yamahaṃpratyayī ; taṃ svapracāraṇasākṣiṇi, antaḥkaraṇapracārasākṣiṇi, caitanyodāsīnatābhyāṃ pratyagātmanyadhyasya /
tadanena kartṛtvabhoktṛtve upapādite /
caitanyamupapādayati- taṃ ca pratyagātmānaṃ sarvasākṣiṇaṃ tadviparyayeṇa, antaḥkaraṇādiviparyayeṇa- antaḥkaraṇādyacetanam, tasya viparyayaḥ caitanyam, tena, itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā-antaḥkaraṇādiṣvadhyasyati /
tadanena antaḥkaraṇādyavacchinnaḥ pratyagātmā idamanidaṃrūpaścetanaḥ kartā bhoktā kāryakāraṇāvidyādvayādhāro 'haṅkārāspadaṃ saṃsārī sarvānarthasaṃbhārabhājanaṃ jīvātmā itaretarādhyāsopādānaḥ tadupādānaścādhyāsa ityanāditvāt bījāṅkuravannetaretarāśrayatvamityuktaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text:
Having thus elaborated the property-superimposition through this exposition, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states its root, the substrate-superimposition (<s>dharmy-adhyāsa</s>): 'Thus, the one who is the locus of the I-cognition' (<s>evam ahaṃ-pratyayinam</s>).
The '<s>ahaṃ-pratyayin</s>' is that in which the I-cognition (<s>ahaṃ-pratyaya</s>), a modification (<s>vṛtti</s>), [occurs] — namely, the inner organ etc. That [inner organ] is superimposed upon the witness (<s>sākṣin</s>) of its own operations — the witness of the operations of the inner organ — upon the inner Self (<s>pratyag-ātman</s>), through [its having] the impartial consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>).
By this, agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>) and enjoyership (<s>bhoktṛtva</s>) are established.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] establishes consciousness: 'And that inner Self, the witness of all' (<s>taṃ ca pratyag-ātmānaṃ sarva-sākṣiṇam</s>) — 'by the converse of that' (<s>tad-viparyayeṇa</s>), meaning by the converse of the inner organ etc. — the inner organ etc. being insentient, its converse is consciousness; by that — [the third case being] in the sense of characterizing the manner — [consciousness] is superimposed upon the inner organ etc.
By this, the inner Self, delimited by the inner organ etc., having the form of 'this' and 'not-this,' conscious, an agent, an enjoyer, the substrate of the twofold <s>avidyā</s> — causal and effectual — the locus of ego-sense, the transmigrating self (<s>saṃsārin</s>), the receptacle of the entire mass of harm — the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>) — is the material of mutual superimposition, and that superimposition is its material [in turn]. And since this is beginningless, like the seed and sprout, there is no mutual dependence — this is what has been stated.

body.text:
pramāṇaprameyavyavahāradṛḍhīkṛtameva śiṣyahitāya svarūpābhidhānapūrvakaṃ sarvalokapratyakṣatayā adhyāsaṃ sudṛḍhīkaroti- evamayamanādiranantaḥ, tattvajñānamantareṇāśakyasamucchedaḥ /
anādyanantatve heturuktaḥ- naisargika iti /
mithyāpratyayarūpaḥ mithyāpratyayānāṃ rūpamanirvacanīyatvam ; tadyasya sa tathoktaḥ ; anirvacanīya ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Having consolidated [the argument] through the transactions of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], for the benefit of the student, makes the superimposition — which is evident to all people — even more firmly established, by first stating its nature: 'Thus, this [superimposition] is beginningless and endless' (<s>evam ayam anādir anantaḥ</s>); 'impossible to eradicate without the knowledge of reality' (<s>tattva-jñānam antareṇa aśakya-samucchedaḥ</s>).
The reason for its beginninglessness and endlessness has been stated: '<s>naisargika</s>' (innate).
'Having the form of false cognition' (<s>mithyā-pratyaya-rūpaḥ</s>) — the form (<s>rūpa</s>) of false cognitions is indescribability (<s>anirvacanīyatva</s>); that which has that [quality] is so called; meaning: indescribable.

body.text:
prakṛtamupasaṃharati- asyānarthahetoḥ prahāṇāya /
virodhipratyayaṃ vinā kuto 'sya prahāṇamityaya uktam- ātmaikatvavidyāpratipattaye /
pratipattiḥ prāptiḥ, tasyai, na tu japamātrāya, nāpi karmasu pravṛttaye /
ātmaikatvaṃ vigalitanikhilaprapañcatvam ānandarūpasya sataḥ /
tatpratipattiṃ nirvicikitsāṃ bhāvayanto vedāntāḥ samūlaghātamadhyāsamupaghnanti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- asmatpratyayasyātmaviṣayasya samīcīnatve sati brahmaṇo jñātatvāt niṣprayojanatvācca na jijñāsā syāt ; tadabhāve ca na brahmajñānāya vedāntāḥ paṭhyeran ; api tu avivakṣitārthā japamātre upayujyeran /
na hi tadaupaniṣadātmapratyayaḥ pramāṇatāmaśnute /
na cāsāvapramāṇamabhyasto 'pi vāstavaṃ kartṛtvabhoktṛtvādyātmano 'panetumarhati /
āropitaṃ hi rūpaṃ tattvajñānenāpodyate, na tu vāstavamatattvajñānena /
na hi rajjvā rajjutvaṃ sahasramapi sarpadhārāpratyayā apavaditumutsahante /
mithyājñānaprasañjitaṃ tu rūpaṃ śakyaṃ tattvajñānena apavaditum, mithyājñānasaṃskāraśca sudṛḍho 'pi tattvajñānasaṃskāreṇādaranairantaryadīrdhakālāsevitatattvajñānābhyāsajanmaneti /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes the topic at hand: 'For the removal of this cause of harm' (<s>asyānartha-hetoḥ prahāṇāya</s>).
Without a contradicting cognition, whence its removal? — to this it is said: 'For the attainment of the knowledge of the unity of the Self' (<s>ātmaikatva-vidyā-pratipattaye</s>).
<s>Pratipatti</s> means attainment — for the sake of that; not merely for the sake of recitation (<s>japa</s>), nor for engagement in ritual actions.
The unity of the Self (<s>ātmaikatva</s>) is the state of being devoid of all phenomenal elaboration (<s>prapañca</s>), of that which is of the nature of bliss.
The <s>Vedānta</s>s, cultivating the unwavering realization of that [unity], uproot superimposition utterly.
What is meant is this: if the ego-cognition's reference to the Self were correct, then, since <s>Brahman</s> would already be known and since there would be no purpose [for further inquiry], there would be no desire to know (<s>jijñāsā</s>). In the absence of that, the <s>Vedānta</s>s would not be studied for the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>; rather, having no intended meaning, they would serve merely for recitation.
For the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> cognition of the Self does not attain the status of a [valid] means of knowledge [if the ego-cognition is already valid].
Nor can that [ego-cognition], even when cultivated extensively, though not a [valid] means of knowledge, remove the real agency, enjoyership, etc. of the Self.
For a superimposed form is removed by the knowledge of reality, but not a real [form] by the non-knowledge of reality.
For not even a thousand currents of snake-cognition can sublate the rope-ness of a rope.
But a form produced by false knowledge can be sublated by the knowledge of reality; and even a very firm impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of false knowledge [is removed] by the impression of the knowledge of reality — [arising from] the practice of the knowledge of reality that is cultivated with devotion, continuity, and over a long period.

body.text:
syādetat /
prāṇādyupāsanā api vedānteṣu bahulamupalabhyante /
tatkathaṃ sarveṣāṃ vedāntānāmātmaikatvapratipādanamartha ityata āha- yathā cāyamarthaḥ ityādi /
śarīrameva śarīrakam ; tatra nivāsī śārīrako jīvātmā /
tasya tvaṃpadābhidheyasya tatpadābhidheyaparamātmarūpatayā yā mīmāṃsā sā tathoktā /
body.translated_text:
One might [object] thus:
Meditations on <s>prāṇa</s> etc. are also abundantly found in the <s>Vedānta</s>s.
Then how can all <s>Vedānta</s>s have as their purpose the teaching of the unity of the Self?
To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And as this meaning [is established]' (<s>yathā cāyam arthaḥ</s>) etc.
The body (<s>śarīra</s>) itself is the <s>śārīraka</s> (that which pertains to the body); the one who dwells in that is the <s>śārīraka</s> — the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>).
The inquiry (<s>mīmāṃsā</s>) into the nature of that [individual self], as denoted by the word 'you' (<s>tvam</s>-<s>pada</s>), being identical with the Supreme Self (<s>paramātman</s>) denoted by the word 'that' (<s>tat</s>-<s>pada</s>) — that is called <s>Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā</s>.

body.text: etāvānatrārthasaṃkṣepaḥ- yadyapi svādhyāyādhyayanavidhinā svādhyāyapadavācyasya vedarāśeḥ phalavadarthāvabodhaparatāṃ āpādayatā karmavidhiniṣedhānāmiva vedāntānāmapi svādhyāyaśabdavācyānāṃ phalavadarthāvabodhaparatvamāpāditam, yadyapi ca 'aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ' iti nyāyāt mantrāṇāmiva vedāntānāmarthaparatvamautsargikam, yadyapi ca vedāntebhyaḥ caitanyānandaghanaḥ kartṛtvabhoktṛtvarahito niṣprapañca ekaḥ pratyagātmā avagamyate, tathāpi kartṛtvabhoktṛtvaduḥkhaśoka-
body.translated_text: This is the summary of the meaning here: Although, by the injunction of <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study) — 'One should study one's own [portion of the <s>Veda</s>]' — which establishes that the entire body of the <s>Veda</s>, denoted by the word '<s>svādhyāya</s>,' is oriented toward the comprehension of meaning that yields fruit, just as for the ritual injunctions and prohibitions, so too for the <s>Vedānta</s>s — which are also denoted by the word '<s>svādhyāya</s>' — orientation toward the comprehension of meaningful, fruitful content is established; and although, by the principle 'the sentence-meaning is not differentiated [from the word-meaning],' the orientation toward meaning of the <s>Vedānta</s>s, like that of mantras, is the general rule; and although from the <s>Vedānta</s>s a single inner Self (<s>pratyag-ātman</s>) is understood — a mass of consciousness and bliss, devoid of agency and enjoyership, without phenomenal elaboration — nevertheless, due to the [ego-experience of] suffering, grief,

body.text:
mohamayamātmānamavagāhamānenāhaṃpratyayena sedehabādhavirahiṇā virudhyamānā vedāntāḥ svārthātpracyutā upacaritārthā vā japamātropayogino vā ityavivakṣitasvārthāḥ /
tathā ca tadarthavicārātmikā caturlakṣaṇī śārīrakamīmāṃsā nārabdhavyā /
body.translated_text:
and delusion, the ego-cognition (<s>ahaṃ-pratyaya</s>), which apprehends a self plunged in [suffering] — being unrebutted by experience [to the contrary] — contradicts the <s>Vedānta</s>s. [If so, the <s>Vedānta</s>s would be] displaced from their own meaning, or would have a figurative meaning, or would serve merely for recitation — thus [they would be] without their intended meaning.
In that case, the <s>Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā</s> — the inquiry into [the meaning of the <s>Vedānta</s>s], consisting of the four characteristics (<s>catur-lakṣaṇī</s>) — should not be undertaken.

body.text: na ca sarvajanīnāhamanubhavasiddha ātmā saṃdigdho vā saprayojano vā, yena jijñāsyaḥ san vicāraṃ prayuñjīta- iti pūrvapakṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Nor is the Self — established through the ego-experience common to all people — either doubtful or purposeful, such that, being a fit subject for inquiry, it would prompt investigation — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view).

body.text:
siddhāntastu- bhavedetadevaṃ yadyahaṃpratyayaḥ pramāṇam /
tasya tu uktena krameṇa śrutyādibādhakatvānupapatteḥ, śrutyādibhiśca samastatīrthakaraiśca prāmāṇyānabhyupagamādadhyāsatvam /
evaṃ ca vedāntā nāvivakṣitārthāḥ, nāpi upacaritārthāḥ, kiṃ tu uktakṣaṇāḥ /
pratyagātmaiva teṣāṃ mukhyor'thaḥ /
tasya ca vakṣyamāṇena krameṇa saṃdigdhatvāt prayojanatvācca yuktā jijñāsā- ityāśayavān sūtrakāraḥ tajjijñāsāmasūtrayat, athāto brahmajijñāsā iti /
body.translated_text:
But the <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion) is: this would be so if the ego-cognition were a [valid] means of knowledge.
But since, by the method stated, [the ego-cognition] is not tenable as sublating scripture etc., and since its status as a [valid] means of knowledge is not accepted by scripture etc. and by all the founders of philosophical schools — [therefore] it is [an instance of] superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>).
This being so, the <s>Vedānta</s>s do not have an unintended meaning, nor a figurative meaning; rather, they are as characterized [above].
The inner Self (<s>pratyag-ātman</s>) alone is their primary meaning.
And since that [Self] is doubtful and purposeful in the manner to be described, the inquiry [into it] is fitting — with this intent, the author of the <s>sūtra</s>s composed the aphorism concerning the desire to know it: '<s>athāto brahma-jijñāsā</s>' (Now, therefore, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>).

body.text:
jijñāsayā ca saṃdehaprayojane sūcayati /
tatra sakṣādicchāvyāpyatvādbrahmajñānaṃ kaṇaṭhoktaṃ prayojanam /
na ca karmajñānātparācīnamanuṣṭhānamiva brahmajñānātparācīnaṃ kiñcidasti, yenaitadavāntaraprayojanaṃ bhavet /
kiṃ tu brahmamīmāṃsākhyatarketikartavyatānujñātaviṣayairvedāntairāhitaṃ nirvicikitsaṃ brahmajñānameva samastaduḥkhopaśamarūpamānandaikarasaṃ paramaṃ prayojanam /
tamarthamadhikṛtya hi prekṣāvantaḥ pravartantetarām /
tacca prāptamapyanādyavidyāvaśādaprāptamiveti prepsitaṃ bhavati ; yathā svagrīvāgatamapi graiveyakaṃ kutaścidbhramānnāstīti manyamānaḥ pareṇa pratipāditamaprāptamiva prāpnoti /
jijñāsā tu saṃśayasya kāryamiti svakāraṇaṃ saṃśayaṃ sūcayati /
saṃśayaśca mīmāṃsārambhaṃ prayojayati /
tathā ca śāstre prekṣāvatpravṛttihetusaṃśayaprayojanasūcanāt yuktamasya sūtrasya śāstrāditvam, ityāha bhagavānbhāṣyakāraḥ-
body.translated_text: And by the [word] '<s>jijñāsā</s>' (desire to know), [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] indicates the doubt and the purpose [of the inquiry]. Therein, since it is pervaded by the desire for direct experience (<s>sākṣāt-icchā</s>), the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> as stated by <s>Kaṇṭha</s> is the purpose. And there is nothing subsequent to the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> in the way that performance [of ritual] is subsequent to the knowledge of <s>karma</s>, such that this [knowledge] would be a subsidiary purpose. Rather, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> itself — established through the <s>Vedānta</s> passages whose subject-matter is sanctioned by reasoning called <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>, free from all doubt — being of the nature of the cessation of all suffering and of the single essence of bliss, is the supreme purpose. For it is with reference to that goal that the discerning engage themselves all the more. And that [knowledge], though already attained, appears as if not attained due to the force of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and so becomes something desired to be obtained — just as a necklace already on one's own neck, when one mistakenly thinks 'it is not here' due to some confusion, is, when pointed out by another, obtained as if it had not been obtained. And '<s>jijñāsā</s>' (desire to know), being the effect of doubt, indicates its own cause, namely doubt. And doubt motivates the commencement of <s>mīmāṃsā</s> (inquiry). And thus, since in the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) there is the indication of doubt as the purpose — the cause of the engagement of the discerning — it is fitting that this <s>sūtra</s> is the beginning of the treatise. This is what the revered commentator (<s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>) says —

body.text:
vedāntamīmāṃsāśāstrasya vyācikhyāsitasya asmābhiḥ, idamādimaṃ sūtram /
pūjitavicāravacano mīmāṃsāśabdaḥ /
paramapuruṣārthahetubhūtasūkṣmatamārthanirṇayaphalatayā ca vicārasya ca pūjitatā /
tasya mīmāṃsāyāḥ śāstram, sā hyanena śiṣyate śiṣyebhyo yathāvatpratipādyata iti /
sūtraṃ ca bahvarthasūcanāt bhavati /
yathāhuḥ-
body.translated_text: Of the <s>Vedānta-mīmāṃsā-śāstra</s> (the treatise of inquiry into <s>Vedānta</s>) that is to be explained by us, this is the first <s>sūtra</s>. The word '<s>mīmāṃsā</s>' denotes revered inquiry. And the reveredness of inquiry [derives] from its fruit being the ascertainment of the most subtle matter that is the cause of the supreme human goal (<s>parama-puruṣārtha</s>). Its <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) — for by this [treatise], it [the inquiry] is taught, i.e., properly communicated to students. And a <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism) is so [called] because it indicates many meanings. As they say —

body.text: laghūni sūcitārthāni svalpākṣarapadāni ca /
body.translated_text: Concise, indicating their meanings, with few syllables and words,

body.text: sarvataḥ sārabhūtāni sūtrāṇyāhurmanīṣiṇaḥ //
body.translated_text: Containing the essence of everything — such [compositions] the wise call <s>sūtra</s>s. //

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text:
tadevaṃ sūtratātparyaṃ vyākhyāya tasya prathamapadaṃ atha iti vyācaṣṭe- tatrāthaśabda ānantaryārthaḥ parigṛhyate /
teṣu sūtrapadeṣu madhye yo 'yaṃ athaśabdaḥ sa ānantaryārtha iti yojanā /
body.translated_text: Having thus explained the purport of the <s>sūtra</s>, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] explains its first word '<s>atha</s>' (now/then) — 'Therein, the word <s>atha</s> is taken in the sense of sequence (<s>ānantarya</s>).' Among those words of the <s>sūtra</s>, this word '<s>atha</s>' has the meaning of sequence — this is the syntactic connection.

body.text:
nanu adhikārārtho 'pyathaśabdo dṛśyate, yathā 'athaiṣa jyotiḥ' iti vede, yathā vā loke 'atha śabdānuśāsanam' iti, 'atha yogānuśāsanam' iti ca ; tatkimatrādhikārārtho na gṛhyata ityata āha- nādhikārārthaḥ /
kutaḥ ? brahmajijñāsāyā anadhikāryatvāt /
jijñāsā tāvadiha sūtre brahmaṇaśca tajjñānācca śabdataḥ pradhānaṃ pratīyate /
na ca yathā 'daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha' ityatra apradhānamapi daṇḍaśabdārtho vivakṣyate evamihāpi brahmatajjñāne iti yuktam, brahmamīmāṃsāśāstrapravṛttyaṅgasaṃśayaprayojanasūcanārthatvena jijñāsāyā eva vivakṣitatvāt /
tadavivakṣāyāṃ tadasūcanena kākadantaparīkṣāyāmiva na brahmamīmāṃsāyāṃ prekṣāvantaḥ pravarteran /
na hi tadānīṃ brahma tajjñānaṃ ca abhidheyaprayojane bhavitumarhataḥ, anadhyastāhaṃpratyayavirodhena vedāntānāmevaṃvidher'the prāmāṇyānupapatteḥ ; karmapravṛttyupayogitayā upacaritārthānāṃ vā japopayogināṃ vā 'hum' ityevamādīnāmivāvivakṣitārthānāmapi svādhyāyādhyayanavidhyadhīnagrahaṇatvasya saṃbhavāt /
tasmātsaṃdehaprayojanasūcanī jijñāsā iha padato vākyataśca pradhānaṃ vivakṣitavyā /
na ca tasyā adhikāryatvam, aprastūyamānatvāt, yena tatsamabhivyāhṛto 'thaśabdo 'dhikārārthaḥ syāt /
jijñāsāviśeṣaṇaṃ tu brahmajñānamadhikāryaṃ bhavet /
na ca tadapyathaśabdena saṃbadhyate, prādhānyābhāvāt /
na ca jijñāsā mīmāṃsā yena yogānuśāsanavadadhikriyeta ; nāntatvaṃ nipātya 'māṅ māne' ityasmādvā 'mānapūjāyām' ityasmādvā dhātoḥ 'mānbandha-' ityādinā anicchārthe sani vyutpāditasya mīmāṃsāpadasya pūjitavicāravacanatvāt ; jñānecchāvācakatvājjijñāsāpadasya /
pravartikā hi mīmāṃsāyāṃ jījñāsā syāt /
na ca pravartyapravartakayoraikyam, ekatve tadbhāvānupapatteḥ /
na ca svārthaparatvasyopapattau satyāṃ anyārthaparatvakalpanā yuktā, atiprasaṅgāt /
tasmātsuṣṭhūktam 'jijñāsāyā anadhikāryatvāt' iti /
body.translated_text: Now, the word '<s>atha</s>' is also seen with the meaning of commencement (<s>adhikāra</s>), as in the <s>Veda</s> '<s>athaiṣa jyotiḥ</s>' (now, this light), or in common usage '<s>atha śabdānuśāsanam</s>' (now, the instruction on words) and '<s>atha yogānuśāsanam</s>' (now, the instruction on <s>yoga</s>). So why is the sense of commencement not taken here? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Not in the sense of commencement.' Why? Because '<s>brahmajijñāsā</s>' (the desire to know <s>Brahman</s>) is not something to be commenced. For in this <s>sūtra</s>, '<s>jijñāsā</s>' (desire to know) is understood from the words as primary, along with <s>Brahman</s> and the knowledge of it. And it is not reasonable that, just as in '<s>daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha</s>' (the staff-bearer recites the directive formulas), where the non-primary meaning of the word '<s>daṇḍa</s>' (staff) is also intended — so too here <s>Brahman</s> and its knowledge [would be primary]. For '<s>jijñāsā</s>' alone is intended, being for the purpose of indicating the doubt and purpose that are accessories to the commencement of the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā-śāstra</s>. Without intending that [doubt and purpose], through not indicating it, the discerning would not engage in <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>, as in the examination of a crow's teeth.
