rāgādikaṣāyamadirāmattaṃ hi manaḥ teṣu teṣu viṣayeṣūccāvacamindriyāṇi pravartayat vividhāśca pravṛttīḥ puṇyāpuṇyaphalā bhāvayat puruṣamatighore vividhaduḥkhajvālājaṭāle saṃsārahutabhuji juhoti /
prasaṃkhyānābhyāsalabdhavairāgyaparipākabhagnarāgādikaṣāyamadirāmadaṃ tu manaḥ puruṣeṇāvajīyate vaśīkriyate /
so 'yamasya vairāgyahetuko manovijayaḥ śama iti vaśīkarasaṃjña iti cākhyāyate /
vijitaṃ ca manastattvaviṣayaviniyogayogyatāṃ nīyate ; seyamasya yogyatā damaḥ, yathā dānto 'yaṃ vṛṣabhayuvā halaśakaṭādivahanayogyaḥ kṛta iti gamyate /
ādi-grahaṇena ca viṣayatitikṣātaduparamatattvaśraddhāḥ saṃgṛhyante /
ata eva śrutiḥ- 'tasmācchānto dānta uparatastitikṣuḥ śraddhāvitto bhūtvātmanyevātmānaṃ paśyet, sarvamātmani paśyati' iti /
tadetasya śamadamādirūpasya sādhanasya saṃpat, prakarṣaḥ, śamadamādisādhanasaṃpat /
tato 'sya saṃsārabandhanānmumukṣā bhavatītyāha- mumukṣutvaṃ ca iti /
tasya ca nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvabrahmajñānaṃ mokṣasya kāraṇamityupaśrutya tajjijñāsā bhavati dharmajijñāsāyāḥ prāgūrdhvaṃ ca ; tasmātteṣāmevānantaryaṃ na dharmajijñāsāyā ityāha- teṣu hi iti /
na kevalaṃ jijñāsāmātram, api tu jñānamapītyāha- jñātuṃ ca /
upasaṃharati- tasmāt iti /
body.translated_text:
Then, from this contemplation characterized by the discrimination of permanent and impermanent things, there arises dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter.
'<s>Artha</s>' means that which is desired, i.e., the fruit.
Dispassion (<s>virāga</s>) toward that is an attitude of indifference characterized by non-attachment.
Thereafter [comes] the collection of means (<s>sādhana-saṃpat</s>) [consisting of] tranquility (<s>śama</s>), self-restraint (<s>dama</s>), and the like.
For the mind, intoxicated by the liquor of passions (<s>rāga</s>) and afflictions (<s>kaṣāya</s>), directing the senses — higher and lower — toward various objects and producing various activities bearing meritorious and demeritorious fruits, casts the person into the sacrificial fire of <s>saṃsāra</s>, [which is] a most terrible mass of flames of manifold suffering.
But the mind whose intoxication by the liquor of passions and afflictions has been broken through the maturation of dispassion obtained by the practice of contemplation — that [mind] is conquered and subdued by the person.
This conquest of the mind, caused by dispassion, is called <s>śama</s> (tranquility) and is designated as 'mastery' (<s>vaśīkara</s>).
And the conquered mind is brought to fitness for application to the reality [of <s>Brahman</s>]; this fitness is <s>dama</s> (self-restraint) — just as [one says] 'this tamed bull or [draft animal] has been made fit for pulling a plough, cart, etc.'
By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.), forbearance toward [pairs of] opposites (<s>titikṣā</s>), withdrawal [from sense-objects] (<s>uparama</s>), and faith in reality (<s>tattva-śraddhā</s>) are included.
Hence the <s>Śruti</s>: 'Therefore, having become tranquil, self-restrained, withdrawn, forbearing, and full of faith, one should see the Self in the Self alone; one sees everything in the Self.'
This collection (<s>saṃpat</s>), i.e., excellence, of the means (<s>sādhana</s>) consisting of tranquility, self-restraint, and the like is the collection of means of tranquility, self-restraint, etc.
Then the desire for liberation (<s>mumukṣā</s>) from the bondage of <s>saṃsāra</s> arises — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And the desire for liberation (<s>mumukṣutva</s>).'
And having heard that the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> — whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free — is the cause of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), the desire to know it arises, both before and after the desire to know <s>dharma</s>; therefore, the sequence is to these [prerequisites] alone, not to the desire to know <s>dharma</s> — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For in the case of these...'
Not merely the desire to know, but even the knowledge itself [follows from these] — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And to know.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes: 'Therefore.'

body.text:
kramaprāptamataḥśabdaṃ vyācaṣṭe- ataḥśabdo hetvarthaḥ /
tamevātaḥśabdasya heturūpamarthamāha- yasmādveda eva iti /
atraivaṃ paricodyate- satyaṃ yathoktasādhanasaṃpattyanantaraṃ brahmajijñāsā bhavati /
saiva tvanupapannā, ihāmutraphalabhogavirāgasyānupapatteḥ /
anukūlavedanīyaṃ hi phalam, iṣṭalakṣaṇatvātphalasya /
na cānurāgahetāvasya vairāgyaṃ bhavitumarhati /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] glosses the word '<s>ataḥ</s>' (therefore), which comes next in order: 'The word <s>ataḥ</s> is in the sense of reason (<s>hetu</s>).'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states that very meaning of the word '<s>ataḥ</s>' as a reason: 'Because from the <s>Veda</s> alone...'
Here the following examination is raised: True, the desire to know <s>Brahman</s> arises in sequence with the prerequisites as stated.
But that [desire] itself is unjustified, since dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter is unjustified.
For the fruit is that which is favorable to experience — since the definition of fruit is that which is desired.
And it is not reasonable that dispassion should arise toward that which is a cause of attraction.

body.text: duḥkhānuṣaṅgadarśanātsukhe 'pi vairāgyamiti cet, hanta bhoḥ sukhānuṣaṅgādduḥkhe 'pyanurāgo na kasmādbhavati ? tasmāt sukhe upādīyamāne duḥkhaparihāre prayatitavyam ; avarjanīyatayā duḥkhamāgatamapi parihṛtya sukhamātraṃ bhokṣyate /
body.translated_text: If it be said that dispassion toward pleasure [arises] from seeing that suffering is inseparably connected [with it] — well then, sir! Why does not attachment to suffering also arise from the inseparable connection of pleasure [with it]? Therefore, when pleasure is being obtained, one should make effort to avoid suffering; and even suffering that has come unavoidably, having been warded off, one will enjoy pleasure alone.

body.text:
tadyathā- matsyārthī saśalkānsakaṇṭakānmatsyānupādatte, sa yāvadādeyaṃ tāvadādāya nivartate ; yathā vā dhānyārthī sapalālāni dhānyānyāharati, sa yāvadādeyaṃ tāvadādāya nivartate /
tasmādduḥkhabhayānnānukūlavedanīyamaihikaṃ vāmuṣmikaṃ vā sukhaṃ parityaktumucitam /
na hi mṛgāḥ santīti śālayo nopyante, bhikṣukāḥ santīti sthālyo nādhiśrīyante /
api ca dṛṣṭaṃ sukhaṃ candanavanitādisaṅgajanma kṣayitālakṣaṇena duḥkhenāghrātatvādatibhīruṇā tyajyetāpi, na tvāmuṣmikaṃ svargādi, tasyāvināśitvāt /
śrūyate hi- 'apāma somamamṛtā abhūma' iti ; tathā ca 'akṣayyaṃ ha vai cāturmāsyayājinaḥ sukṛtaṃ bhavati' iti /
na ca kṛtakatvahetukaṃ vināśitvānumānamatra saṃbhavati, naraśiraḥkapālaśaucānumānavadāgamabādhitaviṣayatvāt /
tasmādyathoktasādhanasaṃpattyabhāvānna brahmajijñāseti prāptam /
evaṃ prāpte āha bhagavānsūtrakāraḥ 'ataḥ' iti ; tasyārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe bhāṣyakāraḥ- yasmādveda eva iti /
body.translated_text:
For example — one who desires fish takes fish that have scales and bones; he takes what is to be taken and then desists. Or, one who desires grain brings grain together with its chaff; he takes what is to be taken and then desists.
Therefore, it is not proper to abandon pleasure — whether pertaining to this world or to the next — that is experienced as agreeable, out of fear of suffering.
For rice is not left unplanted because deer exist, nor are cooking pots left unused because beggars exist.
Moreover, visible (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>) pleasure born from the contact of sandalwood, butter, and the like might be abandoned even by the exceedingly timid, because it is tinged with suffering characterized by perishability; but not pleasure pertaining to the next world, such as heaven and the like, because of its imperishability.
For the <s>Śruti</s> declares: 'We have drunk the <s>Soma</s>; we have become immortal.' And likewise: 'The merit of one who performs the <s>Cāturmāsya</s> sacrifice is imperishable.'
Nor is the inference of perishability based on [the reasoning that it is] produced applicable here, because — like the inference of purity from a human skull — it pertains to a domain contradicted by scripture (<s>āgama</s>).
Therefore, since the requisite conditions as stated are not fulfilled, the conclusion reached is that there should be no inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>.
When this prima facie view has been arrived at, the revered author of the <s>sūtra</s>s says '<s>ataḥ</s>' (therefore); the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) explains its meaning: 'Because the <s>Veda</s> alone...'

body.text:
ayamabhisaṃdhiḥ- satyaṃ mṛgabhikṣukādayaḥ śakyāḥ parihartuṃ pācakakṛṣīvalādibhiḥ ; duḥkhaṃ tvanekavidhānekakāraṇasaṃpātajamaśakyaparihāram ; antataḥ sādhanāpāratantryakṣayitalakṣaṇayorduḥkhayoḥ samastakṛtakasukhāvinābhāvaniyamāt /
na hi madhuviṣasaṃpṛktamannaṃ viṣaṃ parityajya madhumiśraṃ śakyaṃ śilpivareṇāpi bhoktum /
kṣayitānumānopodvalitaṃ ca 'tadyatheha karmacitaḥ' ityādivacanaṃ kṣayitāpratipādakam, 'apāma somam' ityādikaṃ vacanaṃ mukhyāsaṃbhave jaghanyavṛttitāmāpādayati /
yathāhuḥ paurāṇikāḥ-
body.translated_text:
The intention is this: True, deer, beggars, and the like can be warded off by cooks, farmers, and such. But suffering — born from the convergence of manifold causes of many kinds — cannot be warded off. At the very least, [this is so] because all produced pleasure is invariably accompanied by the two kinds of suffering: dependence on means and perishability.
For one cannot eat food mixed with honey and poison, discarding the poison and [retaining only] the honey-mixture, even if one is the most skilled artisan.
And the scriptural statement '<s>tadyatheha karmacitaḥ</s>' ('just as here [the merit] accumulated by action [is exhaustible]') etc., which is corroborated by the inference of perishability, does not teach imperishability; the statement '<s>apāma somam</s>' ('we have drunk the <s>Soma</s>') and the like, when the primary meaning is impossible, resorts to a secondary meaning.
As the <s>Paurāṇika</s>s (narrators of the <s>Purāṇa</s>s) say —

body.text: 'ābhūtasaṃplavaṃ sthānamamṛtatvaṃ hi bhāṣyate' iti /
body.translated_text: 'Immortality is spoken of as lasting until the dissolution of all beings' (<s>ābhūtasaṃplava</s>).

body.text:
atra ca brahmapadena tatpramāṇaṃ veda upasthāpitaḥ /
sa ca yogyatvāt 'tadyatheha karmacitaḥ' ityādiḥ 'ataḥ' iti sarvanāmnā parāmṛśya hetupañcamyā nirdiśyate /
body.translated_text:
And here, by the word '<s>brahma</s>' [in the <s>sūtra</s>], the <s>Veda</s> — which is its means of knowledge — is invoked.
And that [<s>Veda</s>], being appropriate, is referred to by the pronoun '<s>ataḥ</s>' (therefore) together with the statement '<s>tadyatheha karmacitaḥ</s>' etc., and is expressed with the fifth-case suffix in the sense of reason.

body.text:
syādetat /
yathā svargādeḥ kṛtakasya sukhasya duḥkhānuṣaṅgaḥ tathā brahmaṇo 'pītyata āha- tathā brahmavijñānādapi iti /
tenāyamarthaḥ- ataḥ svargādīnāṃ kṣayitāpratipādakāt brahmajñānasya ca paramapuruṣārthatāpratipādakāt āgamāt yathoktasādhanasaṃpat ; tataśca jijñāseti siddham /
body.translated_text:
One might object thus:
Just as produced pleasure such as heaven has the inseparable connection with suffering, so too does <s>Brahman</s> — therefore [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And from the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> also...'
Thus the meaning is: Therefore — from the scripture that teaches the perishability of pleasures like heaven, and that teaches the supreme human goal (<s>parama-puruṣārtha</s>) of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> — the requisite conditions as stated [are fulfilled]; and from that, the desire to know [<s>Brahman</s>] is established.

body.text:
brahmajijñāsāpadavyākhyānamāha- brahmaṇa iti /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsapradarśanena prācāṃ vṛttikṛtāṃ brahmaṇe jijñāsā brahmajijñāseti caturthīsamāsaḥ parāsto veditavyaḥ /
'tādarthyasamāse prakṛtivikṛtigrahaṇaṃ kartavyam' iti kātyāyanīyavacanena yūpadārvādiṣveva prakṛtivikārabhūteṣu caturthīsamāsaniyamāt aprakṛtivikārabhūte ityevamādau tanniṣedhāt, 'aśvaghāsādayaḥ ṣaṣṭhīsamāsā bhaviṣyanti' ityaśvaghāsādiṣu ṣaṣṭhīsamāsapratividhānāt /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāse 'pi ca brahmaṇo vāstavaprādhānyopapatteriti /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] explains the word '<s>brahmajijñāsā</s>': '<s>brahmaṇaḥ</s>' (of <s>Brahman</s>) etc.
By showing [this to be] a genitive compound (<s>ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa</s>), the dative compound '<s>brahmaṇe jijñāsā</s>' — 'desire to know for <s>Brahman</s>' — [which was the reading] of the earlier commentators (<s>prācāṃ vṛttikṛtām</s>) — should be understood as rejected.
[This is] because of <s>Kātyāyana</s>'s statement that 'In a compound denoting purpose, the mention of original substance and modification (<s>prakṛti-vikṛti</s>) must be made' — since dative compounds are restricted to cases involving original substance and modification, as in '<s>yūpa-dāru</s>' (wood for the sacrificial post) and the like; and since [the dative compound] is precluded in cases not involving original substance and modification, as in this case; and since, by the provision '<s>aśvaghāsādayaḥ</s> (horse-fodder etc.) will be genitive compounds,' genitive compounds are prescribed for cases like '<s>aśvaghāsa</s>' etc.
Moreover, even in a genitive compound, the genuine primacy of <s>Brahman</s> is logically established — [hence the genitive is appropriate].

body.text:
syādetat /
brahmaṇo jijñāsetyukte tatrānekārthatvādbrahmaśabdasya saṃśayaḥ- kasya brahmaṇo jijñāsā ?- iti /
asti brahmaśabdo vipratvajātau, yathā- brahmahatyeti ; asti ca vede, yathā- brahmojjhamiti ; asti ca paramātmani, yathā- 'brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati' iti /
tamimaṃ saṃśayamapākaroti- brahma ca vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇam iti /
yato brahmajijñāsāṃ pratijñāya tajjñāpanāya paramātmalakṣaṇaṃ praṇayati tato 'vagacchāmaḥ paramātmajijñāsaiveyaṃ na vipratvajātyādijijñāsā, ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
One might object thus:
When it is said '<s>brahmaṇo jijñāsā</s>' (desire to know <s>Brahman</s>), since the word '<s>brahman</s>' has multiple meanings, there is doubt: Of which '<s>brahman</s>' is the desire to know?
The word '<s>brahman</s>' is used for the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> caste, as in '<s>brahmahatyā</s>' (killing a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>); it is used for the <s>Veda</s>, as in '<s>brahmojjha</s>' (one who abandons the <s>Veda</s>); and it is used for the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>), as in '<s>brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati</s>' (one who knows <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] removes this doubt: '<s>Brahman</s> is that which will be characterized [by the definition to follow].'
Since, having proposed the desire to know <s>Brahman</s>, he formulates the definition of the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>) for the purpose of making it known, we understand that this is the desire to know the Supreme Self, not the desire to know the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> caste and the like — this is the meaning.

body.text:
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaparigrahe 'pi neyaṃ karmaṣaṣṭhī, kiṃ tu śeṣalakṣaṇā ; saṃbandhamātraṃ ca śeṣa iti brahmaṇo jijñāsetyukte brahmasaṃbandhinī jijñāsetyuktaṃ bhavati /
tathā ca brahmasvarūpapramāṇayuktisādhanaprayojanajijñāsāḥ sarvā brahmajijñāsārthā brahmajijñāsayāvaruddhā bhavanti, sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa vā brahmasaṃbandhāt /
karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhyāṃ tu brahmaśabdārthaḥ karma ; sa ca svarūpameveti tatpramāṇādayo nāvarudhyeran ; tathā cāpratijñātārthacintā pramāṇādiṣu bhavet- iti ye manyante tānpratyāhabrahmaṇa iti karmaṇi iti /
atra hetumāha- jijñāsya iti /
icchāyāḥ pratipattyanubandho jñānam, jñānasya ca jñeyaṃ brahma /
no khalu jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ vinā nirūpyate, na ca jijñāsā jñānaṃ vinā, iti pratipattyanubandhatvāt prathamaṃ jijñāsā karmaivāpekṣate, na tu saṃbandhimātram, tadantareṇāpi sati karmaṇi tannirūpaṇāt /
na hi candramasamādityaṃ vopalabhya kasyāyamiti saṃbandhyanveṣaṇā bhavati /
bhavati tu jñānamityukte viṣayānveṣaṇā kiṃviṣayamiti /
tasmātprathamamapekṣitatvāt karmatayaiva brahma saṃbadhyate, na tu saṃbandhitāmātreṇa, tasya jaghanyatvāt /
tathā ca karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī, ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Even accepting the genitive compound, this is not an objective genitive (<s>karma-ṣaṣṭhī</s>), but rather one denoting general relation (<s>śeṣa-lakṣaṇā</s>). And since <s>śeṣa</s> (relation) is merely connection in general, when it is said '<s>brahmaṇo jijñāsā</s>' (desire to know of <s>Brahman</s>), what is stated amounts to: a desire to know that is related to <s>Brahman</s>.
Accordingly, the desires to know <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature, means of knowledge, reasoning, means [of realization], and purpose — all of these are encompassed within the meaning of '<s>brahmajijñāsā</s>,' being included in the desire to know <s>Brahman</s>, either directly or indirectly, by virtue of their connection with <s>Brahman</s>.
But if the genitive were objective (<s>karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī</s>), then the referent of the word '<s>brahman</s>' would be [merely] the object [of desire]; and since that is just [<s>Brahman</s>'s] essential nature, its means of knowledge and the like would not be encompassed. And thus there would be consideration of matters not proposed — namely, the means of knowledge and the like — to those who think thus, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '<s>brahmaṇaḥ</s> — in the objective sense' (<s>karmaṇi</s>).
Here he states the reason: '<s>jijñāsya</s>' (that which is to be known). Desire (<s>icchā</s>) has knowledge as its concomitant of realization, and <s>Brahman</s> is the object to be known (<s>jñeya</s>) of that knowledge.
Indeed, knowledge cannot be determined without the object to be known, nor can the desire to know be [determined] without knowledge. Therefore, since [the desire to know] has realization as its concomitant, the desire to know first requires its object (<s>karma</s>), not merely a related thing (<s>saṃbandhi-mātra</s>), since [the desire] can be determined through [the object] alone even without [specifying the] related thing.
For indeed, having perceived the moon or the sun, no inquiry into their relation arises — 'to whom does this belong?'
But when knowledge is mentioned, the inquiry into its object does arise — 'what is its object?'
Therefore, since [<s>Brahman</s>] is required first as the object, <s>Brahman</s> is connected precisely as the object, not merely as a related thing, since [the latter] is secondary.
Thus the genitive is objective — this is the meaning.

body.text: nanu satyaṃ na jijñāsyamantareṇa jijñāsā nirūpyate ; jijñāsyāntaraṃ tvasyā bhaviṣyati ; brahma tu śeṣatayā saṃbhantsyata ityata āha- jijñāsyāntara iti /
body.translated_text: But surely, the desire to know cannot be determined without an object to be known; yet some other thing may be its object, while <s>Brahman</s> will be related to it as a <s>śeṣa</s> (general relation) — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'some other object to be known' (<s>jijñāsyāntara</s>).

body.text:
nigūḍhābhiprāyaścodayati- nanu śeṣaṣaṣṭhīparigrahe 'pi iti /
sāmānyasaṃbandhasya viśeṣasaṃbandhāvirodhena karmatāyā avighātena jijñāsānirūpaṇopapatterityarthaḥ /
nigūḍhābhiprāya eva dūṣayati- evamapi pratyakṣaṃ brahmaṇa iti /
vācyasya karmatvasya jijñāsayā prathamamapekṣitasya prathamasaṃbandhārhasya cānvayaparityāgena paścātkathañcidapekṣitasya saṃbandhimātrasya saṃbandho, jaghanyaḥ prathamaḥ prathamaśca jaghanyaḥ, iti suvyāhṛtaṃ nyāyatattvam /
pratyakṣaparokṣatābhidhānaṃ ca prāthamyāprāthamyasphuṭatvāsphuṭatvābhiprāyam /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection with a hidden intent: 'But even accepting the <s>śeṣa</s>-genitive...' (<s>nanu śeṣaṣaṣṭhīparigrahe 'pi</s>).
The meaning is: since general relation does not conflict with specific relation, the objectivity [of <s>Brahman</s>] is not obstructed, and the determination of the desire to know is logically established.
With the very same hidden intent, he refutes: 'Even so, the direct [meaning]...' (<s>evamapi pratyakṣam</s>).
Abandoning the connection of the expressed objecthood — which is the first relation appropriate for first connection — and [instead] connecting the general relation that is sought only subsequently, [amounts to saying] what is secondary is primary and what is primary is secondary — this is a well-articulated principle of logic (<s>nyāya-tattva</s>).
And the reference to directness and indirectness is intended [to convey] the clarity and unclarity of priority and non-priority.

body.text:
cedakaḥ svābhiprāyamudghāṭayati- na vyarthaḥ brahmāśritāśeṣa iti /
vyākhyātametadadhastāt /
samādhātā svābhisaṃdhimudghāṭayati- na, pradhānaparigraha iti /
vāstavaṃ prādhānyaṃ brahmaṇaḥ /
śeṣaṃ sanidarśanamatirohitārtham /
śrutyanugamaścātirohitaḥ /
body.translated_text:
The objector reveals his own intent: 'The <s>śeṣa</s>-[genitive] dependent on <s>Brahman</s> is not purposeless' (<s>na vyarthaḥ brahmāśritāśeṣa</s>).
This has been explained below.
The respondent reveals his own intent: 'No, because of the acceptance of the principal' (<s>na, pradhānaparigraha</s>).
The genuine primacy belongs to <s>Brahman</s>.
The rest is clear with examples and has an unhidden meaning.
And the conformity with <s>Śruti</s> is also unhidden.

body.text:
tadevamabhimataṃ samāsaṃ vyavasthāpya jijñāsāpadārthamāha- jñātum iti /
syādetat /
na jñānamicchāviṣayaḥ /
sukhaduḥkhāvāptiparihārau vā tadupāyo vā taddvāreṇecchāgocaraḥ /
na caivaṃ brahmajñānam /
na khalvetadanukūlamiti vā pratikūlanivṛttiriti vānubhūyate /
nāpi tayorupāyaḥ ; tasminsatyapi sukhabhedasyādarśanāt, anuvartamānasya ca duḥkhasyānivṛtteḥ /
tasmānna sūtrakāravacanamātrādiṣikarmatā jñānasyetyata āha- avagatiparyantam iti /
na kevalaṃ jñānamiṣyate kiṃ tvavagatiṃ sākṣātkāraṃ kurvadavagatiparyantaṃ sanvācyāyā icchāyāḥ karma /
kasmāt ? phalaviṣayatvādicchāyāḥ tadupāyaṃ phalaparyantaṃ gocarayatīccheti śeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Having thus established the intended compound, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] explains the meaning of the word '<s>jijñāsā</s>': '<s>jñātum</s>' (to know).
One might object thus:
Knowledge is not the object of desire (<s>icchā</s>).
Rather, the obtaining or removal of pleasure and suffering, or their means, becomes the object of desire through them.
But the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is not such [a means].
For it is not experienced either as 'this is agreeable' or as 'this removes what is disagreeable.'
Nor is it a means to either of those — since even when it is present, no distinct [kind of] pleasure is seen, and continuing suffering does not cease.
Therefore, knowledge cannot be made an object [of desire] merely by the statement of the author of the <s>sūtra</s>s — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'culminating in realization' (<s>avagatiparyantam</s>).
Not mere knowledge is desired, but rather [knowledge] that, producing realization — i.e., direct experience (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) — and thus culminating in realization, is the object of the expressible desire.
Why? Because desire, having its object in the fruit, encompasses as its object the means to the fruit, [extending] up to the fruit — [the word] '<s>icchā</s>' (desire) is to be supplied.

body.text:
nanu bhavatvavagatiparyantaṃ jñānam ; kimetāvatāpīṣṭaṃ bhavati ? na hyanapekṣaṇīyaviṣayamavagatiparyantamapi jñānamiṣyata ityata āha- jñānena hi pramāṇenāvagantumiṣṭaṃ brahma /
bhavatu brahmaviṣayāvagatiḥ, evamapi kathamiṣṭetyata āha- brahmāvagatirhi puruṣārthaḥ /
kimabhyudayaḥ ? na, kiṃ tu niḥśreyasaṃ vigalitanikhiladuḥkhānuṣaṅgaparamānandaghanabrahmāvagatirbrahmaṇaḥ svabhāva iti saiva niḥśreyasaṃ puruṣārtha iti /
body.translated_text:
But granted that knowledge culminates in realization — is anything desired accomplished even by that much? For knowledge culminating in realization is not desired if its object is not worthy of regard — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For <s>Brahman</s> is desired to be realized through knowledge, which is a means of valid cognition.'
Granted that there is realization having <s>Brahman</s> as its object — even so, how is it desired? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For the realization of <s>Brahman</s> is the supreme human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).'
Is it worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>)? No — rather, it is the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>): the realization of <s>Brahman</s> — a mass of supreme bliss free from all taint of suffering — is the very nature of <s>Brahman</s>, and that itself is the highest good, the supreme human goal.

body.text:
syādetat /
na brahmāvagatiḥ puruṣārthaḥ /
puruṣavyāpāravyāpyo hi puruṣārthaḥ /
na cāsyā brahmasvabhāvabhūtāyā utpattivikārasaṃskāraprāptayaḥ saṃbhavanti, tathā satyanityatvena tatsvābhāvyānupapatteḥ /
na cotpattyādyabhāve vyāpāravyāpyatā /
tasmānna brahmāvagatiḥ puruṣārtha ityata āha-niḥśeṣasaṃsārabījāvidyādyanarthanibarhaṇāt /
satyam, brahmāvagatau brahmasvabhāve notpattyādayaḥ saṃbhavanti ; tathāpyanirvacanīyānādyavidyāvaśādbrahmasvabhāvo 'parādhīnaprakāśo 'pi pratibhānapi na pratibhātīva parādhīnaprakāśa iva dehendriyādibhyo bhinno 'pyabhinna iva bhāsata iti saṃsārabījāvidyādyanarthanibarhaṇātprāgaprāpta iva tasminsati prāpta iva bhavatīti puruṣeṇārthyamānatvātpuruṣārtha iti yuktam /
body.translated_text:
One might object thus:
The realization of <s>Brahman</s> is not a human goal. For a human goal is something attainable through human effort. And for this [realization], which is of the very nature of <s>Brahman</s>, neither origination, modification, refinement (<s>saṃskāra</s>), nor attainment are possible — since, being eternal, its having such a nature would be contradicted.
Nor, in the absence of origination etc., is there any susceptibility to human effort.
Therefore, the realization of <s>Brahman</s> is not a human goal — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Because it eradicates <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and all other harm that is the seed of the entire cycle of existence (<s>saṃsāra</s>).'
True, in the realization of <s>Brahman</s>, which is of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, origination and the like are not possible. Nevertheless, due to the force of beginningless, indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) <s>avidyā</s>, the nature of <s>Brahman</s> — though self-luminous and not dependent on another for its manifestation — does not shine forth, as it were; though independent in its luminosity, it appears as if dependent; though distinct from the body, senses, and the like, it appears as if non-distinct. Thus, through the eradication of <s>avidyā</s> and all other harm that is the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>, [<s>Brahman</s>], which was as if unattained before, becomes as if attained when that [<s>avidyā</s>] is removed. Therefore, since it is something sought by a person, it is rightly called a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).

body.text:
avidyādītyādigrahaṇena tatsaṃskāro 'varudhyate /
avidyādinivṛttistūpāsanākāryādantaḥ karaṇavṛttibhedāt sākṣātkārāditi draṣṭavyam /
upasaṃharati- tasmādbrahma jijñāsitavyam uktalakṣaṇena mumukṣuṇā /
na khalu tajjñānaṃ vinā savāsanavividhaduḥkhanidānamavidyocchidyate /
na ca taducchedamantareṇa vigalitanikhiladuḥkhānuṣaṅgānandaghanabrahmātmatāsākṣātkārāvirbhāvo jīvasya /
tasmādānandaghanabrahmātmatāmicchatā tadupāyo jñānameṣitavyam /
tacca na kevalebhyo vedāntebhyaḥ api tu brahmamīmāṃsopakaraṇebhya iti icchāmukhena brahmamīmāṃsāyāṃ pravartyate, na tu vedānteṣu tadarthavivakṣāyāṃ vā ; tatra phalavadarthāvabodhaparatāṃ svādhyāyādhyayanavidheḥ sūtrayatā 'athāto dharmajijñāsā' ityanenaiva pravartitatvāt, dharmagrahaṇasya ca vedārthopalakṣaṇatvenādharmavadbrahmaṇo 'pyupalakṣaṇatvāt /
yadyapi ca dharmamīmāṃsāvat vedārthamīmāṃsayā brahmamīmāṃsāpyākṣeptuṃ śakyate, tathāpi prācyā mīmāṃsayā na tadvyutpādyate, nāpi brahmamīmāṃsāyā adhyayanamātrānantaryamiti brahmamīmāṃsārambhāya nityānityavivekādyānantaryapradarśanāya cedaṃ sūtramārambhaṇīyamityapaunaruktyam /
body.translated_text:
By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) in '<s>avidyādi</s>,' the latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of <s>avidyā</s> are also included.
The cessation of <s>avidyā</s> etc., however, should be understood as [resulting] from direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>), which differs from meditation (<s>upāsanā</s>) and its effects by being a distinct modification of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes: 'Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is to be inquired into by the seeker of liberation (<s>mumukṣu</s>) who possesses the stated qualifications.'
For without that knowledge, <s>avidyā</s> — which is the cause of manifold suffering together with its latent impressions — cannot be destroyed.
Nor, without its destruction, can there be the manifestation of the direct experience of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) as identical with <s>Brahman</s> — which is a mass of bliss, free from all taint of suffering.
Therefore, one who desires identity with <s>Brahman</s>, which is a mass of bliss, should seek knowledge as the means to that.
And that [knowledge comes] not from the <s>Vedānta</s> texts alone, but from the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> (inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>) and its instruments — thus one is directed toward <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> through the channel of desire, not [directly] toward the <s>Vedānta</s> texts or the intention to expound their meaning. [This is] because, there, the injunction of self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) — which, by the <s>sūtra</s> '<s>athāto dharmajijñāsā</s>' (now, therefore, the desire to know <s>dharma</s>), has already set in motion [the understanding] that all that is denoted by the word '<s>svādhyāya</s>' is oriented toward the comprehension of meaningful, fruitful content — and because the mention of '<s>dharma</s>' serves as an indication for the entire meaning of the <s>Veda</s>, thereby indicating <s>Brahman</s> as well, just as it indicates <s>adharma</s> (non-duty).
And although, like the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> (<s>dharmamīmāṃsā</s>), the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmamīmāṃsā</s>) could also be subsumed under the inquiry into the meaning of the <s>Veda</s>, nevertheless [<s>Brahman</s>] is not taught by the earlier <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, nor does the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> follow immediately after mere <s>Vedic</s> study. Therefore, this <s>sūtra</s> is to be commenced in order to show that the sequence [to <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>] is from the [prerequisites of] discrimination between the eternal and non-eternal (<s>nityānityaviveka</s>) etc. — and thus there is no redundancy.

body.text:
syādetat /
etena sūtreṇa brahmajñānaṃ pratyupāyatā mīmāṃsāyāḥ pratipādyata ityuktam ; tadayuktam, vikalpāsahatvāt, iti codayati- tatpunarbrahma iti /
vedāntebhyo 'pauruṣeyatayā svataḥsiddhaprāmāṇyebhyaḥ prasiddhamaprasiddhaṃ vā syāt /
yadi prasiddham, vedāntavākyasamutthena niścayajñānena viṣayīkṛtam ; tato na jijñāsitavyam, niṣpāditakriye karmaṇi aviśeṣādhāyinaḥ sādhanasya sādhananyāyātipātāt /
athāprasiddhaṃ vedāntebhyaḥ, tarhi na tadvedāntāḥ pratipādayantīti sarvathāprasiddhaṃ naiva śakyaṃ jijñāsitum /
anubhūte hi priye bhavatīcchā na tu sarvathānanubhūtāpūrve /
na ceṣyamāṇamapi śakyaṃ jñātum, pramāṇābhāvāt /
śabdo hi tasya pramāṇaṃ vaktavyam /
yathā vakṣyati 'śāstrayonitvāt' iti /
sa cettannāvabodhayati, kutastasya tatra prāmāṇyam ? na ca pramāṇānantaraṃ brahmaṇi prakramate /
tasmātprasiddhasya jñātuṃ śakyasyāpyajijñāsanāt aprasiddhasyecchāyā aviṣayatvāt aśakyajñānatvācca na brahma jijñāsyamityākṣepaḥ /
pariharati- ucyate- asti tāvadbrahma nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvam /
ayamarthaḥ- prāgapi brahmamīmāṃsāyā adhītavedasya nigamaniruktavyākaraṇādipariśīlanaviditapadatadarthasaṃbandhasya 'sadeva somyedamagra āsīt' ityupakramāt 'tattvamasi' ityantātsaṃdarbhāt nityatvādyupetabrahmasvarūpāvagamastāvadāpātato vicārādvināpyasti /
atra ca brahmetyādināvagamyena tadviṣayamavagamaṃ lakṣayati, tadastitvasya sati vimarśe vicārātprāganirṇayāt /
nityeti kṣayitālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkhamupakṣipati /
śuddheti dehādyupādhikamapi duḥkhamapākaroti /
buddhetyaparādhīnaprakāśamānandātmānaṃ darśayati, ānandaprakāśayorabhedāt /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
It was stated that by this <s>sūtra</s>, the serviceability of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> as a means to the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is established; that is improper, because it cannot withstand the dilemma — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises the objection: 'That <s>Brahman</s>, again...'
From the <s>Vedānta</s>s — which, being impersonal (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), possess self-established authority — [<s>Brahman</s>] would be either known or unknown.
If known — [that is,] made the object of a determinate cognition arising from <s>Vedānta</s> sentences — then it need not be inquired into, because when the purpose of an action has been accomplished, a subsidiary that adds nothing further would violate the principle governing subsidiaries.
But if unknown from the <s>Vedānta</s>s, then since the <s>Vedānta</s>s do not convey it, [<s>Brahman</s>], being completely unknown, simply cannot be desired to be known.
For desire arises with respect to a pleasant thing that has been experienced, not with respect to something utterly unexperienced and unprecedented.
Nor can what is desired [to be known] actually be known, due to the absence of a means of knowledge.
For verbal testimony must be stated as the means of knowledge for it.
As [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] will say: 'Because scripture is its source' (<s>śāstrayonitvāt</s>).
And if that [scripture] does not make it known, whence its authority regarding it? Nor does any other means of knowledge apply to <s>Brahman</s>.
Therefore, since even what is known and capable of being known need not be inquired into; since what is unknown is not an object of desire; and since it cannot be known — <s>Brahman</s> is not something to be inquired into — this is the objection.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves it: 'It is said: <s>Brahman</s> certainly exists, having the nature of being eternal, pure, conscious, and free.'
The meaning is this: Even before the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>, for one who has studied the <s>Veda</s> and who, through the examination of the <s>Nigama</s>, <s>Nirukta</s>, <s>Vyākaraṇa</s>, and the like, has come to know the words, their meanings, and the relations between them — from the textual sequence beginning with 'In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone' (<s>sadeva somyedamagra āsīt</s>) and ending with 'You are That' (<s>tattvamasi</s>) — an apprehension of the nature of <s>Brahman</s> as endowed with eternality and the like is available even prima facie, without deliberation.
And here, by the word '<s>Brahman</s>' and the like, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] indicates the apprehension regarding it as its object, since [<s>Brahman</s>'s] existence, when there is deliberation, remains undetermined prior to inquiry.
'Eternal' (<s>nitya</s>) — by this he introduces suffering characterized by destruction.
'Pure' (<s>śuddha</s>) — by this he also removes suffering due to limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) such as the body and the like.
'Conscious' (<s>buddha</s>) — by this he shows [<s>Brahman</s>] as having a self-luminous nature that does not depend on another, and as being of the nature of bliss — because consciousness and bliss are non-different.

body.text:
syādetat /
muktau satyāmasyaite śuddhatvādayaḥ prathante, tatastu prāk dehādyabhedena taddharmajanmajarāmaraṇādiduḥkhayogādityata uktam- mukta iti /
sadaiva muktaḥ sadaiva kevalo 'nādyavidyāvaśāttu bhrāntyā tathāvabhāsata ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
When liberation (<s>mukti</s>) obtains, these [qualities] of purity and the like become manifest; but prior to that, due to non-difference from the body and the like, there would be connection with the suffering of birth, old age, death, and the like that belongs to them — therefore [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] has said 'free' (<s>mukta</s>).
[<s>Brahman</s>] is ever free, ever alone (<s>kevala</s>); but due to the force of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), through delusion it merely appears so — this is the meaning.

body.text:
tadevamanaupādhikaṃ brahmaṇo rūpaṃ darśayitvā avidyopādhikaṃ rūpamāha- sarvajñaṃ sarvaśaktisamanvitam /
tadanena jagatkāraṇatvamasya darśitam, śaktijñānabhāvābhāvānuvidhānātkāraṇatvabhāvābhāvayoḥ /
kutaḥ punarevaṃbhūtabrahmasvarūpāvagatiḥ ityata āha- brahmaśabdasya hi iti /
na kevalam 'sadeva somyedam' ityādīnāṃ vākyānāṃ paurvāparyaparyālocanayā itthaṃbhūtabrahmāvagatiḥ /
api tu brahmapadamapi nirvacanasāmarthyādimamevārthaṃ svahastayati /
nirvacanamāha- bṛhaterdhātorarthānugamāt /
body.translated_text:
Having thus shown the unconditioned (<s>anaupādhika</s>) form of <s>Brahman</s>, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states its form as conditioned by <s>avidyā</s>: 'Omniscient, endowed with all powers.'
By this, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] has shown its being the cause of the world, since the presence or absence of being a cause follows from the presence or absence of power and knowledge.
Whence, then, the apprehension of the nature of <s>Brahman</s> as being of such a character? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For the word <s>Brahman</s>...'
Not only from the sentences 'Being alone, dear one, was this in the beginning' and the like, through considering their contextual coherence, is there the apprehension of <s>Brahman</s> as being of such a character;
but the very word '<s>Brahman</s>' too, by the force of its etymology, points to precisely this meaning.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the etymology: 'Because of following the meaning of the root <s>bṛh</s>.'

body.text:
vṛddhikarmā hi bṛhatiratiśāyane vartate /
taccedamatiśāyanamanavacchinnaṃ padāntarāvagamitaṃ nityaśuddhabuddhatvādyasyābhyanujānātītyarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
For the root <s>bṛh</s>, which takes the action of growth, is used in the sense of surpassing.
And this surpassing, being unlimited, is consistent with what has been conveyed by other words — eternality, purity, consciousness, and the like — this is the meaning.

body.text: tadevaṃ tatpadārthasya śuddhatvādeḥ prasiddhimabhidhāya tvaṃpadārthasyāpyāha- sarvasyātmatvācca brahmāstitvaprasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: Having thus stated the well-knownness of purity and the like, which are the meaning of the word 'That' (<s>tat-pada</s>), [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] also states [the well-knownness] of the meaning of the word 'You' (<s>tvam-pada</s>): 'And because <s>Brahman</s>'s existence is well-known, on account of its being the Self of all.'

body.text:
sarvasya pāṃsulapādakasya hālikasyāpi brahmāstitvaprasiddhiḥ ; kutaḥ ? ātmatvāt /
etadeva sphuṭayati- sarvo hi iti /
pratītimeva apratītinirākaraṇena draḍhayati- na na iti /
na na pratyeti 'ahamasmi' iti, kiṃ tu pratyetyeveti yojanā /
nanu 'ahamasmi' iti ca jñāsyati mā ca jñāsīdātmānamityata āha- yadi iti /
ahamasmīti na pratīyāt /
ahaṅkārāspadaṃ hi jīvātmānaṃ cenna pratīyāt 'aham' iti na pratīyādityarthaḥ /
nanu pratyetu sarvo jana ātmānamahaṅkārāspadam, brahmaṇi tu kimāyātam ityata āha- ātmā ca brahma ; tadaḥ tvamāsāmānādhikaraṇyāt /
tasmāttatpadārthasya śuddhabuddhatvādeḥ śabdataḥ tvaṃpadārthasya ca jīvātmanaḥ pratyakṣataḥ prasiddheḥ, padārthajñānapūrvakatvācca vākyārthajñānasya, tvaṃpadārthasya brahmabhāvāvagamaḥ 'tattvamasi' iti vākyādupapadyata iti bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text:
The existence of <s>Brahman</s> is well-known to everyone, even to the lowliest person or the ploughman. Why? Because of its being the Self.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] makes this very point explicit: 'For everyone...'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] strengthens this cognition by negating its negation: 'Not not...'
'Does not not cognize "I am"' — rather, he certainly does cognize — this is the syntactic connection.
But one might object: 'Let him cognize "I am," but let him not know the Self' — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'If...'
If he did not cognize 'I am' — if he did not cognize the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>) that is the locus of ego-sense — then he would not cognize 'I' — this is the meaning.
But one might object: Let everyone cognize the self as the locus of ego-sense; but what bearing does this have on <s>Brahman</s>? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And the Self is <s>Brahman</s>' — because of the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of 'That' and 'You' [in 'You are That'].
Therefore, since the meaning of the 'That'-word — purity, consciousness, and the like — is well-known from verbal testimony, and since the meaning of the 'You'-word — the individual self — is well-known from direct perception, and since the knowledge of sentence-meaning is preceded by the knowledge of word-meanings, the apprehension that the meaning of the 'You'-word is identical with <s>Brahman</s> is established from the sentence 'You are That' (<s>tattvamasi</s>) — this is the purport.

body.text:
ākṣeptā prathamakalpāśrayaṃ doṣamāha- yadi tarhi loka iti /
adhyāpakādhyetṛparamparā lokaḥ /
tatra 'tattvamasi' iti vākyādyadi brahma ātmatvena prasiddhamasti /
'ātmā brahmatvena' iti vaktavye 'brahma ātmatvena' iti abhedavivakṣayā gamayitavyam /
pariharati- naḥ ; kutaḥ ? tadviśeṣaṃ prati vipratipatteḥ /
tadanena vipratipattiḥ sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāve sati saṃśayabījamuktam /
tataśca saṃśayājjijñāsopapadyata iti bhāvaḥ /
vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dharmī sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddho 'bhyupeyaḥ ; anyathā anāśrayā bhinnāśrayā vā vipratipattayo na syuḥ /
viruddhā hi pratipattayo vipratipattayaḥ ; na cānāśrayāḥ pratipattayo bhavanti, anālambanatvāpatteḥ ; na ca bhinnāśrayā viruddhāḥ /
na hi 'anityā buddhiḥ' 'nitya ātmā' iti pratipattivipratipattī /
tasmāttatpadārthasya śuddhatvādervedāntebhyaḥ pratītiḥ, tvaṃpadārthasya ca jīvātmano lokataḥ siddhiḥ sarvatantrasiddhāntaḥ /
tadābhāsatvānābhāsatvatattadviśeṣeṣu paramatra vipratipattayaḥ /
tasmāt sāmānyataḥ prasiddhe dharmiṇi viśeṣato vipratipattau yuktastadviśeṣeṣu saṃśayaḥ /
body.translated_text:
The objector states a fault in the first alternative: 'If, then, in the world...'
The 'world' (<s>loka</s>) means the succession of teachers and students.
If, in that [succession], through the sentence 'You are That,' <s>Brahman</s> is well-known as being the Self...
[Where it says] '<s>Brahman</s> as being the Self,' it should be understood — by the expression of non-difference — as meaning 'the Self as being <s>Brahman</s>.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves it: 'No. Why? Because of the conflicting views regarding its specific nature.'
By this, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] has stated that conflicting views (<s>vipratipatti</s>), in the absence of supporting and refuting means of knowledge, are the seed of doubt.
Consequently, from doubt the desire to know is justified — this is the purport.
The subject of the dispute (<s>vivādādhikaraṇa</s>) — the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) — must be accepted as established by a universally accepted principle (<s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s>); otherwise, the conflicting views would be either without a substrate or with different substrates — and that cannot be.
For conflicting views are contradictory cognitions; and cognitions cannot be without a substrate, since that would lead to the absurd consequence of being without an object (<s>anālambana</s>). Nor are [cognitions] with different substrates contradictory.
For 'the intellect is impermanent' and 'the self is eternal' are not mutually contradictory cognitions.
Therefore, the cognition of the 'That'-word's meaning — purity and the like — from the <s>Vedānta</s>s, and the establishment of the 'You'-word's meaning — the individual self — from worldly [experience], is a universally accepted principle.
The conflicting views pertain to the specific features of those very things — whether they are apparent or real.
Therefore, since the <s>dharmin</s> is well-known in general, and since there are conflicting views regarding its specific features, doubt concerning those specific features is justified.

body.text:
tatra tvaṃpadārthe tāvadvipratipattīrdarśayati- dehamātram ityādinā bhoktaiva kevalaṃ na karttā ityantena /
atra dehendriyamanaḥkṣaṇikavijñānacaitanyapakṣe na tatpadārthanityatvādayaḥ tvaṃpadārthena saṃbadhyante, yogyatāvirahāt /
śūnyapakṣe 'pi sarvopākhyārahitamapadārthaḥ kathaṃ tattvamorgocaraḥ ? kartṛbhoktṛsvabhāvasyāpi pariṇāmitayā tatpadārthanityatvādyasaṃgatireva /
akartṛtve 'pi bhoktṛtvapakṣe pariṇāmitayā nityatvādyasaṃgatiḥ /
abhoktṛtve 'pi nānātmatvapakṣe nānātvenāvacchinnatvādanityatvādiprasaktāvadvaitahānācca tatpadārthāsaṃgatistadavasthaiva /
tvaṃpadārthavipratipattyā ca tatpadārthe 'pi vipratipattirdarśitā- vedāprāmāṇyavādino hi laukāyatikādayastatpadārthapratyayaṃ mithyeti manyante, vedaprāmāṇyavādino 'pyaupacārikaṃ tatpadārthamavivakṣitaṃ vā manyanta iti /
tadevaṃ tvaṃpadārthavipratipattidvārā tatpadārthe vipratipattiṃ sūcayitvā sākṣāttatpadārthe 'pi vipratipattimāha- asti tadvyatirikta īśvaraḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvaśaktiriti kecit /
#tat#iti jīvātmanaḥ parāmṛśati /
na kevalaṃ śarīrādibhyaḥ jīvātmabhyo 'pi vyatiriktaḥ /
sa ca sarvasyaiva jagata īṣṭe /
aiśvaryasiddhyarthaṃ svābhāvikamasya rūpadvayamuktam 'sarvajñaḥ sarvaśaktiḥ' iti /
tasyāpi jīvātmabhyo 'pi vyatirekāt na tvaṃpadārthena sāmānādhikaraṇyamiti svamatamāha- #atmā sa bhokturityapare# /
bhokturjīvātmano 'vidyopādhikasya sa īśvaraḥ tatpadārtha ātmā ; tata īśvarādabhinno jīvātmā, paramākāśādiva ghaṭākāśādaya ityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] first shows the conflicting views regarding the meaning of the 'You'-word: beginning with 'the body alone' and ending with 'merely an enjoyer, not an agent.'
Herein, on the positions that [the self is] the body, the senses, the mind, momentary consciousness, or [pure] consciousness — the eternality and other [attributes] of the 'That'-word's meaning are not compatible with the 'You'-word's meaning, due to the absence of fitness.
On the position of the void (<s>śūnya</s>) too — that which is devoid of all designation, being a non-entity, how can it be the object of [the sentence] 'You are That'? Even for one whose nature is agency and enjoyership, due to [the self] being subject to transformation, there is indeed incompatibility with the eternality and the like of the 'That'-word's meaning.
Even on the position of non-agency with enjoyership, due to [the self] being subject to transformation, there is incompatibility with eternality and the like.
Even on the position of non-enjoyership [but] with multiplicity of selves — since [each self] is delimited by multiplicity, there arises impermanence and the like; and since non-duality would be lost, incompatibility with the 'That'-word's meaning remains just the same.
And through the conflicting views regarding the 'You'-word's meaning, conflicting views regarding the 'That'-word's meaning are also shown — for the materialists (<s>Laukāyatika</s>s) and others who deny the authority of the <s>Veda</s> consider the cognition of the 'That'-word's meaning to be false; and even those who accept the authority of the <s>Veda</s> consider the 'That'-word's meaning to be figurative or unintended.
Having thus hinted at the conflicting views regarding the 'That'-word's meaning through the conflicting views regarding the 'You'-word's meaning, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] directly states the conflicting views regarding the 'That'-word's meaning as well: 'Some [say] there is a Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), distinct from that [individual self], omniscient and omnipotent.'
The word 'that' refers back to the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>).
[<s>Īśvara</s> is] distinct not only from the body and the like, but even from the individual selves.
And He rules over the entire world.
To establish His sovereignty, His two natural attributes are stated: 'omniscient, omnipotent.'
Since He too, being distinct from the individual selves, would not be in co-referential relation with the 'You'-word's meaning, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states his own position: 'He is the Self of the enjoyer — say others.'
That <s>Īśvara</s>, the 'That'-word's meaning, is the Self of the enjoyer, the individual self — who is conditioned by the limiting adjunct of <s>avidyā</s>. Therefore, the individual self is non-different from <s>Īśvara</s>, just as pot-space and the like [are non-different] from the supreme space — this is the meaning.

body.text:
vipratipattīrupasaṃharan vipratipattibījamāha- #evaṃ bahava#iti /
yuktiyuktyābhāsavākyavākyābhāsasamāśrayāḥ santa iti yojanā /
nanu santu vipratipattayaḥ tannimittaśca saṃśayaḥ ; tathāpi kimarthaṃ brahmamīmāṃsā ārabhyate ityata āha- #tatrāvicārya#iti /
tattvajñānācca niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ, nātattvajñānādbhavitumarhati /
api ca atattvajñānānnāstikye sati anarthaprāptirapītyāha- #anarthaṃ ca#iti /
sūtratātparyamupasaṃharati- #tasmāt#iti /
vedāntamīmāṃsā tāvattarka eva, tadavirodhinaśca ye 'nye 'pi tarkā adhvaramīmāṃsāyāṃ nyāye ca vedapratyakṣādiprāmāṇyapariśodhanādiṣūktāḥ t upakaraṇaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
tasmātparamaniḥśreyasasādhanabrahmajñānaprayojanā brahmamīmāṃsā ārabdhavyeti siddham /
body.translated_text:
Summarizing the conflicting views, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the seed of the conflicting views: 'Thus, many...'
The syntactic connection is: being dependent on reasoning and pseudo-reasoning, [genuine] scriptural statements and pseudo-scriptural statements.
But one might say: let there be conflicting views and the doubt caused by them; still, for what purpose is the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> undertaken? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Therein, without inquiry...'
And from the knowledge of reality comes the attainment of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>); it cannot arise from the non-knowledge of reality.
Moreover, from the non-knowledge of reality, when nihilism (<s>nāstikya</s>) results, there is even the attainment of harm — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And harm...'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes the purport of the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Therefore...'
The <s>Vedānta-mīmāṃsā</s> is indeed reasoning; and those other reasonings that are not in conflict with it — [reasonings] stated in the <s>Karmamīmāṃsā</s>, in <s>Nyāya</s>, and in the purification of the authority of the <s>Veda</s>, perception, and the like — are its instruments (<s>upakaraṇa</s>); the [<s>Vedānta-mīmāṃsā</s>] that has these [as its instruments] is so described.
Therefore, the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s> — whose purpose is the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, which is the means to the supreme good — should be undertaken — thus it is established.

body.text:
brahma jijñāsitavyamityuktam /
kiṃlakṣaṇaṃ punastadbrahma ityata āha bhagavānsūtrakāraḥ -
body.translated_text:
It was stated: '<s>Brahman</s> is to be inquired into.'
What, then, is the defining characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) of that <s>Brahman</s>? To this the revered author of the <s>sūtra</s>s says —

body.text: #janmādyasya yataḥ# //2 //
body.translated_text: 'That from which the origin and the rest [of this world proceed].' // 2 //

body.text:
tadevaṃ prathamasūtreṇa mīmāṃsārambhamupapādya brahmamīmāṃsāmārabhate- #janmādyasya yataḥ# /
etasya sūtrasya pātanikāmāha bhāṣyakāraḥ - #brahma jijñāsitavyamityuktam ; kiṃlakṣaṇaṃ# #punastadbrahma# /
atra yadyapi brahmasvarūpajñānasya pradhānasya pratijñayā tadaṅgānyapi pramāṇādīni pratijñātāni, tathāpi svarūpasya prādhānyāttadevākṣipya prathamaṃ samarthyate /
tatra yadyāvadanubhūyate tatsarvaṃ parimitamaviśudadhamabuddhaṃ vidhvaṃsi ca ; na tenopalabdhena tadviruddhasya nityaśuddhabuddhasvabhāvasya brahmaṇaḥ svarūpaṃ śakyaṃ lakṣayitum /
na hi jātu kaścitkṛtakatvena nityaṃ lakṣayati /
na ca taddharmeṇa nityatvādinā tallakṣyate, tasyānupalabdhacaratvāt /
prasiddhaṃ hi lakṣaṇaṃ bhavati, nātyantāprasiddham /
evaṃ ca na śabdo 'pyatra prakramate, atyantāprasiddhatayā brahmaṇo 'padārthasyāvākyārthatvāt /
tasmāt lakṣaṇābhāvāt na brahma jijñāsitavyamityātyākṣepābhiprāyaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Having thus justified the commencement of the inquiry through the first <s>sūtra</s>, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] commences the <s>Brahmamīmāṃsā</s>: 'That from which the origin and the rest [of this world proceed].'
The commentator states the occasion (<s>pātanikā</s>) of this <s>sūtra</s>: 'It was stated that <s>Brahman</s> is to be inquired into; what then is the defining characteristic of that <s>Brahman</s>?'
Here, although by the announcement of the principal [topic] — the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>'s essential nature — the accessories such as the means of knowledge and the like are also announced, nevertheless, due to the primacy of the essential nature, that alone is taken up and examined first.
Therein, whatever is experienced is all limited, impure, non-conscious, and perishable; by that which is experienced, the essential nature of <s>Brahman</s> — which is of the contrary nature: eternal, pure, and conscious — cannot be defined.
For no one ever defines something eternal by means of something produced.
Nor is it defined by its own property of eternality and the like, since that has not been observed as obtaining.
For a defining characteristic must be well-known, not utterly unknown.
And thus, even verbal testimony does not apply here, since <s>Brahman</s>, being utterly unknown, is a non-entity and hence not a sentence-meaning.
Therefore, due to the absence of a defining characteristic, <s>Brahman</s> is not something to be inquired into — this is the intent of the objection.

body.text:
tamimamākṣepaṃ bhagavān sūtrakāraḥ pariharati- #'janmādyasya yataḥ'#iti /
mā bhūdanubhūyamānaṃ jagattaddharmatayā tādātmyena vā brahmaṇo lakṣaṇam ; tadutpattyā tu bhaviṣyati deśāntaraprāptiriva saviturvrajyāyā iti tātparyārthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
The revered author of the <s>sūtra</s>s resolves this objection: 'That from which the origin and the rest [of this world proceed].'
Let the world as experienced not be the defining characteristic of <s>Brahman</s> by way of sharing its properties or by way of identity with it; but it will serve [as a defining characteristic] through its origination — just as the arrival at another place [serves as a sign] of the sun's motion — this is the purport.

body.text:
sūtrāvayavān vibhajate- #janmotpattirādirasya#iti /
lāghavāya sūtrakṛtā janmādīti napuṃsakaprayogaḥ kṛtaḥ ;
tadupapādanāya samāhāramāha- #janmasthitibhaṅgam#iti /
#janmanaśca#ityādiḥ #kāraṇanirdeśaḥ#ityantaḥ saṃdarbho nigadavyākhyātaḥ /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] analyzes the components of the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Origin (<s>janma</s>) is birth; that is the beginning (<s>ādi</s>) of this [world].'
For the sake of brevity, the author of the <s>sūtra</s>s has used the neuter gender in the compound '<s>janmādi</s>.'
To justify this, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the aggregate: 'Origin, subsistence, and dissolution (<s>janmasthitibhaṅga</s>).'
The passage beginning with 'And of origin' and ending with 'indication of the cause' is explained as a running gloss (<s>nigadavyākhyāta</s>).

body.text:
syādetat /
pradhānakālagrahalokapālakriyāyadṛcchāsvabhāvābhāveṣūpaplavamāneṣu satsu sarvajñaṃ sarvaśaktisvabhāvaṃ brahma jagajjanmādikāraṇamiti kutaḥ saṃbhāvanetyata āha- #asya jagata#iti /
atra #nāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākṛtasya#iti cetanabhāvakartṛkatvasaṃbhāvanayā pradhānādyacetanakartṛkatvaṃ nirupākhyakartṛkatvaṃ ca vyāsedhati /
yatkhalu nāmnā rūpeṇa ca vyākriyate taccetanakartṛkaṃ dṛṣṭam, yathā ghaṭādi /
vivādādhyāsitaṃ ca jagannāmnā rūpeṇa ca vyākṛtam ; tasmāccetanakartṛkaṃ saṃbhāvyate /
cetano hi buddhāvālikhya nāmarūpe ghaṭa iti nāmnā rūpeṇa ca kambugrīvādinā bāhyaṃ ghaṭaṃ niṣpādayati /
ata eva ghaṭasya nirvartyasyāpyantaḥ saṃkalpātmanā siddhasya karmakārakabhāvaḥ 'ghaṭaṃ karoti' iti /
yathāhuḥ-'buddhisiddhaṃ tu na tadasat' iti /
tathā cācetano buddhāvanālikhitaṃ karotīti na śakyaṃ saṃbhāvayitumiti bhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
When [the theories of] <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), time (<s>kāla</s>), planets (<s>graha</s>), world-guardians (<s>lokapāla</s>), action (<s>kriyā</s>), chance (<s>yadṛcchā</s>), and inherent nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) are being refuted — why should the conjecture arise that <s>Brahman</s>, whose nature is omniscient and omnipotent, is the cause of the origin etc. of the universe? To this he says: 'Of this universe.'
Here, [the phrase] 'differentiated by name and form' — by conjecturing that the agent must be a conscious being — refutes the agency of an insentient [cause] such as <s>Pradhāna</s> etc., and also the agency of a non-entity.
For indeed, whatever is differentiated by name and form is observed to have a conscious agent — like a pot and the like.
And the universe under dispute is differentiated by name and form; therefore it is conjectured to have a conscious agent.
For a conscious [agent], having depicted name and form in the intellect, produces the external pot by means of the name 'pot' and the form with a neck-like shape (<s>kambugrīva</s>) etc.
Hence even a pot — though [actually] being produced — since it is already established internally in the form of volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>), has the relation of object to agent (<s>karmakārakabhāva</s>) [as in] 'he makes a pot.'
As they say: 'What is established in the intellect is not non-existent.'
Thus, it cannot be conjectured that an insentient [agent] produces what has not been depicted in the intellect — this is the purport.

body.text:
syādetat /
cetanā grahā lokapālā vā nāmarūpe buddhāvālikhya jagajjanayiṣyanti, kṛtam uktasvabhāvena brahmaṇetyata āha- #anekakartṛbhoktṛsaṃyuktasya#iti /
kecitkartāro bhavanti, yathā sūdartvigādayaḥ, na bhoktāraḥ /
kecittu bhoktāraḥ, yathā śrāddhavaiśvānareṣṭyādiṣu pitāputrādayaḥ, na kartāraḥ /
tasmādubhayagrahaṇam /
deśakālanimittakriyāphalāni itītaretaradvandvaḥ /
deśādīni ca tāni pratiniyatāti ceti vigrahaḥ /
tadāśrayo jagat ; tasya /
kecitkhalu pratiniyatadeśotpādāḥ, yathā kṛṣṇamṛgādayaḥ /
kecitpratiniyatakālotpādāḥ, yathā kokilāravādayaḥ /
kecitpratiniyatanimittāḥ, yathā navāmbudadhvānādinimittā balākāgarbhādayaḥ /
kecitpratiniyatakriyāḥ, yathā brāhmaṇānāṃ yājanādayaḥ, netareṣām /
evaṃ kecitpratiniyataphalāḥ, yathā kecitsukhinaḥ kecidduḥkhinaḥ, evaṃ ya eva sukhinasta eva kadācidduḥkhinaḥ /
sarvametadākasmikāparanāmni yādṛcchikatve ca svābhāvikatve cāsarvajñāsarvaśaktikartṛkatve ca na ghaṭate, parimitajñānaśaktibhirgrahalokapālādibhirjñātuṃ kartuṃ cāśakyatvāt /
tadidamuktam- #manasāpyacintyaracanārūpasya#
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
Conscious beings — planets or world-guardians — having depicted name and form in the intellect, will produce the universe. [So] what need is there of <s>Brahman</s> of the nature described? To this he says: 'Connected with many agents and enjoyers.'
Some are agents — such as cooks, priests (<s>ṛtvij</s>), and the like — but not enjoyers.
Some, however, are enjoyers — such as fathers, sons, and the like in the <s>śrāddha</s>, <s>Vaiśvānara</s>-sacrifice, and other rites — but not agents.
Therefore both [terms] are mentioned.
'Place, time, cause, action, and fruit' — this is an <s>itaretara-dvandva</s> (copulative compound).
The analysis is: those [place etc.] are each specifically determined.
The universe has that [determination] as its basis.
Indeed, some [beings] have a specifically determined place of origin — like the black antelope (<s>kṛṣṇamṛga</s>) and the like.
Some have a specifically determined time of origin — like the cuckoo's call and the like.
Some have a specifically determined cause — like the eggs of the crane (<s>balākā</s>), caused by the sound of fresh clouds and the like.
Some have specifically determined actions — such as the officiating at sacrifices for <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s, but not for others.
Likewise, some have specifically determined fruits — such as some being happy, some being miserable; and moreover, the very ones who are happy at one time are miserable at another.
All of this does not fit with chance — also called the accidental — nor with inherent nature, nor with a creator who is not omniscient and omnipotent, since it cannot be known or done by [beings like] planets and world-guardians who have limited knowledge and power.
Thus it is stated: 'Whose form of construction is inconceivable even by the mind.'

body.text:
iti /
ekasyā api hi śarīraracanāyā rūpaṃ manasā na śakyaṃ cintayituṃ kadācit, prāgeva jagadracanāyāḥ ; kimaṅga punaḥ kartumityarthaḥ /
sūtravākyaṃ pūrayati- #tadbrahmeti vākyaśeṣaḥ# /
body.translated_text:
For the form [design] of even a single bodily construction can never be conceived by the mind — much less the construction of the universe; how much less then can it be created — this is the meaning.
He completes the <s>sūtra</s>-statement: 'That is <s>Brahman</s> — this is the remainder of the sentence.'

body.text:
syādetat /
kasmātpunarjanmasthitibhaṅgamātramihādigrahaṇena gṛhyate na tu vṛddhipariṇāmāpakṣayā apītyata āha- #anyeṣāmapi bhāvavikārāṇāṃ#vṛddhyādīnān #triṣvevāntarbhāva#iti /
vṛddhistāvadavayavopacayaḥ /
tenālpāvayavādavayavino dvitantukāderanya eva mahānpaṭo jāyata iti janmaiva vṛddhiḥ /
pariṇāmo 'pi trividhaḥ dharmalakṣaṇāvasthālakṣaṇaḥ utpattireva /
dharmiṇo hi hāṭakāderdharmalakṣaṇaḥ pariṇāmaḥ kaṭakamukuṭādiḥ tasyotpattiḥ /
evaṃ kaṭakāderapi pratyutpannatvādilakṣaṇaḥ lakṣaṇapariṇāma utpattiḥ /
evamavasthāpariṇāmo navapurāṇatvādirutpattiḥ /
apakṣayastu avayavahrāso nāśa eva /
tasmājjanmādiṣu yathāsvamantarbhāvādvṛddhyādayaḥ pṛthaṅnoktā ityarthaḥ /
athaite vṛddhyādayo na janmādiṣvantarbhavanti, tathāpyutpattisthitibhaṅgamevopādātavyam /
tathā sati hi tatpratipādake 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni' iti vedavākye buddhisthīkṛte jaganmūlakāraṇaṃ brahma lakṣitaṃ bhavati /
anyathā tu jāyate asti vardhate ityādīnāṃ grahaṇe tatpratipādakaṃ nairuktavākyaṃ buddhau bhavet ; tacca na mūlakāraṇapratipādanaparam, mahāsargādūrdhvaṃ sthitikāle 'pi tadvākyoditānāṃ janmādīnāṃ bhāvavikārāṇāmupapatteḥ,- iti śaṅkānirākaraṇārthaṃ vedoktotpattisthitibhaṅgagrahaṇamityāha- #yāska-#
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
Why is only origination, persistence, and dissolution grasped here by the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc., beginning with), and not also growth (<s>vṛddhi</s>), transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), and decline (<s>apakṣaya</s>)? To this he says: 'Of the other modifications of beings too' — of growth etc. — 'there is inclusion within just these three.'
Growth, to begin with, is the accretion of parts.
Thereby, from a two-threaded [fabric] and the like possessing few parts, a great cloth etc. that is altogether different comes into being — thus growth is simply origination.
Transformation too is threefold — in terms of property (<s>dharma</s>), characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and state (<s>avasthā</s>) — and is [a form of] origination.
For the property-transformation of a substance such as gold etc. — [taking the form of] a bracelet, crown, and the like — is the origination of that [product].
Likewise, the characteristic-transformation of a bracelet etc. — being present etc. — is [its] origination.
Similarly, state-transformation — being new, old, etc. — is [its] origination.
Decline, however, is the diminution of parts, which is simply destruction.
Therefore, since growth etc. are each included, as appropriate, within origination etc., they are not separately mentioned — this is the meaning.
Now, even if these — growth etc. — are not included within origination etc., still only origination, persistence, and dissolution should be adopted.
For if so, when the Vedic statement 'from which these beings [are born]' — which teaches [these three] — is accepted in the intellect, <s>Brahman</s> as the root cause of the universe is [thereby] defined.
Otherwise, if origination, existence, growth, etc. were grasped [separately], the <s>Nairukta</s> (etymological) statement would come to mind; and that is not primarily directed toward teaching the root cause, since the modifications of beings — origination etc. — as stated in that statement, are possible even during the period of persistence after the great creation. — To ward off this doubt, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says that the adoption of origination, persistence, and dissolution as stated in the <s>Veda</s> [is preferred] — '<s>Yāska</s>-'

body.text: #paripaṭhitānāṃ tu#iti /
body.translated_text: 'Of those enumerated [by <s>Yāska</s>].'

body.text:
nanvevamapi utpattimātraṃ sūcyatām ; tannāntarīyakatayā tu sthitibhaṅgaṃ gamyata ityata āha- #yotpattirbrahmaṇaḥ kāraṇāt#iti /
tribhirasyopādānatvaṃ sūcyate ; utpattimātraṃ tu nimittakāraṇasādhāraṇamiti nopādānatvaṃ sūcayet ; tadidamuktam- #tatraiva#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might object: Even so, let only origination be indicated; persistence and dissolution would be understood as entailed by it. To this he says: 'The origination that [proceeds] from <s>Brahman</s> as cause.'
By [all] three, [<s>Brahman</s>'s nature as] the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) is indicated; origination alone is common to the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) as well, and so would not indicate the material cause. This is what is stated: 'In that very [<s>Brahman</s>].'

body.text:
pūrvoktānāṃ kāryakāraṇaviśeṣaṇānāṃ prayojanamāha- #na yathokta#iti /
tadanena prabandhena pratijñāviṣayasya brahmasvarūpasya lakṣaṇadvāreṇa saṃbhāvanoktā /
tatra pramāṇaṃ vaktavyam /
yathāhurnaiyāyikāḥ-
body.translated_text:
He states the purpose of the qualifications of effect and cause stated earlier: 'Not as stated [by others].' 
By this line of argument, the conjecture regarding the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, the subject of the thesis, has been stated by way of its defining characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>).
Therein, the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) must be stated.
As the <s>Naiyāyika</s>s say —

body.text: 'saṃbhāvitaḥ pratijñāyāṃ pakṣaḥ sādhyeta hetunā /
body.translated_text: 'The thesis, having been conjectured, would be established by a reason (<s>hetu</s>);

body.text: na tasya hetubhistrāṇamutpatanneva yo hataḥ //
body.translated_text: There is no protection by reasons for one who is destroyed at the very moment of arising. //

body.text: yathā ca vandhyā jananī' ityādiriti /
body.translated_text: Just as a barren woman is a mother' — and so on.

body.text:
itthaṃ nāma janmādi saṃbhāvanāhetuḥ /
yadanye vaiśeṣikakādaya ita evānumānādīśvaraviniścayamicchanti, iti saṃbhāvanāhetutāṃ draḍhayitumāha- #etadeva#iti /
body.translated_text:
Thus, origination etc. is the ground for conjecture (<s>saṃbhāvanāhetu</s>).
Since others — the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s and the like — wish to arrive at the certainty of God (<s>Īśvara</s>) from this very inference, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], in order to strengthen [the status of origination etc. as] a ground for conjecture, says: 'This very [inference].'

body.text:
codayati- #nanvihāpi#iti /
etāvataivādhikaraṇārthe samāpte vakṣyamāṇādhikaraṇārthamanuvadansuhṛdbhāvena pariharati- #na, vedānta#iti /
vedāntavākyakusumagrathanārthatvameva darśayati- #vedānta#iti /
vicārasyādhyavasānaṃ savāsanāvidyādvayocchedaḥ /
tato hi brahmāvagaternivṛttirāvirbhāvaḥ /
tatkiṃ brahmaṇi śabdādṛte na mānāntaramanusaraṇīyam ? tathā ca kuto mananam ? kutaśca tadanubhavaḥ sākṣātkāraḥ ? ityata āha- #satsu tu vedāntavākyeṣu#iti /
anumānaṃ vedāntāvirodhi tadupajīvi cetyapi draṣṭavyam /
śabdāvirodhinyā tadupajīvinyā ca yuktyā vivecanaṃ mananam /
yuktiśca arthāpattiranumānaṃ vā /
body.translated_text:
He raises an objection: 'But here too.'
The topic of this <s>adhikaraṇa</s> (section) having been completed with just this much, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], while recapitulating the topic of the upcoming <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, resolves [the objection] with friendly intent: 'No, [because] <s>Vedānta</s>-'
He shows that [the inquiry] has the very purpose of stringing together the flowers of <s>Vedānta</s> sentences: '<s>Vedānta</s>-'
The conclusion (<s>adhyavasāna</s>) of inquiry is the eradication of the twofold <s>avidyā</s> along with its impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>s).
For from that [eradication] arises the manifestation (<s>āvirbhāva</s>) of the realization of <s>Brahman</s>, which is [its] cessation [from concealment].
Then, apart from scripture, should no other means of knowledge be pursued regarding <s>Brahman</s>? And if so, whence reflection (<s>manana</s>)? And whence the experience (<s>anubhava</s>) of it — the direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>)? To this he says: 'But when <s>Vedānta</s> sentences are available.'
Inference too should be seen as not contradicting <s>Vedānta</s> and as dependent upon it.
Reflection (<s>manana</s>) is the discrimination through reasoning that does not contradict scripture and that depends upon it.
And reasoning is either presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) or inference (<s>anumāna</s>).

body.text:
syādetat /
yathā dharmo na puruṣabuddhisāhāyyam, evaṃ brahmaṇyapi kasmānna bhavatītyata āha- #na dharmajijñāsāyāmiva#iti /
#śrutyādaya#iti ; śrutītihāsapurāṇāsmṛtayaḥ pramāṇam /
anubhavaḥ antaḥkaraṇavṛttibhedo brahmasākṣātkāraḥ ; tasyāvidyānivṛttidvāreṇa brahmasvarūpāvirbhāvaḥ pramāṇaphalam /
tacca phalamiva phalamiti gamayitavyam /
yadyapi dharmajijñāsāyāmapi sāmagryāṃ pratyakṣādīnāṃ vyāpāraḥ tathāpi sākṣānnāsti /
brahmajijñāsāyāṃ tu sākṣādanubhavādīnāṃ saṃbhavo 'nubhavārthā ca brahmajijñāsetyāha- #anubhavāvasānatvāt# /
brahmānubhavo brahmasākṣātkāraḥ paramapuruṣārthaḥ, nirmṛṣṭanikhiladuḥkhaparamānandarūpatvāditi /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
Just as <s>dharma</s> does not [require] the assistance of personal understanding, why should <s>Brahman</s> not also [be independent of it]? To this he says: 'Not as in the inquiry into <s>dharma</s>.'
'<s>Śruti</s> and the rest' means: <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Smṛti</s> are the means of knowledge.
Experience (<s>anubhava</s>) is a modification of the inner organ that is the direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>; the manifestation of the true nature of <s>Brahman</s> through the removal of <s>avidyā</s> is the fruit of the means of knowledge.
And that fruit should be understood as 'like a fruit' (quasi-fruit).
Although in the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> too, perception and the like operate within the aggregate [of means], they do not do so directly.
But in the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>, the direct involvement of experience and the like is possible; and the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> has experience as its culmination — thus he says: 'Because it culminates in experience.'
The experience of <s>Brahman</s>, the direct realization of <s>Brahman</s>, is the supreme human goal (<s>parama-puruṣārtha</s>), because it has the form of supreme bliss with all suffering completely removed.

body.text:
nanu bhavatu brahmānubhavārthā jijñāsā ; tadanubhava eva tvaśakyaḥ, brahmaṇastadviṣayatvāyogyatvāt ityata āha- #bhūtavastuviṣayatvācca brahmajñānasya#iti /
vyatirekasākṣātkārasya vikalparūpo viṣayaviṣayibhāvaḥ /
na tvevaṃ dharmajñānamanubhavāvasānam, tadanubhavasya svayamapuruṣārthatvāt, tadanuṣṭhānasādhyatvātpuruṣārthasya, anuṣṭhānasya ca vināpyanubhavaṃ śābdajñānamātrādeva siddheḥ ityāha- #kartavye hi#ityādinā /
na cāyaṃ sākṣātkāraviṣayatāyogyo 'pi, avartamānaścānavasthitatvādityāha- #puruṣādhīna#iti /
puruṣādhīnatvameva laukikavaidikakāryāṇāmāha- #kartumakartuṃ#iti /
laukikaṃ kāryamanavasthitamudāharati- #yathāśvena#iti /
laukikenodāharaṇena saha vaidikamudāharaṇaṃ samuccinoti- #tathātirātra#iti /
kartumakartumityasyedamudāharaṇamuktam /
kartumanyathā vā kartumityasyodāharaṇamāha - #udita#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might object: Let the inquiry be for the sake of the experience of <s>Brahman</s>; but that very experience is impossible, since <s>Brahman</s> is not fit to be the object of such [experience]. To this he says: 'Because the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> has an existing entity as its object.'
The relation of object and subject in the direct realization through negation (<s>vyatireka</s>) has the form of alternatives.
But the knowledge of <s>dharma</s> does not culminate in experience in this way, since the experience of <s>dharma</s> itself is not a human goal, since the human goal is to be accomplished through the performance [of dharmic action], and since performance is accomplished merely through verbal knowledge alone without [requiring] experience — thus he says: 'For in what is to be done' etc.
Nor is this [<s>Brahman</s>] unfit to be the object of direct realization, nor is it non-existent and therefore unstable — thus he says: 'Dependent on a person.'
He states the dependence on a person of worldly and Vedic effects: 'To do or not to do.'
He illustrates a worldly effect that is unstable: 'As with a horse.'
He conjoins a Vedic illustration with the worldly illustration: 'Likewise, the <s>Atirātra</s> [sacrifice].'
What was said was an illustration of 'to do or not to do.'
He gives an illustration of 'to do or to do otherwise': 'The <s>udita</s> [procedure].'

body.text:
syādetat /
puruṣasvātantryāt kartavye vidhipratiṣedhānāmānarthakyam, atadadhīnatvāt puruṣapravṛttinivṛttyoḥ ityata āha- #vidhipratiṣedhāścātrārthavantaḥ syuḥ# /
gṛhṇātīti vidhiḥ ; na gṛhṇātīti pratiṣedhaḥ /
uditānuditahomayorvidhiḥ /
evaṃ nārāsthitasparśananiṣedho brahmaghnaśca tadvāraṇavidhiḥ- ityevañjātīyakā vidhipratiṣedhā arthavantaḥ /
kuta ityata āha- #vikalpotsargāpavādāśca# /
co hetau /
yasmādgrahaṇāgrahaṇayoruditānuditahomayośca virodhāt samuccayāsaṃbhave tulyabalatayā ca bādhyabādhakabhāvābhāve sati agatyā vikalpaḥ /
nārāsthisparśananiṣedhatadvāraṇāyośca viruddhayoratulyabalatayā na vikalpaḥ ; kiṃ tu sāmānyaśāstrasya sparśananiṣedhasya dhāraṇavidhiviṣayeṇa viśeṣaśāstreṇa bādhaḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- vidhipratiṣedhaireva sa tādṛśo viṣayo 'nāgatotpādyarūpa upanītaḥ yena puruṣasya vidhiniṣedhādhīnapravṛttinivṛttyorapi svātantryaṃ bhavatīti /
bhūte vastuni tu neyamasti vidhā, ityāha- #na tu vastvevaṃ naivam#iti /
tadanena prakāravikalpo nirastaḥ /
prakārivikalpaṃ niṣedhati - #asti nāsti#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
Due to the person's independence, injunctions and prohibitions would be pointless, since the engagement and disengagement of the person do not depend on them. To this he says: 'And the injunctions and prohibitions would here be meaningful.'
'Grasps' (<s>gṛhṇāti</s>) is the injunction; 'does not grasp' (<s>na gṛhṇāti</s>) is the prohibition.
The injunction pertains to the <s>udita</s> and <s>anudita</s> oblations.
Likewise, the prohibition of touching a human bone, and the injunction of warding it off — injunctions and prohibitions of such a kind are meaningful.
Why? To this he says: 'Alternatives, general rules, and exceptions.'
The word '<s>ca</s>' (and) is in the sense of reason.
Because, since grasping and not-grasping — the <s>udita</s> and <s>anudita</s> oblations — being contradictory and accumulation being impossible, and being of equal force so that there is no sublation-relation — an alternative [is established] by necessity.
But between the prohibition of touching a human bone and the injunction of warding it off — being contradictory but not of equal force — there is no alternative; rather, the specific scripture of the injunction of warding overrides the general scripture of the prohibition of touching.
What is stated amounts to this: by injunctions and prohibitions themselves, such a subject-matter is introduced — [one that is] yet-to-come, to-be-produced in nature — whereby the person, though his engagement and disengagement depend on injunction and prohibition, yet has independence.
But in the case of an existing entity, this method does not apply — thus he says: 'Not that the entity is thus or not thus.'
By this, the alternative regarding the mode [of an entity] is refuted.
He refutes the alternative regarding the entity [itself]: 'It exists or it does not exist.'

body.text:
syādetat /
bhūte 'pi vastuni vikalpo dṛṣṭaḥ, yathā 'sthāṇurvā puruṣo vā' iti /
tatkathaṃ na vastu vikalpyate, ityata āha- #vikalpanāstu#iti /
#puruṣabuddhiḥ#antaḥkaraṇaṃ ; tadapekṣā vikalpanāḥ saṃśayaviparyāsāḥ /
savāsanamanomātrayonayo vā yathā svapne ; savāsanendriyamanoyonayo vā yathā 'sthāṇurvā puruṣo vā' iti sthāṇau saṃśayaḥ, 'puruṣa eva' iti ca viparyāsaḥ ; #anya#śabdena vastutaḥ sthāṇoranyasya puruṣasyābhidhānāt /
na tu puruṣatattvaṃ vā sthāṇutattvaṃ vāpekṣante, samānadharmadharmidarśanamātrādhīnajanmatvāt /
tasmādayathāvastato vikalpanā na vastu vikalpayanti vā anyathayanti vetyarthaḥ /
tattvajñānaṃ tu na buddhitantram, kiṃ tu vastutantram ; atastato vastuviniścayo yuktaḥ, na tu vikalpanābhya ityāha- #na vastuyāthātmya#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
Alternatives are observed even regarding an existing entity — as in 'Is it a post or a person?'
So how can an entity not be subject to alternatives? To this he says: 'But the alternatives.'
'<s>Puruṣabuddhi</s>' (personal understanding) is the inner organ; the alternatives — doubts and errors — depend on that.
Or, [they are] born of mind alone together with its impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>s), as in dream; or born of senses together with mind and impressions, as in 'Is it a post or a person?' — [this is] doubt regarding the post; and 'It is indeed a person' — this is error. By the word 'other' (<s>anya</s>), a person who is actually other than the post is referred to.
But they do not depend on the reality of the thing [as it truly is] — whether it is a person or a post — since their arising depends merely on the perception of common properties and substrata.
Therefore, [these] alternatives — which are not in accordance with reality — do not subject the entity to alternatives nor alter it — this is the meaning.
But the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>) is not mind-dependent, but rather reality-dependent; therefore, from that [knowledge], ascertainment of the entity is reasonable, not from alternatives — thus he says: 'Not the reality of the entity.'

body.text:
evamuktena prakāreṇa bhūtavastuviṣayāṇāṃ jñānānāṃ prāmāṇyasya vastutantratāṃ prasādhya brahmajñānasya vastutantratāmāha- #tatraivaṃ sati#iti /
atra codayati- #nanu bhūta#iti /
yatkila bhūtārthaṃ vākyaṃ tatpramāṇāntaragocarārthatayānuvādakaṃ dṛṣṭam, yathā- nadyāstīre phalāni santīti /
tathā ca vedāntāḥ /
tasmāt bhūtārthatayā pramāṇāntaradṛṣṭamevārthamanuvadeyuḥ /
uktaṃ ca brahmaṇi jagajjanmādihetukamanumānaṃ pramāṇāntaram /
evaṃ ca maulikaṃ tadeva parīkṣaṇīyam, na tu vedāntavākyāni tadadhīnasatyatvānīti kathaṃ vedāntavākyagrathanārthatā sūtrāṇāmityarthaḥ /
pariharati-
body.translated_text: Having thus established, by the method stated, the object-dependence (<s>vastutantratā</s>) of the authoritativeness of cognitions that pertain to existing reality, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the object-dependence of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>: 'This being so' (<s>tatraivaṃ sati</s>). Here [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection: 'But surely, an existing [entity]...' (<s>nanu bhūta</s>). Indeed, a sentence that concerns an existing entity is seen to be merely reiterative (<s>anuvādaka</s>), since its content is within the scope of another means of knowledge — as in 'There are fruits on the bank of the river.' And so too the <s>Vedānta</s>s. Therefore, being about existing entities, they would merely reiterate what is already known through another means of knowledge. And it has been said that inference — based on the world's origination and the like — is another means of knowledge regarding <s>Brahman</s>. And if so, that [inference] alone, being primary, should be examined, and not the <s>Vedānta</s> sentences whose validity depends on it. How then can the <s>sūtra</s>s have as their purpose the systematic presentation of <s>Vedānta</s> sentences? — this is the meaning. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves this —

body.text:
#na, indriyāviṣayatvena#iti /
kasmātpunarnendriyaviṣayatvaṃ pratīca ityata āha- #svabhāvata#iti /
ata eva śrutiḥ-
body.translated_text: 'No, because [<s>Brahman</s>] is not an object of the senses' (<s>na, indriyāviṣayatvena</s>). Why then is it not an object of the senses? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'By its very nature' (<s>svabhāvataḥ</s>). For this very reason the <s>Śruti</s> [says] —

body.text:
'parāñci khāni vyatṛṇatsvayaṃbhūstasmātparāṅ paśyati nāntarātman' iti /
#sati hīndriya#iti pratyagātmanastvaviṣayatvamupapāditam /
yathā ca sāmānyato dṛṣṭamapyanumānaṃ brahmaṇi na pravartate tathopariṣṭānnipuṇataramupapādayiṣyāmaḥ /
upapāditaṃ caitadasmābhirvistareṇa nyāyakaṇikāyām /
na ca bhūtārthatāmātreṇānuvādatetyupariṣṭādupapādayiṣyāmaḥ /
tasmātsarvamavadātam /
śrutiśca 'yato vā' iti janma darśayati, 'yena jātāni jīvanti' iti jīvanaṃ stitim, 'yatprayanti-' iti tatraiva layam /
#tasya ca nirṇayavākyam# /
atra ca pradhānādiviṣayatvasaṃśaye nirṇayavākyam- ānandādhyeva iti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-yathā rajjvajñānasahitarajjūpādānā dhārā rajjvāṃ satyāmasti rajjvāmeva ca līyate, evamavidyāsahitabrahmopādānaṃ jagat brahmaṇyevāsti tatraiva ca līyata iti siddham /
body.translated_text: 'The Self-existent (<s>Svayaṃbhū</s>) pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one sees outward, not the inner Self (<s>antarātman</s>).'
