iti /
tathā cārthāntarasaṃsargaparatāmātreṇa vākyārthapratyayopapattau na kāryasaṃsargaparatvaniyamaḥ padānām /
evaṃ ca sati kūṭasthanityabrahmarūpaparatve 'pyadoṣa iti /
body.translated_text: Thus. And when the possibility of sentence-meaning cognition is established merely through the orientation [of words] toward connection with another meaning, there is no restriction that words must be oriented toward connection with a producible entity. And this being so, even if [the words are] oriented toward the nature of the immutably eternal <s>Brahman</s> (<s>kūṭastha-nitya-brahma</s>), there is no defect.

body.text:
bhavyaṃ kāryam /
nanu yadbhavyārthaṃ bhūtamupadiśyate na tadbhūtam, bhavyasaṃsargiṇā rūpeṇa tasyāpi bhavyatvādityata āha- #na hi bhūtamupadiśyamānam#iti /
na tādātmyalakṣaṇaḥ saṃsargaḥ ; kiṃ tu kāryeṇa saha prayojanaprayodanilakṣaṇo 'nvayaḥ /
tadviṣayeṇa tu bhāvārthena bhūtārthānāṃ kriyātmatvamityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: '<s>Bhavya</s>' means producible (<s>kārya</s>). But surely, when an established entity is taught for the purpose of something producible, that [established entity] is not [truly] an established entity, since, in the form of its connection with the producible, it too becomes producible — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For an established entity that is being taught...' (<s>na hi bhūtam upadiśyamānam</s>). The connection is not one of identity (<s>tādātmya</s>); rather, it is a relation of purpose-and-purposer (<s>prayojana-prayojanī</s>) with the producible entity. But through the prescriptive meaning (<s>bhāvārtha</s>) pertaining to that [producible entity], the action-nature of the established entities [is explained] — this is the meaning.

body.text:
śaṅkate- #akriyātve 'pi#iti /
evaṃ cākriyārthakūṭasthanityabrahmopadeśānupapattiriti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati- #naiṣa doṣaḥ ; kriyārthatve 'pi#iti /
na hi kriyārthaṃ bhūtamupadiśyamānamabhūtaṃ bhavati, api tu kriyānivartanayogyaṃ bhūtameva tat /
tathā ca bhūter'the 'vadhṛtaśaktayaḥ śabdāḥ kvacitsvaniṣṭhabhūtaviṣayā dṛśyamānā mṛtvā śīrtvā vā na kathañcitkriyāniṣṭhatāṃ gamayitumucitāḥ /
na hyupahitaṃ śataśo dṛṣṭamapyanupahitaṃ kvaciddṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ bhavati /
tathā ca vartamānāpadeśā astikriyopahitā akāryārthā apyaṭavīvarṇakādayo loke bahulamupalabhyante /
evaṃ kriyāniṣṭhā api saṃbandhamātraparyavasāyinaḥ ; yathā"kasyaiva puruṣaḥ"iti praśne uttaraṃ"rājñaḥ"iti /
tathā prātipadikārthamātraniṣṭhāḥ ; yathā"kīdṛśāstaravaḥ"iti praśne uttaraṃ"phalinaḥ"iti /
na hi pṛcchatā puruṣasya vā tarūṇāṃ vāstitvanāstitve pratipitsite ; kiṃ tu puruṣasya svāmibhedastarūṇāṃ ca prakārabhedaḥ /
praṣṭurapekṣitaṃ cācakṣāṇaḥ svāmibhedameva prakārabhedameva ca prativyakti, na punarastitvam, tasya tenāpratipitsitatvāt /
upapāditā ca bhūte 'pyarthe vyutpattiḥ prayojanavati padānām /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] raises a doubt: 'Even if not action-oriented...' (<s>akriyātve 'pi</s>). And thus the implication is: the teaching of the immutably eternal <s>Brahman</s>, which has a non-action-oriented meaning, would be unjustified. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: 'This is no defect; even if action-oriented...' (<s>naiṣa doṣaḥ; kriyārthatve 'pi</s>). For an established entity that is being taught as action-oriented does not become non-established; rather, it remains an established entity that is fit for subordination to action. And thus, words whose capacity is established regarding established meanings — being seen in some cases with self-referential established-entity content — having died or withered [in those contexts], cannot by any means be made to have action-oriented content. For what has been seen a hundred times in one [context] does not become unseen when seen in another [context]. And thus, statements in the present tense accompanied by the verb 'is' (<s>asti-kriyā</s>) — such as descriptions of a forest and the like — are abundantly found in the world, even though they are not oriented toward producible entities. Similarly, even action-oriented [usages] terminate merely in a relation — as in the question 'Whose man is this?' the answer is 'The king's.' Likewise, [there are usages] that terminate in the mere nominal stem-meaning — as in the question 'What are the trees like?' the answer is 'Fruit-bearing.' For the questioner does not desire to ascertain the existence or non-existence of the man or the trees; rather, [he desires to know] the distinction of owner for the man and the distinction of kind for the trees. And the answerer, expressing precisely the distinction of owner and the distinction of kind that the questioner desires, communicates just that, not existence — since existence is not desired to be known by the questioner. And the verbal competence (<s>vyutpatti</s>) of purposeful words has been established even regarding established-entity meanings.

body.text:
codayati- #yadi nāmopadiṣṭaṃ#bhūtaṅ #kiṃ tava,#upadeṣṭuḥ śroturvā prayojanaṃ #syāt#? tasmādbhūtamapi prayojanavadevopadeṣṭavyaṃ nāprayojanam ; aprayojanaṃ ca brahma, tasyodāsīnasya sarvakriyārahitatvenānupakārakatvāt iti bhāvaḥ /
pariharati- #ucyata#iti /
#anavagatātmavastūpadeśaśca tathaiva#prayojanavāneva #bhavitumarhati# /
apyarthaścakāraḥ /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-yadyapi brahmodāsīnam, tathāpi tadviṣayaṃ śābdajñānamavagatiparyantaṃ vidyā svavirodhinīṃ saṃsāramūlanidānamavidyāmucchindatprayojanavadityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: [The opponent] objects: 'Granted that the established entity is taught — but what purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) would it serve for you' — for the teacher or the hearer? Therefore, even an established entity should be taught only if it is purposeful, not if purposeless. And <s>Brahman</s> is purposeless, since being indifferent and devoid of all activity, it cannot be of any benefit — this is the purport. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: 'It is said...' (<s>ucyate</s>). 'And the teaching of the hitherto-unknown reality of the Self is likewise' — purposeful indeed — 'ought to be' (<s>bhavitum arhati</s>). The word '<s>ca</s>' has the sense of 'also.' What is stated amounts to this: although <s>Brahman</s> is indifferent, nevertheless, the verbal knowledge (<s>śābdajñāna</s>) pertaining to it — culminating in realization — being <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), uproots the <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) that is opposed to it and that is the root cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, and is therefore purposeful. This is the meaning.

body.text:
api ca ye 'pi kāryaparatvaṃ sarveṣāṃ padānāmāsthiṣata, tairapi 'brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ', 'na surā pātavyā' ityādīnāṃ na kāryaparatā śakyā āsthātum /
kṛtyupahitamaryādaṃ hi kāryaṃ kṛtyā vyāptaṃ tannivṛttau nivartate, śiṃśapātvamiva vṛkṣatvanivṛttau /
kṛtirhi puruṣaprayatnaḥ ; sa ca viṣayādhīnanirūpaṇaḥ /
viṣayaścāsya sādhyasvabhāvatayā bhāvārtha eva pūrvāparībhūto 'nyotpādānukūlo bhavitumarhati, na dravyaguṇau /
sākṣātkṛtivyāpyo hi kṛterviṣayaḥ ; na ca dravyaguṇayoḥ siddhayorasti kṛtivyāpyatā /
ata eva śāstrakṛdvacaḥ- 'bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāstebhyaḥ kriyā pratīyeta' iti /
dravyaguṇaśabdānāṃ naimittikāvasthāyāṃ kāryāvamarśe 'pi, bhāvasya svataḥ dravyaguṇaśabdānāṃ tu bhāvayogātkāryāvamarśa iti bhāvārthebhya evāpūrvāvagatiḥ, na dravyaguṇaśabdebhya iti /
na ca 'dadhnā juhoti', 'saṃtatamāghārayati' ityādiṣu dadhyādīnāṃ kāryaviṣayatā ; tatrāpi hi homaghārabhāvārthaviṣayameva kāryam /
na caitāvatā 'somena yajeta' itivat dadhisāṃtatyādiviśiṣṭahomāghāravidhānāt, 'agnihotraṃ juhoti', 'āghāramāghārayati' iti tadanuvādaḥ /
yadyapyatrāpi bhāvārthaviṣayameva kāryam, tathāpi bhāvārthānubandhatayā dravyaguṇāvaviṣayāvapi vidhīyete /
bhāvārtho hi kārakavyāpāramātratayāviśiṣṭaḥ kārakaviśeṣeṇa dravyādinā viśeṣyata iti dravyādistadanubandhaḥ /
tathā ca bhāvārthe vidhīyamāne sa eva sānubandho vidhīyata iti dravyaguṇāvaviṣayāvapi tadanubandhatayā vihitau bhavataḥ /
evaṃ ca bhāvārthapraṇālikayā dravyādisaṃkrānto vidhirgauravādbibhyatsvaviṣayasya cānyataḥ prāptatayā tadanuvādena tadanubandhībhūtadravyādiparo bhavatīti sarvatra bhāvārthaviṣaya eva vidhiḥ /
body.translated_text:
Moreover, even those who have maintained that all words are oriented toward action (<s>kārya</s>) cannot maintain that orientation toward action for [prohibitions] such as 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should not be killed,' 'Liquor should not be drunk,' and the like.
For an action that is delimited by effort (<s>kṛti</s>) is pervaded by effort, and ceases upon the cessation of that [effort] — just as the property of being a <s>śiṃśapā</s> [tree] ceases upon the cessation of tree-ness.
For effort (<s>kṛti</s>) is human exertion; and that [exertion] depends for its determination on [its] object.
And its object, being of the nature of what is to be accomplished (<s>sādhya</s>), must be a <s>bhāvārtha</s> (positive act) that is temporally ordered — conducive to producing something else — and not a substance or a quality.
For the object of effort is what is directly pervaded by effort; and substances and qualities, being already established, do not have the character of being pervaded by effort.
For this very reason, the author of the <s>Śāstra</s> (<s>Jaimini</s>) has said: 'Action-words (<s>karmaśabda</s>s) have a positive-act meaning (<s>bhāvārtha</s>); from them, action is understood.'
Although substance-words and quality-words too, in an occasioned state, may imply an action, the action-implication of positive-act [words] is self-established (<s>svataḥ</s>), while that of substance- and quality-words is by virtue of [their] connection with the positive act — hence the apprehension of the unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>) comes from positive-act words alone, not from substance- and quality-words.
Nor in [sentences like] 'He offers with curds,' 'He continuously pours the <s>āghāra</s> oblation,' and the like, do curds and the like have action as their object; for even there, the action has only the positive act of oblation and pouring as its object.
Nor, by this alone — since there is an injunction of oblation and pouring qualified by curds, continuity, and the like, as in 'He should sacrifice with <s>Soma</s>' — is [the sentence] 'He offers the <s>agnihotra</s>,' 'He pours the <s>āghāra</s>,' a restatement of that [already enjoined sacrifice].
Even though here too the action has only the positive act as its object, nevertheless, by virtue of being an adjunct (<s>anubandha</s>) of the positive act, substances and qualities too — though not themselves objects [of the injunction] — are enjoined [as adjuncts].
For the positive act, being unspecified as mere instrumental operation, is specified by a particular instrument (<s>kāraka</s>) such as a substance and the like — hence the substance and the like are adjuncts of that [positive act].
And thus, when the positive act is being enjoined, that very [positive act] together with its adjuncts is enjoined — hence substances and qualities too, though not themselves objects, are enjoined by virtue of being adjuncts.
Thus, the injunction that has been transmitted to substances and the like through the channel of the positive act, fearing verbosity and [recognizing] that its own object [the positive act] is already obtained from elsewhere, through restating that [positive act] becomes oriented toward the substance and the like that are adjuncts of it — so everywhere the injunction has the positive act alone as its object.

body.text:
etena 'yadāgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo bhavati' ityatra saṃbandhaviṣayo vidhiriti parāstam /
nanu na bhavatyartho vidheyaḥ ; siddhe bhavitari labdharūpasya bhavanaṃ pratyakartṛtvāt ; na khalu gaganaṃ bhavati ; nāpyasiddhe, asiddhasyāniyojyatvāt, gaganakusumavat ; tasmādbhavanena prayojyavyāpāreṇākṣiptaḥ prayojakasya bhāvayiturvyāpāro vidheyaḥ ; sa ca vyāpāro bhāvanā, kṛtiḥ, prayatna iti ; nirviṣayaścāsāvaśakyapratipattiḥ ; ato viṣayāpekṣāyāmāgneyaśabdopasthāpito dravyadevatāsaṃbandha evāsya viṣayaḥ /
nanu vyāpāraviṣayaḥ puruṣaprayatnaḥ kathamavyāpārarūpaṃ saṃbandhaṃ gocarayet ? na hi 'ghaṭaṃ kuru' ityatrāpi sākṣānnāmārthaṃ ghaṭaṃ puruṣaprayatno gocarayati ; api tu daṇḍādi hastādinā vyāpārayati /
tasmādghaṭārthāṃ kṛtiṃ vyāpāraviṣayāmeva pratipadyate, na tu svarūpato ghaṭaviṣayām /
uddeśyatayā tvasyāmasti ghaṭo na tu viṣayatayā /
viṣayatayā tu hastādivyāpāra eva /
ata eva 'āgneyaḥ' ityatrāpi dravyadevatāsaṃbandhākṣipto yajireva kāryaviṣayo vidheyaḥ /
kimuktaṃ bhavati"āgneyo bhavati"iti ? āgneyena yāgena bhāvayediti /
ata eva 'ya evaṃ vidvān paurṇamāsyāṃ yajate', 'ya evaṃ vidvānamāvāsyāṃ yajate' ityanuvādo bhavati 'yadāgneyaḥ' ityādivihitasya yāgaṣaṭkasya /
ata eva ca vihitānūditasya tasyaiva 'darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta' ityādhikārasaṃbandhaḥ /
body.translated_text:
By this, the [view] that in 'when there is an <s>Āgneya</s> eight-kapāla [offering]' the injunction has the relation [of deity to offering] as its object, is set aside.
But one might object: The positive act cannot be what is to be enjoined; for if <s>bhavati</s> (being) already exists as established, its being (<s>bhavana</s>) — since it has already obtained its form — is not [subject to] agency; for surely space does not 'come into being.' Nor [can it be enjoined] if not yet established, since what is unestablished cannot be enjoined — like a sky-flower. Therefore, what is to be enjoined is the operation of the causer (<s>bhāvayitṛ</s>) — [namely,] the operation that is prompted by the [verb] <s>bhū</s> (to be) as used with a causal meaning (<s>bhāvanā</s>); and that operation is productive activity (<s>bhāvanā</s>), effort (<s>kṛti</s>), exertion (<s>prayatna</s>). And that [exertion], without an object, cannot be apprehended; hence, when an object is required, the relation of deity and substance — presented by the word '<s>āgneya</s>' — is its object.
But [one may counter:] how can human exertion, whose object is operation, take as its object a relation, which is not an operation? For even in 'Make a pot,' it is not the case that human exertion directly takes as its object the thing called a pot; rather, it operates upon the staff and the like through the hands and the like. Therefore, one apprehends the effort as having an operation directed toward the pot, not as having the pot itself as its object in terms of its essential nature. The pot is an end-in-view (<s>uddeśya</s>) of it, but not an object; while the operation of the hands and the like is the object.
For this very reason, even in [the sentence] '<s>āgneya</s>,' the sacrifice (<s>yaji</s>) itself — which is implied by the relation of deity and substance — is the object of the action; it is what is to be enjoined.
What does [the sentence] '<s>āgneyo bhavati</s>' mean? It means: 'One should bring about [a sacrifice] with the <s>Āgneya</s> offering.'
For this very reason, 'One who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon,' 'One who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon' — [these sentences] are restatements of the sixfold sacrifice enjoined by '<s>yadāgneyaḥ</s>' and the like.
And for this very reason, that very [sacrifice] which has been both enjoined and restated has the qualification-connection [expressed by] 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>.'

body.text:
tasmātsarvatra kṛtipraṇālikayā bhāvārthaviṣaya eva vidhirityekāntaḥ /
tathā ca 'na hanyāt', 'na pibet' ityādiṣu yadi kāryamabhyupeyeta, tatastadvyāpikā kṛtirabhyupetavyā, tadvyāpakaśca bhāvārtho viṣayaḥ /
evaṃ ca prajāpativratanyāyena paryudāsavṛttyāhananāpānasaṃkalpalakṣaṇayā tadviṣayo vidhiḥ syāt /
tathā ca prasajyapratiṣedho dattajalāñjaliḥ prasajyeta /
na ca sati saṃbhave lakṣaṇā nyāyyā /
'nekṣetodyantam' ityādau tu 'tasya vratam' ityadhikārātprasajyapratiṣedhāsaṃbhavena paryudāsavṛttyānīkṣaṇasaṃkalpalakṣaṇā yuktā /
tasmāt 'na hanyāt', 'na pibet' ityādiṣu prasajyapratiṣedheṣu bhāvārthābhāvāttadvyāptāyāḥ kṛterabhāvaḥ ; tadabhāve ca tadvyāptasya kāryasyābhāva iti na kāryaparatvaniyamaḥ sarvatra vākye ityāha- #brahmaṇo na hantavya ityevamādyā#iti /
body.translated_text:
Therefore, everywhere, the injunction has the positive act alone as its object, through the channel of effort — this is the invariable rule.
And thus, in [prohibitions like] 'One should not kill,' 'One should not drink,' and the like — if action (<s>kārya</s>) were accepted, then the effort pervading it would have to be accepted, and the positive-act object pervading that effort [would also have to be accepted].
And thus, through the principle of the <s>Prajāpati</s> vow, by way of exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), the injunction would have as its object the resolution characterized by non-killing, non-drinking.
In that case, the absolute negation (<s>prasajya-pratiṣedha</s>) would be dismissed.
But when [absolute negation] is possible, a figurative [interpretation] is not justified.
In [sentences like] 'One should not look at the rising [sun]' and the like, however, because of the context 'this is his vow,' — since absolute negation is not possible — the exclusion-interpretation characterized by a resolution of non-looking is fitting.
Therefore, in absolute negations like 'One should not kill,' 'One should not drink,' and the like — due to the absence of a positive act — there is the absence of effort pervaded by it; and in the absence of that [effort], the absence of the action pervaded by it — hence there is no invariable rule that every sentence is oriented toward action. Thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should not be killed — and sentences of this kind.'

body.text:
nanu kasmānnivṛttireva kāryaṃ na bhavati, tatsādhanaṃ vetyata āha- #na ca sā kriyā#iti /
kriyāśabdaḥ kāryavacanaḥ /
etadeva vibhajate- #akriyārthānām#iti /
body.translated_text:
But why should cessation itself not be the action, or the means to it? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Nor is that an action.'
The word 'action' (<s>kriyā</s>) here means 'what is to be done' (<s>kārya</s>).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] analyzes this very [point]: 'Of those [sentences] which do not have action as their meaning' etc.

body.text:
syādetat /
vidhivibhaktiśravaṇātkāryaṃ tāvadatra pratīyate ; tacca na bhāvārthamantareṇa ; na ca rāgataḥ pravṛttasya hananapānādāvakasmādaudāsīnyamupapadyate vinā vidhārakaprayatnam ; tasmātsa eva pravṛttyunmukhānāṃ manovāgdehānāṃ vidhārakaḥ prayatno niṣedhavidhigocaraḥ kriyeti nākriyāparamasti vākyaṃ kiñcidapīti āha- #na ca hananakriyānivṛttyaudāsīnyavyatirekeṇa nañaḥ śakyamaprāptakriyārthatvaṃ kalpayitum# /
kena hetunā na śakyamityata āha- #svabhāvaprāptahantyarthānurāgeṇa#nañaḥ /
ayamarthaḥ- hananapānaparo hi vidhipratyayaḥ pratīyamānaste eva vidhatte ityutsargaḥ /
na caite śakye vidhātum, rāgataḥ prāptatvāt /
na cātra nañaḥ prasajyapratiṣedho vidheyaḥ. tasyāpyaudāsīnyarūpasya siddhatayā prāptatvāt /
na ca vidhārakaḥ prayatnaḥ, tasyāśrutatvena lakṣyamāṇatvāt, sati saṃbhave ca lakṣaṇāyā anyāyyatvāt, vidhivibhakteśca rāgataḥ prāptapravṛttyanuvādakatvena vidhiviṣayatvāyogāt /
tasmādyatpibeddhanyādvetyanūdya tanneti niṣidhyate, tadabhāvo jñāpyate ; na tu nañartho vidhīyate /
abhāvaśca svavirodhibhāvanirūpaṇatayā bhāvacchāyānupātīti siddhe siddhavat, sādhye ca sādhyavadbhāsata iti sādhyaviṣayo nañarthaḥ sādhyavadbhāsata iti nañarthaḥ kārya iti bhramaḥ /
tadidamāha- #nañaścaiṣa svabhāva#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
From the hearing of the optative suffix and the like, an action is at least understood [in the prohibition]; and that [action] cannot [exist] without a positive act; and the indifference of the mind, speech, and body — which are inclined toward the activity [of killing, drinking, etc.] out of passion — is not possible without a restraining effort. Therefore, that very restraining effort of those [faculties] inclined toward activity is the action that is the object of the prohibitive injunction — hence there is no sentence that is devoid of an action-content. To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Nor is it possible to attribute to the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) the meaning of an un-attained action, beyond the indifference [that results from] the cessation of the action of killing.'
For what reason is it not possible? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'By virtue of the attachment inherent in the meaning of "kills"' — of the negative particle.
The meaning is this: The optative suffix, being understood as oriented toward killing, drinking, and the like, enjoins precisely those — this is the general rule.
But those [actions] cannot be enjoined, since they are already obtained through passion.
Nor is the absolute negation (<s>prasajya-pratiṣedha</s>) of the negative particle what is to be enjoined — since that too, being of the nature of indifference, is already obtained as established.
Nor is a restraining effort [to be enjoined], since that [restraining effort] — being unheard [in the text] — would have to be figuratively implied; and when [a literal interpretation] is possible, a figurative one is not justified; and since the optative suffix — being a restater of activity already obtained through passion — is not fit to have an injunctive object.
Therefore, what the [sentence] restates as 'one would drink' or 'one would kill' — that is negated by 'not' (<s>na</s>), i.e., its absence is indicated; the meaning of the negative particle is not being enjoined.
And absence, since it is determined through [reference to] its contradictory positive entity, follows the shadow of a positive entity — hence in an established [entity], it appears as if established; and in what is to be accomplished, it appears as if to be accomplished. Thus, the meaning of the negative particle — which has what-is-to-be-accomplished as its object — [merely] appears as if it is to be accomplished; hence [the belief that] the meaning of the negative particle is an action is an error.
This is what [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states: 'And this is the nature of the negative particle' etc.

body.text:
nanu bodhayatu svasaṃbandhino 'bhāvaṃ nañ ; pravṛttyunmukhānāṃ tu manovāgdehānāṃ kuto 'kasmānnivṛttirityata āha- #abhāvabuddhiścaudāsīnya#paripālana #kāraṇam# /
ayamabhiprāyaḥ- 'jvaritaḥ pathyamaśnīyāt', 'na sarpāyāṅguliṃ dadyāt'
body.translated_text:
But let the negative particle indicate the absence of what it is connected with; however, whence does the sudden cessation of the mind, speech, and body — which are inclined toward activity — [arise]? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And the cognition of absence is the cause of the preservation of indifference.'
The intent is this: '<s>jvaritaḥ pathyamaśnīyāt</s>' (a fever-patient should eat wholesome food), '<s>na sarpāyāṅguliṃ dadyāt</s>' (one should not give a finger to a serpent)' —

body.text:
ityādivacanaśravaṇasamanantaraṃ prayojyavṛddhasya pathyāśane pravṛttiṃ bhujaṅgāṅgulidānonmukhasya ca tato nivṛttimupalabhya bālo vyutpitsuḥ prayojyavṛddhasya pravṛttinivṛttihetū icchādveṣāvanumimīte /
tathā hi- icchādveṣahetuke vṛddhasya pravṛttinivṛttī, svatantrapravṛttinivṛttitvāt, madīyasvatantrapravṛttinivṛttivat /
kartavyataikārthasamaveteṣṭāniṣṭasādhanabhāvāvagamapūrvakau cāsyecchādveṣau, pravṛttinivṛttihetubhūtecchādveṣatvāt, matpravṛttihetubhūtecchādveṣavat /
na jātu mama śabdatadvyāpārapuruṣāśayatraikālyānavicchannabhāvanāpūrvapratyayapūrvāvicchādveṣāvabhūtām ; api tu bhūyo bhūyaḥ svagatamālocayata uktakāraṇapūrvāveva pratyavabhāsete /
tasmādvṛddhasya svatantrapravṛttinivṛttī icchādveṣabhedau ca kartavyataikārthasamaveteṣṭāniṣṭasādhanabhāvāvagamapūrvāvityānupūrvyā siddhaḥ kāryakāraṇābhāva itīṣṭāniṣṭasādhanatāvagamātprayojyavṛddhapravṛttinivṛttī iti siddham /
sa cāvagamaḥ prāgabhūtaḥ śabdaśravaṇānantaramupajāyamānaḥ śabdaśravaṇahetuka iti pravartakeṣu vākyeṣu 'yajeta' ityādiṣu śabda eva kartavyamiṣṭasādhanaṃ vyāpāramavagamayaṃstasyeṣṭasādhanatāṃ kartavyatāṃ cāvagamayati ; ananyalabhyatvādubhayoḥ, anantyalabhyasya ca śabdārthatvāt /
yatra tu kartavyatānyata eva labhyate, yathā 'hanyāt', 'na pibet' ityādiṣu, hananapānapravṛttyo rāgataḥ pratilambhāt, tatra tadanuvādena nañsamabhivyāhṛtā liṅādivibhaktiranyato 'prāptamanayoranarthahetubhāvamātramavagamayati /
pratyakṣaṃ hi tayoriṣṭasādhanabhāvo 'vagamyate, anyathā rāgaviṣayatvāyogāt /
tasmādrāgādiprāptakartavyatānuvādenānarthasādhanatāprajñāpanaparam 'na hanyāt', 'na pibet' ityādivākyam, na tu kartavyatāparamiti suṣṭhūktamakāryaniṣṭhatvaṃ niṣedhānām /
niṣedhyānāṃ cānarthasādhanatābuddhireva niṣedhyābhāvabuddhiḥ /
tayā khalvayaṃ cetana āpātato ramaṇīyatāṃ paśyannapyāyatimālocya pravṛttyabhāvaṃ nivṛttimavabudhya nivartate /
audāsīnyamātmano 'vasthāpayatīti yāvat /
body.translated_text:
Immediately upon hearing such sentences, a child desiring to learn [the language], observing the engagement of the instructed elder in eating wholesome food, and the cessation [of the one] who was inclined to offer a finger to a snake, infers that the causes of the engagement and cessation of the instructed elder are desire and aversion [respectively].
That is as follows: The engagement and cessation of the elder are caused by desire and aversion, because they are autonomous engagement and cessation — just like my own autonomous engagement and cessation.
And his desire and aversion are preceded by the apprehension of the status of being a means to what is beneficial or harmful, co-occurring with [the notion of] what is to be done — because they are desire and aversion that cause engagement and cessation — just like the desire and aversion that cause my engagement.
At no time have my desire and aversion been preceded by a cognition of <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented potency) [arising] through the unbroken practice of contemplating [the chain of] word → word-function → person's intention → [the three] time-frames; rather, upon repeated self-reflection, they manifest as preceded by the stated causes alone.
Therefore, by the stated sequence — the autonomous engagement and cessation of the elder are caused by desire and aversion, and the desire and aversion are preceded by the apprehension of the status of being a means to what is beneficial or harmful, co-occurring with what is to be done — the absence of a causal relation with action [i.e., <s>apūrva</s>] is established.
Hence, the engagement and cessation of the instructed elder [result] from the apprehension of the status of being a means to what is beneficial or harmful — this is established.
And that apprehension, which did not exist before, arising immediately after the hearing of the sentence, is caused by the hearing of the sentence. Thus, in injunctive sentences such as '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice) and the like, the sentence itself — making known the operation that is a means to the desired [end] — makes known its status as a means to the desired [end] and its status as what is to be done; since both are obtainable from no other source, and since what is obtainable from no other source is the meaning of the sentence.
But where the status of what is to be done is obtained from another source — as in 'one would kill' (<s>hanyāt</s>), 'one should not drink' (<s>na pibet</s>), and the like, where the engagement in killing, drinking, and the like is obtained from passion — there, by restating that [already-obtained engagement], the optative suffix combined with the negative particle makes known merely the status of being a cause of harm [for those activities], which is not obtained from elsewhere.
For the status of being a means to the desired [end] for those [activities] is apprehended by direct perception; otherwise, they could not be objects of passion.
Therefore, the sentence 'One should not kill,' 'One should not drink,' and the like — restating the status as what-is-to-be-done that is already obtained through passion and the like — has as its purpose the disclosure of the status of being a cause of harm; it is not oriented toward what is to be done. Thus, it is well said that prohibitions are not oriented toward action.
And the cognition of the absence of the prohibited [actions] is itself the cognition of the harmfulness of those prohibited [actions].
By that [cognition], this conscious being — even though prima facie seeing the attractiveness [of the prohibited act] — upon mature reflection, understanding the absence of activity, i.e., cessation, ceases.
[That is,] he establishes indifference in himself — this is the meaning.

body.text:
syādetat /
abhāvabuddhiścedaudāsīnyasthāpanākāraṇam, yāvadaudāsīnyamanuvarteta ; na cānuvartate ; na hyudāsīno 'pi viṣayāntaravyāsaktacittastadabhāvabuddhimān ; na cāvasthāpakakāraṇābhāve kāryāvasthānaṃ dṛṣṭam ; na hi stambhāvapāte prāsādo 'vatiṣṭhate /
ata āha- #sā ca dagdhendhanāgnivatsvayamevopaśāmyati# /
tāvadeva khalvayaṃ pravṛttyunmukho na yāvadasyānarthahetubhāvamadhigacchati /
anarthahetutvādhigamo 'sya samūloddhāraṃ pravṛttimuddhṛtya dagdhendhanāgnivatsvayamevopaśāmyati /
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
If the cognition of absence is the cause of establishing indifference, it should persist as long as the indifference persists; but it does not persist — for one who is indifferent, with his mind engaged in another object, does not have the cognition of absence [of the prohibited act]; and it is not observed that an effect persists in the absence of its maintaining cause — for a palace does not stand when the pillar is removed.
To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And that [cognition], like a fire whose fuel has been consumed, subsides of its own accord.'
For this [person] is inclined toward activity only so long as he does not apprehend [the prohibited act's] status as a cause of harm.
The apprehension of its being a cause of harm, having uprooted the inclination toward activity root and all, subsides of its own accord like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.

body.text:
etaduktaṃ bhavati- yathā prāsādāvasthānakāraṇaṃ stambho naivamaudāsīnyāvasthānakāraṇamabhāvabuddhiḥ ; api tvāgantukādvināśahetostrāṇenāvasthānakāraṇam, yathā kamaṭhapṛṣṭhaniṣṭhuraḥ kavacaḥ śāstraprahāratrāṇena rājanyajīvāvasthānahetuḥ /
na ca kavacāpagame ca asati ca śastraprahāre, rājanyajīvanāśa iti /
upasaṃharati- #tasmātprasaktakriyānivṛttyaudāsīnyameva#iti /
audāsīnyamajānato 'pyastīti prasaktakriyānivṛttyopalakṣya viśinaṣṭi /
tatkimakriyārthatvenānarthakyamāśaṅkya kriyārthatvopavarṇanaṃ jaiminīyamasamañjasamevetyupasaṃhāravyājena pariharati- #tasmātpuruṣārtha#iti /
puruṣārthānupayogyupākhyānādiviṣayāvakriyārthatayā kriyārthatayā ca pūrvottarapakṣau ; na tūpaniṣadviṣayau, upaniṣadāṃ svayaṃ puruṣārtharūpabrahmāvagatamaparyanasānādityarthaḥ /
body.translated_text:
What is stated amounts to this: Just as a pillar is the cause of a palace remaining standing, so too the cognition of non-existence is not the cause of the state of indifference remaining. Rather, [indifference remains] through the protection from an adventitious cause of destruction — just as a tortoise-shell-hard armor, by protecting from the blow of a weapon, is the cause of a warrior's life remaining.
Nor, upon the removal of the armor and in the absence of a weapon-blow, does the warrior's life perish.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes: 'Therefore, indifference is simply the cessation of ongoing activity.'
Since indifference exists even for one who does not know [the Self], [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] qualifies it as indicated by the cessation of ongoing activity.
Then — anticipating the objection that, due to not being oriented toward action, [<s>Vedānta</s> texts] would be purposeless — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves it under the guise of a conclusion [to the effect] that <s>Jaimini</s>'s description of their orientation toward action is incoherent: 'Therefore, the human goal...'
The two positions — of non-orientation toward action and of orientation toward action — are the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view) and the <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion) [respectively], regarding the subject-matter of stories (<s>upākhyāna</s>) and the like that are not conducive to the human goal; but not regarding the subject-matter of the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s, since the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s culminate in the realization of <s>Brahman</s> — which is itself the form of the human goal — this is the meaning.

body.text:
#yadapi#aupaniṣadātmajñānamapuruṣārthaṃ manyamānena #uktam-kartavyavidhyanupraveśamantareṇa#iti, atra nigūḍhābhisaṃdhiḥ pūrvoktaṃ parihāraṃ smārayati- #tatparihṛtam#iti /
atrākṣeptā svoktamarthaṃ smārayati- #nanu śrutabrahmaṇo 'pi#iti /
nigūḍhamabhisaṃdhiṃ samādhātodghāṭayati- #atrocyate-nāvagatabrahmātmabhāvasya#iti /
satyaṃ na brahmajñānamātraṃ sāṃsārikadharmanivṛttikāraṇam, api tu sākṣātkāraparyantam /
brahmasākṣātkāraścāntaḥkaraṇavṛttibhedaḥ śravaṇamananādijanitasaṃskārasacivamanojanmā, ṣaḍjādibhedasākṣātkāra iva gāndharvaśāstraśravaṇābhyāsasaṃskṛtamanoyoniḥ /
sa ca nikhilaprapañcamahendrajālasākṣātkāraṃ samūlamunmūlayannātmānamapi prapañcatvāviśeṣādunmūlayatītyupapāditamadhastāt /
tasmādrajjusvarūpakathanatulyataivātreti siddham /
atra ca vedapramāṇamūlatayā #vedapramāṇajanita#ityuktam /
atraiva sukhaduḥkhānutpādabhedena nidarśanadvayamāha- #na hi dhanina#iti /
śrutimatrodāharati- #taduktam#iti /
body.translated_text:
As for what was said by one who considers <s>Upaniṣadic</s> self-knowledge to be not a human goal — 'Without entering into the injunction of what is to be done...' — here, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], with a hidden intent, reminds [us] of the previously stated resolution: 'That has been refuted.'
Here the objector reminds [us] of his own stated meaning: 'But even for one who has heard about <s>Brahman</s>...'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>], unveiling the hidden intent to resolve [the objection], says: 'To this we say: For one who has realized the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s>...'
True, mere knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is not the cause of the cessation of <s>saṃsāric</s> properties — rather, [knowledge] culminating in direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) [is].
And the direct realization of <s>Brahman</s> is a distinct modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), born of the mind assisted by the impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and the like — just as the direct perception of the notes beginning with <s>ṣaḍja</s> is born of the mind refined by the impressions of hearing and practicing the science of music (<s>gāndharvaśāstra</s>).
And that [realization], while uprooting from the root the direct perception of the entire phenomenal world as a grand illusion (<s>mahendrajāla</s>), also uproots itself — since there is no distinction [between itself and the phenomenal] in being phenomenal — this has been demonstrated below.
Therefore, it is established that [the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>] is analogous to telling [someone] the true nature of a rope [mistaken for a snake].
And here, since it is rooted in the Vedic means of knowledge, it is said: 'Generated by the Vedic means of knowledge.'
Here itself, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] gives two illustrations by way of the non-production of pleasure and suffering: 'For one who possesses wealth...'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] cites the <s>Śruti</s> alone: 'That has been said.'

body.text:
codayati- #śarīre patite#iti /
pariharati- #na; saśarīratvasya#iti /
yadi vāstavaṃ saśarīratvaṃ bhavet, na jīvatastannivarteta ; mithyājñānanimittaṃ tu tat ; taccotpannatattvajñānena jīvatāpi śakyaṃ nivartayitum /
yatpunaraśarīratvaṃ tadasya svabhāva iti na śakyaṃ nivartayitum, svabhāvahānena bhāvavināśaprasaṅgādityāha- #nityamaśarīratvam#iti /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection: 'When the body falls...'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves it: 'No; because the state of being embodied...'
If the state of being embodied were real, it would not cease even while [the person is] alive. But it is caused by false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>); and that can be removed even while alive by the arisen knowledge of reality.
But the state of being without a body (<s>aśarīratva</s>) is [the Self's] own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), and so cannot be removed — since the removal of its nature would lead to the unwanted consequence of the destruction of the entity — thus he says: 'The state of being without a body is eternal.'

body.text:
syādetat /
na mithyājñānanimittaṃ saśarīratvam api tu dharmādharmanimittam ; tacca svakāraṇadharmādharmanivṛttimantareṇa na nivartate ; tannivṛttau ca prāyaṇameveti na jīvato 'śarīratvamiti śaṅkate- #tatkṛta#iti /
tat ityātmānaṃ parāmṛśati /
nirākaroti- #na ; śarīrasaṃbandhasya#iti /
na tāvadātmā sākṣāddharmādharmau kartumarhati, vāgbuddhiśarīrārambhajanitau hi tau nāsati śarīrasaṃbandhe bhavataḥ ; tābhyāṃ tu śarīrasaṃbandhaṃ rocayamāno vyaktaṃ parasparāśrayatvaṃ doṣamāvahati ; tadidamāha- #śarīrasaṃbandhasya#iti /
yadyucyeta satyamasti parasparāśrayatvam, na tveṣa doṣaḥ, anāditvāt, bījāṅkuravat ityata āha- #andhaparamparaiṣānāditvakalpanā# /
yattu manyate-neyamandhaparamparātulyā anāditā ; na hi yato dharmādharmabhedādya ātmaśarīrasaṃbandhabhedastata eva śarīrasaṃbandhāt sa dharmādharmabhedaḥ ; kiṃ tveṣa pūrvasmādātmaśarīrasaṃbandhātpūrvadharmādharmabhedajanmanaḥ ; eva tvātmaśarīrasaṃbandho 'nyasmāddharmādharmabhedāt -iti, taṃ pratyāha- #kriyāsamavāyābhāvāt#iti /
śaṅkate- #saṃnidhānamātreṇa#iti /
pariharati- #na#iti /
#upārjanaṃ#svīkaraṇam /
na tviyaṃ vidhātmanītyāha- #na#
body.translated_text:
One might say this:
The state of being embodied is not caused by false knowledge, but rather by merit and demerit (<s>dharmādharma</s>). And that [embodiment] does not cease without the cessation of its cause — merit and demerit. And upon the cessation of those, [the self departs] only at death (<s>prāyaṇa</s>) — therefore there is no state of being without a body while alive. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises this doubt: 'Produced by that.'
The word 'that' (<s>tat</s>) refers back to the self.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: 'No; because the connection with the body...'
The self cannot directly produce merit and demerit (<s>dharmādharma</s>), for these two are produced from the activity of speech, mind, and body, and do not exist in the absence of a connection with the body. But one who maintains that [the self] produces the connection with the body through these two [merit and demerit] clearly incurs the defect of mutual dependence (<s>parasparāśrayatva</s>). This is what is stated: 'Because the connection with the body...'
If one says: True, there is mutual dependence, but this is not a defect, because [the series] is beginningless, like the seed and sprout — to this he says: 'This postulation of beginninglessness is a blind succession.'
As for the view that this is not like a blind succession — 'For it is not the case that from the very distinction of merit and demerit from which comes the distinction of the self-body connection, from that very [body-]connection comes that [very] distinction of merit and demerit. Rather, this particular distinction of merit and demerit arises from a previous self-body connection, and this particular self-body connection from another [prior] distinction of merit and demerit' — to this he replies: 'Because of the absence of conjunction with action.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises a doubt: 'By mere proximity.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: 'No.'
'Appropriation' (<s>upārjana</s>) means making one's own.
But this [appropriation] does not pertain to the self as the agent — thus he says: 'No,

body.text: #tvātmana#iti /
body.translated_text: but of the self...'

body.text:
ye tu dehādāvātmābhimāno na mithyā, api tu gauṇaḥ, māṇavakādāviva siṃhābhimāna iti manyante, tanmatamupanyasya dūṣayati- #atrāhuḥ#iti /
prasiddho vastubhedo yasya puruṣasya sa tathoktaḥ /
upapāditaṃ caitadasmābhiradhyāsabhāṣya iti nehopapādyate /
yathā mandāndhakāre sthāṇurayamityagṛhyamāṇaviśeṣe vastuni puruṣāt sāṃśayikau puruṣaśabdapratyayau sthāṇuviṣayau ; tatra hi puruṣatvamaniyatamapi samāropitameva /
evaṃ saṃśaye samāropitamaniścitamudāhṛtya viparyayajñāne niścitamudāharati- #yathā vā śuktikāyām#iti /
śuklabhāsvarasya dravyasya puraḥsthitasya sati śuktikārajatasādhāraṇye yāvadatra rajataviniścayo bhavati tāvatkasmācchuktiviniścaya eva na bhavati ? saṃśayo vā dvedhā yuktaḥ ; samānadharmadharmiṇo darśanāt upalabghyanupalabdhyavyavasthātaḥ ; viśeṣadvayasmṛteśca saṃskāronmeṣahetoḥ sādṛśyasya dviṣṭhatvenobhayatra tulyametaditi /
ata uktam- #akasmāt#iti /
anena dṛṣṭasya hetoḥ samānatve 'pyadṛṣṭaṃ heturuktam ; tacca kāryadarśanonneyatvenāsādhāraṇamiti bhāvaḥ /
#ātmānātmavivekinām#iti /
śravaṇamananakuśalatāmātreṇa paṇḍitānām ; anutpannatattvasākṣātkārāṇāmiti yāvat /
taduktam- #paśvādibhiścāviśeṣāt#iti /
śeṣamatirohitārtham /
body.translated_text:
Those who hold that the identification of the self with the body and the like is not erroneous (<s>mithyā</s>) but rather figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>) — like the identification of a boy as a lion — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] presents their view and refutes it: 'Here, others say...' etc.
'One for whom the real distinction [between self and body] is well-established' — such is the [type of] person described.
And this [matter] has been demonstrated by us in the commentary on the superimposition (<s>adhyāsa-bhāṣya</s>) — therefore it is not demonstrated here.
Just as in dim darkness, when the distinguishing features of an object — 'this is a post' — are not grasped, the two — the word 'person' and the cognition [of a person] — which pertain to a post, are doubtful and have the post as their object; for therein, even the indeterminate person-hood has been superimposed.
Thus, having illustrated superimposition in the case of doubt — where it is indeterminate — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] illustrates it in the case of error — where it is determinate: 'Or, as with mother-of-pearl...'
When a shining white substance stands before [one], given the common features between mother-of-pearl and silver, the question arises: So long as there is a determinate cognition of silver here, why is there not a determinate cognition of mother-of-pearl instead? Or a twofold doubt would be appropriate — since the perception of common properties and substrata [applies equally to both]; since the indeterminate condition arising from memory of both alternatives, which is the cause of the awakening of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), applies equally to both due to the similarity being applicable in both directions.
Therefore it is said: 'Without any [apparent] cause.'
By this, in addition to the observed cause (similarity) being equal [in both directions], an unobserved cause is invoked — and that, being inferrable from the effect observed, is extraordinary (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>) — this is the purport.
'Of those who discriminate between self and non-self' — [this means:] of the learned (<s>paṇḍita</s>s), merely by virtue of their skill in hearing and reflection; [i.e.,] those in whom the direct realization of reality has not yet arisen.
As was said: 'And because there is no distinction from animals and the like.'
The rest has an unhidden meaning.

body.text:
jīvato viduṣo 'śarīratve ca śrutismṛtī udāharati- #tathā ca#iti /
subodham /
prakṛtamupasaṃharati- #tasmānnāvagatabrahmātmabhāvasya#iti /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] cites <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s> for the state of being without a body of the living knower: 'And thus...' etc.
This is easily understood.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes the topic at hand: 'Therefore, for one who has realized the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s>...'

body.text:
nanūktaṃ yadi jīvasya brahmātmatvāvagatireva sāṃsārikadharmanivṛttihetuḥ, hanta mananādividhānānarthakyam ; tasmātpratipattividhiparā vedāntā iti, tadanubhāṣya dūṣayati- #yatpunaruktaṃ śravaṇātparācīnayoḥ#iti /
manananididhyāsanayorapi na vidhiḥ, tayoranvayavyatirekasiddhasākṣātkāraphalayorvidhisarūpairvacanairanuvādāt ; tadidamuktam- #avagatyarthatvāt#iti /
brahmasākṣātkāro 'vagatiḥ ; tadarthatvaṃ manananididhyāsanayoranvayavyatirekasiddhamityarthaḥ /
atha kasmānmananādividhireva na bhavatītyata āha- #yadi hyavagatam#iti /
na tāvanmanananididhyāsane pradhānakarmaṇī apūrvaviṣaye amṛtatvaphale ityuktamadhastāt /
ato guṇakarmatvamanayoravaghātaprokṣaṇādivatpariśiṣyate ; tadapyayuktam, anyatropayuktopayokṣyamāṇatvābhāvādātmanaḥ ; viśeṣatastvaupaniṣadasya karmānuṣṭhānavirodhāt- ityarthaḥ /
prakṛtamupasaṃharati- #tasmāt#iti /
body.translated_text:
One might object: If the realization of the individual self's identity with <s>Brahman</s> is itself the cause of the cessation of <s>saṃsāric</s> properties, then alas! the injunctions of reflection (<s>manana</s>) and the like would be purposeless. Therefore, the <s>Vedānta</s>s are oriented toward the injunction of realization — thus, having restated [the objection], [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes it: 'As for what was further said: regarding reflection and meditation (<s>nididhyāsana</s>), which are subsequent to hearing...'
Reflection and meditation too are not [the objects of] injunctions, since they have the fruit of direct realization established through positive and negative concomitance, and since the statements [about them] — being injunction-like in form — are restatements (<s>anuvāda</s>). This is what is stated: 'Because they are for the purpose of realization.'
The realization (<s>avagati</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> is the direct experience of <s>Brahman</s>; the purpose of reflection and meditation is for that [realization] — this being established through positive and negative concomitance — this is the meaning.
Then why should there not simply be an injunction of reflection and the like? To this he says: 'For if [<s>Brahman</s>] has been realized...'
Reflection and meditation are not principal actions directed toward the <s>apūrva</s> (unseen potency) having the fruit of immortality — this has been stated below.
Therefore, what remains for them is the status of subsidiary actions, like threshing (<s>avaghāta</s>), sprinkling (<s>prokṣaṇa</s>), and the like; but even that is not appropriate, since the self — not being employed for anything else or about to be employed — [does not need subsidiaries]; especially because the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> [self-knowledge] conflicts with the performance of [ritual] action — this is the meaning.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes the topic at hand: 'Therefore...'

body.text:
evaṃ ca siddharūpabrahmaparatve upaniṣadām, brahmaṇaḥ śāstrārthasya dharmādanyatvāt, bhinnaviṣayatvena śāstrabhedāt, 'athāto brahmajijñāsā' ityasya śāstrārambhatvamupapadyata ityāha- #evaṃ ca sati#iti /
itarathā tu dharmajijñāsaiveti na śāstrāntaramiti na śāstrāntarārambhatvaṃ syādityāha- #pratipattividhiparatva#iti /
na kevalaṃ siddharūpatvādbrahmātmaikyasya dharmādanyatvam, api tu tadvirodhādapītyupasaṃhāravyājenāha- #tasmādahaṃ brahmāsmi#iti /
#iti#karaṇena jñānaṃ parāmṛśati /
vidhayo hi dharme pramāṇam /
te ca sādhyasādhanetikartavyatābhedādhiṣṭhānā dharmotpādinaśca tadadhiṣṭhānā na brahmātmaikye sati prabhavanti, virodhāt ityarthaḥ /
na kevalaṃ dharmapramāṇasya śāstrasyeyaṃ gatiḥ, api tu sarveṣāṃ pramāṇānāmityāha- #sarvāṇi cetarāṇi pramāṇāni#iti /
kutaḥ ? #na hi#iti /
advaite hi viṣayaviṣayibhāvo nāsti ; na ca kartṛtvam, kāryābhāvāt ; na ca kāraṇatvam, ata eva /
tadidamuktam- #apramātṛkāṇi ca#iti cakāreṇa /
body.translated_text:
And thus, when the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s are oriented toward <s>Brahman</s> as an established reality; since <s>Brahman</s>, the subject-matter of scripture, is different from <s>dharma</s>; and since, due to the difference in subject-matter, the scripture is different [from the <s>Karmakāṇḍa</s>] — the commencement of '<s>athāto brahmajijñāsā</s>' (Now, therefore, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>) as a separate treatise is justified — thus he says: 'And when this is so...'
Otherwise, if [the Vedāntas were oriented toward] the inquiry into <s>dharma</s> alone, there would be no separate treatise and hence no commencement of a separate treatise — thus he says: 'If [they were] oriented toward the injunction of realization...'
Not only is the identity of the Self with <s>Brahman</s> different from <s>dharma</s> by virtue of being an established reality, but also because it contradicts [<s>dharma</s>] — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says this under the guise of a conclusion: 'Therefore, "I am <s>Brahman</s>"...'
By the word '<s>iti</s>' (thus), [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refers to the knowledge [expressed by the statement].
For injunctions are the means of knowledge regarding <s>dharma</s>.
And they — based on the distinctions of what is to be accomplished, the means, and the procedural details — are productive of <s>dharma</s> and are based on those [distinctions]. They are not possible when the identity of the Self with <s>Brahman</s> obtains — because of contradiction — this is the meaning.
Not only is this the situation for scripture as the means of knowledge of <s>dharma</s>, but for all means of knowledge — thus he says: 'And all other means of knowledge...'
Why? 'For...' — in non-duality (<s>advaita</s>), there is no relation of object and subject; nor is there agency, because of the absence of an effect; nor is there causality, for the same reason.
This is what is stated: 'And non-knowers' — [indicated] by the word '<s>ca</s>' (and).

body.text:
atraiva brahmavidāṃ gāthā udāharati- #api cāhuḥ#iti /
putradārādiṣvātmābhimāno gauṇaḥ /
yathā svaduḥkhena duḥkhī, yathā svasukhena sukhī, tathā putrādigatenāpīti so 'yaṃ gauṇaḥ /
na tvekatvābhimānaḥ, bhedasyānubhavasiddhatvāt /
tasmāt 'gaurvāhīkaḥ' itivadgauṇaḥ /
dehendriyādiṣu tvabhedānubhavānna gauṇa ātmābhimānaḥ ; kiṃ tu śuktau rajatajñānavanmithyā /
tadevaṃ dvividho 'yamātmābhimāno lokayātrāṃ vahati /
tadasattve tu na lokayātrā, nāpi brahmātmaikatvānubhavaḥ, tadupāyasya śravaṇamananāderabhāvāt /
tadidamāha- #putradehādibādhanāt# /
gauṇātmano 'sattve putrakalatrādibādhanam ; mamakārābhāva iti yāvat /
mithyātmano 'sattve dehendriyādibādhanaṃ śravaṇādibādhanaṃ ca /
tataśca na kevalaṃ lokayātrāsamucchedaḥ ; #sadbrahmāhamityevaṃ bodhi#bodhaśīlaṃ yat #kāryam#, advaitasākṣātkāra iti yāvat, tadapi #kathaṃ bhavet ?#kutastadasaṃbhava ityata āha- #anveṣṭavyātmavijñānātprākpramātṛtvamātmanaḥ# /
upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat ; pramāprameyapramāṇavibhāga ityapi draṣṭavyam /
etaduktaṃ bhavati- eṣa hi vibhāgo 'dvaitasākṣātkārakāraṇam, tato niyamena prāgbhāvāt ; tena tadabhāve kāryaṃ notpadyata iti /
na ca pramāturātmano 'nveṣṭavya ātmānya ityāha- #anviṣṭaḥ syātpramātaiva pāpmadoṣādivarjitaḥ# /
uktaṃ hi grīvāsthagraiveyakanidarśanam /
body.translated_text:
Here itself, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] cites the verse (<s>gāthā</s>) of the knowers of <s>Brahman</s>: 'Moreover, they say...'
The identification of the self with sons, wife, and the like is figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>).
Just as one is unhappy with one's own unhappiness, and happy with one's own happiness, so too with the happiness and unhappiness of one's son and the like — this is that figurative [identification].
But [it is] not an identification of oneness, since the difference [between self and son etc.] is established through experience.
Therefore, [it is] figurative, like 'the ox is a <s>Vāhīka</s> [man].'
But with respect to the body, senses, and the like, the self-identification is not figurative — because of the experience of non-difference. Rather, [it is] erroneous, like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.
Thus this twofold self-identification sustains worldly transaction (<s>lokayātrā</s>).
In the absence of that [twofold identification], there would be neither worldly transaction nor the experience of the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s> — since the means to it, hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and the like, would be absent.
This is what is stated: 'Because of the sublation of sons, body, etc.'
In the absence of the figurative self, there is the sublation of sons, wife, and the like — meaning: the absence of the possessive sense (<s>mamakāra</s>).
In the absence of the erroneous self, there is the sublation of body, senses, and the like, as well as the sublation of hearing and the like.
Consequently, not only is there the destruction of worldly transaction; 'How can there be the effect' — namely, the direct realization of non-duality — 'that is of the nature of the understanding (<s>bodhi</s>) "I am the real <s>Brahman</s>"?' Whence its impossibility? To this he says: 'Before the attainment of the knowledge of the Self that is to be sought, there is the knower-status (<s>pramātṛtva</s>) of the Self.'
And this is indicative [of more]; the division into valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>), and means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) should also be understood.
What is stated amounts to this: this division [into knower etc.] is the cause of the direct realization of non-duality, and necessarily precedes it in time; therefore, in its absence, the effect is not produced.
And the self that is to be sought is not other than the self that is the knower — thus he says: 'The very knower, free from sin, defect, and the like, would be the one sought.'
For the illustration of the necklace on one's own neck has been stated.

body.translated_text: One might object: How can the experience of ultimate non-duality arise from something that is not a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>)? To this he says: 'Just as the cognition identifying the body with the Self is accepted as a valid means of knowledge, so too is this worldly [means of knowledge] a <s>pramāṇa</s>.' He states the limit of this: 'Until the ascertainment of the Self' — meaning until the direct realization of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. What is being said is this: Even those who hold that the phenomenal world is ultimately real must admit that the identification of the Self with the body and such is false, since it is sublated by valid knowledge. And it must be acknowledged that this [false identification] is the cause of all valid cognitions and sustains future worldly transactions. This same method will apply in our case too, for the direct realization of non-duality (<s>advaita</s>). Nor is this direct realization of non-duality, being a modification of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), absolutely ultimate. But the realization that is to come is not a produced effect, since it is of the nature of <s>Brahman</s> itself. If <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) were to destroy <s>avidyā</s> or to produce [knowledge], there is no impossibility in that. And the <s>Śruti</s> also says:

body.text: vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca yastadvedobhayaṃ saha /
body.translated_text: He who knows both <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) together,

body.text: avidyayā mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā vidyayāmṛtamaśnute //
body.translated_text: Having crossed death through <s>avidyā</s>, he attains immortality through <s>vidyā</s>.

children.translated_text: Thus.
Therefore, everything is fully explained.

body.text: #iti catuḥsūtrī samāptā# /
body.translated_text: Thus the <s>Catuḥsūtrī</s> (section of four <s>sūtra</s>s) is completed.

children.translated_text: Thus: 'The authoritativeness of the <s>Vedānta</s>s regarding <s>Brahman</s>, whose nature is already established without connection to any effect,
Has been demonstrated by itself with respect to the highest human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).'

body.text:

tacca brahmaṇīti paramārthataḥ /
tvadyāpi brahmaṇyeveti vyutpāditam /

atra ca vipratipatteḥ pravādīnāṃ viśeṣānupalambhe sati saṃśayaḥ /

jīvāṇuvyatiriktacetaneśvaranimittādhiṣṭhitāścaturvidhāḥ paramāṇavo jagadupādānakāraṇamanumitamanuvadantīti kāṇādāḥ /
ādigrahaṇenābhāvopādānatvādi grahītavyam /
anirvacanīyānādyavidyāśaktimañcetanopādānaṃ jagadāgamikamiti brahmavidaḥ /

children.translated_text: The source of these divergent views is inference, scripture, pseudo-inference, and pseudo-scriptural [arguments].
Given this doubt arising from the divergent views, what is initially concluded?
Since <s>Brahman</s> lacks the powers of knowledge and action and is not subject to transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>),
There is no possibility [of it being the cause]; but in <s>Pradhāna</s>, which possesses all powers, there is such possibility.

body.translated_text: Having proposed the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmajijñāsā</s>), the authoritativeness of the <s>Vedānta</s>s regarding the omnipotent cause of the origination, sustenance, and dissolution of the world has been established through the sequence of <s>sūtra</s>s beginning with 'From which [<s>Brahman</s>] the origin and so forth of this [world]' (<s>janmādyasya yataḥ</s>) and ending with 'But that [is established] through harmonious interpretation' (<s>tattu samanvayāt</s>). And that [cause] is <s>Brahman</s> — this is the ultimate [meaning]. Even now it has been demonstrated that it is <s>Brahman</s> alone. Here a doubt arises: Is that material cause (<s>upādānakāraṇa</s>) of the world conscious (<s>cetana</s>) or unconscious (<s>acetana</s>)? And here the doubt arises from the divergent views of proponents, when no distinguishing characteristic is perceived. The <s>Sāṃkhya</s>s hold that the unconscious <s>Pradhāna</s>, established by inference as the material cause of the world, is merely reiterated by the <s>Upaniṣad</s>s. The <s>Kāṇāda</s>s (Vaiśeṣikas) hold that the four types of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>s), supervised by a conscious <s>Īśvara</s> distinct from individual souls (<s>jīva</s>s), inferred as the material cause of the world, are reiterated [by scripture]. By the word 'and so forth' (<s>ādi</s>), [positions such as] the void (<s>abhāva</s>) being the material cause should also be understood. The knowers of <s>Brahman</s> hold that the world, known through scripture (<s>āgama</s>), has a conscious being as its material cause, endowed with the power of beginningless, indescribable <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).

body.text:

na ca jñānakriye cidātmani staḥ, tasyāpariṇāmitvādekatvācca /
triguṇe tu pradhāne pariṇāmini saṃbhavataḥ /
yadyapi ca sāmyāvasthāyāṃ pradhāne samudācaradvṛttinī kriyājñāne na staḥ, tathāpyavyaktena śaktyātmanā rūpeṇa saṃbhavata eva /
tathā ca pradhānameva sarvajñaṃ ca sarvaśakti ca /
na tu brahma /
svarūpacaitanyaṃ tvasyāvṛttitamanupayogi jīvātmanāmivāsmākam /
na ca svarūpacaitanye kartṛtvam, akāryatvāttasya /
kāryatve vā na sarvadā sarvajñatā /
bhogāpargalakṣaṇapuruṣārthadvayaprayuktānādipradhānapuruṣasaṃyoganimittastu mahadahaṅkārādikrameṇācetanasyāpi cetanānadhiṣṭhitasya pradhānasya pariṇāmaḥ sargaḥ /
dṛṣṭaṃ cācetanaṃ cetanānadhiṣṭhitaṃ puruṣārthe pravartamānam /

children.translated_text: Just as unconscious milk flows for the nourishment of the calf.

children.text: 'tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya' ityādyāśca śrutayo 'cetane 'pi cetanavadupacārātsvakāryonmukhamādarśayanti, yathā kūlaṃ pipatiṣatīti /
children.translated_text: And the scriptures such as 'It willed: May I become many, may I be born' (<s>tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya</s>) show even the unconscious [<s>Pradhāna</s>] as if it were conscious, through figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>), as being directed toward its own effect — just as [one says] 'the riverbank wishes to fall.'
'When something is heard in a context where [the primary meaning] predominates, it is understood accordingly;
When heard in a context where the secondary meaning (<s>bhākta</s>) predominates, it is understood as figurative (<s>bhākta</s>).'

body.translated_text: The powers of knowledge and action are indeed to be inferred from the observed effects of knowledge and action. And knowledge and action do not exist in the conscious Self (<s>cidātman</s>), since it is not subject to transformation and is one. But in the <s>Pradhāna</s>, consisting of the three <s>guṇa</s>s and subject to transformation, they are possible. Although in the state of equilibrium (<s>sāmyāvasthā</s>), action and knowledge, which function as ongoing modifications, do not exist in <s>Pradhāna</s>, nevertheless in the unmanifest form as potency they indeed exist. Thus <s>Pradhāna</s> alone is omniscient and omnipotent, not <s>Brahman</s>. The essential consciousness (<s>svarūpacaitanya</s>) of this [<s>Pradhāna</s>], being without modification, is useless — just like our own [consciousness] as individual souls (<s>jīvātman</s>s). And there is no agency in essential consciousness, since it is not an effect. Or if it were an effect, then omniscience would not be constant. The transformation of <s>Pradhāna</s>, which is unconscious and not supervised by any conscious being, into creation proceeds through the sequence of <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, and so forth, occasioned by the beginningless conjunction of <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, impelled by the two human purposes (<s>puruṣārtha</s>s) characterized as enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). And it is observed that unconscious [things], not supervised by a conscious being, operate for the sake of a person —

' api cāhurvṛddhāḥ- yathāgryaprāye likhitaṃ dṛṣṭvā vadanti bhavedayamagryaḥ iti, tathedapi 'tā āpa aikṣanta' tatteja aikṣata ityādyupacāraprāye kṣutam tadaikṣata ityaupacārikameva vijñeyam /
anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi iti ca pradhānasya jīvātmatvaṃ jīvārthakāritayāha /
yathā hi bhadraseno rājārthakārī rājñā bhadraseno mamātmetyupacaryate, evaṃ tattvamasi ityādyāḥ śrutayo bhāktāḥ saṃpattyarthā vā draṣṭavyāḥ /
svamapīto bhavati iti ca niruktaṃ jīvasya pradhāne svakīye 'pyayaṃ suṣuptāvasthāyāṃ brūte /
pradhānāṃśatamaḥsamudrake hi jīvonidrāṇastamasīva magno bhavati /

body.translated_text: And the elders also say: Just as, seeing something written in a context where the primary meaning predominates, people say 'this must be the chief [meaning],' so too, in the case of scriptural statements like 'Those waters willed' (<s>tā āpa aikṣanta</s>) and 'That fire willed' (<s>tatteja aikṣata</s>), which are in a context where figurative usage predominates, the statement 'It willed' (<s>tadaikṣata</s>) should be understood as merely figurative. And by the statement 'Having entered with this living Self, let me manifest names and forms' (<s>anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi</s>), he teaches that the <s>Pradhāna</s> has the nature of the individual soul (<s>jīvātman</s>), since it acts for the sake of the <s>jīva</s>. Just as <s>Bhadrasena</s>, acting for the king's sake, is figuratively called by the king 'my self' — so too, scriptures like 'You are that' (<s>tattvamasi</s>) should be understood as figurative or as meditative identification (<s>saṃpatti</s>). And the statement 'He has gone to his own' (<s>svamapīto bhavati</s>) describes the <s>jīva</s>'s [mergence] into its own <s>Pradhāna</s> in the state of deep sleep. For the <s>jīva</s>, sleeping in the ocean of darkness that is a portion of <s>Pradhāna</s>, becomes as if submerged in darkness. As they say: 'Sleep is a mental modification based on the cognition of absence' (<s>abhāvapratyayālambanā vṛttirnidrā</s>). The meaning is: The absence of other modifications such as valid cognition and so forth is its cause; darkness (<s>tamas</s>) is its support; sleep is the modification of the <s>jīva</s>. Similarly, the <s>Śvetāśvatara</s> <s>mantra</s>, having introduced the omniscient one, says 'The lord of the lords of the instruments that are causes' (<s>sakāraṇāṃ karaṇādhipādhipaḥ</s>) — this is intended with reference to <s>Pradhāna</s>. The omniscience of <s>Pradhāna</s> alone has been established above. Therefore, the scriptures reiterate that the unconscious <s>Pradhāna</s> is the material cause of the world — this is the prior position (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>). In the same way, the scriptures should somehow be interpreted in accordance with the doctrine of the <s>Kāṇāda</s>s and others as well. The literal meaning, however, is: 'Even in the position where <s>Pradhāna</s> is the cause' — meaning 'of <s>Pradhāna</s> also.' The particles '<s>api</s>' have the sense of emphasis (<s>eva</s>). One might object: If its omniscience is due to the preponderance of <s>sattva</s>, then why does not its total ignorance result from the preponderance of <s>tamas</s>? To this he says: 'And through that property of <s>sattva</s>, namely knowledge.' For <s>sattva</s> is luminous by nature, and its unsurpassed excellence is the seed of omniscience. As they say: 'The unsurpassed seed of omniscience.' Whatever is surpassable is seen to reach an unsurpassed [degree] somewhere — just as among the jujube fruit, emblic myrobalan, and wood-apple, magnitude is surpassable, but in space, the supremely great, it is unsurpassed. Similarly, knowledge too, being surpassable in having one, two, or many objects, must somewhere reach an unsurpassed [degree]. And this very unsurpassedness of it is its knowing all that is to be known. This omniscience is possible when <s>sattva</s> reaches unsurpassed excellence. What is being said is this: Although <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> also exist, nevertheless, due to the extreme imbalance of the <s>guṇa</s>s impelled by the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>, when <s>sattva</s> reaches unsurpassed excellence, omniscience as an effect is produced; and even in the state of <s>Pradhāna</s>, by intending only that [<s>sattva</s> aspect] and disregarding the effect of <s>tamas</s>, <s>Pradhāna</s> is figuratively called omniscient. He states what is excluded by the emphatic particles: 'Not of [consciousness] alone.' For no single thing produces just one effect, but rather many. The conscious Self (<s>cidātman</s>) is one, whereas <s>Pradhāna</s> consists of three <s>guṇa</s>s — therefore effects can arise from that [<s>Pradhāna</s>] alone, not from the conscious Self. And he says that even according to your view, the omniscience of the conscious Self is accepted merely on the basis of capacity, not through the connection with any effect: 'Even by you.' He elaborates the point that [omniscience does not belong] to that which alone is without effect, with a backward glance [at the previous argument]: 'Before origination. Moreover, of <s>Pradhāna</s>.' The word 'ca' means 'moreover.' When this [<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>] has been thus presented, he states: '<s>Īkṣaternāśabdam</s>' (Because of willing/seeing, [<s>Pradhāna</s> is] not [the cause, as it is] not scriptural).

children.text: nāmarūpaprapañcalakṣaṇakāryadarśanādetatkāraṇamātravaditi sāmānyakalpamāyāmiti pramāṇaṃ, na tu tadacetanaṃ cetanamiti vā viśeṣakalpanāyāmastyanumānamityupariṣṭātpravedayiṣyate /
children.translated_text: From the observation of the effect characterized as the phenomenal world of names and forms, inference is valid only for the general determination that 'this has some cause' — but there is no inference for the specific determination that it is unconscious or conscious. This will be explained later.
Therefore, with respect to the knowledge of the specific nature of the cause of the phenomenal world of names and forms, scripture (<s>āmnāya</s>) alone is the revered authority.
When the cause of the world, to be known solely through scripture, [is examined] — 'Through consideration of the sequential context, when scripture directly states

children.text: jagadbījaṃ tadeveṣṭaṃ cetane ca sa āñjasaḥ //
children.translated_text: The seed of the world, that alone is to be accepted; and in the case of a conscious [cause], that [direct statement] is indeed direct (<s>āñjasa</s>).'

body.text:
teṣu teṣu khalvāmnāyapradeśeṣu tadaikṣata ityevañjātīyakairvākyairīkṣituḥ kāraṇajjagajjanmākhyāyata iti /
na ca pradhānaparamāṇvāderacetanasyekṣitṛtvamāñjasam /
sattvāṃśenekṣitṛ pradhānaṃ, tasya prakāśakatvāditi cenna /
tasya jāḍyena tattvānupapatteḥ /
kastarhi rajatastamobhyāṃ sattvasya viśeṣaḥ /
svacchatāṣa /
svacchaṃ hi sattvam /
asvacche ca rajastamasī /
body.translated_text: In those various scriptural passages, by statements of the type 'It willed' (<s>tadaikṣata</s>), the birth of the world is declared from a cause that is a willer (<s>īkṣitṛ</s>). And the capacity to will cannot directly belong to something unconscious like <s>Pradhāna</s> or atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>). If it be said that <s>Pradhāna</s> wills through its <s>sattva</s> aspect, since <s>sattva</s> is illuminating — no, because due to its inertness (<s>jāḍya</s>), that [illuminating capacity] is not tenable. What then is the distinguishing characteristic of <s>sattva</s> from <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>? Transparency (<s>svacchatā</s>). For <s>sattva</s> is transparent, while <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> are non-transparent.

body.text:

nahi prādhānikānyantarbahiḥkaraṇāni trayodaśa sattvaguṇapradhānānyapi svayamevācetanāni, tadvṛttayā svaṃ vā paraṃ vā veditumutsahante /
no khalvandhāḥ sahasramapi pānthāḥ panthānaṃ vidanti /
cakṣuṣmatā caikena cedvedyate, sa eva tarhi mārgadarśī svatantraḥ kartā netā teṣām /
evaṃ buddhisattvasya svayamacetanasya citibimbasaṃkrāntyā cedāpannaṃ caitanyasya jñātṛtvaṃ, citireva jñātrī svatantrā, nāntarbahiṣkaraṇānyandhasahasrapratimānyasvasantrāṇi /
na cāsyaściteḥ asti vyāpārayogaḥ /
na ca tadayoge 'pyajñātṛtvaṃ, vyāpāravatāmapi jaḍānāmajñatvāt /
tasmādantaḥkaraṇavartinaṃ vyāpāramāropya citiśaktau kartṛtvābhimānaḥ /
antaḥkaraṇe vā caitanyamāropya tasya jñātṛtvābhimānaḥ /
sarvathā bhavanmateṣaḍapi nedaṃ svābhāvikaṃ kvacidapi jñātṛtvaṃ, api tu sāṃvyavahārārikameveti paramārthaḥ /
nityasyātmano jñānaṃ pariṇāma iti ca bhedābhedapakṣamapākurvadbhirapāstam /

children.text: kūṭasthasya nityasyātmano 'vyāpāravata eva bhinnaṃ jñānaṃ dharma iti copariṣṭādapākariṣyate /
children.translated_text: And the [view] that knowledge is a distinct property (<s>dharma</s>) of the immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), eternal Self, which has no activity, will be refuted later.

children.text: tasmādvastuto 'navacchinnaṃ caitanyaṃ tattvānyatvābhyāmanirvacanīyāvyākṛtavyācikīrṣitanāmarūpaviṣayāvacchinnaṃ sajjñānaṃ kāryaṃ, tasya kartā īśvaro jñātā sarvajñaḥ sarvaśaktiriti siddham /
children.translated_text: Therefore, in reality, consciousness — which is undivided — delimited by name and form that are inexpressible (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) as either identical with or different from [<s>Brahman</s>], [and that are] unevolved (<s>avyākṛta</s>) [and] intended to be manifested — is the effect, endowed with knowledge (<s>sajjñāna</s>). Its maker is <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), the knower, the omniscient (<s>sarvajña</s>), the omnipotent (<s>sarvaśakti</s>) — this is established.

children.text: tathā ca śrutiḥ- tapasā cīyate brahma tato 'nnamabhijāyate /
children.translated_text: And thus the <s>Śruti</s> [states]: '<s>Brahman</s> is augmented by <s>tapas</s> (knowledge-austerity); from that, food (<s>anna</s>) is born;

children.text: annātprāṇo manaḥ satyaṃ lokāḥ karmasu cāmṛtam //
children.translated_text: from food, <s>Prāṇa</s> (the vital breath), mind, truth (<s>satya</s>), the worlds, and in actions, immortality (<s>amṛta</s>).'

body.translated_text: And the designation of the transparent [<s>sattva</s>] as 'illuminating' is due to its capacity to receive the reflection of consciousness (<s>caitanyabimba</s>), not so for the other two, since they lack the capacity to receive that [reflection] due to their non-transparency. Just as among earthen [substances], only a gem has the capacity to receive reflections, not clods of earth and the like. But <s>Brahman</s>'s capacity to will is direct, since its nature as eternal knowledge is ascertained from scripture. One might object: For this very reason it does not will, since its willing, being of the nature of eternal knowledge, is not an action, and hence <s>Brahman</s> has no causal relation to it. And when there is cessation of the general [category of] being a cause for something that has no action as its cause, there is cessation of its specific form, namely agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>), which is pervaded by that [general category]. True — the consciousness that is the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, being eternal, is not an action. But while it is undivided, its delimitation by this or that object, with differences superimposed [upon it], admits of non-eternality and the character of being an effect. And in willing so characterized, which encompasses all objects, the agency of <s>Brahman</s> in the form of independence (<s>svātantrya</s>) is well established. Although the absolute indifference of the immutable, eternal, untransformable [<s>Brahman</s>] is its real [nature], nevertheless, as delimited by beginningless, indescribable <s>avidyā</s>, the appearance of having activity occurs — thus agency is established. Even the opponents must accept this kind of agency — namely, the agency of the immutable, eternal [consciousness] with respect to modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>s) — since the knower-nature is perceived as sharing a common substratum with consciousness in general (<s>caitanyasāmānya</s>). For indeed the thirteen internal and external instruments (<s>karaṇa</s>s), which belong to <s>Pradhāna</s> and are predominantly of the <s>sattva</s> <s>guṇa</s>, being themselves unconscious, are unable by their modifications to know either themselves or anything else. A thousand blind travelers cannot know the path. But if one person with eyes knows it, then he alone is the guide, the independent agent, the leader of those [blind travelers]. Similarly, if the knower-nature of the intellect's <s>sattva</s>, which is itself unconscious, is obtained through the transference of the reflection of consciousness (<s>citibimba</s>), then consciousness (<s>citi</s>) alone is the knower, independent — not the internal and external instruments, which are like a thousand blind [travelers], lacking independence. And this consciousness has no connection with activity. Nor does the absence of activity entail that it is not a knower, since even things possessed of activity, if inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), are not knowers. Therefore, by superimposing the activity residing in the inner organ onto the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>), there is the false identification of agency; or by superimposing consciousness onto the inner organ, there is the false identification of knower-ship in it. In every way, according to your [<s>Sāṃkhya</s>] doctrine, this knower-nature does not intrinsically belong to anything, but is merely conventional (<s>sāṃvyavahārika</s>) — this is the ultimate truth. And the position that knowledge is a transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of the eternal Self has been refuted by those who reject the doctrine of identity-in-difference (<s>bhedābheda</s>).

children.translated_text: 'He who is omniscient (<s>sarvajña</s>), all-knowing (<s>sarvavid</s>), whose <s>tapas</s> is of the nature of knowledge —
from Him this <s>Brahman</s> — name, form, and food — is born.'

body.text:
iti /
tapasā jñānena avyākṛtanāmarūpaviṣayeṇa cīyate tadvyācikīrṣavadbhavati, yathā kuvindādiravyākṛtaṃ paṭādi buddhāvālikhya cikīrṣati /
ekadharmavān dvitīyadharmopajananena upacita ucyate /
vyācikīrṣāyāṃ copacaye sati tato nāmarūpamannamadanīyaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ saṃsāriṇāṃ vyācikīrṣitamabhijāyate /
tasmādavyākṛtādvyācikīrṣitādannātprāṇo hiraṇyagarbho brahmaṇo jñānakriyāśaktyadhiṣṭhānaṃ jagatsūtrātmā sādhāraṇe jāyate, yathāvyākṛtāt vyacikīrṣitātpaṭādavāntarakāryaṃ dvitantukādi /
tasmācca prāṇānmana ākhyaṃ saṃkalpavikalpādivyākaraṇātmakaṃ jāyate /
tato vyākaraṇātmakānmanasaḥ satyaśabdavācyānyākāśādīni jāyante /
tebhyaśca satyākhyebhyo 'nukrameṇa lokāḥ bhūrādayaḥ teṣu manuṣṭādiprāṇino varṇāśramakrameṇa karmāṇi dharmādharmarūpāṇi jāyante /
karmasu cāmṛtaṃ phalaṃ svarganarakādi /
tacca svaninittayordharmādharmayoḥ satorna vinaśyatītyamṛtam /
yāvaddharmādharmabhāvīti yāvat /
yaḥ sarvajñaḥ sāmānyataḥ, sarvavidviśeṣataḥ /
yasya bhagavato jñānamayaṃ tapo dharmo nāyāsamayam, tasmādbrahmamaḥ pūrvasmādetatparaṃ kāryaṃ brahma /
kiñca nāmarūpamannaṃ ca vrīhiyavādi jāyata iti /
tasmātpradhānasya sāmyāvasthāyāmanīkṣitṛtvāt, kṣetrajñānāṃ ca satyapi caitanye sargādau viṣayānīkṣaṇāt, mukhyasaṃbhave copacārasyānyāyyatvāt, mumukṣoścāyathārthopadeśānupapatteḥ, muktivirodhitvāt, tejaḥprabhṛtīnāṃ ca mukhyāsaṃbhavenopacārāśrayaṇasya yuktisiddhatvāt, saṃśaye ca tatprāyapāṭhasya niścāyakatvāt, iha tu mukhyasyautsargikatvena niścaye sati saṃśayābhāvāt, anyathā kirātaśatasaṃkīrṇadeśanivāsino brāhmaṇāyanasyāpi kirātatvāpatteḥ, brahmaivekṣitranādyanirvācyāvidyāsacivaṃ jagadupādānaṃ, śuktiriva samāropitasya rajatasya, marīcaya iva jalasya, evaścadramā iva dvatīyasya cadramasaḥ /
na tvacetanaṃ pradhānaparamāṇatvādi /
aśabdaṃ hi tat /
na ca pradhānaṃ paramāṇavo vā tadatiriktasarvajñeśvarādhiṣṭhitā jagadupādānamiti sāṃprataṃ kāryatvāt /
kāraṇātkāryāṇāṃ bhedābhāvāt kāraṇajñānena samastakāryaparijñānasya mṛdādinidarśanenāgamena prasādhitvāt, bhede ca tadanupapatteḥ /
sākṣācca 'ekamevādvitīyam' 'neha nānāsti kiñcana' mṛtyoḥ , mṛtyumāpnoti' ityādibhirbrahmātiriktasya prapañcasya pratiṣedhācetanopādānameva jagat, bhujaṅga ivāropiti gajjūpādāna iti siddhāntaḥ /
sadupādānatve hi siddhe jagatastadupādānaṃ cetanamacetanaṃ veti saṃśayya mīmāṃsyeta /
adyāpi tu sadupādānatvamasiddhamityata āha- #tatredaṃśabdavācyam#ityādi #darśayati#ityantena /
tathāpīkṣitā pāramārthikapradhānakṣetrajñātirikta īśvaro bhaviṣyati; yathāhurhairaṇyagarbhā ityataḥ śrutiḥ patitā- 'ekamevādvitīyaṃ' iti /
bahu syām' iti cācetanaṃ kāraṇamātmana eva bahubhāvamāha /
tenāpi kāraṇaccetanābhinnaṃ kāryamabhyupagamyate /
yadyapyākāśādyā bhūtasṛṣṭistathāpi tejo 'bannānāmeva trivṛtkaraṇasya vivakṣitatvāttatra tejasaḥ prāthamyāttejaḥ prathamamuktam /
ekamadvitīyaṃ jagadupādānamityatra śrutyantaramapi paṭhati- #tathānyatreti# /
brahma catuṣpādaṣṭāśaphaṃ ṣoḍaśakalaśam /
tadyathā- prācī pratīcī dakṣiṇodīcīti catasraḥ kalā brahmaṇaḥ prakāśavānnāma prathamaḥ pādaḥ /
tadardhaṃ śaphaḥ /
tathā pṛthivyantarīkṣaṃ dyauḥ samudra ityaparaścatasraḥ kalā dvitīyaḥ pādo 'nantavānnāma /
tathāgniḥ sūryacadramā vidyuditi catasraḥ kalāḥ, sa jyotiṣmānnāma tṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ /
prāṇaścakṣuḥ śrotraṃ vāgiti catasraḥ kālāḥ, sa caturthaṃ āyatanavānnāma brahmaṇaḥ pādaḥ /
tadevaṃ ṣoḍaśakalaṃ ṣoḍaśāvayavaṃ brahmopāsyamiti siddham /
syādetat /
īkṣateriti tipā dhātusvarūpamucyate /
na cāvivakṣitārthasya dhātusvarūpasya cetanopādānasādhanatvasaṃbhava ityata āha- #īkṣateriti#dhātvarthanirdeśo 'bhimataḥ, viṣayiṇaṃ niṣayalakṣaṇāt /
prasiddhā ceyaṃ lakṣaṇetyāha- #yajataritivaditi# /
'yaḥ sarvajñaḥ iti sāmānyataḥ; sarvavit iti viśeṣataḥ /
sāṃkhyīyaṃ svamatasamādhānamupanyasya dūṣayati- #yattūktaṃ sattvadharmeṇeti# /
punaḥ sāṃkhyamutthāpayati- #nanūktamiti# /
pariharati- #tadapīti# /
sāmudācaradvṛtti tāvanna bhavati sattvaṃ, guṇavaiṣamyaṃ sāmyānupapatteḥ /
na cāvyaktena rūpeṇa jñānamapapayujyate, rajatastamasostatpratibandhasyāpi sūkṣmeṇa rūpeṇa sadbhāvādityarthaḥ /
apica caitanyapradhānavṛttivacano jānātirna cācetane vṛttimātre dṛṣṭacaraprayoga ityāha- #apica nāsākṣiketi# /
kathaṃ tarhi yogināṃ sattvāśotkarṣahetukaṃ sarvajñatvamityata āha- #yogināṃ tviti# /
sattvāṃśotkarṣo hi yogināṃ cetanyacakṣuṣmatāmupakaroti, nāndhasya pradhānasyetyarthaḥ /
yadi tu kāpilamatamapahāya hairaṇyagarbhamāsthīyeta tatrāpyāha- #atha punaḥ sākṣinimittamiti# /
teṣāmapi hi prakṛṣṭasattvopādānaṃ puruṣaviśeṣasyaiva kleśakarmavipākāśayāparābhṛṣṭasya sarvajñatvaṃ, na tu pradhānasyācetanasya /
tadapi cādvaitaśrutibhirapāstamiti bhāvaḥ /
pūrvapakṣabījamanubhāṣate- #yatpunaruktaṃ brahmaṇo 'pīti# /
cetanyasya śuddhasya nityatve 'pyupahitaṃ sadanityaṃ kāryaṃ, ākāśamiva ghaṭāvacchinnamityabhisaṃdhāya pariharati- #idaṃ tāvadbhavāniti /
pratatauṣṇyaprakāśe savitari#ityetadapi viṣayāvacchinnaprakāśaḥ kāryamityetadabhaiprāyam /
vaiṣamyaṃ codayati- #nanu savituriti# /
kiṃ vāstavaṃ karmābhāvamabhipretya vaiṣamyamāha bhavān uta tadvivakṣābhāvam /
tatra yadi tadvivakṣābhāvaṃ, tadā prakāśayatītyanena mā bhūtsāmyaṃ, prakāśata ityanena tvasti /
nahyatra karma vivakṣaitam /
atha ca prakāśasvabhāva pratyāsta svātantryaṃ savituriti pariharati- #na /
asatyapi karmaṇīti# /
asatyapītyavivakṣite 'pītyarthaḥ /
atha vāstavaṃ karmābhāvamabhisaṃdhāya vaiṣamyamucyeta, tanna, asiddhatvātkarmābhāvasya, vivikṣitatvāccātra karmaṇa iti pariharati- #karmāpekṣāyāṃ tviti# /
yāsāṃ sati karmaṇyavivakṣite śrutīnāmupapattistāsāṃ sati karmaṇi vivakṣite sutarāmityarthaḥ /
#yatprasādāditi# /
yasya bhagavata īśvarasya prasādāt tasya nityasiddhasyeśvarasya nityaṃ jñānaṃ bhavatīti kimu vaktavyamiti yojanā /
yathāduryogaśāstrakārāḥ- 'tataḥ pratyakcetanādhigamo 'pyantarāyābhāśca' iti /
tadbhāṣyakārāśca bhaktiviśeṣādāvarjita īśvarastamanugṛhṇāti jñānavairāgyādinā iti /
#savitṛprakāśavaditi# /
vastuto nityasya kāraṇānapekṣāṃ svarūpeṇoktvā vyatirekamukhenāpyāha- #api cāvidyādimata ityādi# /
ādigrahaṇena kāmakarmādayaḥ saṃgṛhyante /
