children.translated_text: Nor is the superimposed snake different from the rope.
Therefore, there is no violation of the <s>sūtra</s>.

children.text: avidyākalpitaṃ ca kartṛtvabhoktṛtvaṃ yathālokasiddhamupāśritya karmavidhayaḥ pravṛttāḥ, śyenādividhaya iva niṣiddhe 'pi 'na hiṃsyātsarvā bhūtāni' iti sādhyāṃśe 'bhicāre 'tikrāntaniṣedhaṃ puruṣamāśrityāvidyāvatpuruṣāśrayatvācchastrasyetyuktam /
children.translated_text: And the ritual injunctions operate by presupposing the agency and enjoyership that are imagined through <s>avidyā</s> as established in common experience — just as the injunctions of the <s>Śyena</s> (hawk-sacrifice) and the like, even though [harming] is prohibited by 'one should not harm any being,' operate by presupposing a person who has transgressed the prohibition and is intent upon sorcery in the condemned portion — because scripture presupposes a person possessed of <s>avidyā</s>. This has been stated.
This is what [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Of all of them' etc. // [End of <s>Sūtra</s>] 19 //

body.translated_text:
Having taught the <s>jīva</s> — which is in reality different from the <s>Paramātman</s> — as identical with the immortal and fearless Self, like the shadow-person, <s>Prajāpati</s> subsequently teaches the <s>Paramātman</s> as possessing immortality, fearlessness, and the like — but he is not declaring the <s>jīva</s>'s identity with the <s>Paramātman</s>, just as [he did not declare it] for the shadow-person — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Nor is this one identified in the eye the shadow-person' etc.
The Self indicated in the eye is indeed taught [as the Self], not the shadow-person.
Therefore, the illustration is unestablished.
Moreover, in the second and other stages too, since the introduction is 'I shall explain this very [Self] to you further,' what is indicated in the first stage is not the shadow-person, but rather it is shown to be another, i.e., the Self that is different from that [shadow-person] — otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of <s>Prajāpati</s> being a deceiver — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Likewise in the second [stage] too' etc.
But why should the shadow-person itself not be the <s>jīva</s>? And thus the pronoun 'this' (<s>etam</s>) would refer back to the shadow-person — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Moreover, "Today in a dream I [saw] an elephant"' etc.
The word 'moreover' (<s>kiñca</s>) indicates a cumulative statement, declaring conjunction with the previous argument; and that [argument] is through the channel of refuting an objection.
The shadow-person is impermanent, whereas this Self shines as permanent, because of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) — this is the meaning.
'For indeed, this one does not [become] thus' etc.
This one — the one who is asleep.
At present — in the state of deep sleep.
[He] does not know the self — the self that is the locus of ego-sense.
In what manner does he not know? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'That I am this, these beings too' etc. — as in waking and dream.
By the passage 'For there is no cessation of the knowing of the knower, because of its imperishability' — using imperishability as an established reason — the recognition of the Self by one who has awakened from sleep is stated: 'The very one who, having been awake, slept — that very one is now awake.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the view of the Teacher's school: 'But some [say]' etc.
If the pronoun 'this' (<s>etam</s>) referred back to the person located in the eye that was just mentioned, and if his Self-hood were being stated, then [the referent] would not be the shadow-person.
But this is not the case.
Because the pronoun refers back to the supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>) indicated by the opening of the passage.
For indeed, the qualities of being free from sin etc. are not possible in the individual self — this is the meaning.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes this: 'Of those [who hold this view], [the pronoun] "this"' etc.
This is easy to understand.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states another view: 'But others, the disputants' etc.
If the <s>jīva</s> is not in reality an agent and enjoyer, then the ritual injunctions that depend on that [agency and enjoyership] would be obstructed.
And the <s>Sūtrakāra</s>'s statement 'Not because of impossibility' (<s>nāsaṃbhavāt</s>) would be violated.
For that [<s>sūtra</s>] states the impossibility of the qualities of <s>Brahman</s> in the <s>jīva</s>.
And since <s>Brahman</s> and the <s>jīva</s>s are non-different, the impossibility of <s>Brahman</s>'s qualities in the <s>jīva</s>s [would not hold] — this is their intent.
The reply to those disputants has been given by the <s>Śārīraka</s> (the treatise on the embodied Self) itself.
Namely: Through the consideration of the textual sequence, the purport of the <s>Vedānta</s>s is understood to be one non-dual Self-reality, while the <s>jīva</s>s are imagined through the superimposition of <s>avidyā</s>.
And the qualities of <s>Brahman</s>, which truly exists, are not possible in the <s>jīva</s>s, which are superimposed.
For indeed, the real properties of a real rope — such as being approachable — are not possible in a superimposed snake.

children.text: nanu brahmacedatra vaktavyaṃ kṛtaṃ jīvaparāmarśenetyuktamityata āha- #anyārthaśca parāmarśaḥ# /
children.translated_text: But if <s>Brahman</s> is what is to be spoken of here, then — since it has been said that the reference to the <s>jīva</s> is already accomplished — [what more is needed]? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And the reference [to the <s>jīva</s>] has another purpose' etc.

children.text: jīvasyopādhikalpitasya brahmabhāva upadeṣṭavyaḥ, na cāsau jīvamaparāmṛśya śakya upadeṣṭumiti tisṛṣvavasthāsu jīvaḥ parāmṛṣṭaḥ /
children.translated_text: The <s>Brahman</s>-nature of the <s>jīva</s> — which is imagined through limiting adjuncts — is to be taught. And that [teaching] cannot be accomplished without referring to the <s>jīva</s>. Hence the <s>jīva</s> has been referred to in the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
The dissolution of that [<s>jīva</s>-]state — [the purpose is] to show its ultimately real <s>Brahman</s>-nature — this is the meaning. // [End of <s>Sūtra</s>] 20 //
'Because of the brief scriptural statement (<s>alpaśruti</s>)' — if [it be objected] thus, that has been answered.
This is explained by the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, which is explained by the running gloss (<s>nigadavyākhyāta</s>). // [End of <s>Sūtra</s>] 21 //
'Because of imitation, and because of that [being appropriate only for <s>Brahman</s>].'
'The non-manifestation of light is observed when a superior light is present;
Therefore, that which is within [all] lights is understood from imitation.' //

' balīyasā hi saureṇa tejasā mandaṃ tejaścandratārakādyabhibhūyamānaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ, na tu tejaso 'nyena /
ye 'pi pidhāyakāḥ pradīpasya gṛhaghaṭādayo na te svabhāsā pradīpaṃ bhāsayitumīśate /
śrūyate ca-'tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti' iti /
sarvaśabdaḥ prakṛtasūryādyapekṣaḥ /
na cātulyarūpe 'nubhānamityanukāraḥ saṃbhavati /
nahi gāvo varāhamanudhāvantīti kṛṣṇavihaṅgānudhāvanamupapadyate gavām, api tu tādṛśasūkarānudhāvanam /
tasmādyadyapi 'yasmin dyauḥ pṛthivī cāntarikṣamotam' iti brahma prakṛtaṃ, tathāpyabhibhavānukārasāmarthyalakṣaṇena liṅgena prakaraṇabādhayā tejodhāturavagamyate, na tu brahma, liṅgānupapatteḥ /
tatra taṃ tasyeti ca sarvanāmapadāni pradarśanīyamevāvamrakṣyanti /

children.translated_text: And there is no fixed rule that the word '<s>tat</s>' (that) refers back only to what was previously mentioned.

children.text: nahi 'tena raktaṃ rāgāt' 'tasyāpatyam' ityādau pūrvoktaṃ kiñcidasti /
children.translated_text: For in expressions like '<s>tena raktaṃ rāgāt</s>' (dyed red by that, because of the dye) and '<s>tasyāpatyam</s>' (the offspring of that one), there is nothing previously mentioned.

children.text: tasmātpramāṇāntarāpratītamapi tejo 'ntaramalaukikaṃ śabdādupāsyatvena gamyata iti prāpte ucyate-'brahmaṇyeva hi talliṅgaṃ na tu tejasyalaukike /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even though not apprehended by another means of knowledge, some supramundane light-element is understood from scripture as the object of meditation — when this prima facie view has been arrived at, it is said: 'For in <s>Brahman</s> alone does that indicatory mark [fit], not in a supramundane light-element;

children.text: tasmānna tadupāsyatve brahma jñeyaṃ tu gamyate //
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is not to be worshipped [as a light-element]; rather, it is to be known.' //

body.translated_text:
For a weaker light — of the moon, stars, and the like — is observed to be overpowered by the stronger, solar light; but not [overpowered] by something other than light.
Even those objects that obstruct a lamp — such as a house, a pot, and the like — cannot, by their own luminosity, illuminate the lamp.
And the <s>Śruti</s> declares: 'By the light of That, all this shines' (<s>tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti</s>).
The word 'all' (<s>sarva</s>) is relative to the sun and the like that are under discussion.
And imitation is not possible when [two things are] not of the same kind.
For 'cows chase a boar' does not justify [saying that] cows chase black birds; rather, [it means they chase] pigs of that kind.
Therefore, even though <s>Brahman</s> is the topic in 'In which heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven,' nevertheless, by the indicatory mark (<s>liṅga</s>) characterized by the capacity for overpowering and imitation, overriding the context (<s>prakaraṇa</s>), the element of light (<s>tejodhātu</s>) is understood — not <s>Brahman</s>, because the indicatory mark is inapplicable [to <s>Brahman</s>].
Therein, the pronominal words 'him' (<s>tam</s>) and 'of that' (<s>tasya</s>) would protect what is to be indicated [i.e., they could refer to light].

body.text:
' 'tameva bhāntat' ityatra kimalaukikaṃ tejaḥ kalpayitvā sūryādīnāmanubhānamupapadyatām, kiṃvā 'bhārūpaḥ satyasaṃkalpaḥ' iti śrutyantaraprasiddhena brahmaṇo bhānena sūryādīnāṃ bhānamupapādyatāmiti viśaye na śrutasaṃbhave 'śrutasya kalpanā yujyata ityaprasiddhaṃ nālaukikamupāsyaṃ tejo yujyate, api tu śrutiprasiddhaṃ brahmaiva jñeyamiti /
tadetadāha- #prājña evātmā bhavitumarhati# /
virodhamāha- #samatvācceti# /
nanu svapratibhāne sūryādayaścākṣuṣaṃ tejo 'pekṣante /
na hyandhenaite dṛśyante /
tathā tadeva cākṣuṣaṃ tejo bāhyasauryāditejāpyāyitaṃ rūpādi prakāśayati nānāpyāyitam, andhakāre 'pi rūpadarśanaprasaṅgādityata āha- #yaṃ bhāntamanubhāyuriti# /
nahi tejontarasya tejo 'ntarāpekṣāṃ vyāsedhāmaḥ, kintu tadbhānamanubhānam /
naca locanabhānamanubhānti sūryādayaḥ /
tadidamuktam- #nahi pradīpa iti# /
pūrvapakṣamanubhāṣya vyabhicāramāha- #yadapyuktamiti# /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-yadi svarūpasāmyābhāvamabhipretyānukāro nirākriyate, tadā vyabhāciraḥ /
atha kriyāsāmyābhāvaṃ, so 'siddhaḥ /
asti hi vāyurajasoḥ svarūpavisadṛśayorapi niyatadigdeśavahanakriyāsāmyam /
vanhyayaḥ piṇḍayostu yadyapi dahanakriyā na bhidyate tathāpi dravyabhedena kriyābhedaṃ kalpayitvā kriyāsādṛśyaṃ vyākhyeyam /
tadevamanukṛteriti vibhajya tasya ceti sūtrāvayavaṃ vibhajate- #tasya ceti caturthamiti# /
jyotiṣāṃ sūryādīnāṃ brahma jyotiḥprakāśakamityarthaḥ /
tejo 'ntareṇānindriyabhāvamāpannena sūryāditejo vibhātītyaprasiddham /
sarvaśabdasya hi svarasato niḥśeṣābhidhānaṃ vṛttiḥ /
sā tejedhātāvalaukike rūpamātraprakāśake saṃkucet /
brahmaṇi tu niḥśeṣajagadavabhāsake na sarvaśabdasya vṛttiḥ saṃkucatīti- #tatraśabdamāharanniti# /
sarvatra khalvayaṃ tatraśabdaḥ pūrvoktaparāmarśī /
'tena raktaṃ rāgāt' ityādāvapi prakṛteḥ parasminpratyayer'thabhede 'nvākhyāyamāne prātipadikapratyarthasya pūrvavṛttatvamastīti teneti tatparāmarśānna vyabhāciraḥ /
tathāca sarvanāmaśrutireva brahmopasthāpayati /
tena bhavatu nāma prakaraṇālliṅgaṃ balīyaḥ, śrutistu liṅgādbalīyasīti śrautamiha brahmaiva gamyata iti /
api cāpekṣitānapekṣitābhādhānayorapekṣitābhidhānaṃ yuktaṃ, dṛṣṭārthatvādityāha- #anantaraṃ ca hiraṇyamaye pare kośa iti# /
asminvākye jyotiṣāṃ jyotirityuktaṃ, tatra kathaṃ tat jyotiṣāṃ jyotirityapekṣāyāmitadamupatiṣṭhate- #na tatra sūrya iti# /
svātantryeṇa tūcyamāne 'napekṣitaṃ syādadṛṣṭārthamiti /
brahmaṇyapi caiṣāṃ bhānapratiṣedho 'nakalpata iti /

children.text: ayamabhiprāyaḥ-'na tatra sūryo bhāti' iti neyaṃ satisaptamī, yataḥ sūryādīnāṃ tasmin satyabhibhavaḥ pratīyeta /
children.translated_text: The purport is this: 'There the sun does not shine' — this is not a <s>satīsaptamī</s> (locative of attendant circumstance), for from that one would understand the eclipse of the sun and others in Its presence.
Rather, it is a <s>viṣayasaptamī</s> (locative of domain).

children.text: tena na tatra brahmaṇi prakāśayitavye sūryādayaḥ prakāśakatayā bhānti, kintu brahmaiva sūryādiṣu prakāśayitavyeṣu prakāśakatvena bhāti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the sun and others do not shine as illuminators in that [domain of] <s>Brahman</s> which is to be illuminated; rather, <s>Brahman</s> alone shines as the illuminator in [the domain of] the sun and others which are to be illuminated.

children.text: tacca svayaṃprakāśam, #agṛhyo nahi gṛhyata ityādiśrutibhya iti# //22 //
children.translated_text: And That is self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), 'ungraspable, for It is not grasped' — [this is established] from <s>Śruti</s>s such as these. //22//

body.translated_text:
In the passage 'Him alone shining,' [the question is]: should one postulate some supramundane light (<s>tejas</s>) and thereby explain the shining of the sun and others, or should the shining of the sun and others be explained through the radiance of <s>Brahman</s>, which is established by another <s>Śruti</s> — 'luminous in nature, of true will' (<s>bhārūpaḥ satyasaṃkalpaḥ</s>)? In this matter, when the heard [meaning] is possible, the postulation of something unheard is not appropriate — hence a supramundane, unestablished object of meditation (<s>tejas</s>) is not fitting; rather, <s>Brahman</s> itself, established by <s>Śruti</s>, is to be known.
This is what [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states: 'The <s>Prājña</s> (the intelligent one) alone deserves to be the self.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the contradiction: 'Because of equality' (<s>samatvāt</s>).
Now, [the objection is:] for their own manifestation, the sun and others require visual light (<s>cākṣuṣa tejas</s>), for they are not seen by a blind person. Likewise, that very visual light, when nourished by external solar and other light, illuminates forms and the like, but not when unnourished — otherwise forms would be seen even in darkness. To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] replies: 'Which, shining, they shine after' (<s>yaṃ bhāntam anubhāyuḥ</s>).
For we do not deny that one light depends on another light; rather, [what we deny is] that their shining is a 'shining-after' [i.e., derivative illumination]. And the sun and others do not shine after the shining of the eye.
This is what is stated: 'For not a lamp...' (<s>nahi pradīpa</s>).
Having restated the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (objection), [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] points out the deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>): 'What was also said...' (<s>yadapyuktam</s>).
What is stated is this: if imitation (<s>anukāra</s>) is rejected on the grounds that there is no similarity of essential nature (<s>svarūpasāmya</s>), then there is deviation [from the rule]. But if [one says it is rejected] because of the absence of similarity of action (<s>kriyāsāmya</s>), that is unestablished. For wind and dust, though dissimilar in essential nature, have similarity in the action of blowing in a fixed direction and place. As for the balls of fire and iron, although the action of burning does not differ [between them], still, by positing a difference of action based on the difference of substance, the dissimilarity of action should be explained.
Having thus analyzed [the sūtra-portion] 'of imitation,' [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] divides the sūtra-component 'and of that': 'And of that — this is the fourth' (<s>tasya ceti caturtham</s>).
The meaning is: <s>Brahman</s> is the illuminator of the lights (<s>jyotis</s>) such as the sun and others.
The claim that the light of the sun etc. shines through another light that has not attained the status of a sense-organ is unestablished.
For the natural function of the word 'all' (<s>sarva</s>) is to denote everything without remainder. That [function] would be restricted in the case of a non-mundane substance that illuminates mere form. But in the case of <s>Brahman</s>, which manifests the entire world without remainder, the function of the word 'all' is not restricted — hence: 'Adducing the word "there"' (<s>tatraśabdam āharan</s>).
Everywhere indeed this word 'there' (<s>tatra</s>) refers back to what was previously stated.
Even in [expressions like] 'colored by that, due to passion' (<s>tena raktaṃ rāgāt</s>) etc., when the meaning-difference of the suffix applied after the base is being explained, since the meaning of the nominal base has already occurred previously, by the reference back to that through 'by that' (<s>tena</s>), there is no deviation.
Thus the pronoun (<s>sarvanāman</s>) itself presents <s>Brahman</s>.
Therefore, let it be that contextual indication (<s>prakaraṇa</s>) is stronger than inferential sign (<s>liṅga</s>); but <s>Śruti</s> (direct scriptural statement) is stronger than inferential sign — hence what is understood here through <s>Śruti</s> is <s>Brahman</s> alone.
Moreover, between the expression of what is relevant and what is irrelevant, the expression of what is relevant is appropriate, since it serves a perceived purpose — so [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And next, in the golden, in the highest sheath' (<s>anantaraṃ ca hiraṇyamaye pare kośa</s>).
In this sentence it is said 'the light of lights' (<s>jyotiṣāṃ jyotiḥ</s>); when the question arises how it is the light of lights, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] supplies [the answer]: 'There the sun [does not shine]' (<s>na tatra sūrya</s>).
But if stated independently, it would be irrelevant and serve no perceived purpose.
And the negation of their shining in <s>Brahman</s> too is not unfitting.

children.translated_text: 'Moreover, it is remembered (<s>smaryate</s>).'
'That does not illumine' (<s>na tad bhāsayate</s>) — [by this] the ungraspability of <s>Brahman</s> is stated.
'That which is in the sun' (<s>yad ādityagatam</s>) — by this, the illuminating capacity of That very [<s>Brahman</s>] is stated. //23//
'Known from the word alone' (<s>śabdādeva pramitaḥ</s>).
'There is no straightforward difference of means of knowledge regarding the Supreme, which is beyond [all] means of knowledge;
lordship over past and future is not straightforward in the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) — hence the doubt.'

body.text:
' kimaṅguṣṭhamātraśrutyanugrahāya jīvopāsanāparametadvākyamastu, tadanurodhena ceśānaśrutiḥ kathañcidvāyākhyāyatām, āhosvidīśānaśrutyanugrahāya brahmaparametadastu, tadanurodhenāṅguṣṭhamātraśrutiḥ kathañcinnīyatām /
tatrānyatarasyānyatarānurodhaviṣaye prathamānurodho nyāṭya ityaṅguṣṭhaśrutyanurodheneśānaśrutirnetavyā /
apica yuktaṃ hṛtpuṇḍarīkadaharasthānatvaṃ paramātmānaḥ, parimāṇamātranirdeśāt /
naca 'madhya ātmani' ityatra sthānabhedo 'vagamyate /
ātmaśabdo hyayaṃ svabhāvavacano vā jīvavacano vā brahmavacano vā syāt /
tatra svabhāvasya svabhavitradhīnanirūpaṇatayā svasya ca bhavituranirdeśānna jñāyate kasya madhya iti /
naca jīvaparayorasti madhyamañjaseti naiṣa sthānanirdeśo vispaṣṭaḥ /
spaṣṭastu parimāṇanirdeśaḥ /
parimāṇabhedaśca parasminna saṃbhavatīti jīvātmaivāṅguṣṭhamātraḥ /
sa khalvantaḥkaraṇādyupādhikalpito bhāgaḥ paramātmanaḥ /
antaḥkaraṇaṃ ca prāyeṇa hṛtkamalakośasthānaṃ, hṛtkamalakośaśca manuṣyāṇāmaṅguṣṭhamātra iti tadavacchinno jīvātmāpyaṅguṣṭhamātraḥ, nabha iva vaṃśaparvāvacchinnamaratnimātram /
api ca jīvātmanaḥ spaṣṭamaṅguṣṭhamātratvaṃ smaryate-'aṅguṣṭhamātraṃ puruṣaṃ niścakarṣa yamo balāt' iti /
nahi sarveśasya brahmaṇo yamena balānniṣkarṣaḥ kalpate /
yamo hi jagau-'hariguruvaśago 'smi na svatantraḥ prabhavati saṃyamane mamāpi viṣṇuḥ' iti /
tenāṅguṣṭhamātratvasya jīve niśchayādāpekṣikaṃ kiñcidbhūtabhavyaṃ prati jīvasyeśānatvaṃ vyākhyeyam /

children.translated_text: 'This verily is That' (<s>etad vai tat</s>) — [this expression] refers to the directly perceived form of the <s>jīva</s>.
Therefore, the object of meditation here is the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>) alone — this is the prima facie conclusion (<s>prāpta</s>).
This being the prima facie view, [the <s>Siddhāntin</s>] states: 'Because of the question-and-answer [format], and because the hearing of [the word] "Lord" (<s>Īśāna</s>) is without distinction;
the statement is meant to convey the <s>Brahman</s>-nature of the <s>jīva</s>.'

body.translated_text:
[The question is:] Should this passage, in deference to the <s>Śruti</s> about the thumb-sized [<s>puruṣa</s>], be taken as referring to the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) as object of meditation, and should the <s>Śruti</s> about lordship (<s>Īśāna</s>) be explained away somehow accordingly? Or should it, in deference to the <s>Śruti</s> about lordship, be taken as referring to <s>Brahman</s>, and should the <s>Śruti</s> about the thumb-sized [<s>puruṣa</s>] be explained away somehow accordingly?
In this matter, where one of the two must be accommodated to the other, whichever is first accommodated is the stronger — hence the <s>Śruti</s> about lordship should be led to conform with the <s>Śruti</s> about the thumb-sized [<s>puruṣa</s>].
Moreover, it is fitting that the <s>Paramātman</s> (supreme Self) should have as its location the space within the lotus of the heart, [only] because of the teaching of a specific measure. And in [the phrase] 'in the middle, in the self' (<s>madhya ātmani</s>), no specific location is ascertained. For the word <s>ātman</s> here could mean either essential nature, or the individual soul, or <s>Brahman</s>. Among these, since essential nature depends on that whose nature it is for its determination, and since that whose essential nature it is has not been specified, one does not know whose 'middle' it is. And there is no straightforward 'middle' for either the individual soul or the Supreme — hence this designation of location is not clear. But the designation of measure is clear. And a difference of measure is not possible in the Supreme — hence the thumb-sized one is the individual self (<s>jīvātman</s>) alone.
That [<s>jīvātman</s>] is indeed a portion of the <s>Paramātman</s> imagined through limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>s) such as the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) and the rest. And the inner organ generally has its seat in the lotus-sheath of the heart, and the lotus-sheath of the heart in human beings is thumb-sized — hence the individual self delimited by that is also thumb-sized, just as space delimited by the hollow of a bamboo joint is a cubit in measure.
Moreover, the thumb-sized nature of the individual self is clearly stated in <s>Smṛti</s>: '<s>Yama</s> forcibly extracted the thumb-sized <s>puruṣa</s>' (<s>aṅguṣṭhamātraṃ puruṣaṃ niścakarṣa yamo balāt</s>). For forcible extraction by <s>Yama</s> is not conceivable for <s>Brahman</s>, the Lord of all. <s>Yama</s> himself declared: 'I am under the control of <s>Hari</s>, the supreme teacher; I am not independent. <s>Viṣṇu</s> has dominion even over my power of punishment.'
Therefore, since the thumb-sized nature is established in the <s>jīva</s>, [any] lordship over past and future attributed to the <s>jīva</s> should be explained as merely relative.

body.text:
' iha hi bhūtabhavyamātraṃ prati niraṅkuśamīśānatvaṃ pratīyate /
prāk pṛṣṭaṃ cātra brahma 'anyatra dharmādanyatrādharmāt' ityādinā /
tadanantarasya saṃdarbhasya tatprativacanateciteti 'etadvai tat' iti brahmābhidhānaṃ yuktam /

children.text: tathā cāṅguṣṭhamātratayā yadyapi jīve 'vagamyate tathāpi na tatparametadvākyaṃ, kintvaṅguṣṭhamātrasya jīvasya brahmarūpatāpratipādanaparam /
children.translated_text: And thus, although from the thumb-sized measure the passage may seem to refer to the <s>jīva</s>, nevertheless it is not ultimately about the <s>jīva</s>; rather, it is meant to teach the <s>Brahman</s>-nature of the thumb-sized <s>jīva</s>.
Thus, the unrestricted lordship should not be narrowed down.
Nor should the question-and-answer relationship regarding <s>Brahman</s> be abandoned.

children.text: tena yathā 'tattvamasti' iti vijñānātmanastvaṃpadārthasya taditi paramātmanaikatvaṃ pratipādyate, tathehāpyaṅguṣṭhaparimitasya vijñānātmana īśānaśrutyā brahmabhāvaḥ pratipādya iti yuktam //24 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as in 'You are That' (<s>tat tvam asi</s>) the identity of the referent of 'you' — the cognitive self (<s>vijñānātman</s>) — with the <s>Paramātman</s> (supreme Self), the referent of 'That,' is taught, so too here it is appropriate that the <s>Brahman</s>-nature of the cognitive self, which is measured as thumb-sized, is taught through the <s>Śruti</s> about lordship (<s>Īśāna</s>). //24//

body.translated_text: For here, unrestricted lordship over the past and future alone is understood. And <s>Brahman</s> was asked about at the outset with [the words] 'other than <s>dharma</s>, other than <s>adharma</s>' (<s>anyatra dharmād anyatrādharmāt</s>) and so on. The subsequent passage, being the answer to that [question], fits as a reply to that — hence the statement 'This verily is That' (<s>etad vai tat</s>) as a designation of <s>Brahman</s> is appropriate.

body.text:
#hṛdyapekṣayā tu manuṣyādhikāratvāt /
sarvagatasyāpi parabrahmaṇo hṛdaye 'vasthānamapekṣyeti#jīvābhiprāyam /
na cānyaḥ paramātmāna iha grahaṇamarhatīti na jīvaparametadvākyamityarthaḥ /
#manuṣyāneveti# /
traivarṇikāneva /
#arthitvāditi# /
antaḥsaṃjñānāṃ mokṣamāṇānāṃ ca kāmyeṣu karmasvadhikāraṃ niṣedhati- #śaktatvāditi#tiryagdevarṣīṇāmaśaktānāmadhikāraṃ nivartayati /
#upanayanādiśāstrācceti#śūdrāṇāmanadhikāritāṃ darśayati /
#yadapyuktaṃ parimāṇopadeśātsmṛteśceti# /
yadyetatparamātmaparaṃ kimiti tarhi jīva ihocyate /

children.translated_text: Well, let the <s>Paramātman</s> alone be spoken of [one might say].
But the <s>jīva</s> is [also] spoken of — hence [the passage] is about the <s>jīva</s> alone — this is the purport [of the objection].
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves this: 'To that we reply' (<s>tatpratyucyata</s>).

children.text: jīvasya hi tattvaṃ paramātmabhāvaḥ, tadvaktavyam, naca tajjīvamanabhidhāya śakyaṃ vaktumiti jīva ucyata ityarthaḥ //25 //
children.translated_text: For the true nature (<s>tattva</s>) of the <s>jīva</s> is its <s>Paramātman</s>-nature; that is what is to be stated. And that cannot be stated without mentioning the <s>jīva</s> — hence the <s>jīva</s> is spoken of — this is the meaning. //25//

body.translated_text:
'With reference to the heart, because of the eligibility of human beings alone.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s> comments:] 'Even for the all-pervading supreme <s>Brahman</s>, the location in the heart is to be understood with reference [to meditation]' — this is [said] with the intention [of establishing] the <s>jīva</s> [interpretation].
The meaning is: no other than the <s>Paramātman</s> is eligible for being grasped here; hence this passage is not about the <s>jīva</s> alone.
'Human beings alone' (<s>manuṣyān eva</s>) — [means] the three upper castes (<s>traivarṇika</s>s) alone.
'Because of fitness' (<s>arthitvāt</s>) — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] denies eligibility in desire-motivated rituals for those who are inner-dwellers (<s>antaḥsaṃjñā</s>s, i.e., ascetics) and those who are on the verge of liberation.
'Because of capability' (<s>śaktatvāt</s>) — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] removes the eligibility of animals, gods, and sages who are incapable.
'Because of the scripture on initiation (<s>upanayana</s>) etc.' — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] shows the ineligibility of <s>Śūdra</s>s.
'What was said about the designation of measure and about <s>Smṛti</s>...' — If this [passage] is about the <s>Paramātman</s>, then why is the <s>jīva</s> mentioned here at all?

body.text:
#taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt# /
devarṣīṇāṃ brahmavijñānādhikāracintā samanvayalakṣaṇe 'saṃgatetyasyāḥ prāsaṅgikīṃ saṃgatiṃ darśayituṃ prasaṅgamāha- #aṅguṣṭhamātraśrutiriti# /
syādetat /
devadīnāṃ vividhavicitrānandabhogabhogināṃ vairāgyābhāvānnārthitvaṃ brahmavidyāyāmityata āha- #tatrārthitvaṃ tāvanmokṣaviṣayamiti# /
kṣayātiśayayogyasya svargādyupabhoge 'pi bhāvādasti vairāgyamityarthaḥ /
nanu devādīnāṃ vigrahādyabhāvendriyārthasaṃnikarṣajāyāḥ pramāṇādivṛtteranupapatteravidvattayā sāmarthyābhāvena nādhikāra ityata āha #-tadā sāmarthyamiti teṣāmiti# /
yathā ca mantrādibhyastadavagamastathopariṣṭādupapādayiṣyate /
nanu śudravadupanayanāsaṃbhavenādhyāyanābhāvātteṣāmanadhikāra ityata āha- #na copanayanaśāstreṇeti# /
na khalu vidhivat gurumukhādgṛhyamāṇo vedaḥ phalavatkarmabrahmāvabodhahetuḥ, api tvadhyayanottarakālaṃ nigamaniruktalavyākaraṇādividitapadatarthasaṃgateradhiśābdanyāyatattvasya puṃsaḥ smaryamāṇaḥ /
sa ca manuṣyāṇāmiha janmanīva devadīnāṃ prāci bhave vidhivadhīta āmnāya iha janmani smaryamāṇaḥ /
ata eva svayaṃ pratibhāto vedaḥ saṃbhavatītyarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: And [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says that ineligibility for rituals (<s>karma</s>) does not [entail] ineligibility for <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge: 'What was stated as the reason for ineligibility in rituals...' (<s>yadapi karmasv anadhikāra-kāraṇam uktam</s>).
For the <s>Vasu</s>s and others have no other [set of] <s>Vasu</s>s and others [to worship].
Nor do <s>Bhṛgu</s> and others have other <s>Bhṛgu</s>s and others.
The meaning is: the former <s>Vasu</s>s, <s>Bhṛgu</s>s, and others, their eligibility [for those positions] having been exhausted, are no longer gods and sages at present. //26//

body.translated_text:
'And above that too, <s>Bādarāyaṇa</s> [holds it is so], because of possibility' (<s>taduparyapi Bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt</s>).
To show the incidental connection (<s>prāsaṅgikī saṃgati</s>) of the discussion about the eligibility of gods and sages for <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge with the [first <s>pāda</s>'s] characteristic of <s>samanvaya</s> (harmonization), [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] mentions the occasion: 'The <s>Śruti</s> about the thumb-sized [<s>puruṣa</s>]...'
One might [object] thus: Gods and others, who enjoy various and wonderful pleasures, lack dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) and therefore have no desire (<s>arthitva</s>) for <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge. To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] replies: 'Their desire, to begin with, pertains to liberation' (<s>tatrārthitvaṃ tāvan mokṣaviṣayam</s>).
The meaning is: since even in the enjoyment of heavenly pleasures and the like, their perishable and surpassable nature is recognized, dispassion arises.
Now, [the objection is:] since gods and others, lacking bodies and sense-organs, cannot have valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>) etc. arising from sense-object contact, they lack knowledge and therefore lack capability — hence no eligibility. To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Their capability then...' (<s>tadā sāmarthyam teṣām</s>).
How their understanding [of <s>Brahman</s>] is attained through <s>mantra</s>s and the like will be established later.
Now, [the objection is:] just as <s>Śūdra</s>s [are ineligible] because initiation (<s>upanayana</s>) is impossible and therefore Vedic study is absent, so too gods and others are ineligible. To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And [they are] not [excluded] by the scripture on initiation' (<s>na copanayana-śāstreṇa</s>).
For it is not the <s>Veda</s> as [formally] received from a teacher in accordance with ritual that is the cause of the knowledge of fruitful action and <s>Brahman</s>; rather, [it functions] when, after the time of study, one has learned the meanings of words and sentences through <s>Nigama</s>, <s>Nirukta</s>, grammar, and the like. And this [Veda], just as it was studied according to ritual in this birth for humans, was studied according to ritual by gods and others in a previous birth, and is remembered in this birth.
Hence the meaning is that the <s>Veda</s> that manifests spontaneously [in them] is possible.

body.text:
#virodhaḥ karmaṇīti cennānekapratipatterdarśanāt# /
mantrādipadasamanvayātpratīyamānor'thaḥ pramāṇāntarāvirodhe satyupeyaḥ na tu virodhe /
pramāṇāntaraviruddhaṃ cedaṃ vigrahavattvādi devatāyāḥ /
tasmāt 'yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ' ityādivadupacaritārtho mantrādirvyākhyeyaḥ /
tathāca vigrahādyabhāvācchabdopahitārthor'thopahito vā śabdo devatetyacetanatvānna tasyāḥ kkacidapyadhikāra iti śaṅkārthaḥ /
nirākaroti- #na# /
kasmāt /
#anekarūpapratipatteḥ# /
saiva kuta ityata āha- #darśanāt#śrutiṣu smṛtiṣu ca /
tathāhi-ekasyānekakāyanirmāṇamadarśanādvā na yujyate, bādhadarśanādvā /
tatrādarśanamasiddhaṃ, śrutismṛtibhyāṃ darśanāt /
nahi laukikena pramāṇenādṛṣṭatvādāgamena dṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ bhavati, mā bhūdyāgādīnāmapi svargādisādhanatvamadṛṣṭamiti manuṣyaśararasya mātāpitṛsaṃyogajatvaniyamādapi pitroḥ saṃyoge kutaḥ saṃbhavaḥ, saṃbhave vānagnito 'pi dhūmaḥ syāditi bādhadarśanamiti cet /
hanta kiṃ śarīratvena hetunā devādiśarīramapi mātāpitṛsaṃyogajaṃ siṣādhayiṣasi /
tathā cānekānto hetvābhāsaḥ, svedajodbhijjānāṃ śarīrāṇāmatadbhetutvāt /
icchāmātranirmāṇatvaṃ dehādīnāmadṛṣṭacaramiti cet, na /
bhūtopādānatvenecchāmātranirmāṇatvāsiddheḥ /
bhūtavaśināṃ hi devādīnāṃ nānākāyacikīrṣāvaśādbhūtakriyotpattau bhūtānāṃ parasparasaṃyogena nānākāyamasutpādāt /
dṛṣṭā ca vaśina icchāvaśādvaye kriyā, yathā viṣavidyāvida icchāmātreṇa viṣaśakalapreraṇam /
naca viṣavidyāvido darśanenādhiṣṭhānadarśanādvyavahitaviprakṛṣṭabhūtādarśanāddevādīnāṃ kathamadiṣṭhānamiti vācyam /
kācābhrapaṭalapihitasya viprakṛṣṭasya ca bhaumaśanaiścarāderdarśanena vyabhācirāt /
asaktāśca dṛṣṭayo devādīnāṃ kācābhrapaṭalādivanmahīmahīdharādibhirna vyavadhīyante /
na cāsmadādivatteṣāṃ śarīritvena vyavahitāviprakṛṣṭādidarśanāsaṃbhavo 'numīyata iti vācyam, āgamavirodhino 'numānasyotpādāyogāt /
antārdhānaṃ cāñjanādinā manujānāmiva teṣāṃ prabhavatāmupapadyate, tena saṃnihitānāmapi na kratudeśe darśanaṃ bhaviṣyati /
tasmātsūktam-anekapratipatteriti- #tathāhi kati devā ityupakramyeti# /
vaiśvadevaśāstrasya hi nividi 'kati devāḥ' ityupakramya nividaivottaraṃ dattaṃ śākalyāya yājñavalkyena- #trayaśca trī ca śatā trayaśca trī ca sahasreti# /
vivinnāma śas.mānadevatāsaṃkhyāvācakāni mantrapadāni /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-vaiśvadevasya nividi kati devāḥ śasyamānāḥ prasaṃkhyātā iti śākalyena pṛṣṭe yājñavalkyasyottaraṃ-'trayaśca trī ca śatā' ityādi /
yāvatsaṃkhyākā vaiśvadevanividi saṃkhyātā devāsta etāvanta iti /
punaśca śākalyena 'katame te' iti saṃkhyeyeṣu pṛṣṭeṣu yājñavalkyasyottaram- #mahimāna evaiṣāmete trayastriṃśattveva devā iti# /
aṣṭau vasava ekādaśa rudrā dvādaśādityā indraśca prajāpatiśceti trayastriṃśaddevāḥ /
tatrāgniśca pṛthivī ca vāyuścāntarikṣaṃ cādityaśca dyauśca candramāśca nakṣatrāṇi ceti vasavaḥ /
ete hi prāṇināṃ karmaphalāśrayeṇa kāryakāraṇasaṃghātarūpeṇa pariṇamanto jagadidaṃ sarvaṃ vāsayanti, tasmādvasavaḥ /
katame rudrā iti daśeme puruṣe prāṇāḥ buddhikarmendriyāṇi daśa, ekādaśaṃ ca mana iti /
tadetāni prāṇaḥ, tadvṛttitvāt /
te hi prāyaṇakāla utkrāmantaḥ puruṣaṃ rodayantīti rudrāḥ /
katama ādityā iti dvādaśamāsāḥ saṃvatsarasyāvayavāḥ punaḥ punaḥ paruvartamānāḥ prāṇabhṛtāmāyūṃṣu ca karmaphalopabhogaṃ cādāpayantītyādityāḥ /
aśanirindraḥ, sā hi balaṃ, sā hīndrasya paramā īśatā, tayā hi sarvānprāṇinaḥ pramāpayati, tena stanayitnuraśanirindraḥ /
yajñaḥ prajāpitirita, yajñasādhanaṃ ca yajñarūpaṃ ca paśavaḥ prajāpatiḥ /
eta eva trayastriṃśaddevāḥ ṣaṇṇāmagniṣṭathivīvāṭvantarikṣādityadivāṃ mahimāno na tato bhidyante /
ṣaḍeva tu devāḥ /
te tu ṣaḍagniṃ pṛthivīṃ caikūkṛtyāntarikṣaṃ vāyuṃ caikīkṛtya divaṃ cādityaṃ caikīkṛtya trayo lokāstraya eva devā bhavanti /
eta eva ca trayo 'nnaprāṇayorantarbhavanto 'nnaprāṇau dvau devau bhavataḥ /
tāvapyadhyardho deva ekaḥ /
katamo 'dhyardhaḥ, yo 'yaṃ vāyuḥ pavate /
kathamayameka evādhyardhaḥ, yadasminsati sarvamidamadhyardhaṃ vṛddhiṃ prāpnoti tenādhyardha iti /
katama eka iti, sa evādhyardhaḥ prāṇa eko brahma /
sarvadevātmatvena bṛhattvādbrahma tadeva tyadityācakṣate parokṣābhidhāyakena śabdena /
tasmādekasyaiva devasya mahimavaśādyugapadanekadevarūpatāmāha śrutiḥ /
smṛtiśca nigavyākhyātā /
api ca pṛthagjanānāmapyupāyānuṣṭhānavaśātprāptāṇimadyaiśvaryāṇāṃ yugapadaṅgabhāvapratipattiraṅgamāvagamanaṃ, tasya darśanāt /
tadeva parisphuṭaṃ darśayituṃ vyatirekaṃ tāvadāha- #kkacideka iti# /

children.text: na khalu bahuṣu śrāddheṣveko brāhmaṇo yugapadaṅgabhāvaṃ gantumarhati /
children.translated_text: Indeed, a single <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> cannot simultaneously assume the role of an accessory in multiple <s>Śrāddha</s> ceremonies.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the simultaneous presence of one [deity] in many [places]: '#But sometimes one [in many]#.'

children.text: yathaikaṃ brāhmaṇamuddiśya yugapannamaskāraḥ kriyate bahubhistathā svasthānasthitāmekāṃ devatāmuddiśya bahubhiryajamānairnānādeśāvasthitairyugapaddhavistyajyate, tasyāśca tatrāsaṃnihitāyā apyaṅgabhāvo bhavati /
children.translated_text: Just as salutation is made simultaneously by many [people] directed toward a single <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, so too an oblation is offered simultaneously by many sacrificers situated in different places, directed toward a single deity abiding in her own location; and her accessory-role (<s>aṅgabhāva</s>) obtains there even though she is not physically present.
It has been demonstrated that she possesses the capacity to simultaneously apprehend multiple distant objects. //27//

body.translated_text:
'If [it be said that there is] a contradiction with [their] action — no, because of the apprehension of multiple [forms], as is seen' (#<s>virodhaḥ karmaṇīti cennānekapratipatterdarśanāt</s>#).
The meaning understood from the coordination of words in mantras and the like is to be accepted when there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge, but not when there is contradiction.
If this — the possession of bodily form and the like by the deity — contradicts other means of knowledge,
then mantras and the like should be interpreted as having figurative meaning, as in 'The sacrificer is the grass-bundle (<s>prastara</s>)' and similar [statements].
And thus, since there is no bodily form [for the deity], either the word designates a meaning qualified by sound, or the sound designates a meaning qualified by the object — and being insentient, the deity has no authority anywhere — this is the purport of the objection.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: 'No.'
Why?
'Because of the apprehension of multiple forms.'
Whence this [apprehension]? To this he says: 'As is seen' — in <s>Śruti</s>s and <s>Smṛti</s>s.
Thus: the creation of multiple bodies by a single [deity] is untenable either because it is not seen, or because it is contradicted.
Of these, the 'not seen' [objection] is unestablished, since it is seen in <s>Śruti</s>s and <s>Smṛti</s>s.
For it is not the case that what is seen through scripture becomes unseen merely because it is not seen through ordinary means of knowledge — otherwise, the efficacy of sacrifices and the like in producing heaven and the like would also be 'unseen.' If one objects that since the human body is invariably produced from the union of parents, whence the possibility [of multiple bodies] even when there is a union of parents — or if there were such a possibility, then smoke would also arise from non-fire — this is the 'contradicted' [objection],
Well then! Do you wish to prove with 'being a body' as your reason that even divine bodies are produced from the union of parents?
In that case, this is the fallacy of an inconclusive reason (<s>anekānta hetvābhāsa</s>), since the bodies of sweat-born and plant-born [creatures] do not have that as their cause.
If one says that the creation of bodies and the like by mere will is not observed — no,
because [creation] by mere will is unestablished, since [bodies] have the elements as their material cause.
For the gods and others, who have mastery over the elements, when the activity of the elements arises from their desire to create multiple bodies, the elements, through their mutual combination, do not fail to produce multiple bodies.
And the activity of those who have mastery [over elements] is seen [to occur] from mere will, just as one skilled in the science of poisons (<s>viṣavidyā</s>) propels a piece of poison by mere will.
Nor should it be said that, from observing the wielder of poison-science [requiring proximity], how can the gods and others exercise control (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) over distant and intervening elements, since they are not seen [nearby]?
For this is refuted by the counter-example (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) of seeing the distant planetary Saturn even when covered by glass-like cloud-layers.
And the unobstructed perceptions of the gods and others are not blocked by earth, mountains, and the like, as [ordinary vision is blocked] by glass-like cloud-layers and the like.
Nor should it be said that, as with us, from their being embodied, the impossibility of perceiving what is intervening, distant, and the like can be inferred — for an inference that contradicts scripture cannot arise.
Moreover, becoming invisible (<s>antardhāna</s>) through collyrium and the like is possible for them, as for humans endowed with such powers — hence even those who are present nearby are not seen in the sacrificial precinct.
Therefore it is well said: 'Because of the apprehension of multiple forms.' — '#Thus, beginning with "How many gods are there?"#' (<s>tathāhi kati devā ityupakramya</s>).
For in the litany (<s>nivid</s>) of the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> [rite], beginning with 'How many gods are there?', the answer was given by <s>Yājñavalkya</s> to <s>Śākalya</s> in the litany itself — '#Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three#.'
The mantra-words are denoting the number of deities who are praised.
What is stated amounts to this: When <s>Śākalya</s> asked 'How many gods are there who are praised and enumerated in the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> litany?', <s>Yājñavalkya</s>'s answer was 'Three hundred and three' and so on.
'As many as are enumerated in the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> litany, that many are they.'
And again, when <s>Śākalya</s> asked 'Which are they?', inquiring about the enumerable ones, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>'s answer was — '#These are merely the glories (<s>mahimānaḥ</s>) of those; the gods are indeed thirty-three#.'
Eight <s>Vasu</s>s, eleven <s>Rudra</s>s, twelve <s>Āditya</s>s, <s>Indra</s>, and <s>Prajāpati</s> — these are the thirty-three gods.
Among these, fire, earth, wind, atmosphere, sun, heaven, moon, and the stars are the <s>Vasu</s>s.
For these, by transforming into the aggregate of cause and effect that serves as the repository of the fruits of beings' actions, cause all this world to dwell (<s>vāsayanti</s>) [in them] — hence they are <s>Vasu</s>s ('dwellers').
Which are the <s>Rudra</s>s? The ten vital breaths (<s>prāṇa</s>s) in the person — the ten cognitive and active sense-organs — and the mind as the eleventh.
These are the vital breaths (<s>prāṇa</s>), being modifications of the life-force.
For when they depart at the time of death, they make the person weep (<s>rodayanti</s>) — hence they are <s>Rudra</s>s ('weepers').
Which are the <s>Āditya</s>s? The twelve months, being parts of the year, revolving again and again, carry away (<s>ādāpayanti</s>) the life-spans and the enjoyment of the fruits of actions of living beings — hence they are <s>Āditya</s>s ('carriers').
Thunderbolt is <s>Indra</s>, for it is power, and it is the supreme sovereignty of <s>Indra</s>; for by it he destroys all beings — hence the thunderbolt is <s>Indra</s>.
Sacrifice is <s>Prajāpati</s> — the means of sacrifice and that which has the form of sacrifice are the animals, and [their lord is] <s>Prajāpati</s>.
These very thirty-three gods — the six [pairs] of fire-and-earth, wind-and-atmosphere, sun-and-heaven — are the glories (<s>mahimānaḥ</s>) of these; they do not differ from them.
But the gods are only six.
Those six — combining fire and earth into one, atmosphere and wind into one, heaven and sun into one — the three worlds become three gods.
And these very three, being subsumed under food and breath (<s>anna-prāṇa</s>), become two gods — food and breath.
Those two again are one-and-a-half gods.
Which is the one-and-a-half? This wind that blows.
How is this one alone one-and-a-half? Because when it blows, all this grows (<s>adhyardham</s>) — hence it is called 'one-and-a-half.'
Which is the one? That very one-and-a-half — breath (<s>prāṇa</s>) — is the one <s>Brahman</s>.
Because of being great (<s>bṛhat</s>) through being the self of all gods, it is <s>Brahman</s>; and that they call '<s>tyat</s>' (that) — by a word denoting what is remote.
Therefore, the <s>Śruti</s> declares the simultaneous plurality of divine forms of one single deity by virtue of His glory.
And the <s>Smṛti</s> too has been explained by the litany.
Moreover, even for ordinary people who have attained the powers of <s>aṇimā</s> and the like through the practice of [yogic] means, the simultaneous attainment of multiple embodiments is seen.
To show that very [point] clearly, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] first states the negative case: '#Sometimes one [body]#.'

'[If it be said that this is merely] a word — no, because of [its] origin; [this is established] by direct perception and inference' (#<s>śabda iti cennātaḥ prabhavātpratyakṣānumānābhyām</s>#).
Just as with cow-ness (<s>gotva</s>) and the like, because of the absence of prior apprehension [of the individual], and because even a limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>), being singular, is not perceived [as multiple] — like a cook and the like, or like the words 'space' (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like that denote universals — the words '<s>Vasu</s>' and the like too are merely denotative of individuals (<s>vyakti</s>). And since the individual is eternal, the relation [between word and referent] would be eternal.
But if [the deities] possess bodily form, then being composite, the <s>Vasu</s>s and the like would be non-eternal; and therefore, prior to [their creation], the word '<s>Vasu</s>' and the like would not have been connected with its referent, since the referent itself did not exist.
Consequently, when the <s>Vasu</s> and the like come into being, the connection of the word '<s>Vasu</s>' and the like would emerge — like the connection of the word '<s>Devadatta</s>' — as originating from human convention (<s>puruṣabuddhiprabhava</s>). And the cognition of sentence-meaning based on that [convention] would also be dependent on human understanding.
And human understanding depends on other means of knowledge for its origin — thus the authoritativeness of the <s>Veda</s> would be undermined by [its] dependence on other means of knowledge — this is the purport of the objection.
The answer: 'No. Because of [its] origin.'
From the word denoting the universal '<s>Vasu</s>-ness' and the like, [<s>Brahman</s>], having ascertained in Its mind the individual of that universal that It desires to create, brings about its origination.
This is the 'origination from that' (<s>tatprabhavatvam</s>).
What is stated amounts to this: Although the word is not the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of the <s>Vasu</s>s and the like — since <s>Brahman</s> is their material cause — nevertheless, [the word functions as] the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) in the manner described.
And this does not render the word-referent relation non-eternal, since the universal '<s>Vasu</s>-ness' and the like — or any limiting adjunct whatever — delimited by some form or other, is eternal.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] elaborates this very point through objection and resolution: '#Is it not [the case that] "from which [arise] birth and the rest"#' —
These are explained by the running commentary (<s>nigada</s>).
Then what — was speech created by the Self-existent one (<s>Svayaṃbhū</s>), like the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> and the like by <s>Kālidāsa</s> and others? And if so, [the Veda], being a statement dependent on other means of knowledge, would incur the fault of being unauthoritative — to this he says: '#This emanation (<s>utsarga</s>) of speech too is of the nature of the transmission of tradition (<s>saṃpradāya</s>)#.'
<s>Saṃpradāya</s> is the study [of the Veda] through the lineage of teachers and students.
What is stated amounts to this: Even though the Self-existent is the author of the <s>Veda</s>, [His authorship] is not independent like that of <s>Kālidāsa</s> and others, but rather in conformity with the previous creation.
And this has been demonstrated by us.

And the commentator will establish this further on.
Moreover, this [creative activity] is observed even in the present [age].
From observing that, [the same] nature is inferred even for the earlier creators — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Moreover, what was intended to be done' etc.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection: 'But of what nature, then?' etc.
The intent is this: It must be accepted that the deities originate from expressive words (<s>vācaka śabda</s>), since without an expressive [word], they cannot be imprinted on the intellect.
Therein, the individual phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>s) such as 'v' and the like are not expressive of <s>Vasu</s> and the like, since — being different upon each utterance — the comprehension of their relation [to meanings] is impossible, and since, if relation were not comprehended, there would be over-extension of expressiveness.
Moreover, would they express the sentence-meaning individually or collectively?
Not individually — since after the utterance of a single phoneme, no cognition of meaning is observed, and since the utterance of further phonemes would be purposeless.
Nor collectively — since these [phonemes], employed by a single speaker, perishing at each moment in form or in particular manifestation, cannot coexist with one another.
Nor is any third mode besides individual and collective possible.
Nor is it appropriate [to say] that even without essential coexistence, the phonemes have a mediated coexistence through latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — as with the <s>Āgneya</s> [offerings] and the like — since this cannot withstand the dilemma.
What, pray, is this intended latent impression — is it an unprecedented potency (<s>apūrva</s>) like that produced by the <s>Āgneya</s> and the like, or is it a seed of memory-production, also called <s>bhāvanā</s> (impregnation)?
The first alternative is not [viable].
For a word that is not known — either in its own form or in its subsidiary elements — and whose relation [to meaning] is not known, cannot be a cause of the cognition of meaning, like a sense-organ [which operates without such conditions].
Because a [word] that has been uttered — whether unapprehended by a deaf person, or apprehended [but] without [known] relation — is not communicative.
Therefore, a word must be accepted as communicative only when known, when its relation is known, and when all its communicative subsidiaries are known — like smoke and the like [as signs].
And thus, its latent impression — [which would be] called <s>apūrva</s> — being a subsidiary of communication, must be known prior to the cognition of meaning.
But at that time, there is no means of knowing it.
And one who tries to justify its being known from the cognition of meaning enters into an irrefutable mutual dependence: the cognition of meaning [depends on] the ascertainment of the latent impression, and the ascertainment of that [depends on] the cognition of meaning.
But the latent impression called <s>bhāvanā</s> (impregnation) is merely its own capacity to produce memory.
And it is not reasonable for that very [capacity] to be also the capacity to produce the cognition of meaning.
Nor does the very same capacity [have] a further capacity.
For the burning power of fire is not the same as its illuminating power.
Nor is the illuminating power [a power] of the burning power.
Moreover, from phonemes uttered in reverse order, that very latent impression — being a seed of memory — would exist, and hence a cognition of meaning would follow.
But it does not.
Therefore, phonemes in no way whatsoever are causes of the cognition of meaning.
Nor [is the expressive entity] the <s>sphoṭa</s> (bursting-forth entity) that is distinct from the phonemes.
Because it does not ascend into experience.
And if its knowledge [were to be established] from its effect — the cognition of meaning — there would be the absurd consequence of mutual dependence, as has been said.
But if [the <s>sphoṭa</s>], being eternal, were the cause of the cognition of meaning merely by virtue of its existence, there would be the absurd consequence of the cognition of meaning arising at all times, since an independent cause — being perpetual — [would always produce its effect].
Therefore, the production of the denotatum from a denotative word is untenable — thus.
To this the follower of the Teacher (<s>ācāryadeśīya</s>) says: '[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says "<s>sphoṭa</s>"' — thus.
We accept that phonemes are not communicative.
But that the <s>sphoṭa</s> does not [exist] — that we do not accept.
Because, immediately upon the cognition of it, the cognition of meaning arises for one whose relation [of words to meanings] is known.
Nor is there no experience of it as distinct from the phonemes.
'<s>Gau</s>' (<s>go</s>) is a single word; '<s>gām ānaya śuklām</s>' (bring the white cow) is a single sentence — [in these cases,] the experience of a single word and sentence distinct from the multiple phonemes and words is universal to all people.
Nor can this unsublated experience of a single word and sentence be declared false by [the objection] 'It is not so.'
Nor is it [merely] adventitious (<s>aupādhika</s>).
For the adventitious character (<s>upādhi</s>) would be either the being grasped in a single cognition, or the being a cause of a single cognition of meaning.
As for the first — there is no single cognition that apprehends <s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s>, and <s>palāśa</s> [trees] simultaneously as objects of a single awareness.
If there were, [the separate cognition] '<s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>palāśa</s>' would never arise.
Nor is [the adventitious character] the being a cause of a single cognition of meaning.
Because causation of that [cognition] by phonemes has been refuted.
And in postulating coexistence [of phonemes] by virtue of [their] causing that [cognition], there would be the absurd consequence of mutual dependence.
[Their] coexistence [would depend on] their being the cause of that, and their being the cause of that [would depend on their] coexistence.
Therefore, this unsublated and non-adventitious experience — of a single manifestation — regarding [what appears as] a word and a sentence, grasps a single expressive entity distinct from the phonemes; that is the <s>sphoṭa</s>. And the [individual] sounds (<s>dhvani</s>s), even while manifesting it individually, do not make it vivid in a single instant, which would produce an immediate cognition of meaning.
Rather, just as in the knowledge of the true nature of gems — [where] the reality of word and sentence shines vividly in the final cognition, which is born of a mind assisted by the maturation of the latent impressions generated by the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth observations — so too, the cognition of meaning, not having arisen previously, arises [only] after that [cumulative process]. Hence the later sounds are not purposeless.
Nor are the earlier ones — since without them, the absence of the latent impressions generated by them and their maturation [would mean] the absence of assistance, [and hence no final cognition].
Because the final cognition alone, by itself, is not generative.
Nor, like the word-cognition [where each phoneme contributes],

Because [the standard in epistemology is that] perceptual cognition is invariably [either] distinctly or indistinctly manifest.
And the cognition of the <s>sphoṭa</s> is perceptual.
But the cognition of meaning — being non-perceptual and born from another means of knowledge — may arise vividly or may not arise at all, but not indistinctly. Hence the parallel resolution [between word-cognition and meaning-cognition] does not hold.
Therefore, the eternal <s>sphoṭa</s> alone is the expressive [entity], not the phonemes.
This view of the follower of the Teacher, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] does not refute while establishing his own view: 'But the phonemes alone — and not a [separate] word' — thus.
For the <s>sphoṭa</s> as distinct from phonemes would have to be accepted only if the expressiveness of phonemes were impossible and if it [the <s>sphoṭa</s>] occupied a place in the range of experience.
And the impossibility of the expressiveness of phonemes is twofold: either because of the impossibility of comprehending [their] relation — due to [their] being momentary — or because of the absence of both modes — individual and collective.
The first alternative is not [viable].
Because there is no evidence for the momentariness of phonemes.
But one may object: the difference of phonemes upon each utterance is well-known to all people.
No.
Because they are recognized [as the same].

body.translated_text: Nor is there a clear cognition of a difference in individual instances [of the phoneme] with each pronunciation, as in the case of [the expression] 'svasti' and the like. If that were so, the cognition would be 'Caitra uttered ten ga-sounds,' not 'he uttered the ga-sound ten times.' Nor is this repetition intended in the sense of a universal (<s>jāti</s>), as in '<s>Devadatta</s> ate partridges a hundred times,' for even when a bullock cries out from being struck on the chest, there arises in people the cognition of repeated utterance with respect to the individual instance of the ga-sound and so on. The objector raises an obstacle to recognition: 'For how can many persons utter [the same sound] at one time?' That which possesses a conjunction of mutually contradictory properties simultaneously is many, just as cow, horse, and the like possess [contradictory properties such as] cloven hoof, single hoof, mane, dewlap, and so on. And this <s>varṇa</s> (phoneme) simultaneously possesses contradictory properties such as <s>udātta</s> (raised accent) and <s>anudātta</s> (unraised accent). Therefore it must be many. Nor is it proper to say that <s>udātta</s> and the like are properties of the manifesting [sounds] (<s>vyañjaka</s>), not properties of the <s>varṇa</s>. For the manifestors of this [phoneme] are the air-currents (<s>vāyu</s>). If those are inaudible, how could their properties be audible? Here this much must first be said: a sense-organ whose object is a quality does not also apprehend the quality-bearer — otherwise the nose, tongue, and ear, whose objects are smell, taste, and sound, would also apprehend earth, water, and space that possess those [qualities]. Likewise, even if the ear does not have air-currents as its object, it will apprehend their qualities such as <s>udātta</s> and the like. And those, being apprehended in conjunction with sound, are determined to be properties of sound. But the properties <s>udātta</s> and the like, being mutually contradictory, cannot belong to the intrinsic nature of the phoneme whose unity is established through recognition, without alternation. Therefore, just as a single face appears with illusory differences of location, size, and shape due to the medium of jewels, swords, mirrors, and so on, similarly even for a single <s>varṇa</s>, this illusion of conjunction with various contradictory properties is due to the manifesting <s>dhvani</s>s (sounds), and there is no real conjunction of multiple properties — this being established, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) offers a resolution by conceding [the objection]: 'Or else, it is produced by <s>dhvani</s>' (<s>athavā dhvanikṛta</s>). By 'or else' he sets aside the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view). Even if a quality and its possessor are grasped by one sense-organ, still there is no fault, because <s>dhvani</s>s too, like <s>śabda</s> (sound), are audible. He distinguishes the nature of <s>dhvani</s> from <s>varṇa</s>s through a question: 'What then is this?' Nor is it proper to say that this is merely a cognition of the generic nature of <s>varṇa</s>-hood without determining a specific [dhvani], rather than a cognition of a manifesting <s>dhvani</s> distinct from <s>varṇa</s>. For there is no recognition of it as differentiated by distinctions such as nasality and the like, as there is with individual instances of the ga-sound, etc.; and since what is not recognized lacks unity, the existence of a universal is not established. Therefore this sound is either non-phonemic in nature, or a <s>dhvani</s> distinct from <s>śabda</s>, audible and serving as a manifestor of <s>śabda</s> — and in both cases, properties such as nasality that are cognized through the medium of the particular distinctions of the respective <s>dhvani</s>s among the manifesting [sounds] are understood as properties of those [dhvanis] but appear as if belonging to <s>śabda</s>, and are not intrinsic properties of <s>śabda</s> itself. And thus, let those <s>dhvani</s>s in which mutually contradictory properties such as nasality appear be non-eternal; for there is no recognition in them. But the <s>varṇa</s>s in which there is recognition do not have nasality and the like as their properties, and hence are not non-eternal. 'And this being so' —

body.translated_text: 'has a support' (<s>sālambanā</s>). If this is the opponent's non-apprehension [of the phoneme as such] — that when the property-bearer is not grasped, its properties cannot be grasped either — then let it be so, let the opponent be satisfied. Even so there is no fault — this is the meaning. By this line of argument, the charge that <s>varṇa</s>s are non-denotative because their conjunction cannot be grasped due to their momentariness has been refuted. Now, wishing to refute what was established through the impossibility of both the individual and collective modes, he says: 'And from <s>varṇa</s>s the cognition of meaning' (<s>varṇebhyaś cārthapratīḥ</s>). Not tolerating the [opponent's] construction, the partial advocate says: 'I do not construct' (<s>na kalpayāmi</s>). He refutes this: 'No. Of this cognition too...' (<s>na, asyā api buddheḥ</s>). Let the venerable one examine the cognition that 'go' is a single word. Does this cognition apprehend only the previously experienced ga-sound and the like in their totality, or something distinct from ga-sound and the like, as a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is distinct from a boar and the like? If it were to present something different from the ga-sound and the like, there would be no cognition tinged with the ga-sound and so on. For a cognition of a boar does not apprehend a boar tinged with buffalo. The <s>dhvani</s>s, which individually manifest the one word-reality, being differentiated by differences in effort yet produced at the same place and with the same instrument, through their similarity to the respective <s>dhvani</s>s that manifest other words, impose upon the one word-reality they manifest a resemblance to many mutually dissimilar words, and through different impositions of similarity, they make even a single partless [word] appear as if many, as if possessing parts — just as jewels, swords, mirrors, and the like [make] a single face, which has a fixed number, size, location, and shape of features, [appear] with multiple colors, sizes, and shapes. And if it is said that its parts, the <s>varṇa</s>s, are merely constructed, then do you now propose to declare that the distinction of <s>varṇa</s>s is false even without a sublating cognition? If it is said that the cognition of unity itself subverts plurality — well then, in this [cognition] many <s>varṇa</s>s do appear, so why does the appearance of plurality not subvert the unity? Or rather, like the cognition of a forest or an army, unity and plurality are not contradictory. Indeed, the cognitions of army and forest do not arise while negating the distinctions of elephants, foot-soldiers, horses, and so on, or of campaka, aśoka, kiṃśuka trees and so on; rather, they impose a unity upon things that are indeed distinct, delimited by some single qualifying condition (<s>upādhi</s>). And the superimposed unity does not contradict the intrinsic plurality. For the figurative fire-nature [attributed to] a boy does not contradict his natural man-nature. Therefore, in the single memory-cognition — born from the accumulation of latent impressions (<s>bhāvanā</s>) generated by the experience of each individual <s>varṇa</s> — which encompasses all the <s>varṇa</s>s, the unity of the <s>varṇa</s>s appearing therein is to be understood as figurative (<s>aupacārika</s>), by virtue of their being objects of that single cognition and by virtue of their being causes of the cognition of a single meaning. And there is no mutual dependence [in arguing] that being the cause of a single meaning-cognition [establishes] unity, and that unity [establishes] being the cause of a single meaning-cognition. For prior to the cognition of meaning, these many <s>varṇa</s>s, which ascend into a single memory, do indeed appear.
