yadyapi pratyakṣādīnāṃ tāttvikamabādhitatvaṃ nāsti, yuktyāgamābhyāṃ bādhanāt, tathāpi vyavahāre bādhanābhāvātsāṃvyavahārikamabādhanam /
nahi pratyakṣādibhirarthaṃ paricchidya pravartamāno vyavahāre visaṃbādyate sāṃsārikaḥ kaścit /
tasmādabādhanānna pramāṇalakṣaṇamatipatanti pratyakṣādaya iti /
#satyatvopapatteriti# /
satyatvābhimānopapatteriti /
grahaṇakavākyametat /
vibhajate- #yāvaddhi na satyātmaikatvapratipattiriti# /
vikārāneva tu śarīrādīnahamityātmabhāvena putrapaśvādīnmametyātmīyabhāveneti yojanā /
vaidikaśceti /
karmakāṇḍamokṣaśāstravyavahārasamarthanā /
'svapnavyavahārasyeva' iti vibhajate- #yathā suptasya prākṛtasyeti# /
'kathaṃ cānṛtena mokṣaśāstreṇa' iti yaduktaṃ tadanubhāṣya dūṣayati- #kathaṃ tvasatyeneti# /
śakyamatra vaktuṃ, śravaṇādyupāya ātmasākṣātkāraparyanto vedāntasamuttho 'pi jñānanicayo 'satyaḥ, so 'pi hi vṛttirūpaḥ kāryatayā nirodhadharmā, yastu brahmatvabhāvasākṣātkāro 'sau na kāryastatsvabhāvatvāt, tasmādacodyametat kathamasatyātsatyotpāda iti /
yatkhalu satyaṃ na tadutpadyata iti kutastasyāsatyādutpādaḥ /
yaccotpadyate tatsarvamasatyameva /
sāṃvyavahārikaṃ tu satyatvaṃ vṛttirūpasya brahmasākṣātkārasyeva śravaṇādīnāmapyabhinnam /
tasmādabhyupetya vṛttisvarūpasya brahmasākṣātkārasya paramārthasatyatāṃ vyabhicārodbhāvanamiti mantavyam /
yadyapi sāṃvvahārikasya satyādeva bhayātsatyaṃ maraṇamutpadyate tathāpi bhayaheturahistajjñānaṃ vāsatyaṃ tato bhayaṃ satyaṃ jāyata ityasatyātsatyasyotpattiruktā /
yadyapi cāhijñānamapi svarūpeṇa sattathāpi na tajjñānatvena bhayaheturapi tvanirvācyāhirūṣitatvena /
anyathā rajjujñānādapi bhayaprasaṅgājjñānatvenāviśeṣāt /
tasmādanirvacyāhirūṣitaṃ jñānamapyanirvācyamiti siddhamasatyādapi satyasyopajana iti /
na ca brūmaḥ sarvasyādasatyātsatyasyopajanaḥ, yataḥ samāropitadhūmabhāvāyā dhūmamahiṣyā vahnijñānaṃ satyaṃ syāt /
nahi cakṣuṣo rūpajñānaṃ satyamupajāyata iti rasādijñānenāpi tataḥ satyena bhavitavyam /
yato niyamo hi sa tādṛśaḥ satyānāṃ yataḥ kutaścit kiñcideva jāyata iti /
evamasatyānāmapi niyamo yataḥ kutaścidasatyātsatyaṃ kutaścidasatyaṃ, yathā dīrghatvādervarṇeṣu samāropitatvāviśeṣe 'pyajīnamityato jyānivirahamavagacchanti satyam /
body.translated_text:
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the key to the resolution: 'That non-difference, because of the words "origination" (<s>ārambhaṇa</s>) and the like' — thus.
Since there is no contradiction with the preceding [sūtra], [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the division of this specific exposition: 'And having conceded this' — thus.
One might say this: If the world-effect — <s>ākāśa</s> and the rest — is non-different from the cause that is ultimately real, then why does the proliferation of defects alleged by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s and others not apply? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'The non-existence of the effect apart from [the cause] is understood' — thus.
Indeed, by 'non-difference' (<s>ananyatva</s>) we do not assert identity (<s>abheda</s>); rather, we negate difference (<s>bheda</s>). Therefore, there is no occasion for the defects that attend [the position of] identity.
Rather, the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s and others, in negating identity, are actually rendering assistance to us. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] glosses the reason for negating difference: 'The word "origination" (<s>ārambhaṇa</s>), to begin with' — thus.
For thus — if <s>Brahman</s> alone were the reality of the world — the entire world would be truly known through the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>.
Just as, when the rope is known, the reality of the snake [superimposed on it] is known.
For that [rope] is its [the snake's] reality.
And the knowledge of reality is [true] knowledge; what is other than that is false knowledge — ignorance indeed.
Herein, the Vedic illustration [is given]: 'Just as, dear one, by one lump of clay' — thus.
One might say this: When clay is known, how is the clay-made pot and the like known?
For that [pot] has not been established as being of the nature of clay — [as was] demonstrated above.
Therefore, it is in reality different [from clay].
And when one thing is known, another is not known — to this the <s>Śruti</s> says: 'A modification is a mere verbal elaboration (<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>), a name only.'
By speech alone is the entire class of modifications originated; but it does not exist in reality, since it is a mere name.
Just as 'the consciousness of a person' [is a mere verbal construct], or 'the head of <s>Rāhu</s>' — [these are] mere conceptual constructs (<s>vikalpa</s>).
As the knowers of conceptual construction say: 'A conceptual construct (<s>vikalpa</s>) is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a [corresponding] real object.'
And thus, being unreal by virtue of being non-substantial, the entire class of modifications is false; 'It is clay alone that is real' — [this is the truth].
Therefore, the reality of pots, dishes, water-vessels, and the like is clay alone; hence, when clay is known, the reality of all of them is known.
This is what was stated: 'And otherwise, the knowledge of everything through one knowledge would not be achieved' — thus.
Showing two further illustrations, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] concludes: 'Therefore, just as the spaces [enclosed] in pots, jars, and the like' — thus.
For those whose essential nature is seen [to arise] and [to be] destroyed are not substantially real, like mirage-water and the like. And thus the entire class of modifications [is unreal]; therefore it is not substantially real.
For whatever truly exists, exists [as] real — like the conscious Self (<s>cid-ātman</s>).
For that [Self] does not exist at some time, in some place, or in some manner [only].
Rather, it exists always, everywhere, and in every way — it never does not exist.
But the class of modifications is not like this, since it exists [only] at some time, in some manner, and in some place.
For indeed, form (<s>rūpa</s>) never at any time, in any place, or in any way becomes smell.
Now, if something has the properties of both being (<s>sat</s>) and non-being (<s>asat</s>), and if these [properties], being dependent on their own cause for their origination, exist only at some time, then that class of modifications — being pressed [to answer whether it is real or unreal] — is not eternal; hence there is no modification of anything.
But if at the time of its non-existence it does not exist, then to what does the property of non-existence belong?
For when the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) is not present, its property — non-existence — cannot be present.
But if [one says] this is not its property but rather its identity with something else —
What has come about for the [previously existing] entity?
For when a pot arises, nothing happens to the cloth.
If [one objects that] non-existence is contradictory to existence —
No.
Because a [supposed entity] that accomplishes nothing cannot be a reality.
Or, if it does accomplish something, even in that case, non-existence as applied to it would be possible [i.e., the same problem recurs].
But if one says that its non-existence means that nothing whatsoever arises, but rather it itself simply does not exist —
As they say: 'Nothing whatsoever happens to it; it simply does not exist, that is all.'
Now, let this <s>prasajya-pratiṣedha</s> (verbally-bound negation) be analyzed: is its nature that of an entity (<s>bhāva</s>), or is it an entity whose nature is that [negation]?
In the first alternative — since entities would have that [negation] as their nature, i.e., would be empty (<s>tuccha</s>) — the world would be void.
And thus there would be the absence of the experience of entities.
But in the second alternative — since the entity-nature would be eternal — there would be no usage of non-existence.
Even if the negation is caused by mere conceptual construction alone, the unwanted consequence of the eternality of the entity remains just the same. Therefore, the class of modifications is different from the cause and is not a substantially real entity.
Hence the class of modifications is indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) and false (<s>anṛta</s>).
With this evidence, the falsity of the class of modifications [is established, while] the reality of the cause is expressed as: 'It is clay alone that is real' — by this and similar passages, the <s>Śruti</s> states [this] by way of illustration.
'When the understanding of worldly examiners is in agreement — that is an illustration' — and the <s>sūtra</s> of <s>Akṣapāda</s> (<s>Gautama</s>) has as its purport that an illustration is one established by a means of valid knowledge, not that it need be established by common worldly [knowledge]; otherwise, atoms and the like would not serve as illustrations for them [the <s>Naiyāyika</s>s].
For atoms and the like are not established for ordinary people who lack the superior understanding born of natural or trained intelligence.
Now [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises the <s>anekāntavādin</s> (pluralist) objector: 'But is it not of multiple natures?' — thus.
<s>Brahman</s>, possessing multiple powers (<s>śakti</s>s), whose activities are the creations of diverse effects — it is reasonable [to say] that <s>Brahman</s> is both one and many.
What follows from this? To this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'By its aspect of oneness' — thus.
But if oneness alone were substantially real, then, because of the absence of plurality, the entire Vedic ritual-based (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>) and worldly transactional usage would be completely destroyed.
And all the practices of hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and the like that pertain to <s>Brahman</s> would become as if water poured on sand [i.e., futile].
And thus, if <s>Brahman</s> were of multiple natures, the illustrations of clay and the like would be appropriate — thus.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes this pluralism: 'It would not be so' — thus.
Here, first, this must be said: when one who says that there is oneness by virtue of the clay-nature and plurality by virtue of the pot-and-dish-nature [is asked] — regarding cause and effect mutually — is it identity that is intended, or difference, or both identity and difference?
Therein, if absolute identity — the two descriptions 'by virtue of the clay-nature' and 'by virtue of the pot-and-dish-nature,' and the restriction [that one pertains to oneness and the other to plurality], would be untenable.
If difference — the two descriptions and the restriction would be tenable, but [the expression] 'by virtue of the nature [of]' (<s>ātmanā</s>) would be incoherent.
For one thing cannot be the self (<s>ātman</s>) of another.
Nor would this be [the position of] the pluralist (<s>anekāntavāda</s>).
In the alternative of both identity and difference — the two descriptions might be possible.
But the restriction would be unjustified.
For if the two property-bearers (<s>dharmin</s>s) — cause and effect — are mixed together, it is not possible that their two properties — oneness and plurality — would not be mixed.
And thus, oneness by virtue of the clay-nature would, so long as it persists, also exist by virtue of the pot-and-dish-nature; and similarly, plurality by virtue of the pot-and-dish-nature would, so long as it persists, also be plurality by virtue of the clay-nature.
This restriction posits either absolute difference between cause and effect, or the indescribability (<s>anirvacanīyatā</s>) of the effect.
And this has been thoroughly investigated by us in the first <s>adhyāya</s>.
Let that be for now.
This very point — refuted by reasoning — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] illustrates by citing the <s>Śruti</s> that restates it: 'It is clay alone that is real' — thus.
One might say this: The <s>jīva</s>'s (individual soul's) state of being a <s>jīva</s> is not merely imagined (<s>kālpanika</s>) [i.e., superimposed], but real (<s>bhāvika</s>).
For it is a part (<s>aṃśa</s>) [of <s>Brahman</s>], and through knowledge combined with <s>karma</s>, its <s>Brahman</s>-nature is conferred — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'For it is self-established' — thus.
[This means:] because it is natural and beginningless — thus.
As for what was said — 'By its aspect of plurality, the ritual-based and worldly transactional usage will be sustained' — to that [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And when [duality] is sublated' — thus.
For all this transactional usage [persists] only so long as it is not sublated — just as in the state of dream, the transactional usage regarding the objects presented therein [persists until waking].
And just as that [dream-usage] ceases through the sublating [cognition] of the waking state, so too this [worldly usage] ceases through the direct realization of the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmātmabhāva-sākṣātkāra</s>), born from the maturation of the practice of contemplating [the meaning of] sentences like 'You are That' (<s>tattvamasi</s>).
One might say this: 'Where, however, everything has become the Self alone for him' (<s>yatra tvasya sarvam ātmaivābhūt</s>) — by this and similar [passages], the <s>Śruti</s> does not say that transactional usage characterized by action, agent, and the like — which depends on false knowledge — is removed by true knowledge; rather, it says that transactional usage dependent on a difference of states ceases upon the attainment of another state — just as the child's unrestricted behavior in eating and the like ceases upon the attainment of investiture (<s>upanayana</s>).
And that [change of state] does not thereby make that [prior behavior] dependent on false knowledge — similarly here too — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And this cessation of transactional usage' — thus.
Why? 'Because of [the sentence] "You are That," the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s>' — thus.
Indeed, this sentence does not teach the Self's identity with <s>Brahman</s> as restricted to a particular state of the <s>jīva</s>; rather, like 'This is not a snake, it is a rope,' it declares an eternal [truth].
Moreover, even by the characterization of 'real-and-unreal' (<s>satyānṛta</s>), this very [conclusion] is justified — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And by the illustration of the thief' — thus.
'And in this view' — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s> adds].
For indeed, the knowledge of a piece of wood as possessing a staff, water-pot, and earring — and as an earring-wearer (<s>kuṇḍalin</s>) — does not sublate [the perception of] its staff-nature or water-pot-nature.
For what reason?
Because the staff, earring, and the rest truly belong to that [piece of wood].
Similarly here too — the knowledge of oneness, whose object is what is real (<s>bhāvika</s>), should not sublate the plurality that is [also] real.
For knowledge does not remove a real entity.
Rather, [knowledge removes only] what has been superimposed by false knowledge — this is the meaning.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection: 'But in the commitment to absolute oneness' — thus.
A means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is defined as producing a cognition that is unsublated, previously unacquired, and undoubted — by virtue of this general definition of a means of valid knowledge, perception and the like claim the status of valid means.
But in the commitment to absolute oneness, since all of them — having difference as their object — would be sublated, their invalidity would follow.
Likewise, the scripture of injunction and prohibition too — since it depends on the distinctions of <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force), <s>bhāvya</s> (what is to be produced), <s>kāraka</s> (agent-factors), and <s>itikartavyatā</s> (procedural details) — would be contradicted.
And thus, [there would be] nihilism (<s>nāstikya</s>).
And since by the rejection of one part [of the <s>Veda</s>], the entire <s>Veda</s> is rejected, even the <s>Vedānta</s>s would be invalid — this is the loss [entailed by] the commitment to absolute identity.
Not only is this <s>mokṣa</s>-scripture rejected by the rejection of injunctions and prohibitions, but also in its own right, since it too depends on difference — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'Even of the <s>mokṣa</s>-scripture' — thus.
Moreover, in this [Advaita] view, since phonemes, words, sentences, passages, and the like are unreal, the non-dual knowledge (<s>advaita-jñāna</s>) born from them would be faulty — for surely, valid knowledge of fire does not arise from unreal smoke — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And how, by a false <s>mokṣa</s>-scripture' — thus.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: 'Here it is said' — thus.
Although perception and the like do not possess ultimately real unsublated-ness — since they are sublated by reasoning and scripture — nevertheless, in [the sphere of] transactional usage, because of the absence of sublation, they possess conventionally real (<s>sāṃvyavahārika</s>) unsublated-ness.
For no worldly being (<s>sāṃsārika</s>) who, having ascertained an object through perception and the like, engages in transactional activity, is ever disappointed in that transaction.
Therefore, because of [their] unsublated-ness, perception and the like do not fail to satisfy the definition of a means of valid knowledge — thus.
'Because of the tenability of being real' — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s> comments].
[This means:] because of the tenability of the conviction of being real — thus.
This is a summarizing statement.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] elaborates: 'For so long as the realization of the one real Self does not arise' — thus.
[The construction is:] modifications alone — such as the body and the like — [are regarded] as 'I' with the sense of selfhood, and sons, cattle, and the like as 'mine' with the sense of belonging to the self — thus.
'And the Vedic [usage too]' — thus.
This justifies the transactional usage based on both the ritual section (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>) and the <s>mokṣa</s>-scripture.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] elaborates 'like dream-transaction': 'Just as for one who is asleep, in the natural [state]' — thus.
Having restated what was said — 'And how by a false <s>mokṣa</s>-scripture' — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes it: 'But how by an unreal [scripture]' — thus.
Here it can be said: the means of knowledge — hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>) and the other practices — culminating in the direct realization of the Self, [even though] arising from the <s>Vedānta</s>, are [themselves] unreal, for they too, being of the nature of mental modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>) and being effects, are subject to cessation. But the direct realization of <s>Brahman</s>-hood (<s>brahmatva-bhāva-sākṣātkāra</s>) is not an effect, since it is of the nature of That [<s>Brahman</s>] itself. Therefore, this objection — 'How can the real arise from the unreal?' — is not a valid challenge.
For what is truly real does not originate; so whence its origination from the unreal?
And whatever originates is entirely unreal.
But the conventionally real status (<s>sāṃvyavahārika satyatva</s>) of hearing and the other practices is no different from that of the direct realization of <s>Brahman</s>, which is [also] of the nature of a mental modification.
Therefore, it should be understood that, having conceded the ultimately real status of the direct realization of <s>Brahman</s> — which is of the nature of a mental modification — the demonstration of an inconsistency [follows].
Although the fear of death — being conventionally real — arises from what is [conventionally] real, nevertheless the snake that is the cause of fear, or the cognition of it, is unreal; from that, the fear — which is real — arises. Thus, the origination of the real from the unreal is stated.
And although the cognition of the snake is also real in its own form, nevertheless it is not a cause of fear by virtue of being a cognition, but rather by virtue of being qualified by the indescribable snake-form.
Otherwise, even the cognition of a rope would entail fear — since, qua cognition, there is no distinction.
Therefore, the cognition qualified by the indescribable snake-form is also indescribable — hence it is established that the real can arise even from the unreal.
And we do not say that the real arises from everything that is unreal — for then, from a she-buffalo of smoke superimposed [on fire], the knowledge of fire would be real [which is absurd].
For indeed, just because a valid cognition of form arises from the eye, it does not follow that a valid cognition of taste and the like must also arise from it.
For there is such a restriction among realities: from some particular [cause], only some particular [effect] arises.
Similarly, among unrealities too there is a restriction: from some unreal [thing], the real [arises]; from some other unreal [thing], the unreal [arises]. Just as, despite the equal status of being superimposed upon phonemes, from [the word] <s>ajīna</s> (animal skin), people understand the real absence of old age (<s>jyāni</s>) [by false etymology].

body.text:
ajinamityatastu samāropitadīrghabhāvājjyānivirahamavagacchanto bhavanti bhrāntāḥ /
na cobhayatra dīrghasamāropaṃ prati kaścidasti bhedaḥ /
tasmādupapannamasatyādapi satyasyodaya iti /
nidarśanāntaramāha- #svapnadarśanāvasthasyeti# /
yathā sāṃsāriko jāgradbhujaṅgaṃ dṛṣṭvā palāyate tataśca na daṃśavedanāmāpnoti, pipāsuḥ salilamālokya pātuṃ pravartate tatastadāsādya pāyaṃpāyamāpyāyitaḥ sukhamanubhavati, evaṃ svapnāntike 'pi tadavasthaṃ sarvamityasatyātkāryasiddhiḥ /
śaṅkate- #tatkāryamapyanṛtameveti# /
evamapi nāsatyātsatyasya siddhiruktetyarthaḥ /
pariharati- #tatra brūmaḥ /
yadyapi svapnadarśanāvasthasyeti# /
laukiko hi suptotthito 'vagamyaṃ bādhitaṃ manyate na tadavagatiṃ, tena yadyapi parikṣakā anirvācyarūṣitāmavagatimanirvācyāṃ niścinvanti tathāpi laukikābhiprāyeṇaitaduktam /
atrāntare laukāyatikānāṃ matamapākaroti- #etena svapnadṛśo 'vagatyabādhaneneti# /
yadākhalvayaṃ caitrastārakṣavīṃ vyāttavikaṭadaṃṣṭrākarālavadanāmuttabdhabambhramanmastakāvacumbilāṅgūlāmatiroṣāruṇastabdhaviśālavṛttalocanāṃ romāñcasaṃcayotphullamīṣaṇāṃ sphaṭikācalabhittipratibimbitāmabhyamitrīṇāṃ tanumāsthāya svapne pratibuddho mānuṣīmātmanastanuṃ paśyati tadobhayadehānugatamātmānaṃ pratisaṃdadhāno dehātiriktamātmānaṃ, niścinoti, na tu dehamātram, tanmātratve dehavatpratisaṃdhānābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
kathaṃ caitadupapadyeta yadi svapnadṛśo 'vagatirabādhitā syāt /
tadbādhe tu pratisaṃdhānābhāva iti /
asatyācca satyapratītiḥ śrutisiddhānvayavyatirekasiddhā cetyāha- #tathāca śrutiriti /
tathākārādīti# /
yadyapi rekhāsvarūpaṃ satyaṃ tathāpi tadyathāsaṃketamasatyam /
nahi saṃketayitāraḥ saṃketayantīdṛśena rekhābhedenāyaṃ varṇaḥ pratyetavyo 'pi tvīdṛśo rekhābhedo 'kāra īdṛśaśca kakāra iti /
tathā cāsamīcīnātsaṃketātsamīcīnavarṇāvagatiriti siddham /
yaccoktamekatvāṃśena jñānamokṣavyavahāraḥ setsyati, nānātvāṃśena tu karmakāṇḍāśrayo laukikaśca vyavahāraḥ setsyatīti, tatrāha- #api cāntyamidaṃ pramāṇamiti# /
yadi khalvekatvāvagatinibandhanaḥ kaścidasti vyavahāraḥ, tadavagateḥ sarvettaratvāt /
tathāhi-'tattvamasi' ityaikātmyāvagatiḥ samastapramāṇatatphalatādvyahārānapabādhamānaivodīyate, naitasyāḥ parastātkiñcidanukūlaṃ pratikūlaṃ cāsti, yadapekṣena, yena ceyaṃ pratikṣipyeta, tatrānukūlapratikūlanivāraṇānnātaḥ paraṃ kiñcidākāṅkṣyamiti /
na ceyamavagatirḍulakṣīraprāyetyāha- #na ceyamiti# /
syādetat /
antyā cediyamavagatirniṣprayojanā tarhi tathā ca prekṣāvadbhirupādīyeta, prayojanavattve vā nāntyā syādityata āha- #na ceyamavagatiranarthikā#kutaḥ #avidyānivṛttiphaladarśanāt# /
nahīyamutpannā satī paścādavidyāṃ nivartayati yena nāntyā syāt, kintvavidyāvirodhisvabhāvatayā tannivṛttyātmaivodayate /
avidyānivṛttiśca na tatkāryatayā phalamapi tviṣṭatayā, iṣṭalakṣaṇatvātphalasyeti /
pratikūlaṃ parācīnaṃ nirākartumāha- #bhrāntirveti# /
kutaḥ, #bādhaketi# /
syādetat /

mṛdādidṛṣṭāntena hi kathañcitpariṇāma unneyaḥ, naca śakya unnetum, 'mṛttiketyeva satyam' iti kāraṇamātrasatyatvāvadhāraṇena kāryasyānṛtatvapratipādanāt /
body.translated_text: But those who understand the absence of the bowstring from the animal-skin due to the superimposed lengthening in 'ajinam' are deluded. And there is no difference regarding the superimposition of length in both cases. Therefore it is established that the real can arise even from the unreal. He gives another illustration: 'of one in the state of dream-vision.' Just as a worldly person in waking, having seen a serpent, runs away and thereby does not suffer the pain of a bite, and a thirsty person, seeing water, proceeds to drink and, having obtained it, drinks and is refreshed and experiences happiness — so too in the dream state everything is the same, hence effects arise from the unreal. He raises an objection: 'that effect too is unreal.' Even so, the production of the real from the unreal has not been established — this is the meaning. He resolves it: 'there we say: although of one in the state of dream-vision.' For an ordinary person who has awakened understands that what was cognized has been sublated, not that the cognition itself is sublated. Therefore, although critical examiners determine that the cognition tinged with the indeterminable is itself indeterminable, still this is stated from the standpoint of ordinary people. In this connection, he refutes the view of the <s>Lokāyatikas</s> (materialists): 'by this, the non-sublation of the cognition of the dream-seer.' When indeed this <s>Caitra</s>, having assumed in dream the body of an enemy — a she-jackal with gaping mouth and terrible fangs, with tail raised and touching the whirling head, with eyes reddened, fixed and wide with excessive rage, with hair slightly bristling with goosebumps, reflected on a wall of crystal mountain — and upon awakening sees his own human body, then, connecting his self as continuous through both bodies, he ascertains a self beyond the body, not merely the body; for if he were merely the body, there would be the absurd consequence of no recognition of continuity, just as with the body itself. And how would this be possible if the cognition of the dream-seer were unsublated? But if that is sublated, then the absence of recognition of continuity follows. And the cognition of the real from the unreal is established by <s>śruti</s> (scripture), and is also established through positive and negative concomitance — he says: 'and so the <s>śruti</s>; thus from letters and the like.' Although the form of the written marks is real, still as conventionally designated they are unreal. For those who establish conventions do not say 'this letter is to be understood by such and such a difference of written marks,' but rather 'such and such a written mark is the letter a, and such and such is the letter ka.' Thus it is established that correct apprehension of letters arises from incorrect convention. And regarding what was said — 'through the aspect of oneness, the transaction of knowledge and liberation will be accomplished, and through the aspect of multiplicity, the transaction dependent on the ritual portion and worldly transaction will be accomplished' — to that he says: 'moreover, this is the final <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).' If indeed there is any transaction grounded in the cognition of oneness, that cognition being ultimate among all. For thus: the cognition of identity in '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('you are that') arises without sublating the transactions of all other means of knowledge and their results; there is nothing favorable or unfavorable beyond this, with reference to which or by which this could be rejected. Since both the favorable and the unfavorable are precluded, nothing further is to be expected beyond this. And this cognition is not like an owl's milk — he says: 'nor is this.' One might say: if this cognition is final, then it is purposeless, and thus would not be adopted by the discerning; or if it has a purpose, it would not be final — therefore he says: 'nor is this cognition without purpose.' Why? 'Because the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is seen as its result.' For this cognition, once arisen, does not subsequently remove <s>avidyā</s> such that it would not be final; rather, being of a nature opposed to <s>avidyā</s>, it arises as identical with the cessation of <s>avidyā</s>. And the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> is not a result in the sense of being its effect, but in the sense of being desired, since a result is defined as what is desired. To refute the opposing view, he says: 'error, etc.' Why? 'Because of the sublating cognition.' One might say: let there be no transaction grounded in oneness; but there is one grounded in multiplicity, for that alone sustains the entire course of the world, and therefore, for establishing that, the reality of multiplicity must be posited — to this he says: 'prior to, etc.' For the transaction of those who act with deliberation is possible through cognition, but not through its reality, since it is possible even through error — this has been indicated. And it is real due to non-discordance, and unreal due to being indeterminable as it cannot withstand scrutiny. The sublating power of the final cognition of identity is due to its independence, and the weakness of the cognition of multiplicity due to its dependence on the apprehension of a counterpositive makes it sublatable — stating this, he concludes the topic: 'therefore, by the final <s>pramāṇa</s>.' One might say: we do not posit the reality of multiplicity for establishing the transaction of multiplicity, but rather its reality is itself scriptural — thus he objects: 'but clay and so forth.' He resolves: 'no, it is said.' For by the illustration of clay and the like, some kind of transformation is to be inferred, but it cannot be so inferred, because the statement 'clay alone is real' establishes the unreality of the effect through the determination that only the cause is real.

children.translated_text: It is of the nature of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).'

children.text: nāma ca rūpaṃ ca te eva bījaṃ tasya vyākaraṇaṃ kāryaprapañcastadapekṣatvādaiśvaryasya /
children.translated_text: Name and form — these are the seed of that; its manifestation is the expanse of effects, since sovereignty depends on them.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati-na tāttvikamaiśvaryaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ ca brahmaṇaḥ kintvavidyopādhikamiti tadāśrayaṃ pratijñāsūtraṃ, tattvāśrayaṃ ti tadananyatvasūtram, tenāvirodhaḥ /
children.translated_text: What is meant is this: the sovereignty and omniscience of <s>Brahman</s> are not real but are conditioned by the limiting adjunct of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); the <s>sūtra</s> of the proposition is based on that, while the <s>sūtra</s> of non-difference is based on reality. Hence there is no contradiction.
The rest is straightforward. //14//

body.translated_text: But there are thousands of <s>śruti</s> passages that establish the absolute immutability (<s>kūṭastha-nityatva</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>, hence <s>Brahman</s> does not possess the property of transformation. Now, if even the immutable can undergo transformation, why should it not? — to this he says: 'for not of a single entity.' He raises an objection: 'like rest and motion.' Just as in one and the same arrow, there is both cessation of motion and motion, so in the one <s>Brahman</s> there will be both transformation and the absence thereof, i.e., immutability. He refutes: 'from the qualifier of the immutable.' For the immutability that is <s>kūṭastha</s> is an eternal non-departure from one's own nature. How can that not be contradicted by departure? And a property is not different from its possessor, so that even upon the arising and perishing of that property, the possessor would remain immutable. If the difference were absolute, as between a cow and a horse, there would be no relation of property and possessor. But arrows and the like undergo transformation through rest and motion — they are subject to change. Moreover, since the entire corpus of the <s>Vedas</s> derives its meaningfulness from the injunction to study the <s>Vedas</s>, not even a single letter should be meaningless — how much less so such a large collection of sentences that establishes <s>Brahman</s> as the source of the world. There, in the proximity of the fruitful teaching of the vision of <s>Brahman</s>, the teaching of being the source of the world, though itself without independent fruit, serves that purpose as a means to it, and not for any other purpose — he says: 'and not as regarding <s>Brahman</s>.' Therefore it does not refer to transformation — this is the meaning. He raises the objection of contradiction with the <s>sūtra</s> 'its non-difference' and contradiction with <s>śruti</s>: 'for one who holds the doctrine that <s>Brahman</s> is the immutable self.' He resolves: 'no.

children.translated_text: For if difference is established, then <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) follows, and from <s>samavāya</s>, difference follows.
And there is no other means of establishing difference, since both purposive activity and designation can be accounted for even without difference — this has been shown.
Therefore all this amounts to nothing.

children.text: anayā ca diśā mūlakāraṇaṃ brahmaiva paramārthasat, avāntarakāraṇāni ca tanvādayaḥ sarve 'nirvācyā evetyāha- #tathā ca tantuṣviti# //15 //
children.translated_text: And in this direction, <s>Brahman</s> alone as the root cause is ultimately real, while all intermediate causes such as threads and the like are themselves indeterminable — he says: 'and so in the threads, etc.' //15//

body.translated_text: '<s>Bhāve</s> (existence) and <s>upalabdhi</s> (apprehension).' The existence (<s>bhāva</s>) of the cause and the apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>) — from the apprehension and existence of the effect in that cause. What is meant is this: the word 'object' refers to both object and subject, and the word 'subject' also refers to both subject and object; thus the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is established — from the apprehension and existence that are to be accepted, of the apprehension and existence of the cause. And thus there is no deviation with the visual perception that has a nature of illumination not contrary to form, nor with smoke as distinct from fire whose existence and non-existence follow the existence and non-existence of fire — this is established. There, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator, i.e., <s>Śaṅkara</s>) begins by stating one part of the stated reason: 'and for this reason the non-difference of the effect from the cause' — the absence of difference of the effect — 'because of the very existence of the cause.' He states the probative force of this through the negative method: 'and not invariably.' By the logic of the crow and the palm fruit, one thing is perceived in the presence of another, but not invariably — this is the meaning. To qualify the reason, he raises the objection of deviation: 'but even in the presence of another.' He resolves by the view of a partial adherent: 'no, it is said.' Having refuted the partial resolution through an objection, he states the ultimate resolution: 'now then.' By this, the qualification of the reason has been stated. He explains the same <s>sūtra</s> with an alternative reading: 'not only from words.' By direct perceptual cognition of 'cloth,' only the threads in the state of being stretched out as a covering are apprehended, but no cloth beyond the threads is directly perceived. And the oneness of the threads is due to the delimitation by the single purposive activity characterized as a single covering, even though they are many. Just as trees such as <s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s>, and <s>palāśa</s>, though many, delimited by one place and time, constitute a forest. And in purposive activity, though individually incapable, they are seen to accomplish it when combined, without producing anything additional — just as stones support a pot-stand as one thing. Similarly, threads combined will serve as a single covering without producing anything additional. And it is not proper to say that the non-ascertainment of difference between two distinct things is due to <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), for there is mutual dependence:

children.translated_text: And it is not proper to say that being itself is differentiated because of its non-difference from those two.
For in that case, there would be the absurd consequence that being itself is superimposed.

children.text: tatra bhedābhedayoranyatarasamāropakalpanāyāṃ kiṃ tāttvikābhedopādānābhedakalpanāstu, āho tāttvikabhedopādānābhedakalpaneti /
children.translated_text: Now, in the choice between superimposing either difference or non-difference — should one accept real non-difference and superimpose difference, or accept real difference and superimpose non-difference?

children.text: vayaṃ tu paśyāmo bhedagrahasya pratiyogigrahapekṣatvādbhedagrahamantareṇa ca pratiyogigrahasaṃbhavādanyonyasaṃśrayāpatteḥ, abhedagrahasya ca nirapekṣatayā tadanupapatterekaikāśrayatvācca bhedasyaikābhāve tadanupapatterabhedagrahopādānaiva bhedakalpaneti sarvabhavadātam //16 //
children.translated_text: But we observe that since the apprehension of difference depends on the apprehension of a counterpositive, and since the apprehension of a counterpositive is possible without the apprehension of difference, there would be mutual dependence; whereas the apprehension of non-difference, being independent, suffers no such difficulty; and since difference, being dependent on each individual thing, cannot be established in the absence of even one, the superimposition of difference with non-difference as the basis is established — this is accepted by all. //16//

body.translated_text: 'And because of the existence of the lower.' He analyzes: 'and for this further reason.' Not only <s>śruti</s>, but reasoning too applies here: 'whatever is of the nature of whatever.' For oil does not exist in sand in the nature of sand as a pot exists in clay in the nature of clay. For a pot that has come into being is apprehended as having the nature of clay. But oil that has come into being is not apprehended as having the nature of sand. Therefore, just as oil is never born from sand, so too the world would never be born from the self; but it is born, therefore it is understood that 'it existed as the self itself.' He gives another reasoning: 'just as the cause, <s>Brahman</s>.' For just as a pot is always and everywhere a pot alone and never at any time becomes a cloth, so too being (<s>sat</s>) is always and everywhere being alone and cannot at any time become non-being — this has been established earlier. Therefore the effect in all three times is being alone. If it has being, what follows from that? — to this he says: 'and again, one.' The being of cause and effect is one. For being is not differentiated in each individual. And therefore, since they are non-different in their undivided being, these too are not different from each other.

children.translated_text: 'It is not so, because of the designation as non-being — no, because of another attribute, by the completion of the sentence.'
And the states of being manifest and unmanifest are two attributes that are indeterminable.
This <s>sūtra</s> has been explained by the <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary) which is a verbal paraphrase. //17//

utpādanā hi siddhānāṃ kapālakulālādīnāṃ vyāpāro notpattiḥ /
na cotpādanaivotpattiḥ, prayojyaprayojakavyāpārayorbhedāt /
abhede vā ghaṭamutpādayatītivadghaṭamutpadyata ityapi prasaṅgāt /
tasmāt karotikārayatyoriva ghaṭagocarayorbhṛtyasvāmisamavetayorutpattyutpādanayoradhiṣṭhānabhedo 'bhyupetavyaḥ, tatra kapāsakulālādīnāṃ siddhānāmutpādanādhiṣṭhānānāṃ notpattyadhiṣṭhānatvamastīti pāriśeṣyādghaṭa eva sādhya utpatteradhiṣṭhānameṣitavyaḥ /
na cāsāvasannadhiṣṭhānaṃ bhavitumarhatīti sattvamasyābhyupeyam /
evañca ghaṭo bhavatītila ghaṭavyāpārasya dhātūpāttatvāttatrāsya kartṛtvamupapadyate, taṇḍulānāmiva satāṃ viklittau viklidyanti taṇḍulā iti /
śaṅkate- #atha svakāraṇasattāsaṃbandha evotpattiriti# /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-notpattirnāma kaścidvyāpāraḥ, yenāsiddhasya kathamatra kartṛtvamityanuyujyeta, kintu svakāraṇasamavāyaḥ, svasattasvāyo vā, sa cāsato 'pyaviruddha iti /
so 'pyasato 'nupapanna ityāha- #kathamalabdhātmakamiti# /
api ca prāgutpatterasattvaṃ kāryasteti kāryābhāvasya bhāvena maryādākaraṇanupapannamityāha- #abhāvasya ceti# /
syādetat /
atyantābhāvasya bandhyāsutasya mā bhūnmaryādanupākhyo hi saḥ, ghaṭaprāgabhāvasya tu bhaviṣyatā ghaṭenopākhyeyasyāsti maryādetyata āha- #yadi bandhyāputraḥ kārakavyāpārāditi# /
uktametadadhastādyathā na jātu ghaṭaḥ paṭo bhavatyevamasadapi sanna bhavatīti /
tasmānmṛtpiṇḍe ghaṭasyāsattve 'tyantāsattvameveti /
atrāsatkāryavādī codayati- #nanvevaṃ satīti# /
prāk prasiddhamapi kāryaṃ kadācitkāraṇena yojayituṃ vyāpāror'thavānmavedityata āha-tadananyatvācceti /
pariharati- #naiṣa doṣa iti# /
uktametadyathā bhujaṅgatattvaṃ na rajjorbhidyate, rajjureva hi tat, kālpanikastu bhedaḥ, evaṃ vastutaḥ kāryatattvaṃ na kāraṇādbhidyate kāraṇasvarūpameva hi tat, anirvācyaṃ tu kāryarūpaṃ bhinnamivābhinnamiva cāvabhāsata iti /
body.translated_text: 'From reasoning and from another scriptural text. Because the prior state possesses excellence.' For the attribute of excellence cannot exist in an effect that is unreal. Now, one might say that it is not the excellence of the effect that is the determining factor, but rather the difference in the power of the cause, and that power exists because the cause exists even when the effect is non-existent — to this he says: 'and power.' It is neither different from the cause and the effect, nor is it non-existent as having the nature of the effect — this is the construction. 'Moreover, of cause and effect.' Although this meaning was stated in 'because of existence and apprehension,' still it is repeated here for the purpose of refuting <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). 'And when not accepted' — when the relation of <s>samavāya</s> with the things inhering is not accepted, there would be the absurd consequence of disconnection of parts and wholes, substances and qualities, and so forth from each other. For <s>samavāya</s>, unrelated to the things inhering, cannot relate the things inhering. He raises an objection: 'but if <s>samavāya</s> by itself.' Just as substances, qualities, and actions exist due to their connection with being (<s>sattā</s>), but being itself is inherently existent and does not require connection with another being, so too <s>samavāya</s> does not require connection with another relation to be related to the things inhering, since it is itself of the nature of relation. He refutes this by showing it leads to conflict with another established doctrine: 'then conjunction too.' And one should not say that because conjunction is an effect, and because an effect depends on its inherent cause for its origin, and because without inherence this cannot be accounted for, therefore inherence is postulated for conjunction — for in the case of eternal conjunction, that absence would follow. Moreover, just as <s>samavāya</s>, whose determination depends on the relata, is not differentiated when the two relata differ and does not perish when they perish but is rather eternal and one, so too conjunction would be the same. What fault would there be in that? If, out of fear of this consequence, it is accepted that <s>samavāya</s>, like conjunction, is differentiated for each pair of relata and is non-eternal, then, just as conjunction arises from an efficient cause alone, so too <s>samavāya</s> would arise from an efficient cause alone — the situation is the same. 'And because of the cognition of identity.' For the seed of postulating a relation lies in the cognition of relatedness, not in the cognition of identity, since the latter is contradictory to a relation that rests on duality. He refutes the whole beyond the parts through an alternative analysis: 'and how can the effect be? In its totality.' Because the middle and far parts are separated by the near part. Now if it is said that though pervading all parts collectively, it will be grasped as located in only some parts, to that he says: 'for plurality is not. And if part by part.' For the number of plurality, by its very nature, pervades all the things enumerated; therefore, if even one enumerated item is not grasped, plurality is not grasped, since its nature pervades the totality. But the whole does not pervade its parts by its own nature, but rather part by part. Therefore, just as a thread pervading flowers through its parts does not require the grasping of all flowers together, since it can be perceived even when located in only some flowers, so too the whole — this is the purport. He refutes: 'even so.' He objects: 'like cowness and the like.' He refutes: 'no.' Although the particulars of <s>gotva</s> (cowness), which is a universal, are indeterminable and not ultimately real, and thus there is no complete realization of it in each individual, still this has been stated by way of concession. Since it has no maker, it would therefore be without a self. For in the absence of a cause, an unproduced effect — what would it be? Therefore it is without self — this is the meaning. If it be said that the word 'pot' is applied to its parts through conventional usage, the parts being arranged facing the production of the pot, and since those parts are already established, there is agency, and thus the usage 'the pot comes into being' is justified — to this he says: 'and the origination of the pot being spoken of.' For the activity of established things like potsherds, potters, and the like is production, not origination. And production is not the same as origination, since the action of the one acted upon and the action of the agent are different. Or if they were identical, then just as one says 'he produces the pot,' one could also say 'he originates the pot' — which is absurd. Therefore, just as with the verbs 'to do' and 'to cause to do,' which have the master and servant as their respective loci, so too origination and production, being respectively about the pot, must have different loci. There, the already-established potsherds, potters, and the like are the loci of production but not of origination; therefore, by elimination, the pot itself, which is to be accomplished, must be accepted as the locus of origination. And it cannot be a locus while non-existent, therefore its existence must be accepted. And thus, since the pot is the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal root in 'the pot comes into being,' its agency in that is justified, just as with rice grains that exist and soften: 'the rice grains soften.' He objects: 'but if origination is just the connection with one's own cause's existence.' What is meant is this: origination is not some activity by which the objection 'how can the unestablished have agency here?' would apply; rather it is the inherence in one's own cause, or the connection with one's own existence, and that is not contradicted even for the non-existent. He refutes that too as impossible for the non-existent: 'how can that which has not attained being.' Moreover, since prior to origination the effect is non-existent, the delimitation of the absence of the effect by existence is unjustified — he says: 'and of absence.' One might say: let there be no delimitation for absolute absence, such as a barren woman's son, for that is not subject to delimitation; but for the prior absence of the pot, which is to be delimited by the future pot, there is delimitation — to this he says: 'if the barren woman's son, from the operation of agents.' This has been stated earlier: just as a pot never becomes a cloth, so too non-being does not become being. Therefore, when the pot is non-existent in the lump of clay, it is absolutely non-existent. Here the proponent of <s>asatkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine that the effect is non-existent before origination) objects: 'but if so.' Even a previously well-known effect might sometimes be connected with a cause through some operation — to this he says: 'because of its non-difference from that.' He resolves: 'this is no fault.' This has been stated: just as the reality of the serpent is not different from the rope — for it is the rope itself, the difference being merely imagined — so too in reality the nature of the effect is not different from the cause, for it is the very nature of the cause; but the indeterminable form of the effect appears as if different and as if non-different.

vastutaḥ paramārthato 'nyatvaṃ na viśeṣadarśanamātrādbhavati /

children.translated_text: If the effect is non-different from the cause, then the operation of agents would have a real object, not otherwise — this is the meaning.
'The root cause' — <s>Brahman</s>.
Having taken up the portion of the <s>sūtra</s> 'and from another scriptural text,' he explains: 'thus from reasoning, of the effect.'
The meaning is transparent. //18//

body.translated_text: This has been stated: 'the non-otherness of the real.' In reality, in the ultimate sense, otherness does not arise merely from the perception of a distinction. But in conventional usage, some kind of otherness does exist — this is the meaning. For it is in this very direction that this passage should be construed. He states another refutation against the proponent of <s>asatkāryavāda</s>: 'but for one who holds, etc.'

children.translated_text: 'Like a cloth.'
'And just as <s>prāṇa</s> (breath) and the rest'

children.text: iti ca sūtre nigadavyākhyātena bhāṣyeṇa vyākhyāte //19 //
children.translated_text: — these two <s>sūtras</s> have been explained by the <s>bhāṣya</s> which is a verbal paraphrase. //19//

body.text:
#itaravyapadeśāddhitākaraṇādidoṣaprasaktiḥ# /
yadyapi śārīrātparamātmano bhedamāhuḥ śrutayastathāpyabhedamapi darśayanti śrutayo bahvayaḥ /
naca bhedābhedāvekatra samavetau virodhāt, naca bhedastāttvika ityuktam /
tasmāt paramātmanaḥ sarvajñānna śārīrastattvato bhidyate /
sa eva tvavidyopadhānabhedādghaṭakarakādyākāśavadbhedena prathate /
upahitaṃ cāsya rūpaṃ śārīraḥ, tena mā nāma jīvāḥ paramātmatāmātmano 'nubhūvan, paramātmā tu tānātmano 'bhinnānanubhavati /

children.translated_text: If he did not know them as non-different, there would be a contradiction with his omniscience.
And thus, in binding the individual selves, he would be binding himself.
To this it has been said: 'for no one who is not subject to another's control would make a prison for himself and enter it' — and so forth.
Therefore, a conscious entity is not the cause of the world — this is the prima facie view. //21//

body.translated_text: 'Because of the designation of the other, the fault of failure to act for the welfare and so forth would follow.' Although <s>śruti</s> passages declare a difference between the individual self and the supreme self, nevertheless many <s>śruti</s> passages also demonstrate their non-difference. And difference and non-difference cannot co-exist in one entity due to contradiction, and it has been stated that difference is not real. Therefore, the individual self is not really different from the supreme self who is omniscient. But due to the differentiation imposed by the limiting adjunct of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), like space delimited by a pot, a room, and so forth, it appears as different. And its conditioned form is the individual self (<s>śārīra</s>); therefore, let the individual selves not experience their identity with the supreme self — the supreme self, however, knows them as non-different from itself.

body.text: #adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt# /

children.text: satyamayaṃ paramātmana sarvajñatvādyathā jīvān vastuta ātmano 'bhinnān paśyati, paśyatyevaṃ na bhāvata eṣāṃ sukhaduḥkhādivedanāsaṅgostyavidyāvaśāttveṣāṃ tadvadabhimāna iti /
children.translated_text: True, this supreme self, due to its omniscience, sees the individual selves as they really are — non-different from itself; but it also sees thus: their association with the experience of pleasure, pain, and the like does not really exist; it is only through the power of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) that they have such a false identification.

children.text: tathā ca teṣāṃ sukhaduḥkhādivedanāyāmapyahamudāsīna iti na teṣāṃ bandhanāgāraniveśe 'pyastikṣatiḥ kācinmameti na hitākaraṇādidoṣāpattiriti rāddhāntaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus, even when they experience pleasure, pain, and the like, 'I remain indifferent' — so even when they are confined in the prison of bondage, there is no impairment whatsoever to me; hence there is no consequence of failure to act for the welfare, and so forth — this is the established conclusion.
This has been stated: 'moreover, when "you are that"' —
The word 'moreover' indicates conjunction with the preceding argument, not the introduction of an additional argument. //22//

body.translated_text: 'But it is something additional, because of the indication of difference.'

children.translated_text: One might say:

children.text: yadi brahmaviṣarto jagat, hanta sarvasyaiva jīvavacaitanyaprasaṅga ityata āha- #aśmādivacca tadanupapattiḥ# /
children.translated_text: If the world is a transformation of <s>Brahman</s>, then there would be the absurd consequence that everything, like the individual selves, would be conscious — to this he says: 'and like stones and the like, that is not tenable.'
This has been explained by the <s>bhāṣya</s> whose meaning is transparent. //23//

body.text:
#upasaṃhāradarśanānneti cenna kṣīravaddhi# /
brahma khalvekamadvitīyatayā parānapekṣaṃ krameṇotpadyamānasya jagato vivadhavicitrarūpasyopādānamupeyate tadanupapannam /
nahyekarūpātkāryabhedo bhavitumarhati, tasyākasmikatvaprasaṅgāt /
kāraṇabhedo hi kāryabhedahetuḥ, kṣīrabījādibhedādṛśyaṅkurāhikāryabhedadarśanāt /
na cākramātkāraṇāt kāryakramo jujyato, samarthasya kṣepāyogādadvitīyatayā ca kramavattatsahakārisamavadhānāpapatteḥ /
tadidamuktam- #iha hi loka iti# /
ekaikaṃ mṛdādi kārakaṃ teṣāṃ tu sāmagryaṃ sādhanam, tato hi kāryaṃ sādhayatyeva, tasmānnādvitīyaṃ brahma jagadupādānamiti prāpte, ucyate- #kṣīravaddhi# /
idaṃ tāvadbhavān pṛṣṭo vyācaṣṭām-kiṃ tāttvikamasya rūpamapekṣyemucyate utānādināmarūpabījasahitaṃ kālpanikaṃ sārvajñyaṃ sarvaśaktitvam /
tatra pūrvasmin kalpe kiṃ nāma tato 'dvitīyādasahāyādupajāyate /
nahi tasya śuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvasya vastusatkāryamasti /
tathā ca śrutiḥ-'na tasya kāryaṃ karaṇaṃ ca vidyate' iti /
uttarasmiṃstu kalpe yadi kulālādivadatyantavyatiriktasahakārikāraṇābhāvādanupādānatvaṃ sādhyate, tataḥ kṣīrādibhirvyabhicāraḥ /
te 'pi hi bāhyacetanādikāraṇānapekṣā eva kālaparivaśena svata eva pariṇāmāntaramāsādayanti /
atrāntarakāraṇānapekṣatvaṃ hetuḥ kriyate, tadasiddham, anirvācyanāmarūpabījasahāyatvāt /

children.text: tathā ca śrutiḥ-'māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyānmāyinaṃ ti maheśvaram' iti kāryakrameṇa utparipāko 'pi kramavānunneyaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus the <s>śruti</s> says: 'Know <s>māyā</s> to be <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), and the great Lord to be the wielder of <s>māyā</s>.' The sequential ripening of effects too is to be inferred as sequential.
Moreover, from a single cause possessing varied powers, the production of manifold effects is observed.
Just as from a single fire arise burning and cooking, or from a single action arise conjunction, disjunction, and <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions).

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'Not because of the observation of aggregation, it is said; for it is like milk.' Now, <s>Brahman</s>, being one without a second and thus independent of anything else, is accepted as the material cause of the world which arises in sequence with manifold and varied forms — but this is untenable. For from a cause of uniform nature, differentiation of effects cannot arise, since that would be without reason. It is the differentiation of causes that is the reason for differentiation of effects, as we observe the differentiation of effects such as the rice-shoot and the serpent from differentiated causes such as milk and seed. Nor is a sequential arising of effects justified from a non-sequential cause, since a capable cause cannot delay its operation, and being without a second, the sequential co-presence of auxiliary causes is impossible. This has been stated: 'For in this world...' Each individual [factor] such as clay is a causal agent; their aggregate is the instrument, for it is from that aggregate that the effect is produced. Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> which is without a second cannot be the material cause of the world — when this prima facie view is arrived at, the reply is: 'Like milk.' Now let the honorable opponent explain when asked — is this said with reference to its real nature, or with reference to its provisional <s>sarvajñatva</s> (omniscience) and <s>sarvaśaktitva</s> (omnipotence) together with the beginningless seed of name and form that is superimposed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)? In the former interpretation, what indeed arises from that which is without a second, without an associate? For that which is of the nature of pure, enlightened, and liberated being has no real effect-in-cause. And thus the <s>śruti</s> says: 'Neither effect nor instrument is found in it.' But in the latter interpretation, if what is being established is that it is not a material cause because of the absence of completely external auxiliary causes as in the case of the potter and such, then there is deviation by the examples of milk and the like. For they too, without depending on external conscious agents and such causes, undergo transformation of their own accord through the force of time alone. If independence from external causes is made the reason here, that is unestablished, because [<s>Brahman</s>] is assisted by the beginningless seed of indescribable name and form.

children.text: yadi tu cetanatve satīti viśeṣamānna kṣīrādibhirvyabhicāraḥ, dṛṣṭā hi kulālādayo bāhyamṛdādyapekṣāḥ, cetanaṃ ca brahmeti, tatredamupatiṣṭhate- #devādivadapi loke# /
children.translated_text: If one objects that there is no deviation by the examples of milk and the like because the qualification 'being conscious' is specified — for it is seen that potters and such depend on external clay and the like, and <s>Brahman</s> is conscious — then to this the following is presented: [Sūtra:] 'Also like the gods and others in the world.'
<s>Loka</s> (world) here means 'speech' itself, that by which things are expressed, in that [usage].

body.text:
#kṛtsnaprasaktirniravayavatvaśabdakopo vā# /
nanu na brahmaṇastattvataḥ pariṇāmo yena kārtsnyabhāgavikalpenākṣipyeta /
avidyākalpitena tu nāmarūpalakṣaṇena rūpabhedena vyākṛtāvyākṛtātmanā tattvānyatvābhyāmanirvacanīyena pariṇāmādivyavahārāspadatvaṃ brahma pratipadyate /
naca kalpitaṃ rūpaṃ vastu spṛśati /
nahi candramasi taimirikasya dvitvakalpanā candramaso dvitvamāvahati /
tadanupapattyā vā candramaso 'nupapattiḥ /
tasmādavāstavī pariṇāmakalpanānupapadyamānāpi na paramārthasato brahmaṇo 'nupapattimāvahati /
tasmātpūrvapakṣābhāvādanārabhyamidamadhikaraṇamiti, ata āha- #cetanamekam# /
yadyapi śrutiśatādaikāntikādvaitapratipādanaparāt pariṇāmo vastuto niṣiddhastathāpi kṣīrādidevatādṛṣṭāntena punastadvāstavatvaprasaṅgaṃ pūrvapakṣopapattyā sarvathāyaṃ pakṣo na ghaṭayituṃ śakyata ityapabādhya #śrutestu śabdāmūlatvāt#'ātmani caivaṃ' 'vicitrāśca hi' iti sūtrābhyāṃ vivartadṛḍhīkaraṇenaikāntikādvayalakṣaṇaḥ śrutyarthaḥ pariśodhyata ityarthaḥ /
#tasmādastyavikṛtaṃ brahma#tattvataḥ /

children.translated_text: 'Now, even by the word [of scripture]' — this objection is [raised] in order to demonstrate that it is superimposed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
For there is no third alternative besides partlessness and having parts, since the negation of one is tantamount to the affirmation of the other.

Therefore, due to the absence of any other mode, and because both the modes of partlessness and having parts are untenable, the scriptural statement would be unauthoritative like the <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogistic passage) about stones floating and the like — this is the meaning of the objection.
The refutation is straightforward.

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'The consequence of total transformation, or contradiction of the statement of partlessness.' Now, there is no real transformation of <s>Brahman</s> by which one might object through the alternative of totality or partiality. Rather, through the form characterized by name and form superimposed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — a form that is both manifest and unmanifest, indescribable as either identical or different — <s>Brahman</s> becomes the locus of the conventional usage of transformation and the like. And a superimposed form does not touch the reality. For the superimposition of duality upon the moon by one with an eye-disease does not bring about duality in the moon, nor does the impossibility of that [duality] entail the impossibility of the moon itself. Therefore, the unreal superimposition of transformation, even though untenable [as real], does not entail the impossibility of <s>Brahman</s> which exists in the ultimate sense. Therefore, since there is no prima facie objection, this topic need not be undertaken at all — hence [the author] says: [Sūtra:] 'The one conscious [<s>Brahman</s>].' Although transformation is prohibited in reality by hundreds of <s>śruti</s> passages exclusively establishing non-duality, nevertheless, through the examples of milk and gods as prima facie illustrations, the possibility of transformation being real arises again, and this position cannot be established in any way — therefore, refuting it, [the sūtras] 'But from <s>śruti</s>, since it is rooted in scripture,' 'In the self also thus,' and 'For [powers] are varied' — by firmly establishing <s>vivarta</s> (apparent transformation), the meaning of <s>śruti</s>, characterized by absolute non-duality, is thereby purified. [Sūtra:] 'Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> exists as unmodified' — in reality.

children.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'In the self also thus; for [powers] are varied.'
By this, the <s>māyāvāda</s> (doctrine of illusion) is made explicit.

children.text: svapnadṛgātmā hi manasaiva svarūpānupamardena rathādīn sṛjati //28 //
children.translated_text: For the self in dream, by the mind alone, without any impairment of its own nature, creates chariots and the like.

avyāpnuvanvā tatra na varteta /
nahyasti saṃbhavaḥ sa eva tadānīṃ tatra vartate na vartate ceti /
tathā coparyadhaḥpārśvasthāḥ ṣaḍapi paramāṇavaḥ samānadeśā iti prathimānupapatteraṇumātraḥ piṇḍaḥ prasajyeta /

children.translated_text: Or if [the conjunction] does not pervade, the atom would have six parts — thus the partlessness [of atoms] is contradicted.

children.text: aśakyaṃ ca sāvayavatvamupetuṃ, tathā satyanantāvayavatvena sumerurājasarṣapayoḥ samānaparimāṇatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: And it is impossible to accept that [atoms] have parts, for if so, having infinite parts, there would be the absurd consequence that Mount <s>Meru</s> and a mustard seed would have the same size.
Therefore, the defect is the same [for all opponents].

children.text: āpātamātreṇa sāmyamuktam, paramārthatastu bhāvikaṃ pariṇāmaṃ vā karyakāraṇabhāvaṃ vecchatāmeṣa durvāro doṣo na punarasmākaṃ māyāvādināmityāha- #parihṛtastviti# //29 //
children.translated_text: The similarity has been stated only superficially; but in reality, this inescapable defect belongs to those who accept either real transformation or the cause-effect relation, but not to us who hold the <s>māyāvāda</s> (doctrine of illusion) — hence [the author] says: 'But this has been refuted...'

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'And because of the defect in one's own position.' [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises the objection: 'Now, not so...' [and then] refutes it: 'Not by one of this kind...' Although the aggregate has parts, nevertheless individually <s>sattva</s> (goodness), <s>rajas</s> (passion), and <s>tamas</s> (darkness) are partless. For there is no possibility that <s>sattva</s> alone transforms while <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> do not, since the combined transformation of all is accepted. And if the individually partless [<s>guṇas</s>] undergo total transformation, the consequence would be the complete annihilation of the root-cause. Or if they transform partially, the undesired consequence of their having parts would follow. [Sūtra:] 'Likewise for those who advocate <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) also.' For the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>, the process is that two atoms combine to produce one dyad, and from three such dyads one triad is produced. In that case, the conjunction of two partless atoms would pervade those entire atoms. Or, if it does not pervade, it would not be present there at all. For there is no possibility that it is simultaneously present and not present there. And thus the six atoms on top, bottom, and sides would be co-located, so that due to the impossibility of spatial extension, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom.

body.text: vicitraśaktitvamuktaṃ brahmaṇa, tatra śrutyupanyāsaparaṃ sūtram- #sarvopetā ca taddarśanāt# //30 //
body.translated_text: The varied potency of <s>Brahman</s> has been stated. The <s>sūtra</s> that presents the scriptural evidence for this is: [Sūtra:] 'And [<s>Brahman</s>] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture].'

children.translated_text: The <s>sūtra</s> that addresses the objection and its resolution is: [Sūtra:] 'If it be said that [<s>Brahman</s> cannot create] because of the absence of instruments, that has been stated [already].' Just as the distinction between potters and such who require external instruments, and gods and others who create through their own inner power without external dependence, is observed through valid means and cannot be denied, and just as the creation of chariots and the like in dream — accomplished through inner faculty alone without dependence on external instruments, unlike waking creation which requires external instruments — cannot be denied, so too the creation of the world by the supreme deity who possesses all powers and is independent of inner instruments, being declared by scripture, cannot be denied merely on the basis of general inference.

children.text: kulālādibhyastāvadbāhyakaraṇāpekṣebhyo devādīnāṃ bāhyanapekṣāṇāmāntarakaraṇāpekṣasṛṣṭhīnāṃ pramāṇena dṛṣṭo yathā viśeṣo nāpahnotuṃ śakyaḥ, yathā tu jāgratsṛṣṭerbāhyakaraṇāpekṣāyāstadanapekṣāntarakaraṇamātrasādhyā dṛṣṭā svapne rathādisṛṣṭiraśakyāpahnotum, evaṃ sarvaśakteḥ parasyā devatāyā āntarakaraṇānapekṣāyā jagatsarjanaṃ śrūyamāṇaṃ na sāmānyato dṛṣṭamātreṇāpahnavamarhatīti //31 //

body.text:
#na pa3yojanavattvāt# /
na tāvadunmattavadasya mativibhramājjagatprakriyā, bhrāntasya sarvajñatvānupapatteḥ /
tasmāt prekṣavatānena jagat kartavyam /
prekṣāvataśca pravṛttiḥ svaparahitāhitaprāptiparihāraprayojanā satī nāprayojanālpāyāsāpi saṃbhavati, kiṃ punaraparimeyānekavidhoccāvacaprapañcajagadvibhramaviracanā mahāprayāsā /
ata eva līlāpi parāstā /
alpāyāsasādhyā hi sā /

children.translated_text: Nor is even that [play] purposeless, since it too has the purpose of pleasure.
Or [it functions] for the sake of that [purpose], and in the absence of that [purpose] in the original state, the state of having fulfilled one's purpose cannot be established.
And because of the non-existence of others to be benefited, activity for their benefit too is impossible.

children.text: tasmāt prekṣāvatpravṛttiḥ prayojanavattayā vyāptā tadabhāve 'nupapannā brahmopādānatāṃ jagataḥ pratikṣipatīti prāptam //32 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the activity of a purposeful agent, being invariably accompanied by purposefulness, is impossible in its absence, and thus negates <s>Brahman</s>'s being the material cause of the world — when this prima facie view is arrived at,

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'Not, because of purposelessness.' It is not the case that this world-creation arises from a disturbance of mind like that of a madman, for omniscience cannot be established for one who is deluded. Therefore, this world must have been created by a purposeful agent. And the activity of a purposeful agent, being aimed at the attainment and avoidance of benefit and harm to oneself and others, cannot occur even without minimal effort if it is purposeless — how much less [can it occur in] the creation of the vast elaborate world-illusion of immeasurable, manifold, and graded complexity, which requires enormous effort. For this very reason, even <s>līlā</s> (divine play) is ruled out, for that requires only minimal effort.

body.text:
evaṃ prāpte 'bhidhīyate- #lokavattu līlākaivalyam# /
bhavedetadevaṃ yadi prekṣāvatpravṛttiḥ prayojanavattayā vyāptā bhavet /
tatastannivṛttau nivarteta, śiṃśāpātvamiva vṛkṣatānivṛttau, na tvetadasti, prekṣāvatāmananusaṃhitaprayojanānāmapi yādṛścikīṣu kriyāsu pravṛttidarśanāt /
anyathā 'na kurvīta vṛthā ceṣṭām' iti dharmasūtrakṛtāṃ pratiṣedho nirviṣayaḥ prasajyeta /

anyathā mṛtaśarīre 'pi śvāsapraśvāsapravṛttiprasaṅgāt /

dṛṣṭaṃ ca yadalpabalavīryabuddhināmaśakyamatiduṣkaraṃ vā tadanyeṣāmanalpabalavīryabuddhīnāṃ suśakamīṣatkaraṃ vā /
nahi vānarairmārutiprabhṛtibhirnagairna baddho nīranidhiragādho mahāsattvānām /
na caiṣa pārthena śilīmukhairna baddhaḥ /
na cāyaṃ na pītaḥ saṃkṣipya culukena helayeva kalaśayoninā mahāmuninā /
na cādyāpi na dṛśyante līlāmātravinirmitāni mahāprāsādapramadavanāni śrīmannṛganarendrāṇāmanyeṣāṃ manasāpi duṣkarāṇi nareśvarāṇam /
tasmādupapannaṃ yadṛcchayā vā svabhāvādvā līlayā vā jagatsarjanaṃ bhagavato maheśvarasyeti /

avidyā ca svabhāvata eva kāryonmukhī na prayojanamapekṣate /
nahi dvicandrālātacakragandharvanagarādivibhramāḥ samuddiṣṭaprayojanā bhavanti /

children.translated_text: Nor do the effects thereof — astonishment, fear, trembling, and the like — require a purpose for their own arising.

children.text: sā ca caitanyacchuritā jagadutpādaheturutu cetano jagadyonirākhyāyata ityāha- #na ceyaṃ paramārthaviṣayeti# /
children.translated_text: And that [<s>avidyā</s>], pervaded by consciousness, is the cause of the world's manifestation, and thus a conscious entity is declared to be the source of the world — hence [the author] says: 'And this is not a matter of ultimate reality.'

children.text: api ca na brahma jagatkāraṇamapi tattayā vivakṣantyāgamā api tu jagati brahmātmabhāvam /
children.translated_text: Moreover, the scriptures do not intend to say that <s>Brahman</s> is the cause of the world in the sense of a real causal relation, but rather [they declare] the identity of <s>Brahman</s> with the world.

children.text: tathā ca sṛṣṭeravivakṣāyāṃ tadāśrayo doṣo nirviṣaya evetyāśayenāha- #brahmātmabhāveti# //33 //
children.translated_text: And thus, when creation is not the intended teaching, the defect based on it is entirely without scope — with this intent [the author] says: [Sūtra:] 'The identity of <s>Brahman</s> [with the world].'

body.translated_text: When this prima facie view is thus established, the reply is given: [Sūtra:] 'But it is like [activity] in the world; mere play.' This would be so if the activity of a purposeful agent were invariably accompanied by purposefulness. Then in its absence it would cease, just as the nature of being a tree ceases when the nature of being a <s>śiṃśapā</s> (rosewood) ceases. But this is not so, since we observe the engagement of purposeful agents in actions of a whimsical nature without any premeditated purpose. Otherwise, the prohibition in the <s>dharmasūtra</s>, 'One should not engage in purposeless activity,' would be without scope. And this <s>sūtra</s> is not meaningful only with reference to the insane, since they cannot comprehend its meaning or follow it. Moreover, the activity of breathing — characterized by inhalation and exhalation, caused by unseen merit — is observed in purposeful agents without any premeditation of purpose. And consciousness is not useless even for this [breathing] in a conscious being, since [breathing] exists even in deep sleep — this is appropriate, because even in the state of <s>prājña</s> (deep-sleep consciousness), consciousness does not depart. Otherwise, breathing would absurdly continue even in a dead body. And just as those who have attained all desires through the fulfillment of their own and others' welfare, being fulfilled and with untroubled minds, engage in mere play even when there is no result to be accomplished, without any such intention — so too <s>Brahman</s>'s engagement in world-creation is not untenable. And what is observed to be impossible or extremely difficult for those of little strength, power, and intelligence is easily accomplished or trivially done by others of great strength, power, and intelligence. For was not the fathomless ocean bridged with mountains by the monkeys led by <s>Māruti</s> (Hanuman)? And was it not [bridged] by <s>Pārtha</s> (Arjuna) with arrows? And was it not drunk up, compressed into a handful, effortlessly by the great sage born of <s>Kalaśa</s> (Agastya)? And are there not seen even today great palaces and pleasure-gardens created as mere sport by illustrious kings, which are impossible even to conceive for other rulers? Therefore, it is established that the creation of the world by the blessed great Lord occurs spontaneously, or by nature, or as mere play. Moreover, this creation is not ultimately real, so that purpose might be demanded of it; rather, it is grounded in beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). And <s>avidyā</s>, by its very nature, tends toward producing effects and does not require a purpose. For illusions such as seeing a double moon, a firebrand circle, and a <s>gandharva-nagara</s> (city in the sky) do not serve any deliberately intended purpose.

body.text:
#vaiṣamyanerghṛṇye na sāpekṣatvāttathāhi darśayati# /
atirohito 'tra pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ /
