nahi sabhyaḥ sabhāyāṃ niyukto yuktavādinaṃ yuktavādyasīti cāyuktavādinamayuktavādyasīti bruvāṇa, sabhāpatirvā yuktavādinamanugṛhṇannayuktavādinaṃ ca nigṛhṇannanukto dviṣṭo vā bhavatyapi tu madhyastha iti vītarāgadveṣa iti cākhyāyate, tadvadīśvaraḥ puṇyakarmāṇamanugṛhṇannapuṇyakarmāṇaṃ ca nigṛhṇanmadhyastha eva nāmadhyasthaḥ /
evaṃ hyasāvamadhyasthaḥ syādyakalyāṇakāriṇamanugṛhṇīyātkalyāṇakāriṇaṃ ca nigṛhṇīyāt /
natvetadasti /
tasmānna vaiṣamyadoṣaḥ /
ata eva na nairghṛṇyamapi saṃharataḥ samastān prāṇabhṛtaḥ /
sa hi prāṇabhṛtkarmāśayānāṃ vṛttinirodhasamayaḥ, tamitalaṅghayannayamayuktakārī syāt /
naca karmāpekṣāyāmīśvarasya aiśvaryavyāghātaḥ /
nahi sevādikarmabhedāpekṣaḥ phalabhedapradaḥ prabhuraprabhurbhavati /
na ca 'eṣa hyeva sādhu karma kārayati yamebhyo lokebhya unninīṣate eṣa evāsādhu karma kārayati taṃ yamadho niniṣate' iti śruterīśvara eṣa dveṣapakṣapātābhyāṃ sādhvasādhunī karmaṇī kārayitvā svargaṃ narakaṃ vā lokaṃ nayati, tasmādvaiṣamyadoṣaprasaṅgānneśvaraḥ kāraṇamiti vācyam /
virodhāt /
yasmāt karma kārayitveśvaraḥ prāṇinaḥ sukhaduḥkhinaḥ sṛjati iti śruteravagamyate, tasmānna sṛjatīti viruddhamabhidhīyate /
naca vaiṣamyamātramatra brūmo na tvīśvarakāraṇatvaṃ vyāsedhāma iti vaktavyam /

children.translated_text: What follows from that, even if so?

children.text: tasmādīśvarasya savāsanakleśāparāmarśamabhivadantīnāṃ bhūyasīnāṃ śrutīnāmanugrahāyonninīṣate 'dho ninīṣata ityetadapi tajjātīyapūrvakarmābhyāsavaśātprāṇina ityevaṃ neyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, in deference to the greater number of <s>śruti</s> passages that declare <s>Īśvara</s> to be free from contact with afflictions and their latent impressions, even the passage 'He wishes to lead up... he wishes to lead down' should be interpreted as meaning that beings [are so led] due to the force of habitual practice of their own prior <s>karmas</s> of the same kind.
As they say: 'Whatever — charity, study, and austerity — has been practiced life after life,
by that very force of practice, a person practices that very thing again.'

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'Partiality and cruelty [cannot be alleged], because [creation] is dependent [on the merits and demerits of beings]; for thus [scripture] shows.' The prima facie view is concealed here. But the reply is stated: When [the Lord] creates the manifold array of living beings differentiated by high, low, and middling degrees of happiness and suffering, and creates manifold substances such as nectar and poison that cause happiness and suffering — being assisted by the accumulated merit and demerit of the living beings in their different forms — neither partiality nor cruelty can be attributed to this <s>Parameśvara</s> (Supreme Lord). For a judge appointed in an assembly, who tells a correct speaker 'You are correct' and an incorrect speaker 'You are incorrect,' or a president of the assembly who favors the correct speaker and censures the incorrect one, is not called partial or hostile, but rather is known as impartial and free from attachment and aversion. Similarly, <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), favoring those of meritorious deeds and restraining those of unmeritorious deeds, is indeed impartial, not partial. For he would be partial only if he were to favor the evildoer and restrain the virtuous. But this is not the case. Therefore, there is no defect of partiality. For the same reason, there is no cruelty even when he destroys all living beings. For that [destruction] is the time when the <s>karmāśayas</s> (karmic impressions) of living beings cease their operation, and transgressing that [appointed time], he would be acting improperly. Nor does dependence on <s>karma</s> impair the sovereignty of <s>Īśvara</s>. For a lord who bestows different fruits in dependence on different acts such as service does not thereby become powerless. And one should not say that, because of the <s>śruti</s> 'He indeed causes him whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds to perform good deeds; he indeed causes him whom he wishes to lead down to perform bad deeds,' <s>Īśvara</s>, out of hatred and favoritism, makes beings perform good and bad deeds and then leads them to heaven or hell, and therefore, due to the consequence of partiality, <s>Īśvara</s> is not the cause. Because of contradiction. Since it is understood from <s>śruti</s> that <s>Īśvara</s> creates beings as happy or suffering having caused them to act, it would be contradictory to say that he does not create. And one cannot say 'We are merely pointing out the partiality but not denying that <s>Īśvara</s> is the cause.'

children.translated_text: And this has been said on the assumption that creation is real.
But that creation is indescribable [as either real or unreal] should not be forgotten here either.

children.text: tathā ca māyākārasyevāṅgasākalyavaikalyabedena vicitrān prāṇino darśayato na vaiṣamyadoṣaḥ, sahasā saṃharato vā na nairdhṛṇyam, evamasyāpi bhagavato vividhavicitraprapañcamanirvācyaṃ viśvaṃ darśayataḥ saṃharataśca svabhāvādvā līlayā vā na kaściddoṣaḥ //34 //
children.translated_text: And just as there is no defect of partiality for a magician who displays varied living beings with complete or incomplete limbs, nor cruelty when he makes them suddenly disappear — so too for this blessed Lord, who displays an indescribable universe of manifold and varied expanse and who dissolves it, whether by nature or as divine play, there is no defect whatsoever.

children.text: iti sthite śaṅkāparihāraparaṃ sūtram- #na karmāvibhāgāditi cennānāditvāt# /
children.translated_text: This being established, the <s>sūtra</s> that addresses a further doubt and its resolution is: [Sūtra:] 'If it be said that [creation is impossible] because of the non-differentiation of <s>karma</s>, [we say] no, because of beginninglessness.'
The doubt and its resolution are explained by the <s>bhāṣya</s> passage whose meaning is concealed.

body.text:
anāditvāditi siddhavaduktaṃ, tatsādhanārthaṃ sūtram- #upapadyate cāpyupalabhyate ca# /
akṛte karmaṇi puṇye pāpe vā tatphalaṃ bhoktāramadhyāgacchet, tathā ca vidhiniṣedhaśāstramanarthakaṃ bhavet pravṛttinivṛttyabhāvāditi /
mokṣaśāstrasya coktamānarthakyam /
#na cāvidyā kevaleti# /
layābhiprāyam /
vikṣepalakṣaṇāvidyāsaṃskārastu kāryatvātsvotpattau pūrvaṃ vikṣepamapekṣate, vikṣepaśca mithyāpratyayo mohāparanāmā puṇyāpuṇyapravṛttihetubhūtarāgadveṣanidānaṃ, sa ca rāgādibiḥ sahitaḥ svakāryairna śarīraṃ sukhaduḥkhabhogāyatanamantareṇa saṃbhavati /
naca rāgādvaiṣāvantareṇa ka4ma /
naca bhogasahitaṃ mohamantareṇa rāgadveṣau /
naca pūrvaśarīramantareṇa mohādiriti pūrvapūrvaśarīrāpekṣo mohādirevaṃ pūrvapūrvamohādyapekṣaṃ pūrvapūrvaśarīramityanāditaivātra bhagavatī cittamanākulayati /
tadetadāha- #rāgādikleśavāsanākṣiptakarmāpekṣā tvavidyā vaiṣamyakarī syāditi# /
rāgādveṣamohā rāgādayasta eva hi puruṣaṃ sāsāraduḥkhamanubhāvya kleśayantīti kleśāsteṣāṃ vāsanāḥ karmaparvṛttyanuguṇāstābhirākṣiptāni pravarttitāni karmāṇi tadapekṣā layalakṣaṇā avidyā /

children.translated_text: One might object:
Designation by a future [action] is also observed, as in 'He scatters chaff with the sacrificial cake on a potsherd.'
Hence [the author] says: 'And not because it will sustain — for that reason.'

children.text: tadevamanāditve siddhe 'sadeva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyam' iti prāk sṛṣṭeravibhāgāvadhāramaṃ samudācaradrūparāgādiniṣedhaparaṃ na punaretānprasuptānapyapākarotīti sarvamavadātam //36 //
children.translated_text: Thus, when beginninglessness is established, the passage 'In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one only without a second' — the determination of non-differentiation prior to creation is directed at negating the manifest form of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the like, but does not negate them even in their dormant state — thus everything is clear.

body.translated_text: 'Because of beginninglessness' has been stated as if established; the <s>sūtra</s> to prove it is: [Sūtra:] 'And it is justified, and it is also observed.' If <s>karma</s> — whether meritorious or sinful — were not performed, then its fruit would not reach the one who is to experience it, and thus the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions would become purposeless, since there would be no engagement or disengagement. And the purposelessness of <s>mokṣa-śāstra</s> (scripture of liberation) has already been stated. [Sūtra:] 'And <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is not alone.' This is intended with reference to the state of dissolution. <s>Avidyā</s> in the form of projective power, being an effect, requires a prior projection for its own arising; and projection, which is false cognition also called <s>moha</s> (delusion), is the cause of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) that give rise to meritorious and unmeritorious activity; and that [delusion] together with <s>rāga</s> and the like as its effects cannot exist without a body that is the locus of the experience of pleasure and pain; and without <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s> there is no <s>karma</s>; and without <s>moha</s> accompanied by experience there are no <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s>; and without a prior body there is no <s>moha</s> and the like — thus <s>moha</s> and the like depend on a prior body, and the prior body in turn depends on prior <s>moha</s> and the like, and so this beginninglessness does not trouble the blessed mind. This is what [the author] states: '<s>Avidyā</s>, which produces inequality, depends on <s>karma</s> impelled by the latent impressions of afflictions such as <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the like.' <s>Rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) are the 'afflictions beginning with <s>rāga</s>' — they are called <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) because they torment a person by making him experience the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration). Their <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) are those conducive to the operation of <s>karma</s>; <s>karmas</s> impelled by those [impressions] are the ones on which <s>avidyā</s> in its latent form depends.

body.text:
#sarvadharmopapatteśca# /
atra #sarvajñamiti# /

children.translated_text: [The <s>bhāṣya</s> says] 'possessing all powers.'
It has been established that [<s>Brahman</s>] is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the entire world — [the <s>bhāṣya</s> says] 'possessed of great <s>māyā</s> (illusive power).'
All doubts regarding impossibility have been dispelled.
Therefore, it is established that <s>Brahman</s> is the cause of the world.

body.translated_text: [Sūtra:] 'And because all attributes are established.' Here, [the <s>bhāṣya</s> says] 'omniscient' — the conformity with worldly [observation] that everything operates only when directed by a conscious being has been shown.

body.text: iti śrīvācaspatimiśraviracite bhagavatpādaśārīrikabhāṣyavibhāge bhāmatyāṃ dvitīyasyādhyāyasya prathamaḥ pādaḥ //1 //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the first <s>pāda</s> (quarter) of the second <s>adhyāya</s> (chapter) in the <s>Bhāmatī</s>, the exposition of the venerable master's commentary on the <s>Śārīraka</s> (Brahmasūtra), composed by the illustrious <s>Vācaspati Miśra</s>.

body.text: #iti dvitīyādhyāyasya sāṃkhyāyogakāraṇadādismṛtibhiḥ sāṃkhyādiprayuktatarkaiśca vedāntasamanvayavirodhaparihārākhyaḥ prathamaḥ pādaḥ#
body.translated_text: Thus [ends] the first <s>pāda</s> of the second <s>adhyāya</s>, named 'The resolution of contradictions with <s>Vedānta</s> harmony, [raised] by the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, <s>Yoga</s>, and other <s>smṛtis</s> regarding causation, and by the reasoning adduced by the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and others.'

body.text: #dvitīyādhyāye dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ# /
body.translated_text: [Beginning of] the second <s>pāda</s> of the second <s>adhyāya</s>.

#racanānupapatteśca nānumānam---#syādetat /
iha hi pāde khatantrā vedanirapekṣāḥ pradhānādisiddhiviṣayāḥ sāṃkhyādiyuktayo nirākariṣyante /
tadayuktamaśāstrāṅgatvāt /
nahīdaṃ śāstramucchṛṅkhalatarkaśāstravatpravṛttamapi tu vedāntavākyāni brahmaparāṇīti pūrvapakṣottarapakṣābhyāṃ viniścetum /
tatra kaḥ prasaṅgaḥ śuṣkatarkavatkhatantrayuktinirākaraṇasyetyata āha- #- yadyapīdaṃ vedāntavākyānāmiti# /
nahi vedāntavākyāni nirṇetavyānīti nirṇīyante, kintu mokṣamāṇānāṃ tattvajñānotpādanāya /
yathā ca vedāntavākyebhyo jagadupādānaṃ brahmāvagamyate, evaṃ sāṃkhyādyanumānebhyaḥ pradhānādyacetanaṃ jagadupādānamavagamyate /
na caitadeva cetanopādānamacetanopādānaṃ ceti samuccetuṃ śakyaṃ, virodhāt /
na ca vyavasthite vastuni vikalpo yujyate /
na cāgamabādhitaviṣayatayānumānameva nodīyata iti sāṃpratam. sarvajñapraṇītatayā sāṃkhyādyāgamasya vedāgamatulyatvāt tadbhāṣitasyānumānasya pratikṛtisiṃhatulyatayābādhyatvāt /

naca tattvajñānādṛte mokṣa iti svatantrāṇāmapyanumānānāmābhāsīkaraṇamiha śāstresaṃgatameveti /
yadyevaṃ tataḥ parakīyānumānanirāsa eva kasmātprathamaṃ na kṛta ityata āha- #- vedāntārthanirṇayasya ceti# /
nanu vītarāgakathāyāṃ tattvanirṇayamātramupayujyate na punaḥparapakṣādhikṣepaḥ, sa hi sarāgatāmāvahatīti codayati- #- nanu mumukṣūṇāmiti# /
pariharati #-- bāḍhamevaṃ, tathāpīti# /
tattvanirṇayāvasānā vītarāgakathā /
naca parapakṣadūṣaṇamantareṇa tattvanirṇayaḥ śakyaḥ kartumiti tatvanirṇayāya vītarāgeṇāpi parapakṣo dūṣyate na tu parapakṣatayeti na vītarāgakathātvavyāhatirityarthaḥ /
punaruktatāṃ paricodya samādhatte #-- nanvīkṣateriti /
tatra saṃkhyā iti# /
yāni hi yena rūpeṇā sthaulyādā ca saukṣmyātsamanvīyante tāni tatkaraṇāni dṛṣṭāni, yathā dhaṭādayo rucakādayaścā sthaulyādā ca saukṣmyānmṛtsuvarṇānvitāstatkaraṇāḥ, tathā cedaṃ bāhyamādhyātmikaṃ ca bhāvajātaṃ suḥkhaduḥkhamohātmanānvitamupalabhyate, tasmāttadapi suḥkhaduḥkhamohātmasāmānyakāraṇakaṃ bhavitumarhati /
tatra jagatkāraṇasya yeyaṃ sukhātmatā tatsattvaṃ, yā duḥkhātmatā tadrajaḥ, yā ca mehātmatā tattama iti traiguṇyakāraṇasiddhiḥ /
tathāhi-- pratyekaṃ bhāvāstraiguṇyavanto 'nubhūyante /
yathā maitradāreṣu padmāvatyāṃ maitrasya sukhaṃ, tat kasya hetoḥ,taṃprati satvaguṇasamudbhavāt /
tatsapatnīnāṃ ca duḥkhaṃ,tatkasya hetoḥ, tāḥ pratyasyā rajoguṇasamudbhavāt /
caitrasya tu straiṇasya tāmavindato moho viṣādaḥ,tat kasya hetoḥ, taṃ pratyasyāstamoguṇasamudbhavāt /
padmāvatyā ca sarve bhāvā vyākhyātāḥ /
tasmātsarvaṃ suḥkhaduḥkhamohānvitaṃ jagattatkāraṇaṃ gamyate /
tacca triguṇaṃ pradhānaṃ pradhīyate kriyate 'nena jagaditi,pradhīyate nidhīyate 'sminpralayasamaye jagaditi vā pradhānam /
tacca mṛtsuvarṇavadacetanaṃ cetanasya puruṣasya bhogāpavargalakṣaṇamarthaṃ sādhayituṃ svabhāvata eva pravartate,na tu kenacitpravartyate. tathā hyāhuḥ--- 'puruṣārtha eva heturna kenacitkāryate karaṇam' iti. /
parimāṇādibhirityādigrahaṇena 'śaktitaḥ pravṛtteśca /
kāraṇakāryavibhāgādavibhāgādvaiśvarūpyasya' ityavyaktasiddhihetavo gṛhyante /
etāṃścepariṣṭādvyākhāyāya nirākariṣyata iti /
tadetatpradhānānumānaṃ dūṣayati- #- tatra vadāma iti# /
yadi tāvadacetanaṃ pradhānamanadhiṣṭhitatvena mṛtsuvarṇādau dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi vyāpterupalabdherviruddhatvāt /
nahi mṛtsuvarṇadārvādayaḥ kulālahemakārarathakārādibhiranadhiṣṭhitāḥ kumbharucakarathādyupādadate /
tasmāt kṛtakatvamiva nityatvasādhanayā prayuktaṃ sādhyaviruddhena vyāptaṃ viruddham,evaṃ samanvayādi cetanānadhiṣṭhitatve sādhya iti racanānupapatteriti darśitam /
yaducyeta dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇyacetanaṃ tāvadupādānaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ,tatra yadyapi taccetanaprayuktamapi dṛśyate, tathāpi tatprayuktatvaṃ hetoraprayojakaṃ bahiraṅgatvāt,antaraṅgaṃ tvacaitanyamātramupādānānugataṃ hetoḥ prayojakam /
yathāhuḥ-- 'vyāpteśca dṛśyamānāyāḥ kaściddharmaḥ prayojakaḥ' iti /
tatrāha-- #naca mṛdādīti# /
svabhāvapratibaddhaṃ hi vyāptaṃ vyāpakamavagamayati /
sa ca svabhāvapratibandhaḥ śaṅkitasamāropitopādhinirāse sati niścīyate /
tanniścayaścānvayavyatirekayorāyatate /
tau cānvayavyatirekau na tathopādānācaitanye yathopādānācaitanye yathā cetanaprayuktatve 'tiparisphuṭau /
tadalamatrāntaraṅgatveneti bhāvaḥ /
evamapi cetanaprayuktatvaṃ nābhyupeyeta yadi pramāṇāntaravirodho bhavet, pratyuta śrutiranuguṇatarātretyāha-- #na caivaṃ satīti# /
cakāreṇa suḥkhaduḥkhādisamanvayalakṣaṇasya hetorasiddhatvaṃ samuccinotītyāha #-- anvayādyanupapatteśceti# /
āntarāḥ khalvamī suḥkhaduḥkhamohaviṣādā bāhyebhyaścandanādibhyo 'tivicchinnapratyayapravedanīyebhyo vyatiriktā adhyakṣamīkṣyante /
yadi punareta eva suḥkhaduḥkhādisvabhāvā bhaveyustataḥsvarūpatvādhemante 'pi candanaḥ sukhaḥ syāt /
nahi candanaḥ kadācidacandanaḥ /
tathā nidāgheṣvapi kuṅkumapaṅkaḥ sukho bhavet /
nahyasau kadācidakuṅkumapaṅka iti /
evaṃ kaṇṭakaḥ kramelakasya sukha iti manuṣyādīnāmapi prāṇabhṛtāṃ sukhaḥ syāt /
nahyasau kāṃścitpratyeva kaṇṭaka iti /
tasmādasukhādisvabhāvā api candanakuṅkumādayo jātikālāvasthādyapekṣayā sukhaduḥkhādihetavo na tu svayaṃ sukhādisvabhāvā iti ramaṇīyam /
body.translated_text: And because of the impossibility of design, inference is not valid. One might object: In this <s>pāda</s> (section), the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and other reasonings, which are independent of the <s>Vedas</s> and concern the establishment of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and such, will be refuted like unruly dialectical treatises. That is improper, since it is not a subsidiary of the scripture. For this scripture does not proceed like an unbridled treatise on logic; rather, it is meant to ascertain through objection and reply that the <s>Vedānta</s> sentences are directed toward <s>Brahman</s>. What occasion is there then for refuting unruly reasonings like dry logic? To this he says: 'Although these <s>Vedānta</s> sentences...' For the <s>Vedānta</s> sentences are not being determined merely for the sake of determination, but for producing knowledge of reality in those seeking liberation. And just as from the <s>Vedānta</s> sentences <s>Brahman</s> is understood as the material cause of the world, so too from <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and other inferences, <s>Pradhāna</s> and other insentient entities are understood as the material cause of the world. And it is not possible to combine both — that this very thing has both a sentient and an insentient material cause — because of contradiction. Nor is an alternative appropriate regarding a determined entity. Nor is it correct to say that inference alone, whose domain is contradicted by scripture, should not be upheld — because the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and other <s>āgamas</s> (scriptures), being composed by an omniscient being, are equal to the Vedic <s>āgama</s>, and because the inference taught therein, being like a replica-lion, cannot be sublated. Therefore, due to conflict with that, the coherence of <s>Vedānta</s> passages with <s>Brahman</s> cannot be established, and hence knowledge of reality cannot be proven from them. And since there is no liberation without knowledge of reality, it is entirely appropriate in this scripture to demonstrate that even independent inferences are mere semblances. If so, then why was the refutation of the opponent's inferences not done first? To this he says: 'Because the determination of the meaning of <s>Vedānta</s>...' But one objects: in a dispassionate discourse, only the determination of truth is needed, not the attack on opposing views, for that would introduce passion — thus he raises the objection: 'But for those seeking liberation...' He answers: 'Indeed so, nevertheless...' A dispassionate discourse culminates in the determination of truth. And since the determination of truth is impossible without refuting opposing views, even a dispassionate person refutes opposing views for the sake of determining truth, not for the sake of opposing views as such — thus there is no contradiction with the nature of dispassionate discourse. This is the meaning. Having raised the objection of redundancy, he resolves it: 'But <s>īkṣate</s> (sees)...' 'Therein the enumeration...' For those things that are coherent with something by way of a certain form, from grossness to subtlety, are seen to be its effects — just as pots and the like, and ornaments and the like, being pervaded by clay and gold respectively from grossness to subtlety, are their effects. Similarly, this entire collection of entities, both external and internal, is perceived as pervaded by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therefore it too must have as its cause something whose common nature is pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therein, the pleasure-nature of the world-cause is <s>sattva</s>, its pain-nature is <s>rajas</s>, and its delusion-nature is <s>tamas</s> — thus the establishment of a cause consisting of three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities). For indeed, each entity is experienced as possessing three <s>guṇas</s>. For example, regarding <s>Maitra's</s> wives, <s>Maitra</s> experiences pleasure with <s>Padmāvatī</s> — for what reason? Because she is a product of <s>sattva-guṇa</s> with respect to him. And her co-wives experience pain — for what reason? Because she is a product of <s>rajo-guṇa</s> with respect to them. But <s>Caitra</s>, who is amorous, not finding her, experiences delusion and despair — for what reason? Because she is a product of <s>tamo-guṇa</s> with respect to him. And through <s>Padmāvatī</s> all states are explained. Therefore the entire world, being pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion, points to such a cause. And that three-<s>guṇa</s> cause is called <s>Pradhāna</s> — 'that by which the world is produced,' or 'that in which the world is deposited at the time of dissolution.' And that, like clay or gold, being insentient, operates by its very nature to accomplish the purpose of the sentient <s>Puruṣa</s> (spirit), characterized by enjoyment and liberation, and is not set in motion by anyone. As they say: 'The purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> alone is the cause; the instrument is not activated by anyone.' By 'from measure and so forth,' the word 'and so forth' includes the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> proofs for the unmanifest such as 'from the activity of potency, from the division of cause and effect, from non-division, and from diversity.' These he will explain and refute later. He refutes this <s>Pradhāna</s> inference: 'Therein we say...' If the insentient <s>Pradhāna</s> is unsupervised, then it is contradicted, because in the illustrative subjects such as clay and gold, the pervasion is observed to include supervision — for clay, gold, wood, and the like, unsupervised by potters, goldsmiths, carpenters, and the like, do not produce pots, ornaments, chariots, and the like. Therefore, just as 'being produced' is contradicted when employed to prove eternality because it is pervaded by what contradicts the thesis, similarly coherence and such, being the thesis when proving non-supervision by a sentient being, is shown to be impossible of design. If it were argued that in the illustrative subject, an insentient material cause is indeed observed, and although it is seen to be directed by a sentient being, that direction by a sentient being is not the operative factor of the reason because it is extrinsic, while only insentience as such, which accompanies the material cause, is the intrinsic operative factor of the reason — as they say: 'Of a pervasion that is observed, some property is the operative factor' — to this he says: 'And not clay and so forth...' For a pervasion that is bound to the essential nature reveals the pervader. And that essential binding is ascertained when suspected, superimposed, or adventitious conditions are eliminated. And that ascertainment depends on positive and negative concomitance. And those positive and negative concomitances are not as clearly manifest in the insentience of the material cause as in the direction by a sentient being. Therefore enough of claiming intrinsic status for that — this is the purport. Even so, direction by a sentient being would not be accepted if there were a conflict with another means of knowledge; on the contrary, scripture is more favorable — thus he says: 'And when this is so...' By the word 'and' he combines the unestablished nature of the reason characterized by the coherence of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and says: 'And because of the impossibility of coherence and so forth...' For these internal experiences of pleasure, pain, delusion, and despair are directly perceived as distinct from external things like sandalwood and the like, which are known through entirely different cognitions. If, however, these were by nature pleasure, pain, and so forth, then due to being their essential nature, sandalwood would always be pleasant. For sandalwood is never non-sandalwood. Likewise, saffron paste would be pleasant even in the hot season. For it is never non-saffron-paste. Similarly, if a thorn is pleasant for a camel, it should be pleasant for humans and other living beings too. For it is not a thorn only with respect to some. Therefore, even though sandalwood, saffron, and the like are not by nature pleasant, they serve as causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth depending on species, time, condition, and other factors — they are not themselves of the nature of pleasure and so forth. This is elegant.

tasmātsukhādirūpasamanvayo bhāvānāmasiddha iti nānena tadrūpaṃ kāraṇamavyaktamunnīyata iti /
tadidamuktam- #- śabdādyaviśeṣe 'pi ca bhāvanāviśeṣāditi# /
bhāvanā vāsanā saṃskārastadviśeṣāt /
karabhajanmasaṃvartakaṃ hi karma karabhocitāmeva bhāvanāmabhivyaniktiṃ, yathāsmai kaṇṭakā eva rocante /
evamanyatrāpi draṣṭavyam /
parimāṇāditi sāṃkhyīyaṃ hetumupanyasyati- #- tathā parimitānāṃ bhedānāmiti# /
saṃsargapūrvakatve hi saṃsargasyaikasminnadvaye 'saṃbhavānnānātvaikārthasamavetasya nānākaraṇāni saṃsṛṣṭāni kalpanīyāni,
body.translated_text: Therefore, the coherence of entities with the form of pleasure and so forth is unestablished, and hence the unmanifest cause of that form cannot be inferred from it. This is what is stated: 'Even when there is no difference in sound and so forth, due to the difference in disposition (<s>bhāvanā</s>)...' <s>Bhāvanā</s> means latent impression, <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental imprint) — due to the difference thereof. For the <s>karma</s> (action) that brings about birth as a camel manifests only a disposition suited to a camel, such that thorns alone are relished by it. The same should be understood in other cases as well. With 'from measure and so forth' he presents the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> reason: 'Thus, of limited modifications...' For if preceded by combination, and since combination is impossible in one without a second, the manifold things coherent in a single purpose must have multiple causes that are combined,

body.text:
tāni ca sattvarajastamāṃsyeveti bhāvaḥ /
tadetatparimitatvaṃ sāṃkhyīyarāddhāntālocanenānaikāntikamiti dūṣayati-- #sattvarajastamasāmiti# /
yadi tāvatparimitatvamiyattā, sā nabhaso 'pi nāstītyavyāpako hetuḥ parimāṇāditi /
atha na yojanādimitatvaṃ parimāṇamiyattāṃ nabhaso brūmaḥ kintvavyāpitām, avyāpi ca nabhastanmātrādeḥ /
nahi kāryaṃ kāraṇavyāpi, kintu kāraṇaṃ kāryavyāpīti parimitaṃ nabhastanmātrādyavyāpitvāt /
hanta sattvarajastamāṃsyapi na parasparaṃ vyāpnuvanti, naca tattvāntarapūrvakatvameteṣāmiti vyabhicāraḥ /
nahi yathā taiḥ kāryajātamāviṣṭamevaṃ tāni parasparaṃ viśanti,mithaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvābhāvāt /

children.translated_text: And the mutual combination and interpenetration does not exist in the power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>).

children.text: nahi citiśaṅktiḥ kūṭasthanityā taiḥ saṃsṛjyate, tataśca tadavyāpakā guṇā iti parimitāḥ /
children.translated_text: For <s>citi-śakti</s> (the power of consciousness), being immutably eternal, is not combined with them, and therefore the <s>guṇas</s>, being non-pervasive of it, are limited.

children.text: evaṃ citiśaktirapi guṇairasaṃsṛṣṭeti sāpi parimitetyanaikāntikatvaṃ parimitatvasya hetoriti /
children.translated_text: Similarly, <s>citi-śakti</s> too, being uncombined with the <s>guṇas</s>, is also limited — thus the reason of limitedness is inconclusive.
Likewise, the division of cause and effect is also contradictory like the coherence argument — thus he says: 'But the cause-effect relationship...' (1)

body.translated_text: and those are none other than <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> — this is the purport. He refutes this limitedness as inconclusive by examining the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine itself: '<s>Sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>...' If limitedness means definite quantity, then even <s>ākāśa</s> (space) lacks it, so the reason 'from measure and so forth' fails to pervade. Or if we do not speak of limitedness as measurability in terms of <s>yojanas</s> (leagues) for <s>ākāśa</s>, but rather as non-pervasion — and <s>ākāśa</s> is non-pervasive of <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) and the like — for the effect does not pervade the cause, but rather the cause pervades the effect — then <s>ākāśa</s> is limited because it does not pervade the <s>tanmātras</s> and the like. But wait — <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> also do not pervade each other, and these are not preceded by yet another category, so there is a deviation. For it is not the case that just as the entire collection of effects is pervaded by them, they in turn pervade each other, since there is no mutual cause-effect relationship among them.

tasmānna cetanasya jagatsarjane pravṛttirityarthaḥ /
atraupaniṣado gūḍhābhisaṃdhiḥ praśnapūrvakaṃ vimṛśati-- #kiṃ punaratreti# /
atrāntare sāṃkhyo brūte-- #nanu yasminniti# /
na tāvaccetanaḥ pravṛtyāśrayatayā tatprayojakatayā vā pratyakṣamīkṣyate, kevalaṃ pravṛttistadāśrayaścācetano deharathādiḥ pratyakṣeṇa pratīyate, tatrācetanasya pravṛttistannimittaiva na tu cetananimittā /
sadbhāvamātraṃ tu tatra cetanasya gamyate rathādivailakṣaṇyājjīvaddehasya /
naca sadbhāvamātreṇa kāraṇatvasiddhiḥ /
mā bhūdākāśa utpattimatāṃ ghaṭādīnāṃ nimittakāraṇamasti hi sarvatreti /
tadanena dehātirikte satyapi cetane tasya na pravṛttiṃ prati nimittabhāvo 'stītyuktam /
yataścāsya na pravṛttihetubhāvo 'sti ata eva pratyakṣe dehe sati pravṛttidarśanādasati cādarśanāddehasyaiva caitanyamiti laukāyatikāḥ pratipannāḥ, tathā ca na cidātmanimittā pravṛttiriti siddham /
tasmānna racanāyāḥ pravṛttervā cidātmakāraṇatvasiddhirjagata iti aupaniṣadaḥ pariharati-- #tadabhidhīyate--- na brūma iti# /
na tāvat pratyakṣānumānāgamasiddhaḥ śārīro vā paramātmā vāsmābhiridānīṃ sādhanīyaḥ, kevalamasya pravṛtti prati kāraṇatvaṃ vaktavyam /
tatra mṛtaśarīre vā rathādau vānadhiṣṭhite cetanena pravṛtteradarśanāt tadviparyaye ca pravṛttidarśanādanvayavyatirekābhyāṃ cetanahetukatvaṃ pravṛtterniścīyate, na tu cetanasadbhāvamātreṇa,
body.translated_text: And because of activity — not only do differences in design not occur without the supervision of a sentient being, but also the departure from the state of equilibrium into disequilibrium, and thus whatever arises as predominant, and whatever is subordinate being overpowered by it, remaining as a subsidiary in conformity with it — when such a principal-subsidiary relation obtains, what activity can there be in the effect such as <s>mahat</s> (the great principle) and the rest? That activity too points to supervision by a sentient being alone. For without the supervision of a sentient being, the subsidiary factors such as the wheel, rod, water, thread, and the like do not remain in their subsidiary role in the lump of clay that is the <s>Pradhāna</s>. Therefore, even from activity, the establishment of sentient supervision follows — thus 'because of the activity of potency' is also a <s>Sāṃkhya</s> reason that is contradictory itself, stated obliquely. Here the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> raises an objection: 'But even the sentient being's activity...' The intent is this: You, the <s>Aupaniṣada</s> (Vedāntin), having refuted our reasons by scripture, must then establish that the sentient being alone, independent of anything else, is both the material and the efficient cause of the world. That is improper, because activity of a sentient being alone is not observed in the illustrative subjects. But the <s>Aupaniṣada</s>, intending 'Let this <s>Sāṃkhya</s> first accept that activity is caused by a sentient being, and afterward I shall resolve my own position from that very concession,' says: 'That is true' — it is not observed that a sentient being alone is active. The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> says: 'But not one conjoined with the insentient...' The word 'but' excludes the <s>Aupaniṣada</s> position. All activity is seen to rest on an insentient substrate, but no activity whatsoever rests on a sentient substrate. Therefore the sentient being has no activity in creating the world — this is the meaning. Here the <s>Aupaniṣada</s>, with a hidden intent, deliberates by way of a question: 'What then here...' In the meanwhile, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> says: 'Is it not the case that in which...' The sentient being is not directly perceived as either the substrate of activity or its cause; only activity and its insentient substrate, the body-chariot and the like, are known through perception. Therein, the activity of the insentient is caused by the insentient itself, not by the sentient. Only the mere existence of the sentient being there is understood, because a living body differs from a chariot and the like. But mere existence does not establish causality — otherwise <s>ākāśa</s> (space) would be the efficient cause of produced things like pots, for it exists everywhere. By this it is stated that even though a sentient being exists apart from the body, it has no role as an efficient cause with respect to activity. And because it has no causal role in activity, from the observation that activity is seen when the body, which is perceptible, is present and not seen when it is absent, the <s>Cārvākas</s> (materialists) have concluded that consciousness belongs to the body alone — and thus it is established that activity is not caused by a conscious self. Therefore, the sentient self's causality of the world cannot be established either from design or from activity — the <s>Aupaniṣada</s> replies: 'To that it is said — we do not say...' We do not need to establish right now, whether through perception, inference, or scripture, either the embodied self or the supreme self; we need only state its causality with respect to activity. Therein, since activity is not observed in a dead body or in a chariot unsupervised by a sentient being, and since activity is observed in the opposite case, the causal role of the sentient being in activity is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance — not through the mere existence of the sentient being,

body.text:
yenātiprasaṅgo bhavet /
bhūtacaitanikānāmapi cedanādhiṣṭhānādacetanānāṃ pravṛttirityatrāvivāda ityāha-- #laukāyatikānāmapīti# /
syādetat /
dehaḥ svayaṃ cetanaḥ karacaraṇādimān svavyāpāreṇa pravartayatīti yuktaṃ, na tu tadatiriktaḥ kūṭasthanityaścetano vyāpārarahito jñānaikasvabhāvaḥ pravṛttyabhāvāt pravartako yukta iti codayati-- #nanu taveti# /
pariharati- #- na /
ayaskāntavadrūpādivacceti /
yathā ca rūpādaya iti# /
sāṃkhyānāṃ hi svadeśasthā rūpādaya indriyaṃ vikurvate, tena tadindrayamarthaṃ prāptamarthākāreṇa pariṇamata iti sthitiḥ /
saṃprati codakaḥ svābhiprāyamāviṣkaroti-- #ekatvāditi# /
yeṣāmacetanaṃ cetanaṃ cāsti teṣāmetadyujyate vaktuṃ cetanādhiṣṭhitamacetanaṃ pravartata iti /
yathā yogināmīśvaravādinām /
yeṣāṃ tu cetanātiriktaṃ nāstyadvaitavādināṃ, teṣāṃ pravartyābhāve kaṃ prati pravartakatvaṃ cetanasyetyarthaḥ /
pariharati-- #na avidyeti# /
kāraṇabhūtayā layalakṣaṇayāvidyayā prāksargopacitena ca vikṣepasaṃskāreṇa yat pratyupasthāpitaṃ nāmarūpaṃ tadeva māyā, tadāveśenāsya codyasyāsakṛtprayuktatvāt /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-- neyaṃ sṛṣṭirvastusatī yenādvaitino vastusato dvitīyasyābhāvādanuyujyeta /

children.text: kālpanikyāṃ tu sṛṣṭāvasti kālpanikaṃ dvitīyaṃ sahāyaṃ māyāmayam /
children.translated_text: But in an illusory creation, there does exist an illusory second, an associate made of <s>māyā</s>.
As they say: 'The associates are of the very same kind as one's destiny.',
Thus it is said.

children.text: na caivaṃ brahmopādānatvavyāghātaḥ, brahmaṇa eva māyāveśenopādānatvāttadadhiṣṭhānatvājjagadvibhramasya, rajatavibhramasyeva śuktikādhiṣṭhānasya śuktikopādānatvamiti niravadyam //2 //
children.translated_text: Nor is there any contradiction with <s>Brahman</s> being the material cause, for <s>Brahman</s> alone, through the influence of <s>māyā</s>, serves as the material cause and as the substratum of the world-illusion — just as the mother-of-pearl is the material cause of the silver-illusion, being the substratum of the mother-of-pearl. This is faultless. (2)

body.translated_text: by which there would be over-extension. Even for the materialists (<s>Bhūtacaitanikas</s>), the activity of insentient things proceeds from the supervision of a sentient being — in this there is no dispute, thus he says: 'Even for the <s>Cārvākas</s>...' One might object: The body itself is sentient, possessing hands, feet, and the like, and it acts through its own operation — that is reasonable. But that an entity distinct from it, immutably eternal, devoid of operation, whose sole nature is knowledge, should be an activator — that is unreasonable, since it has no activity. Thus he raises the objection: 'But in your view...' He answers: 'No. Like a magnet, like form and the rest...' 'And just as form and the rest...' For according to the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, form and the rest, situated in their own locus, transform the sense organ, whereby that sense organ, having reached the object, is modified into the form of the object — such is the doctrine. Now the objector reveals his own intent: 'Because of oneness...' For those who accept both an insentient and a sentient principle, it is appropriate to say that the insentient operates under the supervision of the sentient — as for the <s>Yogins</s> and the proponents of <s>Īśvara</s> (God). But for those who accept nothing apart from the sentient, the <s>Advaitins</s> (non-dualists), in the absence of anything to be set in motion, toward whom would the sentient being exercise its agency? — this is the meaning. He answers: 'No — due to <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)...' The <s>nāma-rūpa</s> (name and form) that is presented by the causal <s>avidyā</s> characterized by dissolution, together with the projecting <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) accumulated from prior creation — that itself is <s>māyā</s> (illusion), and through its influence this objection has been repeatedly raised. What is stated amounts to this: this creation is not ultimately real, such that the <s>Advaitin</s> could be challenged on the ground that a real second entity is absent.

body.text:
#payombuvaccettatrāpi# /
yathā payombunoścetanānadhiṣṭhitayoḥ svata eva pravṛttirevaṃ pradhānasyāpīti śaṅkārthaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'Like milk and water, even there...' Just as milk and water, without the supervision of a sentient being, transform of their own accord, so too <s>Pradhāna</s> should — this is the meaning of the objection.

body.text:
tatrāpi cetanādhiṣṭhitatvaṃ sādhyaṃ, na ca sādhyenaiva vyabhicāraḥ, tathā satyanumānamātrocchedaprasaṅgāt, sarvatrāsya sulabhatvāt /
na cāsādhyam /
atrāpi cetanādhiṣṭhānasyāgamasiddhatvāt /
na ca sapakṣeṇa vyabhicāra iti śaṅkānirākaraṇasyārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: 'In the thesis to be proved' is to be understood as illustrative.
It should also be seen as 'because of being included in the co-probative instance.'

children.text: nanu 'upasaṃhāradarśanāt' ityatrānapekṣasya pravṛttirdaśitā, iha tu sarvasya cetanāpekṣā pravṛttiḥ pratipādyata iti kuto na virodha ityata āha-- #upasaṃhāradarśanāditi# /
children.translated_text: But in 'from the observation of aggregation,' unsupervised activity was indicated, whereas here all activity is taught as requiring the sentient being — so how is there no contradiction? To this he says: 'From the observation of aggregation...'

children.text: sthūladarśilokābhiprāyānurodhena taduktaṃ na tu paramārthata ityarthaḥ //3 //
children.translated_text: That was stated in accordance with the intent of ordinary gross perception, but not in the ultimate sense — this is the meaning. (3)

body.translated_text: Even there, supervision by a sentient being is what is to be proved, and there is no deviation through what is itself to be proved, for otherwise there would follow the destruction of all inference, since this fallacy is easily available everywhere. Nor is it unestablished, since even there the supervision of a sentient being is established through scripture. And the objection cannot be raised through the co-probative instance — this is the meaning of the refutation of the objection.

body.text:
#vyatirekānavasthiteścānapekṣatvāt# /
yadyapi sāṃkhyānāmapi vicitrakarmavāsanāvāsitaṃ pradhānaṃ sāmyāvasthāyāmapi tathāpi na karmavāsanāḥ sargasyeśate, kintu pradhānameva svakārye pravartamānamadharmapratibaddhaṃ sanna sukhamayīṃ sṛṣṭiṃ kartumutsahata iti dharmeṇādharmapratibandho 'panīyate /
evamadharmeṇa dharmapratibandho 'panīyate daḥkhamayyāṃ sṛṣṭau /

children.translated_text: And <s>Pradhāna</s> itself proceeds toward creation independently, without depending on anything.

children.text: yathāhuḥ-- 'nimittamaprayojakaṃ prakṛtīnāṃ varaṇabhedastu tataḥ kṣetrikavat' iti /
children.translated_text: As they say: 'The occasion is not the activator of the <s>prakṛtis</s> (natures); rather, it is the removal of the obstruction, like a farmer with a field.'

children.text: tataśca pratibandakāpanayasādhane dharmādharmavāsane api saṃnihite ityāgantorapekṣaṇīyasyābhāvāt sadaiva sāmyena pariṇameta vaiṣamyeṇa vā, na tvayaṃ kādācitkaḥ pariṇāmabheda upapadyeta /
children.translated_text: And since the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> impressions, which serve to remove the obstruction, are always present, in the absence of anything extrinsic to be awaited, <s>Pradhāna</s> should always transform either into equilibrium or disequilibrium; but this occasional difference in transformation cannot be accounted for.

children.text: īśvarasya tu mahāmāyasya cetanasya līlayā vā yadṛcchayā vā svabhāvavaicitryādvā karmaparipākāpekṣasya pravṛttinivṛttī upapadyete eveti //4 //
children.translated_text: For <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), however, who is the great magician, a sentient being, whether through sport, or spontaneously, or through the natural diversity of his nature, and who depends on the ripening of <s>karma</s> — both activity and cessation are well accounted for. (4)

body.translated_text: 'And because of the non-establishment of distinction without dependence' — Although for the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> too, <s>Pradhāna</s> is imbued with the impressions of diverse <s>karmas</s> even in the state of equilibrium, nevertheless the <s>karma</s> impressions do not govern creation; rather, <s>Pradhāna</s> itself, proceeding toward its own effect, being bound by <s>adharma</s> (demerit), is unable to create a blissful creation — so <s>dharma</s> (merit) removes the obstruction of <s>adharma</s>. Similarly, <s>adharma</s> removes the obstruction of <s>dharma</s> in a painful creation.

body.text:
#anyatrābhāvācca na tṛṇādivat# /
dhenūpayuktaṃ hi tṛṇapallavādi yathā svabhāvata eva cetanānapekṣaṃ kṣīrabhāvena pariṇamate na tu tatra dhenūcaitanyamapekṣyate, upayogamātre tadapekṣatvāt /
evaṃ pradhānamapi svabhāvata eva pariṇaṃsyate kṛtamatra cetaneneti śaṅkārthaḥ /

children.text: dhenūpayuktasya tṛṇādeḥ kṣīrabhāve kiṃ nimittāntaramātraṃ niṣidhyate, uta cetanam /
children.translated_text: Regarding the transformation of grass and the like consumed by a cow into milk, is it only some other efficient cause that is denied, or is it the sentient being?

children.text: na tāvannimittāntaraṃ, dhenudehasthasyaudaryasya vahnyādibhedasya nimittāntarasya saṃbhavāt /
children.translated_text: It is not some other efficient cause, since the digestive fire and other differentiating factors present in the cow's body are plausible as another efficient cause.

children.text: buddhipūrvakārī tu tatrāpīśvara eva sarvajñaḥ saṃbhavatīti śaṅkānirākaraṇasyārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: But one who acts with deliberation — even there, it is only <s>Īśvara</s> (God), the omniscient, who is a plausible candidate — this is the meaning of the refutation of the objection.
This is what is stated: 'Something is accomplished by divine providence...' (5)

body.translated_text: 'And because of the absence elsewhere, not like grass and so forth' — For grass, sprouts, and the like consumed by a cow transform of their own accord into the form of milk without depending on the cow's sentience — since sentience is required only for the act of consumption. Similarly, <s>Pradhāna</s> too should transform by its own nature — what need is there of a sentient being? This is the meaning of the objection.

body.text:
#abhyupagame 'pyarthābhāvāt# /
puruṣārthāpekṣābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
tadidamuktam-- #evaṃ prayojanamapi kiñcinnāpekṣiṣyata iti# /
athavā puruṣārthābhāvāditi yojyam /
tadidamuktam-- #tathāpi pradhānapravṛtteḥ prayojanaṃ vivektavyamiti# /
na kevalaṃ tāttviko bhogo 'nādheyātiśayasya kūṭasthanityasya puruṣasya na saṃbhavati, anirmokṣaprasaṅgaśca /
yena hi prayojanena pradhānaṃ pravartitaṃ tadanena kartavyaṃ, bhogena caitatpravartitamiti tameva kuryānna mokṣaṃ, tenāpravartitatvādityarthaḥ /
#apavargaścetprāgapīti# /
citeḥ sadā viśuddhatvānnaitasyāṃ jātu karmānubhavavāsanāḥ santi /
pradhānaṃ tu tāsāmanādīnāmādhāraḥ /
tathā ca pradhānapravṛtteḥ prāk citirmuktaiveti nāpavargārthamapi tatpravṛttiriti /
#śabdādyanupalabdhiprasaṅgaśca# /
tadarthamapravṛttatvātpradhā #nasya /
ubhayārthatābhyupagame 'pīti# /
na tāvadapavargaḥ sādhyastasya pradhānāpravṛttimātreṇa siddhatvāt /
bhogārthaṃ tu pravarteta /
bhogasya ca sakṛcchabdādyupalabghimātrādeva samāptatvānna tadarthaṃ punaḥ pradhānaṃ pravartetetyayatnasādhyo mokṣaḥ syāt /
niḥśeṣaśabdādyupabhogasya cānantyena samāpteranupapatteranirmokṣaprasaṅgaḥ /
kṛtabhogamapi pradhānamāsattvapuruṣānyatākhyāteḥ kriyāsamabhihāreṇa bhojayatīti cet, atha puruṣārthāya pravṛttaṃ kimarthaṃ sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātiṃ karoti /
body.translated_text: 'Even if accepted, because of the absence of purpose' — because there would follow the absence of any need for the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> (spirit). This is what is stated: 'Thus, no purpose whatsoever would be required...' Alternatively, it should be construed as 'because of the absence of purpose for <s>Puruṣa</s>.' This is what is stated: 'Even so, the purpose of <s>Pradhāna's</s> activity must be discriminated...' Not only is genuine enjoyment impossible for <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is immutably eternal and upon whom no excellence can be superimposed, but there also follows the impossibility of liberation. For the purpose for which <s>Pradhāna</s> was set in motion must be accomplished by it — and since it was set in motion for enjoyment, it should accomplish only that, not liberation, since it was not set in motion for that purpose — this is the meaning. 'And liberation would have been prior too...' Since consciousness is always pure, <s>karma</s> impressions and experiential traces never belong to it. <s>Pradhāna</s>, however, is the repository of those beginningless impressions. And so, prior to the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s>, consciousness is already liberated — hence the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s> cannot be for the purpose of liberation either. 'And there would follow the non-apprehension of sound and the rest' — because <s>Pradhāna</s> has not been set in motion for that purpose. 'Even if both purposes are accepted...' Liberation is not something to be achieved, since it is accomplished by the mere cessation of <s>Pradhāna's</s> activity. But <s>Pradhāna</s> might be active for the purpose of enjoyment. And since enjoyment is completed by merely once apprehending sound and the rest, <s>Pradhāna</s> would not be active again for that purpose — hence liberation would be effortlessly attained. And since the complete enjoyment of all sounds and the rest cannot be completed due to their infinity, there follows the impossibility of liberation. If one says that <s>Pradhāna</s>, even after providing enjoyment, continues to make one experience through the continued operation of the discrimination between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> — then, having set out for the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>, why does it produce the discrimination between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>?

body.text:
apavargārthamiti cet, hantāyāṃ sakṛcchabdādyupabhogena kṛtaprayojanasya pradhānasya nivṛttimātrādeva sidhyatīti kṛtaṃ sattvānyatākhyātipratīkṣaṇena /
na cāsyāḥ svarūpataḥ puruṣārthatvam /
tasmādubhayārthamapi na pradhānasya pravṛttirupapadyata iti siddhor'thābhāvaḥ /
sugamamitarat /
śaṅkate-- #dṛkśaktīti# /
puruṣo hi dṛkśaktiḥ /
sā ca dṛśyamantareṇānarthikā syāt /
naca svātmanyarthavatī, svātmani vṛttivirodhāt /
pradhānaṃ ca sargaśaktiḥ /
sā ca sarjanīyamantareṇānarthikā syāditi yatpradhānena śabdādi sṛjyate tadeva dṛkśakterdṛśyaṃ bhavatīti tadubhayārthavatvāya sarjanamiti śaṅkārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: He refutes this: 'Like the non-destruction of the creative power...'

children.text: yathā hi pradhānasya sargaśaktirekaṃ puruṣaṃ prati caritārthāpi puruṣāntaraṃ prati pravartate 'nucchedāt /
children.translated_text: For just as the creative power of <s>Pradhāna</s>, even though it has fulfilled its purpose with respect to one <s>Puruṣa</s>, proceeds toward another <s>Puruṣa</s> because it is not destroyed,

children.text: evaṃ dṛkśaktirapi taṃ puruṣaṃ pratyarthavattvāyānucchedātsarvadā pravartetetyanirmokṣaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, the power of seeing (<s>dṛkśakti</s>) also would always operate for the sake of serving its purpose to that <s>Puruṣa</s>, since it is never cut off, and the consequence would be that there is no liberation (<s>anirmokṣa</s>).

children.text: sakṛddṛśyadarśanena vā caritārthatve na bhūyaḥ pravarteteti sarveṣāmekapade nirmokṣaḥ prasajyeteti sahasā saṃsāraḥ samucchidyeteti //6 //
children.translated_text: Or, if its purpose is fulfilled by a single instance of seeing the seen, it would not operate again, and consequently liberation for all would occur at once — thus <s>saṃsāra</s> would be abruptly annihilated.

body.translated_text: If for the purpose of liberation — well then, this is accomplished by the mere cessation of <s>Pradhāna</s> whose purpose is fulfilled by a single experience of sound and the rest, so there is no need to wait for the discrimination of <s>sattva</s>'s otherness. Nor does that discrimination have intrinsic value for <s>Puruṣa</s>. Therefore, <s>Pradhāna's</s> activity cannot be accounted for even for both purposes — thus the absence of purpose is established. The rest is easy to understand. He raises an objection: 'The power of seeing...' <s>Puruṣa</s> is the power of seeing (<s>dṛk-śakti</s>). And that would be purposeless without something to be seen. Nor is it purposeful with respect to itself, since there is a contradiction in operating upon oneself. And <s>Pradhāna</s> is the power of creation (<s>sarga-śakti</s>). And that would be purposeless without something to be created. So what is created by <s>Pradhāna</s> as sound and the rest becomes the object of seeing for the power of seeing — thus creation serves the purposefulness of both. This is the meaning of the objection.

body.text:
#puruṣāśmavaditi cettathāpi# /
naiva doṣātpracyutiriti śeṣaḥ /
mā bhūtpuruṣārthasya śaktyarthavattvasya vā pravartakatvam, puruṣa eva dṛkśaktisampannaḥ paṅguriva pravṛttiśaktisaṃpannaṃ pradhānamandhamiva pravartayiṣyatīti śaṅkā /

children.translated_text: He states the consequence of non-liberation arising from this defect — 'To begin with, there is the abandonment of what has been accepted.'
Not only is there abandonment of what has been accepted, but this is also unreasonable when examined according to your own doctrine — thus he says, 'How can one who is indifferent...'
The proof of actionlessness is — 'because of being without qualities (<s>nirguṇa</s>).'
The rest is self-evident in meaning.

body.translated_text: 'If it be like the case of <s>Puruṣa</s> and a stone' — the remainder is: even so, there is no escape from the defect. Let it not be that the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> or the purposefulness of the power serves as the impeller; the objection is that <s>Puruṣa</s> himself, endowed with the power of seeing, would impel <s>Pradhāna</s>, which is blind and endowed with the power of activity, just as a lame person would.

body.translated_text: 'And because of the impossibility of being a constituent.' If the state of <s>Pradhāna</s> is immutably eternal, then there can be no departure from it, for that would entail the consequence of non-eternality. As they say — 'The wise call that eternal whose own nature does not perish.' This is what is stated — 'from the fear of the destruction of its essential nature.' Now, if it is eternal in the sense of being subject to transformation (<s>pariṇāminityā</s>), as they say — 'That which, even when undergoing modification, whose essence is not destroyed, that too is eternal' —

children.translated_text: thus.
To this he says — 'and of what is external.'

children.translated_text: How can that which has remained for a long time in the state of equilibrium (<s>sāmyāvasthā</s>) attain disequilibrium without the intervention of a distinct cause?

children.text: anapekṣasya svato vāpi vaiṣamye na kadācitsāmyaṃ bhavedityarthaḥ //8 //
children.translated_text: The meaning is that if it is independent and can attain disequilibrium on its own, then equilibrium would never obtain.

children.translated_text: 'Even so, of <s>Pradhāna</s>' —

children.text: aṅgitvānupapattilakṣaṇo doṣastāvanna bhavadbhiḥ śakyaḥ parihartumiti vakṣyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: We shall say that the defect characterized as the impossibility of being a constituent cannot be resolved by you.
The meaning is: even granting your position, the absence of defect is being stated.
Now he establishes the impossibility of being a constituent — 'Even those capable of attaining disequilibrium...'

body.translated_text: 'And in the case of inference otherwise, because of the separation from the power of the knower.'

body.translated_text: 'And because of contradiction, it is incoherent. Somewhere seven sense-organs' — for indeed, the skin alone is the one cognitive sense-organ (<s>buddhīndriya</s>) capable of grasping multiple forms and so forth; the five organs of action (<s>karmendriyāṇi</s>), and the mind (<s>manas</s>) as the seventh — thus seven sense-organs. 'Somewhere three internal organs' — <s>buddhi</s>, <s>ahaṅkāra</s>, and <s>manas</s>. 'Somewhere one' — <s>buddhi</s> alone. The rest is self-evident. 'Here the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> objects' — 'But the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> texts also...' First, the relation of the heated and the heater cannot obtain in one and the same entity. For the root 'tap' is not like the root 'as' which takes an agent-based construction, but rather like the root 'pac' which takes an object-based construction. And the object is that which bears the fruit of the action residing in another. Thus the heated, being the object bearing the fruit of the action residing in the heater, must be different from the heater. If they were non-different, then even for <s>Caitra</s> who is the agent of going, bearing the fruit of his own action of walking — namely, reaching the city — there would be the absurd consequence of not being an object. But if they are different, then the heated stands to the heater as the city, which receives the fruit of <s>Caitra</s>'s action of walking, stands to the walker — thus the relation of heated and heater is established. Therefore, in non-difference, the relation of heated and heater does not obtain. He states another refutation — 'And if...' For an entity cannot be separated from its own nature — this is the purport. And the waves, surges, and foam of the ocean, being its own nature, possess the properties of appearance and disappearance, yet the ocean is never freed from them. Not only is the otherness of the heated from the heater established by the object-relation, but it is also established by experience — thus he says, 'And this is well-known.' For indeed, wealth, though acquired, being seen to have the defects of earning, protecting, loss, attachment, increase, and harm, becomes a source of suffering and afflicts the one who desires it. The heated is the one who suffers for its sake, and the heater is wealth itself; and these two are known in the world as distinct. And in non-difference, the refutations have been stated. How then can both subsist in one non-dual entity — this is the meaning. Having thus declared the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> view to be incoherent, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> demonstrates liberation in his own system based on the difference between the heated and the heater — 'But when there is a different kind of existence.' The conjunction of the power of seeing and of what is seen is indeed the cause of suffering. Its cause is <s>avidyā</s>, the impression of non-discriminative cognition. And that is removed by <s>vidyā</s>, discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>), which is its opposite. Upon its cessation, the conjunction caused by it ceases, and upon the cessation of that, the suffering caused by it ceases. As stated by the teacher <s>Pañcaśikha</s> — 'By the removal of the cause of that conjunction, this would be the absolute remedy for suffering.' And here, bondage and liberation do not belong directly to <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is beyond transformation, but rather to the <s>sattva</s> aspect of <s>buddhi</s> alone, which has obtained consciousness through the reflection of pure awareness (<s>citicchāyāpatti</s>). For indeed —

body.translated_text: the apprehension of the nature of desirable and undesirable qualities, which has become non-distinct from it, constitutes his experience (<s>bhoga</s>); the apprehension of the nature of the experiencer constitutes liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). By that, it is the <s>sattva</s> aspect of <s>buddhi</s> alone that is liberated. Nevertheless, just as victory or defeat occurring among warriors is attributed primarily to the king, so too bondage and liberation, occurring in the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>, are in some manner attributed to <s>Puruṣa</s>, for he, through non-distinction, is the experiencer of its fruit. Anticipating this, he says — 'It might be that'

children.text: yadā tu 'tattvamasi'iti vākyaśravaṇamananadhyānābhyāsaparipākaprakarṣaparyantajo 'sya sākṣātkāra upajāyate tadā jīvaḥ śuddhabuddhatattvasvabhāvamātmano 'nubhavan nirmṛṣṭanikhilasavāsanakleśajālaḥ kevalaḥ svastho bhavati, na cāsya punaḥ saṃsārabhayamasti taddhetoravāstavatvena samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitatvāt /
children.translated_text: But when, through the culmination of the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditation on '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' ('That thou art'), direct realization arises in him, then the <s>jīva</s>, experiencing the nature of his own self as pure awakened reality, having completely washed away the entire net of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) together with their latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), becomes solitary (<s>kevala</s>) and at ease in himself; and there is no further fear of <s>saṃsāra</s> for him, because its cause, being unreal, has been uprooted entirely.
But for the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, since <s>tamas</s>, being real, cannot be utterly eradicated —
thus it has been said — 'And because of hearing that the distinction of modifications is a mere verbal designation.'

body.translated_text: 'liberation could sometimes be established.' To this it is replied — 'No. Because of oneness alone, the relation of heated and heater does not obtain.' Since in oneness the relation of heated and heater does not obtain, precisely because of oneness, therefore the relation of heated and heater must be accepted by us as resting on conventional distinction. For suffering is merely conventional, not ultimate — this has been declared repeatedly. 'This defect would arise if, in the oneness of self, the heated and the heater were to enter into the relation of object and subject with each other' — thus, according to our position, the remainder is supplied. Even the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, who speaks of the relation of heated and heater as based on difference, cannot declare <s>Puruṣa</s> to be the object of the action of heating, because being beyond transformation, it is impossible for him to bear the fruit produced by the action of heating. It is only that <s>sattva</s> is the heated by this account, and <s>rajas</s> must be accepted as the heater. But since it has been shown that <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s> is what is heated, <s>Puruṣa</s> too, through non-distinction from it, appears as if heated — but is not actually heated, due to being beyond transformation. And that non-distinction is <s>avidyā</s>. Thus the relation of heated and heater is, by your own admission, created by <s>avidyā</s>; this very same thing is being stated by us — why then does it appear harsh to you? Moreover, since you accept the eternality of the heater, there would be the consequence of non-liberation. He raises an objection — 'Even though the powers of the heated and the heater are eternal' — it operates together with its cause, namely non-discrimination (<s>adarśana</s>), thus the conjunction is with-cause and depends on that. He refutes — 'No. Because non-discrimination (<s>adarśana</s>) is <s>tamas</s>.' It has been said that <s>Puruṣa</s> is not the one who is heated. It is only that this heating belongs to <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s>, produced by <s>rajas</s> the heater. And for that <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s>, which through <s>tāmasa</s> error does not perceive its own difference from <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is the false identification that '<s>Puruṣa</s> is heated' — but <s>Puruṣa</s> is not susceptible even to the flaw of error. And for that <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s>, this <s>tāmasa</s> non-discriminative cognition is to be removed by the <s>sāttvika</s> discriminative cognition (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>). But since <s>tamas</s> is the root, it cannot be utterly eradicated. Even when cut, like a cut <s>badarī</s> tree, <s>avidyā</s> would sprout again from <s>tamas</s>, overwhelming <s>sattva</s>, displacing discriminative knowledge, and manifesting with a hundred peaks — and thus this talk of liberation would amount to a farewell libation of water for the ascetic. In our system, however, there is no such defect — he says, 'But in the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> view.' For just as a face, though fair, assumes impurity through the superimposed reflection in a dirty mirror, yet is not really impure, and the reflection does not truly differ from the original — but in that reflection, impurity gains a foothold due to the imposition of the dirty mirror;

body.translated_text: The doctrine of <s>Pradhāna</s> as cause' — just as the doctrine of <s>Pradhāna</s> as cause contradicts the doctrine of <s>Brahman</s> as cause, so too does the doctrine of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) as cause; therefore that too must be refuted. The elaboration of 'By this, the views not accepted by the learned are also explained' is begun. Therein, the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> have criticized the doctrine of <s>Brahman</s> as cause: if a conscious entity is the material cause of space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the rest, then space and the rest, being produced from it, should be conscious. For in the effect, the arising of qualities follows the sequence of qualities in the cause — just as a cloth woven from white threads is white and never black. Likewise, what is produced from a conscious being should be conscious, not unconscious. Therefore, the world has only an unconscious material cause. And that unconscious cause is the atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>). Indeed, the production of gross from subtle is observed — just as cloth from threads, and threads from fibres — and so on until at the limit of reduction there remains an extremely subtle, partless causal substance, and that is the atom. If it were accepted as having parts, then due to infinite divisibility, there would be the absurd consequence of a mustard seed and Mount <s>Meru</s> having equal magnitude. Now, first, through the conjunction of the soul possessing <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) with the atom, motion (<s>karma</s>) arises in the atom; then that atom, conjoining with another atom, produces a dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>). But many atoms conjoined together do not immediately produce a gross object, because despite being many they remain atomic in size — like atoms contained within a pot. For if atoms contained in a pot were to produce the pot, then when the pot is broken apart, potsherds and gravel and the like would not be perceived, since they would not have been produced, only the pot alone having been produced by those atoms. In that case, upon the destruction of the pot by a hammer-blow, nothing would be perceived, since those atoms, being unproduced and being beyond the senses, would not be perceived. Therefore, many atoms are not the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of a substance; rather, only two atoms produce a dyad. And its magnitude, being atomic (<s>aṇutva</s>), different from the spherical magnitude (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>) of the atom, is the duality-number which arises dependent on God's cognition. And no substance is produced from just two dyads, for that would result in pointlessness — it too would be merely a dyad, not something large. For the production of largeness arises from the multiplicity of causes, from the largeness of causes, or from the specific aggregation of causes. The dyads possess neither largeness, from which what is produced from them would be large, nor multiplicity, being only two, nor difference of aggregation as in gross lumps, since their partless components lack the distinction of loosely-connected parts. Therefore, what is produced by them too would have to be atomic like the producing dyad. And since there would be no distinction of enjoyment for <s>Puruṣa</s>, and since the construction of the universe, being for the purpose of enjoyment and caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, would be accomplished by that causal dyad, there would be no need for another dyad as substrate — hence the production would be pointless. For the production to be purposeful, a substance that is large and extended must be produced from many dyads as a triad (<s>tryaṇuka</s>) or tetrad (<s>caturaṇuka</s>). There is indeed a distinction of enjoyment in each of those. And there is the multiplicity-number, arisen dependent on God's cognition, which is the source of the magnitude of largeness.

body.translated_text: An effect-substance produced from triads and the like becomes large either from the multiplicity of causes, or from the largeness of causes, or from the specific aggregation of causes — this is the procedure. The refutation that, by this very procedure, qualities inhering in the cause produce only a quality of the same kind in the effect is rendered ineffective due to deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) — he says, 'Just as with large and long, so from short and spherical.' Just as a large substance such as a triad arises from a short dyad, yet the arising of the quality of largeness does not depend on largeness in the dyad, since the dyad is short. Or just as that same triad, being long, arises from a short dyad, yet does not depend on length in the dyad, since it is absent there. The word 'or' serves to include what is unstated. Just as a dyad, which is atomic and of short magnitude, arises from the spherical atom as something non-spherical — so too from conscious <s>Brahman</s>, an unconscious world can be produced: this is the construction of the <s>sūtra</s>. In the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, 'But the specific quality of the atom' — the mention of sphericality is illustrative. It should also be noted that in the dyad, atomicity too, like the spherical magnitude residing in the atom, does not produce a like quality, since the dyad's magnitude arises from duality-number. The <s>sūtra</s> 'from short and spherical' refers to the qualified substances, not to the qualities themselves. 'Where one should read two-two dyads' — due to an oversight, one word 'two' was not written. Thus the tetrad and so forth are explained. Otherwise, that too would be just a dyad, not something large — as was stated. Alternatively, 'two' denotes duality, as in 'the dual and singular of one or two.' For here the meaning is: of duality and unity. Otherwise, it would have to be 'in some' due to the plurality of countable things. Thus the construction should be: the two dualities that subsist in the dyads — when those two produce a tetrad, since four dyads are the producers of the countable things, the duality-numbers residing in each pair are also productive — this is the meaning. Thus, when the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> procedure is established in this way, the deviation of its refutation has been stated. And even if the procedure is not thus established, the deviation remains in the same condition — he says, 'Even when many atoms...' The construction is: neither an atomic thing nor a short thing is produced. He raises an objection — 'If you think that by a magnitude of a different kind, one's own cause being transcended...' He resolves — 'Do not think so.' Since the desired conclusion is achieved simply by the fact that qualities in the cause do not produce a quality of the same kind in the effect, the mind need not be wearied by pursuing the reason for that. Moreover, a different magnitude supersedes an existing one, but before origination the different magnitude does not yet exist, so how could it supersede? Nor does it supersede its cause. Since sphericality too, being of the same kind, would equally serve as a cause for supersession, both effects would equally fail to arise — with this intent he says, 'Nor is there supersession by a different magnitude.' And there is no engagement of sphericality and the rest in the production of a different magnitude. And the presence or absence of cause-multiplicity and the rest does not affect sphericality — he says, 'Nor in the production of a different magnitude...' He states another deviation — 'From conjunction...' He raises an objection — 'Regarding substance, which is the topic...' He refutes — 'No.

body.translated_text: 'In either case, there is no motion (<s>karma</s>), hence the absence of that.' Whether one accepts or does not accept a cause for the initial motion of atoms, there is no motion, and hence the absence of that — namely, of creation proceeding through dyads and the rest. Alternatively, whether the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> inheres in the atom or in the soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), in either case, since that which is unconscious and not governed by a conscious being does not act, there is no motion, and hence the absence of that — the absence of creation. The governance of God (<s>Īśvara</s>) as merely an efficient cause will be refuted later. Alternatively, whether for the purpose of producing conjunction or for the purpose of producing disjunction — in either case, there is no motion, and hence the absence of that: the absence of conjunction, which is the cause of creation, and the absence of disjunction, which is the cause of dissolution — that is, the absence of both creation and dissolution. He explains that <s>sūtra</s> in its purport — 'Now, the doctrine of atoms as cause...' He states the form of what is to be refuted together with its reasoning — 'And that doctrine...' 'Accompanied by their own' means accompanied by those connected with themselves. And the connection here is <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), which is the relation of container and contained, serving as the basis of 'here'-cognition. Since the fifth element has no parts — 'those four elements.' This is the <s>sūtra</s> stated regarding the atomic doctrine. He gives the first interpretation — 'Of those possessing motion.' The word 'etc.' after 'impact' includes impulse (<s>nodana</s>), tendency (<s>saṃskāra</s>), gravity (<s>gurutva</s>), and fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>). Impulse and tendency share the same conditions as impact; and gravity and fluidity, being perpetually present in atoms, would lead to the consequence of perpetual motion. He states the second interpretation, preceded by an objection — 'If <s>adṛṣṭa</s>' — that is, merit and demerit (<s>dharmādharma</s>). 'Of the initial motion' — 'and of the self' — of the soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), 'whose consciousness has not yet arisen' — 'by a person possessing <s>adṛṣṭa</s>.' The meaning is: through the relation of conjunction-inherence (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>). 'Because of the continuity of the connection' — although the conjunction of atoms and souls arises from the motion of the atom, nevertheless the stream of that conjunction is continuous — this is the purport. And if there were complete coalescence — for in a partial conjunction, since two surfaces of an atom are contiguous, other surfaces are not pervaded by the conjunction, and so the first interpretation is sustained. But in total contiguity, other atoms too would merge into a single atom, and so the first interpretation would not hold — this is the meaning. He raises an objection: even though atoms are without spatial extension, nonetheless conjunction is by nature non-pervasive — such is its inherent character. What is this verbal quibbling that conjunction does not pervade what has no extension? This very verbal quibbling amounts to saying that whatever is apprehended should be accepted as it is. He extracts the purport of this objection — 'The parts of atoms are imagined.' For there is no possibility that a single partless entity is simultaneously conjoined and unconjoined with that very same thing, due to the contradiction of existence and non-existence in a single non-dual entity. Or if there were no contradiction, then contradiction would never find any scope anywhere. But the apprehension can be explained even by imagining spatial parts. This is what is stated — 'the parts are imagined.' And he draws out the conclusion — 'Because what is imagined has no real existence.' He gives the third interpretation — 'Just as in the initial creation.' Why cannot impact, impulse, and the rest serve as causes of the motion that initiates dissolution at the time of dissolution? To this he says — 'For even there, nothing determinate...' Impact and the rest do occur occasionally in some places,

children.translated_text: Therefore, one must say that <s>saṃyoga</s> is related to the two <s>saṃyogin</s>s by <s>samavāya</s>.
This very same [argument] applies equally to <s>samavāya</s>'s relation with its own <s>samavāyin</s>s — [there is no difference] except for a stubborn attachment [to one's own position].
