body.translated_text:
'And because of the acceptance of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), due to parity, there is infinite regress' (<s>samavāyābhyupagamāc ca sāmyād anavasthiteḥ</s>).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] expounds: '<s>samavāyābhyupagamāt</s>' — thus.
To begin with, an independent <s>samavāya</s>, being absolutely different from the two <s>samavāyin</s>s (things related by inherence), cannot connect the two <s>samavāyin</s>s — because of over-extension [i.e., it could connect anything with anything].
Therefore, the two <s>samavāyin</s>s are to be connected by this [<s>samavāya</s>] which is related to the <s>samavāyin</s>s; and thus, when the relation of <s>samavāya</s> to the <s>samavāyin</s>s is accepted through yet another relation, there is an infinite regress.
But [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> may say:] that [<s>samavāya</s>], in its relation to the <s>samavāyin</s>s, does not require another relation, because its essential nature is the connecting of the <s>samavāyin</s>s.
Thus: even though it is different [from the <s>samavāyin</s>s], it cannot be determined without reference to the <s>samavāyin</s>s. And when it exists, the <s>samavāyin</s>s are not non-<s>samavāyin</s>s [i.e., they are necessarily related].
Therefore, <s>samavāya</s> [relates to] the <s>samavāyin</s>s by its very nature, not through another relation — hence there is no infinite regress — [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>] objects.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] answers: 'No, it is said. <s>Saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) too [is] likewise' (<s>saṃyogo 'py evam</s>).
Thus: <s>saṃyoga</s> too has as its essential nature the connecting of the <s>saṃyogin</s>s (things related by conjunction). And even though different [from them], it cannot be determined without the two <s>saṃyogin</s>s. And when it exists, the <s>saṃyogin</s>s are not non-<s>saṃyogin</s>s — hence the same argument applies.
If it were said that <s>saṃyoga</s> is a quality (<s>guṇa</s>), and a quality does not exist without being inherent in a substance, and its being inherent is not possible without <s>samavāya</s>, hence <s>saṃyoga</s> has <s>samavāya</s> — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] removes this doubt: 'And not because of being a quality' (<s>na ca guṇatvāt</s>).
If in the absence of <s>samavāya</s> it would lose its status as a quality — let it! There is no harm to us. This is what was stated: 'And because of the technical definition of quality' (<s>guṇaparibhāṣāyāḥ</s>).
But in reality, it has been said that [a quality] merely has substance as its locus (<s>dravyāśrayī</s>). And that [being the locus of a substance] is possible for <s>saṃyoga</s> from its own nature even without <s>samavāya</s>.
Nor is it correct [to argue] that because <s>saṃyoga</s> is a product (<s>kārya</s>), it requires <s>samavāya</s> as its <s>samavāyi-kāraṇa</s> (inherent cause) and therefore is an <s>samavāyin</s> — because of the unwanted consequence that [even] the <s>saṃyoga</s> of an atom [would be so], since that [atom's saṃyoga] is not [a product] of the same kind.
Moreover, <s>samavāya</s> too, whose existence depends on the <s>samavāyin</s>s, is a product (<s>kārya</s>) — because of its perishability through the perishing of one or both of the <s>samavāyin</s>s.
For it is not possible that a quality, or a quality and its possessor, or a part, or a part and its whole, do not exist, yet their relation [<s>samavāya</s>] exists.
Therefore, <s>samavāya</s> is a product. And thus, just as its origination depends on a mere efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>), so too does <s>saṃyoga</s>.
Alternatively, even if <s>samavāya</s> too requires <s>samavāyi</s> and <s>asamavāyi</s> causes, still that very infinite regress [ensues].
Therefore, like <s>samavāya</s>, <s>saṃyoga</s> too does not require another relation.
If it were said that [<s>saṃyoga</s>] connects the <s>saṃyogin</s>s but not itself with the <s>saṃyogin</s>s — then what, is it unrelated to the <s>saṃyogin</s>s? And if so, being absolutely different and unrelated, how could it relate the <s>saṃyogin</s>s?

children.translated_text: 'And because of eternality [of inherence, conjunction too would be eternal]' (<s>nityam eva ca bhāvāt</s>).
The supplement [to the <s>sūtra</s>] is: '[then there would be] either activity or non-activity [eternally].'
The <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary) on this has a transparent meaning. //14//

body.text:
#rūpādimattvācca viparyayo darśanāt# /
yat kila bhūtabhautikānāṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ tadrūpādimān paramāṇurnitya iti bhavadbhirabhyupeyate, tasya cedrūpādimattvamabhyupeyeta paramāṇutvanityatvaviruddhe sthaulyānityatve prasajyeyātāṃ, so 'yaṃ prasaṅga ekadharmābhyupagame dharmāntarasya /
niyatā prāptirhi prasaṅgalakṣaṇaṃ , tadanena prasaṅgena jagatkāraṇaprasiddhaye pravṛttaṃ sādhanaṃ rūpādimannityaparamāṇusiddheḥ pracyāvya brahmagocaratāṃ nīyate /
tadetadvaiśeṣikābhyupagamopanyāsapūrvakamāha-- #sāvayavānāṃ dravyāṇāmiti# /
paramāṇunityatvasādhanāni ca teṣāmupanyasya dūṣayati-- #yacca nityatve kāraṇamiti /
saditi#prāgabhāvāhyavacchinatti /
#akāraṇavaditi#ghaṭādeḥ /
#yadapi#
body.translated_text:
'And because of possessing form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like, the reverse [i.e., non-eternality and grossness] — because it is observed' (<s>rūpādimattvāc ca viparyayo darśanāt</s>).
As the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s accept: that which is the root cause of the elements and their products is the eternal atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) possessing form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the like. If the possession of form and the like is accepted for it, then grossness and non-eternality — which contradict its atomic nature and eternality — would follow. This is the unwanted consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>) [arising] from the acceptance of one property leading to another.
For the definition of <s>prasaṅga</s> is: the necessary entailment [of an undesired consequence]. By this <s>prasaṅga</s>, the proof that was deployed for establishing [the atom as] the cause of the world is dislodged from its purpose of establishing eternal atoms possessing form and the like, and is redirected toward [establishing] <s>Brahman</s>.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states this, preceded by the presentation of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> position: 'Of substances that have parts' (<s>sāvayavānāṃ dravyāṇām</s>).
Having presented the proofs for the eternality of atoms, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes them: 'And what is the reason for eternality' (<s>yac ca nityatve kāraṇam</s>).
'Being existent' (<s>sat</s>) — [this] excludes prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>).
'Like what has no cause' (<s>akāraṇavat</s>) — like a pot and the like.

body.text:
#nityatve dvitīyamiti# /
labdharūpaṃ hi kvacit kiñcidanyatra niṣidhyate /
tenānityamiti laukikena niṣedhenānyatra nityatvasadbhāvaḥ kalpanīyaḥ, te cānye paramāṇava iti /
tanna /
ātmanyapi nityatvopapatteḥ /
vyapadeśasya ca pratītipūrvakasya tadabhāve nirmūlasyāpi darśanāt /
yatheha vaṭe yakṣa iti /
#yadapi nityatve tṛtīyaṃ kāraṇamavidyeti# /
body.translated_text:
'The second [argument] for eternality' (<s>nityatve dvitīyam</s>).
Something that has been established as obtaining somewhere is negated elsewhere. Hence, by means of the ordinary negation 'non-eternal,' the existence of eternality elsewhere is to be postulated — and those 'others' are the atoms.
This is not [valid].
Because eternality is possible even in the Self (<s>ātman</s>).
And because designation (<s>vyapadeśa</s>), which requires prior cognition, is observed to be baseless even in the absence of that [cognition] — as in 'Here in this <s>vaṭa</s> tree [there is] a <s>yakṣa</s>.'
'And what is the third reason for eternality — <s>avidyā</s> (non-cognition)' (<s>yadapi nityatve tṛtīyaṃ kāraṇam avidyā</s>).

body.text:
yadi satāṃ paramāṇūnāṃ paridṛśyamānasthūlakāryāṇāṃ pratyakṣeṇa kāraṇāgrahaṇamavidyā tayā nityatvam, evaṃ sati dvyaṇukasyāpi nityatvam /
#athādravyatve satīti viśeṣyeta#tathā sati na dvyaṇuke vyabhicāraḥ, tasyānekadravyatvenāvidyamānadravyatvānupapatteḥ /
#tathāpyakāraṇavattvameva nityatānimittamāpadyeta,#yato 'dravyatvamavidyamānakāraṇabhūtadravyatvamucyate, tathā ca punaruktamityāha-- #tasya ceti# /
api cādravyatve sati sattvādityata eveṣṭārthasiddheravidyeti vyartham /
athāvidyāpadena dravyavināśakāraṇadvayāvidyamānatvamucyate,dvividho hi dravyanāśaheturavayavavināśo 'vayavavyatiṣaṅgavināśaśca, tadubhayaṃ paramāṇau nāsti, tasmānnityaḥ paramāṇuḥ /
naca sukhādibhirvyabhicāraḥ, teṣāmadravyatvādityāha-- #athāpīti# /
nirākaroti-- #nāvaśyamiti# /
yadi hi saṃyogasacivāni bahūni dravyāṇi dravyāntaramārabheranniti prakriyā sidhyet sidhyet dravyadvayameva(?) tadvināśakāraṇamiti /
natvetadasti, dravyasvarūpāparijñānāt /
na tāvat tantvādhārastadvyatiriktaḥ paṭo nāmāsti yaḥ saṃyogasacivaistantubhirārabhyetetyuktamadhastāt. ṣaṭpadārthasya dūṣayannagre vakṣyati /
kintu kāraṇameva #viśeṣavadavasthāntaramāpadyamānaṃ#kāryaṃ, tacca sāmānyātmakam /
tathāhi-- mṛdvā suvarṇaṃ vā sarveṣu ghaṭarucakādiṣvanugataṃ sāmānyamanubhūyate /
na caite ghaṭarucakādayo mṛtsuvarṇābhyāṃ vyatiricyanta ityuktam /
agre ca vakṣyāmaḥ /
tasmānmṛtsuvarṇe eva tena tenīkāreṇa pariṇamamāne ghaṭa iti ca rucaka iti ca kapālaśarkarākaṇamiti ca śakalakaṇikācūrṇamiti ca vyākhyāyete /
tatra tatropādānayormṛtsuvarṇayoḥ pratyabhijñānāt /
na tu ghaṭādayo vā kapālādiṣu kapālādayo vā ghaṭādiṣu ca rucakādayo vā śakalādiṣu śakalādayo vā rucakādiṣu pratyabhijñāyante yatra kāryakāraṇabhāvo bhavet /
na ca vinaśyantameva ghaṭakṣaṇaṃ pratītya kapālakṣaṇo 'nupādāna evotpadyate tatkimupādānapratyabhijñāneneti vaktavyam, etasyā api vaināśikaprakriyāyā upariṣṭānnirākariṣyamāṇatvāt /
tasmādupajanāpāyadharmāṇo viśeṣāvasthāḥ sāmānyasyopādeyāḥ, sāmānyātmā tūpādānam /
evaṃ vyavasthite yathā suvarṇadravyaṃ kāṭhinyāvasthāmapahāya dravāvasthayā parigaṇitaṃ, na ca tatrāvayavavibhāgaḥ sannapi dravatve kāraṇaṃ, paramāṇūnāṃ bhavanmate tadabhāvena dravatvānupapatteḥ, tasmādyathā evaṃ guṇādayo na dravyādyanadhīnanirūpaṇāḥ, api tu yadā yadā nirūpyante tadā tadā tadākāratayaiva prathante na tu prathāyāmeṣāmasti svātantryaṃ, tasmānnātiricyante dravyādapi tu dravyameva sāmānyarūpaṃ tathā tathā prathata ityarthaḥ /
dravyakāryatvamātraṃ guṇādīnāṃ dravyādhīnatvamiti manvānaścodayati-- #nanvagreranyasyāpīti# /
pariharati- #bhedapratīteriti# /
na tadadhīnotpādatāṃ tadadhīnatvamācakṣmahe kintu tadākāratāṃ, tathā ca na vyabhicāra ityarthaḥ /
śaṅkate- #guṇānāṃ dravyādhīnatvaṃ dravyaguṇayorayutasiddatvāditi yadyucyeta# /
yatra hi dvāvākāriṇau vibhinnābhyāmākārābhyāmavagamyate tau saṃbaddhāsaṃbaddhau vā vaiyadhikaraṇyena pratibhāsete,yatheha kuṇḍe dadhi yathā vā gauraśva iti, na tathā guṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyāḥ, teṣāṃ dravyakāratayākārāntarāyogena dravyādākāriṇo 'nyatvenākāritayā vyavasthānābhāvāt seyamayutasiddhiḥ /
tathā ca sāmānādhikaraṇyena prathetyarthaḥ /
tāmimāmayutasiddhiṃ vakalpya dūṣayati--
body.translated_text:
If, for existing atoms that have observable gross products, the non-apprehension of their cause through perception constitutes <s>avidyā</s> (non-cognition), and from that [non-cognition] their eternality [is inferred], then in that case, the <s>dyaṇuka</s> (binary atom) too would be eternal [since its cause — the single atom — is also imperceptible].
'But if [the argument] is specified as: provided it is not a [composite] substance' (<s>athādravyatve sati</s>) — then there is no deviation in the case of the <s>dyaṇuka</s>, since the <s>dyaṇuka</s>, being composed of multiple substances, does not have the property of 'being a non-substance whose cause is unknown.'
'Even so, it would amount to the very reason being "the absence of a cause" as the ground for eternality' — because 'non-substancehood' (<s>adravyatva</s>) is said to be [equivalent to] the absence of a substance serving as its cause. And thus, there would be redundancy — so [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'And of that' (<s>tasya ca</s>).
Moreover, if from non-substancehood together with existence, the desired conclusion is already established, then [the argument from] <s>avidyā</s> is superfluous.
Alternatively, if by the word <s>avidyā</s> what is meant is the absence of both types of causes that destroy a substance — for there are two kinds of causes that destroy a substance: the destruction of parts and the destruction of the conjunction of parts, and neither of these exists in the atom, hence the atom is eternal —
and there is no deviation with respect to pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and the like [which also lack parts], since they are non-substances — so [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: 'But even so' (<s>athāpi</s>).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: 'Not necessarily' (<s>nāvaśyam</s>).
If the procedure were that many substances, accompanied by conjunction, produce another substance, then indeed substance-duality alone would be the cause of its destruction.
But this is not so, because the true nature of substance is not [correctly] understood [by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s].
For there is no entity called 'cloth' (<s>paṭa</s>) that is different from and located in the threads — which is supposedly produced by threads accompanied by conjunction — this has been stated above. [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] will further refute [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system] while criticizing the six categories (<s>ṣaṭpadārtha</s>).
Rather, the cause itself, 'undergoing a different state characterized by particularity,' is the effect — and that [effect] has a universal nature (<s>sāmānyātmaka</s>).
Thus: clay or gold, pervading all pots, armlets, and the like, is experienced as a universal [substrate].
And these pots, armlets, and the like are not different from clay and gold — this has been stated.
And we shall state it further.
Therefore, it is clay and gold themselves that, transforming in this way and that, are explained as 'pot,' 'armlet,' 'potsherd,' 'gravel,' 'granule,' and 'shard,' 'particle,' 'powder' — because in each case the material cause — clay or gold — is recognized [as persisting].
But pots and the like are not recognized in potsherds and the like, nor potsherds and the like in pots and the like, nor armlets and the like in shards and the like, nor shards and the like in armlets and the like — where a cause-effect relation [between them] could be posited.
Nor should it be said that the pot-state, while perishing, gives rise to the potsherd-state without [the latter] being a [genuine causal] product — 'then what need is there of the recognition of the material cause?' — because this very <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> (destruction-based) procedure will be refuted further on.
Therefore, the particular states (<s>viśeṣāvasthā</s>s) — characterized by origination and dissolution — are to be accepted as [modes] of the universal [substrate], while the universal-natured [substrate] itself is the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>).
This being established: just as gold, the substance, abandoning the state of hardness and entering the state of fluidity, is enumerated [as the same substance] — and there, the separation of parts, though present, is not the cause of fluidity; since according to the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view, because of the absence of [parts in atoms], fluidity would be impossible for atoms — therefore, just as [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> themselves must account for fluidity without part-separation], so too qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) and the like are not determinable independently of substance and the like; rather, whenever they are determined, they shine forth as having the very form of that [substance], but they have no independence in their manifestation. Therefore, they are not different from substance; rather, substance in its universal form manifests in this way and that — this is the meaning.
[The opponent] objects, conceiving that the dependence of qualities and the like on substance consists merely in being products of substance: 'But is it not the case that even the other [i.e., substance] too' (<s>nanu agrere anyasyāpi</s>).
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: 'Because of the cognition of difference' (<s>bhedapratīteḥ</s>).
We do not declare [their] dependence [to mean] dependence in origination upon that [substance], but rather [their] having the form of that [substance] — and thus there is no deviation [from our position] — this is the meaning.
[The opponent] objects: 'If it is said that the dependence of qualities on substance is due to the inseparable inherence (<s>ayutasiddhatva</s>) of substance and quality' (<s>guṇānāṃ dravyādhīnatvaṃ dravyaguṇayor ayutasiddhatvāt</s>).
For wherever two entities possessing form are cognized through two different forms, they appear as either related or unrelated, through occupying different substrata — as in 'curds in a pot' or 'a white horse.' But qualities, actions, universals, particularities, and <s>samavāya</s> are not [cognized] in this way, since — being of the form of substance — they cannot be established as 'other' through any form other than the form of substance. This is the inseparable inherence (<s>ayutasiddhi</s>).
And thus the meaning is: [they] manifest through co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>).
Having conceived this inseparable inherence, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes —

body.text:
#tatpunarayutasiddhatvamiti# /
tatrāpṛthagdeśatvaṃ tadabhyupagamena virudhyata ityāha-- #apṛthagdeśatva iti# /
yadi tu saṃyoginoḥ kāryayoḥ saṃbandhibhyāmanyadeśatve yutasiddhistato 'nyāyutasiddhiḥ, nityayostu saṃyoginordvayoranyatarasya vā pṛthaggatimattvaṃ yutasiddhistato 'nyāyutasiddhiḥ, tathā cākāśaparamāṇvoḥ paramāṇvośca saṃyuktayoryutasiddhiḥ siddhā bhavati /
guṇaguṇinośca śauklyapaṭayorayutasiddhiḥ siddhā bhavati /
nahi tatra śauklyapaṭābhyāṃ saṃbandhibhyāmanyadeśau śauklyapaṭau /
satyapi paṭasya tadanyatantudeśatve śauklyasya saṃbandhipaṭadeśatvāt /
tanna /
nityayorātmākāśayorajasaṃyoge ubhayasyā api yutasiddherabhāvāt /
na hi tayoḥ pṛthagāśrayāśritatvamanāśrayatvāt /
nāpi dvayoranyatarasya vā pṛthaggatimatvamamūrtatvenobhayorapi niṣkriyatvāt /
na cājasaṃyogo nāsti tasyānumānasiddhatvāt /
tathāhi -- ākāśamātmasaṃyogi, mūrtadravyasaṅgitvāt, ghaṭādivadityanumānam /
pṛthagāśrayāśrayitvapṛthaggatimatvalakṣaṇayutasiddheranyā tvayutasiddhiryadyapi nābhyupetavirodhamāvahati tathāpi na sāmānādhikaraṇyaprathāmupapādayitumarhati /
evaṃ lakṣaṇe 'pi hi samavāye guṇaguṇinorabhyupagamyamāne saṃbaddhe iti pratyayaḥ syānna tādātmyapratyayaḥ /
asya copapādanāya samavāya āsthīyate bhavadbhiḥ /
sa cedāsthito 'pi na pratyayamimamupapādayet kṛtaṃ tatkalpanayā /
na ca pratyakṣaḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyapratyayaḥ samavāyagocaraḥ,tadviruddhārthatvāt /
tadgocaratve hi paṭe śukla ityevamākaraḥ syānna tu paṭaḥ śukla iti /
naca śuklapadasya guṇaviśiṣṭaguṇiparatvādevaṃ pratheti sāṃpratam /
nahi śabdavṛttyanusāri pratyakṣam /
nahyagnirmāṇavaka ityupacaritāgnibhāvo māṇavakaḥ pratyakṣeṇa dahanātmanā prathate /
na cāyamabhedabibhramaḥ samavāyanibandhano bhinnayorapīti vācyam, guṇādisadbhāve tadbhede ca pratyakṣānubhavādanyasya pramāṇasyābhāvāttasya ca bhrāntatve sarvābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
tadāśrayasya tu bhedasādhanasya tadviruddhayotthānāsaṃbhavāt /
tadidamuktam-- #tasya tādātmyenaiva pratīyamānatvāditi# /
body.translated_text:
'#That again [is the notion of] <s>ayutasiddhatva</s> (inseparable co-existence)#.'
Therein, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says that non-separation-of-locus (<s>apṛthagdeśatva</s>) contradicts their own accepted position: '#Non-separation of locus#.'
If, for two things related by conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), when the effects [are said to be] in a different locus from their relata, that constitutes <s>yutasiddhi</s> (separable co-existence), and the opposite is <s>ayutasiddhi</s> (inseparable co-existence); and for two permanent (<s>nitya</s>) things related by conjunction, the capacity of both or either to move independently constitutes <s>yutasiddhi</s>, and the opposite <s>ayutasiddhi</s> — then, the <s>yutasiddhi</s> of space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and atoms, and of atoms mutually conjoined, is established.
And the <s>ayutasiddhi</s> of quality and qualified — whiteness and cloth — is established.
For therein, whiteness and cloth [as] relata are not in a locus different from whiteness and cloth.
Even though the cloth may be in the locus of [its] other [constituent] threads, whiteness is in the locus of the cloth with which it is related.
That [objection] is not [valid].
Because, in the case of the permanent [entities] Self (<s>Ātman</s>) and space (<s>ākāśa</s>) — which are in beginningless conjunction — the <s>yutasiddhi</s> of both is absent.
For there is no separation of substratum and dependent for these two, since they have no substratum.
Nor is there independent motion of both or either, since both are actionless due to being non-corporeal.
Nor can it be said that [their] beginningless conjunction does not exist, since it is established by inference.
Thus: 'Space is conjoined with the Self, because of being in contact with corporeal substances — like a pot' — this is the inference.
Even though a different <s>ayutasiddhi</s> — other than [that defined by] the characteristic of 'having a separate substratum-dependent relationship and separate independent motion' — does not bring about contradiction with what is accepted [by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s], still, it is not able to account for the co-referential cognition (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya-prathā</s>).
For even with <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) defined thus, when the relation of quality and qualified is accepted, the cognition would be 'these are related' — not a cognition of identity (<s>tādātmya</s>).
And it is for accounting for this [identity-cognition] that <s>samavāya</s> is resorted to by you.
And if, even when resorted to, it cannot account for this cognition — then the postulation of it is futile.
Nor is the perceptual co-referential cognition (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya pratyaya</s>) an apprehension of <s>samavāya</s> — because it has a contrary meaning.
For if it were an apprehension of <s>samavāya</s>, the cognition would take the form 'whiteness is in the cloth' — not 'the cloth is white.'
Nor is it correct [to say] that the word 'white' (<s>śukla</s>) conveys [the meaning of] 'a qualified thing possessing a quality' and hence [the cognition] occurs thus — that is not right.
For perception does not follow verbal convention.
For the boy designated as 'fire' in 'The boy is fire' is not apprehended in perception as having the nature of burning.
Nor should it be said that this [co-referential cognition] is a delusion of non-difference, grounded in <s>samavāya</s>, even of things that are [actually] different — because from the perceptual experience of the existence and the difference of qualities and the like, there is no other [valid] means of knowledge [for establishing difference]; and if that [perception] were erroneous, there would be the consequence of the non-existence of everything.
And because the evidence for difference — which depends on that [perceptual experience] — cannot [itself] give rise to what contradicts [its own basis].
This is what was stated: '#Because of its being perceived as identical [with its substrate]#.'

body.text:
api cāyutasiddhaśabdo 'pṛthagutpattau mukhyaḥ, sā ca bhavanmate na dravyaguṇayorasti, dravyasya prāksiddherguṇasya ca paścādutpatteḥ, tasmānmithyāvādo 'yamityāha-- #yutasiddhayoriti# /
atha bhavatu kāraṇasya yutasiddhiḥ, kāryasya tvayutasiddhi kāraṇātirekeṇābhāvādityāśaṅkyānyathā dūṣayati-- #evamapīti# /
saṃbandhidvayādhīnasadbhāvo hi saṃbandho nāsatyekasminnapi saṃbandhini bhavitumarhati /
naca samavāyo nityaḥ svatantra iti coktamadhastāt /
naca kāraṇasamavāyādananyā kāryasyotpattiriti śakyaṃ vaktum, evaṃ hi sati samavāyasya nityatvābhyupagamāt kāraṇavaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ /

body.translated_text:
Moreover, the word '<s>ayutasiddha</s>' (inseparably co-existent) has its primary meaning in [the sense of] co-origination (<s>apṛthagutpatti</s>); and that [co-origination], in your view, does not exist between substance and quality — since substance exists first and quality originates afterwards — hence this [claim of <s>ayutasiddhi</s>] is a false statement — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Of things that are <s>yutasiddha</s> (separately established)#.'
Now, let there be <s>yutasiddhi</s> of the cause — but the effect [has] <s>ayutasiddhi</s>, since it does not exist apart from the cause — having anticipated this objection, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes it differently: '#Even so#.'
For a relation, whose existence depends on both relata, cannot exist when even one of the relata is absent.
And it has been said earlier that <s>samavāya</s> is not eternal and independent.
Nor can it be said that the origination of the effect is non-different from the <s>samavāya</s> of the cause — for if so, since <s>samavāya</s> is accepted as eternal, the consequence would be the purposelessness of the cause.
And if origination [involves] a <s>samavāya</s> [between effect and cause], that very [origination] suffices for the effect — what is the need for <s>samavāya</s>?
But in the relation of [two] already-established [entities], there would be the consequence of <s>yutasiddhi</s>.
And a different <s>ayutasiddhi</s> is not possible — this has been said.
And thus, what was said by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s — that because of the absence of <s>yutasiddhi</s>,
'#there is no conjunction or disjunction between cause and effect#' — that would be a bad statement.
Because of the very absence of <s>yutasiddhi</s> [being unfounded].
By this, the definition '<s>yutasiddhi</s> is [the condition of] non-contact and conjunction' is also shown to be untenable.
Let there be no non-contact between cause and effect — but why can their contact (<s>prāpti</s>) not be [a form of] conjunction? For the <s>ayutasiddhi</s> [that would distinguish their relation] from conjunction must then be stated.
And thus, let that very [<s>ayutasiddhi</s>] be stated — what is the use of this [definition] that is afflicted by the defect of circular dependence (<s>paramparāśraya</s>)?
And another [<s>ayutasiddhi</s>] is not possible — this has been said.
If it be said: contact (<s>prāpti</s>) preceded by non-contact (<s>aprāpti</s>), [and which is] produced by the action of one or both [entities], is conjunction — as in [the conjunction] of a post and a hawk, or of two wrestlers —
but the relation of threads and cloth is not like that, since the cloth is related to the threads from the very moment of its origination —
hence this is <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) alone — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#And just as of the newly originated#.'
For conjunction produced by [another] conjunction too is accepted by you — not only [that produced] by action — this is the meaning.
Nor is it [the case that only] contact preceded by non-contact is conjunction — because in the eternal conjunction of Self and space, that [non-contact] is absent; and because, in the case of the effect at the very first moment of its origination, there is the absence of prior contact with the cause.
Moreover, when a relation distinct from the form of the relata is established, one would seek a definitional distinction for the sub-types within it — but that very relation, distinct from the relata, is not established. For it has been said above: a relation distinct from the relata cannot, being unrelated [to them], unite the relata.
And in the relation-of-the-relation, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, by both reasoning and experience, the effect is not different from the cause; rather, this is an inexpressible (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) modification-difference of the cause itself.
Therefore, since the effect is non-different from the cause — what is related to what? And since conjunction is non-different from the conjoined [entities] — what is their conjunction? — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Nor of conjunction#.'
Without considering the inexpressibility of this [relation], [the opponent] objects: '#That is, apart from the words and cognitions of the relata#.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: '#No. Even in oneness, with reference to the extrinsic forms of the essential nature#.'
With reference to the inexpressible manifold specific states and distinctions — even in a single [entity], the possibility of diverse cognitions and designations [is established].
Just as the one <s>Devadatta</s>, with reference to his own intrinsic distinctions, is a human being, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, fair-complexioned; with reference to his own state-distinctions, [he is] a child, a youth, an old man; with reference to distinctions of his own activities, [he is] a <s>Vedic</s> scholar; and with reference to others, [he is] a father, a son, a grandson, a brother, a son-in-law.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] gives another illustration: '#Just as, even though being a single line#.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] applies [it] to the illustrated case: '#So too, of the relata#.'
The non-intermediacy of [two] fingers is conjunction; the lower-and-upper-ness of curd and pot is conjunction.
But of cause and effect, even though there is identity (<s>tādātmya</s>), when the difference of the inexpressible effect is intended, '#relata#' is said.
'#Nor, when the relata are the objects [of the words and cognitions]#' — this too has the intent of the inexpressible difference.
Moreover, [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s] accept that the first action of atoms and mind arises from the conjunction of the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (field-knower/self) — [motivated by] <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit).
'The upward flaming of fire, the lateral blowing of wind, and the first action of atoms and mind — these are caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>' — thus the statement.
But the conjunction of atoms and mind with the Self, which is partless (<s>apradeśa</s>), is not possible.
And if it were possible — then, since atoms and mind pervade the Self, there would be the consequence of [their being] maximally large and hence not atomic.
Nor is [the conjunction] of atoms and mind with the Self [by means of] a part-based relation (<s>pradeśavṛtti</s>) — because the Self is partless; and because the postulation [of parts in the Self] cannot establish the reality of the thing, and because of over-extension — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Likewise, of atoms, the Self, and mind#.'
'#Something else#' — from two atoms that are causes, the contact (<s>saṃśleṣa</s>) of the composite effect — the dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>) — '#with space, is untenable — like [the case of space itself]#.'
Contact (<s>saṃśleṣa</s>) is grasping together — such that when one relatum is pulled, the other relatum is also pulled — [and] its untenability [is asserted].
For this very reason, another [relation] — '#the substratum-dependent relationship (<s>āśrayāśritabhāva</s>) of cause and effect substances — is otherwise#'

'#untenable; hence <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) must necessarily be postulated — if this be said#' —
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: '#No.'
Why?
'#Because of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśrayatva</s>)#.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] elaborates this: '#For of cause and effect#.'
'#Something else: Of atoms#.'
'#Those that are delimited are composite, like pots and the like.
Similarly atoms [are delimited]; therefore they would be composite and impermanent.#'
If [they are] undelimited, then like space and the like, there would be the undermining of their atomicity — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises the doubt: '#What you [hold]#.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes: '#No. Because of grossness#.'
Is it that atoms do not perish because of subtlety, or because of partlessness? — regarding the former alternative, this was said: '#Even though being a real thing#.'
Anticipating [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>'s] response to the latter alternative and refuting it: '#Even though perishing, by the division of parts#.'
'#For just as of ghee, gold, and the like — whose parts are not [actually] separated#' —
Just as a ball of dough — without the destruction of the conjunction of its parts — [merely] expands,

children.text: prathamānaścāśvaśaphākāratāṃ nīyamānaḥ puroḍāśatāmāpadyate,tatra piṇḍo naśyati puroḍāśaścotpadyate, nahi tatra piṇḍāvayavasaṃyogā vinaśyanti,api tu saṃyuktā eva santaḥ paraṃ prathanena nudyamānā adhikadeśavyāpakā bhavanti, evamagnisaṃyogena suvarṇadravyāvayavāḥ saṃyuktā eva santo dravībhāvamāpadyante, natu mitho vibhajyante /
children.translated_text: and [the ball], while expanding, being shaped into the form of a horse-hoof, attains the form of a <s>puroḍāśa</s> (sacrificial offering-cake) — therein, the ball perishes and the <s>puroḍāśa</s> arises; for the conjunctions of the parts of the ball are not destroyed there — rather, the parts, while remaining conjoined, being pushed by expansion, come to pervade a greater extent of space. Similarly, the parts of the gold substance, being conjoined, attain liquidity through conjunction with fire — they are not mutually separated.

children.text: tasmādyathāvayavasaṃyogavināśāvantareṇāpi suvarṇapiṇḍo vinaśyati, saṃyogāntarotpādamantareṇa ca suvarṇe drava upajāyate, evamantareṇāpyavayavasaṃyogavināśaṃ paramāṇavo vinaṅkṣyantyanye cotpatsyanta iti sarvamavadātam //17 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as the gold-ball perishes without the destruction of the conjunction of [its] parts, and liquidity arises in the gold without the production of a new conjunction — so too, atoms will perish without the destruction of the conjunction of [their] parts, and others will arise — thus everything is clear. //17//

children.translated_text: Those of middling [intellect] — through [the doctrine of] the existence of consciousness alone — are led into voidness.

children.text: ye tu prakṛṣṭamatayastebhyaḥ sākṣādeva śūnyatātattvaṃ pratipādyate /
children.translated_text: But those of superior intellect — to them the reality of voidness (<s>śūnyatā-tattva</s>) is directly taught.
As stated in the <s>Bodhicittavivaraṇa</s>: 'The teachings of the Lords of the World (<s>Lokanātha</s>s) follow the dispositions of beings.'
The worlds are divided in many ways, and again by many methods. //1//

body.translated_text:
'#The aggregate (<s>samudāya</s>), even though having both as its cause, [is such that] there is no attainment of that [purpose]#.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the sub-connection: '#The established conclusion of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>#.'
The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s are indeed half-annihilationists (<s>ardhavaināśika</s>).
For they, having accepted the permanence of atoms, space, directions, time, self, and mind, as well as [the permanence] of the universals (<s>sāmānya</s>), particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>), <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), and certain qualities — accept the traceless annihilation of the remainder. Hence they are half-annihilationists.
Therefore, the presentation of [the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system] — through its similarity with [full] annihilationism — reminds [us] of the complete annihilationists, and hence the refutation of the annihilationist doctrine [follows] immediately after — this is [the connection].
The aggregate-origination (<s>samudāyārambha</s>) would be tenable for the half-annihilationists who hold the doctrine of enduring entities; but for the momentarists (<s>kṣaṇikabhāvavādin</s>s), it is far removed — this we shall demonstrate.
Hence '#all the more so#' is said.
In order to present the annihilationist doctrine for refutation, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states its varieties: '#And that is of many kinds#.'
Due to the diversity of proponents: some accept the established conclusion of the existence of everything (<s>sarvāstitva</s>); some, the existence of consciousness alone (<s>jñānamātrāstitva</s>).
Some [accept] the complete voidness of everything (<s>sarvaśūnyatā</s>).
But [one might say:] among all your omniscient ones, a difference in the apprehension of reality is not possible — because reality has a uniform nature — expressing dissatisfaction with this, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Or, because of the difference of those to be instructed (<s>vineya</s>)#.'
For the disciples are of inferior, middling, and superior intellects.
Therein, those of inferior intellect — through the doctrine of the existence of everything, in conformity with their disposition — are led into [the truth of] voidness (<s>śūnyatā</s>).

children.translated_text: With the distinction of profound and shallow, and sometimes characterized by both,
though divided, the teaching is undivided — characterized by the twofold <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness). //2//

body.translated_text:
Thus.
Although there is an internal doctrinal difference between the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>s and the <s>Sautrāntika</s>s, nevertheless — since there is agreement [between them] regarding the doctrine of 'everything exists' (<s>sarvāstitā</s>) — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] presents them as one.
And thus the number three [i.e., three Buddhist schools] is justified.
Earth is of the nature of hardness; water is of the nature of viscosity; fire is of the nature of heat; air is of the nature of propulsion.
<s>Īraṇa</s> (propulsion) means impelling.
Having mentioned the <s>bhūta</s>s (elements) and the <s>bhautika</s>s (derivatives), he states the <s>citta</s> (mind) and <s>caittika</s>s (mental factors): '#Thus, <s>rūpa</s>#' (<s>tathā rūpeti</s>).
By the etymologies 'they are formed (<s>rūpyante</s>) by these' and 'they form (<s>rūpyante</s>),' the sense-organs together with their objects constitute the <s>rūpa-skandha</s> (aggregate of form).
Although the things being formed — earth and the like — are external, nevertheless they become internal (<s>ādhyātmika</s>) either because of being located in the body or because of [their] connection with the sense-organs.
The <s>vijñāna-skandha</s> (aggregate of consciousness) is the cognition having the form 'I,' or having form and the like as its objects, or born from the sense-organs and the like — [which is] being illustrated.
The <s>vedanā-skandha</s> (aggregate of feeling) is that special state of the mind that arises upon contact with objects that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neither — [namely,] the specific states of pleasure, pain, and [that which is] free from both.
The <s>saṃjñā-skandha</s> (aggregate of perception) is determinate cognition (<s>savikalpapratyaya</s>), the appearance fit for association with a name — such as '<s>Ḍittha</s>, wearing earrings, fair-complexioned, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, is going' — of this sort.
The <s>saṃskāra-skandha</s> (aggregate of volitional formations) consists of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>s) such as passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the like, the secondary afflictions (<s>upakleśa</s>s) such as pride (<s>mada</s>), conceit (<s>māna</s>), and the like, and merit (<s>dharma</s>) and demerit (<s>adharma</s>).
Thus, the aggregate (<s>samudāya</s>) of these is the <s>pañcaskandhī</s> (five aggregates).
'#In that [aggregate], though caused by both [sets of factors]#.'
In the external aggregate of elements and their derivatives caused by dyads (<s>dvyaṇu</s>) of earth and the like, and in the internal aggregate caused by the aggregates of form, consciousness, and the like — when this [aggregate] is being referred to — its non-attainment, i.e., the unjustifiability of that aggregate, [is shown].
'#Why?
Because the constituents (<s>samudāyin</s>s) are non-conscious#.'
For a conscious [agent] such as a potter and the like, having gathered together clay, staff, and the like, is observed to fashion a pot that is of the nature of an aggregate.
For without a knowledgeable potter who operates the clay, staff, and the like, the non-conscious clay, staff, and the like never operate on their own to fashion a pot.
Nor, without a weaver, do the threads, shuttle, and the like weave a cloth.
Therefore, the production of an effect depends on the appropriate arrangement of causes conforming to [that effect] — in the absence of that [arrangement], it does not occur.

children.translated_text: Otherwise, the [relation of] causality and basis-hood would be untenable.
And between [two entities that are] simultaneous, there is no cause-and-effect relationship.
Nor between [two entities of] different times is there a container-contained relationship.
And thus there would be the abandonment of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) — he says: '#Because of the acceptance of momentariness#.' //18//

body.translated_text:
And the arrangement of causes conforming to the production of an effect depends on the oversight of a conscious [agent] — in the absence of conscious oversight, it cannot occur. Thus, the production of effects — being pervaded by dependence on conscious oversight — by the logical argument of the perception of what contradicts the pervasion (<s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s>), turning away from causes that are not superintended by a conscious [agent], settles upon [causes that are] superintended by a conscious [agent] — thus the invariable concomitance (<s>pratibandha</s>) is established.
If it be said: 'Indeed, the production of effects depends on a conscious [agent], and there does exist <s>citta</s> (mind) which is conscious — that, upon the contact of the sense-organs and the like with their objects, blazing forth, illuminates the causal nexus as suitable for [producing] the effect in whatever way [is needed], and superintending the non-conscious causes, brings about the effect' — to that he says: '#And because the blazing forth of <s>citta</s> (mind) depends on the establishment of the aggregate#.'
For without the prior establishment of the external and internal aggregate, there is no blazing forth of <s>citta</s> — and one who desires that [blazing forth] would encounter the irresolvable fault of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>).
Nor does the blazing forth of <s>citta</s> from a previous birth assemble the subsequent aggregate.
Because at the time of assembly, that [previous blazing forth], having long since passed away, lacks the capacity [to act].
[This is] just as in our own established view — '#because of the non-acceptance of another conscious experiencer or ruler who is stable and is the maker of the aggregate#.'
For a maker who is knowledgeable about the different arrangements of causes is [necessary].
And he cannot know the different arrangements without [the method of] positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>).
And one who is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) — unable to endure for the time [required to perform] positive and negative concomitance — cannot know [those methods].
Hence it was said: '#of a stable [one]#.'
If it be said: 'The causes, without being arranged [by a conscious agent], will produce the effect by themselves, independent of one another — there is no need for a conscious [agent] to arrange them' — to this he says: '#And in the acceptance of activity without dependence [on a conscious agent]#.'
If it be said: 'There exists the <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness), which is the locus of the ego-sense and which connects the earlier and later [moments]; that very [<s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>] will be the assembler of the causes' — to that he says: '#Of the <s>āśaya</s> (repository/storehouse) too#.'
If indeed that one [<s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>] is accepted as stable, then by another name it is simply the <s>ātman</s> (self).
But if it is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), then the stated fault applies.
And if [one resorts to] its continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>) — if that [continuum] is different [from the <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>], then by another name the <s>ātman</s> is accepted; and if it is not different, then it is simply <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) — and that too is momentary — hence the stated fault applies.
The <s>karmānubhava-vāsanā</s>s (latent impressions of the experience of <s>karma</s>) rest (<s>āśerate</s>) in it — hence it is the '<s>āśaya</s>' (repository), i.e., the <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> — of that [<s>āśaya</s>].
Moreover, <s>pravṛtti</s> (activity) is the operation of the constituents (<s>samudāyin</s>s).
And the operation of momentary [entities] is not tenable.
For operation is well-known in the world as having a basis (<s>āśraya</s>) for the operation and having a cause for it.
Therefore, the one that possesses operation must exist both before the operation and at the time of the operation.

'#If [it be said that there is] mutual causation (<s>itaretarapratyayatva</s>) — no, because [each is] a mere occasion (<s>nimitta</s>) for the arising [of the other]#.'
'#Even if#' (<s>yadyapi</s>).
The meaning is this: In brief, the characteristic of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination) has been stated by the <s>Buddha</s>: 'This is the effect of that condition.'
'Whether <s>Tathāgata</s>s arise or do not arise, this nature of <s>dharma</s>s (phenomena) is established —'
'the stability of <s>dharma</s>s, the regularity of <s>dharma</s>s, the conformity to dependent origination.'
Now, this <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination) arises from two kinds of causes — from the binding of the <s>hetu</s> (root cause) and from the binding of the <s>pratyaya</s> (condition).
And it is of two kinds — external and internal.
Therein, the <s>hetu</s>-binding (root-cause binding) of the external <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> is as follows: from the seed arises the sprout; from the sprout, the leaf; from the leaf, the stalk; from the stalk, the stem; from the stem, the bud; from the bud, the husk; from the husk, the flower; from the flower, the fruit.
When there is no seed, the sprout does not arise — and so on until — when there is no flower, the fruit does not arise.
But when there is a seed, the sprout arises — and so on until — when there is a flower, the fruit [arises].
Therein, the seed does not have the cognition: 'I produce the sprout.'
Nor does the sprout have the cognition: 'I was produced by the seed.'
Similarly, up to: the flower does not have [the cognition]: 'I produce the fruit.'
Similarly, the fruit too does not have [the cognition]: 'I was produced by the flower.'
Therefore, even without the consciousness of the seed and the like, and without any other superintendent, the regularity of cause-and-effect is observed.
The <s>hetu</s>-binding has been stated.
The <s>pratyaya</s>-binding (condition-binding) of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> is now stated.
A <s>pratyaya</s> (condition) is the concurrence (<s>samavāya</s>) of [multiple] causes.
Each cause serves as the condition for the other causes — [and] the coming together of those [causes] is the <s>pratyaya</s> (condition),
i.e., concurrence.
Thus, from the concurrence of six elements (<s>dhātu</s>s), the sprout — whose root cause is the seed — is born.
And therein, the earth-element performs the function of holding the seed together, because of which the sprout becomes firm; the water-element moistens the seed; the fire-element ripens the seed; the air-element draws the seed out, because of which the sprout emerges from the seed; the space-element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed; and the season (<s>ṛtu</s>) too brings about the transformation of the seed. Thus, when these elements are complete in their concurrence, the sprout grows in the seed and is born — not otherwise.
Therein, the earth-element does not have [the cognition]: 'I perform the function of holding the seed together' — and so on until — the season does not have [the cognition]: 'I bring about the transformation of the seed.'
Nor does the sprout have [the cognition]: 'I was produced by these conditions.'
Similarly, the internal <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> arises from two kinds of causes — from the <s>hetu</s>-binding and from the <s>pratyaya</s>-binding.
Therein, the <s>hetu</s>-binding of the internal [<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>] is as follows: conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are the <s>saṃskāra</s>s (volitional formations) — and so on until — conditioned by birth, old age, death, and the like arise.
Therein, <s>avidyā</s> does not have [the cognition]: 'I produce the <s>saṃskāra</s>s.'
Nor do the <s>saṃskāra</s>s have [the cognition]: 'We were produced by <s>avidyā</s>.'
Similarly, up to: birth does not have [the cognition]: 'I produce old age, death, and the like.'
Nor do old age, death, and the like have [the cognition]: 'We were produced by birth and the like.'
And yet, when <s>avidyā</s> and the like exist — themselves non-conscious and not superintended by another conscious [agent] — the arising of <s>saṃskāra</s>s and the like [occurs], just as when seeds and the like exist — non-conscious and not superintended by another conscious [agent] — [the arising of] sprouts and the like [occurs].
'Depending on this, this arises' — only this much has been observed, [while] the superintendence of a conscious [agent] has not been perceived.
This is the <s>hetu</s>-binding of the internal <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.
Now the <s>pratyaya</s>-binding: from the concurrence of the elements — earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) — the body comes into being.
Therein, the earth-element produces the hardness of the body.
The water-element moistens the body.
The fire-element digests what is eaten and drunk by the body.
The air-element produces the breathing and the like of the body.
The space-element produces the hollowness within the body.
And that which produces the sprout of name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>), which is connected with the activity of the five consciousnesses and which is the impure (<s>sāsrava</s>) mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) — that is called the <s>vijñāna-dhātu</s> (consciousness-element).
When the internal elements — earth and the like — are complete, then from the concurrence of all, the arising of the body occurs.
Therein, the earth-element and the like do not have [the cognition]: 'We produce the hardness and the like of the body.'
Nor does the body have the cognition: 'I was produced by these conditions.'
And yet, from the elements — earth and the like — which are non-conscious and not superintended by another conscious [agent], the body arises, just like a sprout.
This <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), being observed, should not be otherwise explained.
Therein, in these very six elements (<s>dhātu</s>s), the notion of a single [entity], the notion of a mass, the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure —

na ca cetanamantareṇānyaḥ saṃnidhāpayitāsmi kāraṇānāmityuktam /
bījādaṅkurotpatterapi pratyayopanibaddhāyā vivādādhyāsitatvena pakṣanikṣiptatvāt, pakṣeṇa ca vyabhicārodbhāvanāyāmatiprasaṅgena sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅgāt /
syādetat /
anapekṣā evāntyakṣaṇaprāptāḥ kṣityādayo 'ṅkuramārabhante /
teṣāṃ tūpasarpaṇapratyayavaśātparasparasamavadhānam /
na caikasmādeva kāraṇātkāryasiddheḥ kimanyaiḥ kāraṇairiti vācyam /
kāraṇacakrānantaraṃ kāryotpādāt siddhamityeva nāsti /
na caiko 'pitatkāraṇasamarthaṃ ityanya udāsata iti yuktam /
nahi te prekṣāvanto yenaisamālocayeyurasmāsu samartha eko 'pi kārye iti kṛtaṃ naḥ saṃnidhineti /
kintūpasarpaṇapratyayādhīnaparasparasaṃnidhānotpādā nānutpattuṃ nāpyasaṃnidhātumīśate /
tāṃśca sarvananapekṣān pratītya kāryamapi na netpattumarhati /
naca svamahimnā sarve kāryamutpādayanto 'pi nānākāryāṇāmīsate tatraiva teṣāṃ sāmarthyāt /
na ca kāraṇabhedāt kāryabhedaḥ, sāmagryā ekatvāt /
tadbhedasya ca kāryānānātvahetutvāttathā darśanāt /
tanna /
yadyantyakṣaṇaprāptā anapekṣāḥ svakāryopajanane, hantānena krameṇa tataḥ pūrve tataḥ pūrve sarva evānapekṣāstattatsvakāryopajanana iti kusūlasthatvāviśeṣe 'pi yena bījakṣaṇena kusūlasthena svakāryakṣaṇaparamparayāṅkurotpattisamartho bījakṣaṇo janayitavyaḥ so 'napekṣa eva bījakṣaṇaḥ svakāryopajanane evaṃ sarva eva tadantarānantapavartino bījakṣaṇa anapekṣā iti kusūlanihitabīja eva syāt kṛtī kṛṣīvalaḥ kṛtamasya duḥkhabahulena kṛṣikarmaṇā /
yena hi bījakṣaṇena svakṣaṇaparamparayāṅkuro janayitavyastasyānapekṣāsau kṣaṇaparamparā kusūla evāṅkuraṃ kariṣyatīti /
tasmātparasparāpekṣā evāntyā vā madhyā vā pūrve vā kṣaṇāḥ kāryopajanana iti vaktavyam /
yathāhuḥ-- 'na kiñcidekamekasmātsāmagryāḥ sarvasaṃbhavaḥ' iti /
taccedaṃ samavadhānaṃ kāraṇānāṃ vinyāsabhedatatprayojanābhijñaprekṣāvatpūrvakaṃ dṛṣṭamiti nācetanādbhavitumarhati /
tadidamuktam-- #bhavedupapannaḥ saṃghāto yadi saṃghātasya kiñcinnimittamavagamyeteti /
itaretarapratyayatve 'pīti# /
itaretarahetutve 'pītyarthaḥ /
uktamabhisaṃdhimavidvān paricodayati-- #nanvavidyādibhirarthādākṣīpyata iti# /
pariharati-- #atrocyate, yadi tāvaditi# /
kimākṣepa utpādanam,āho jñāpanam /
tatra na tāvat kāraṇamanyathānupapadyamānaṃ kāryamutpādayati, kintu svasāmarthyena /
tasmājjñāpanaṃ vaktavyam /
tathā ca jñāpitasyānyadutpādakaṃ vaktavyam /
.tacca sthirapakṣe 'pi satyapi ca bhoktaryaghiṣṭhātāraṃ cetanamantareṇa na saṃbhavati kimaṅga,punaḥ kṣaṇikeṣu bhāveṣu /
bhokturbhogenāpi kadācidākṣipyeta saṃghātaḥ,sa tu bhoktāpi nāstīti dūrotsāritatvaṃ darśayati-- #bhoktṛrahiteṣviti# /
api ca bahava upakāryopakārakabhāvena sthitāḥ kāryaṃ janayanti /
naca kṣaṇikapakṣa upakāryopakārakabhāvo 'sti,bhāvasyopakārānāspadatvāt /
kṣaṇasyābhedyatvādanupakṛtopakṛtatvāsaṃbhavāt /
kālabhedena vā tadupapattau kṣaṇikatvavyāghātāt /
tadidamāha-- #āśrayāśrayiśūnyeṣu ceti /
athāyamabhiprāya iti# /
yadā hi pratyayopanibandhaḥ pratītyasamutpādo bhavettadā cetano 'dhiṣṭhātāpekṣetāpi, na tu pratyayopanibandhane 'pi tu hetūpanibandhaḥ /
tathāca kṛtamadhiṣṭhātrā /
hetuḥ svabhāvata eva kāryasaṃghātaṃ kariṣyati kevala iti bhāvaḥ /
astu tāvadyathā kevalādhetoḥ kāryaṃ nopajāyata iti, anyonyāśrayaprasaṅgo 'smin pakṣa ityāśayavānāha- #- kathaṃ tameveti# /
saṃprati pratyayopanibandhanaṃ pratītyasamutpādamāstāya codayati-- #atha manyase saṃghātā eveti# /
asthirā api hi bhāvāḥ sadā saṃhatā evodayante vyante ca /
na punaratistato 'vasthitāḥ kenacit puñjīkriyante /
tathā ca kṛtamatra saṃhantrā cetaneneti bhāvaḥ /
#anādau#iti parasparāśrayaṃ nivartayati /
tadetadvikalpya dūṣayati-- #tathāpi saṃghātāditi# /
sa khalu saṃghātasaṃtativarti dharmādharmāhvayaḥ saṃskārasaṃtāno yathāyathaṃ sukhaduḥkhe janayannāgantukaṃ kañcanānāsādya svata eva janayet,āsādya vā /
anāsādyajanane sadaiva sukhaduḥkhe janayet, samarthasyānapekṣasyākṣepāyogāt /
āsādya janane tadāsādanakāraṇaṃ prekṣāvānabhyupeyaḥ /
tathāca na pratyayopanibandhanaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ /
tasmādanenāgatantukānapekṣasya saṃdhātasaṃtānasyaiva sadṛśajanane visadṛśajanane vā svabhāva āstheyaḥ /
tathā ca bhāṣyoktaṃ dūṣaṇamiti /
#api ca yadbhogārthaḥ saṃghātaḥ syāditi# /
aprāptabhogo hi bhogamāptukāmastatsādhane pravartata iti pratyātmasiddham /
seyaṃ pravṛttirbhogādanyasmin sthire bhoktari bhogatatsādhanasamayavyāpini kalpyate nāsthire /
naca bhogādananyasmin /
nahi bhogo bhogāya kalpate nāpyanyo bhogāyānyasya /
evaṃ mokṣe 'pi draṣṭavyam /
tatra bubhukṣumumukṣū cet sthirāvāsthīyeyātāṃ tadābhyupetahānam, asthairyā vā pravṛttiprasaṅga ityarthaḥ /
#na tu saṃghātaḥ sidhyedbhoktrabhāvāditi# /
bhoktrabhāvena pravṛttyanupapatteḥ kartrabhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: Consequently, because of the absence of action, the aggregate is not established — this is the meaning. //19//

body.translated_text:
[The Buddhist explains:] The notion of a being (<s>sattvasaṃjñā</s>), the notion of a person (<s>pudgalasaṃjñā</s>), the notion of a human (<s>manuṣyasaṃjñā</s>), the notions of mother and daughter (<s>mātṛduhitṛsaṃjñā</s>), the notions of 'I' and 'mine' (<s>ahaṅkāramamakārasaṃjñā</s>) — '#this <s>avidyā</s>#' (ignorance) is the root cause of the entire accumulation of <s>saṃsāric</s> misfortune. When that <s>avidyā</s> obtains, '#<s>saṃskāra</s>s#' (dispositions) — namely attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>) — operate toward objects.
Cognition directed toward a real object is '#<s>vijñāna</s>#' (consciousness). From consciousness arise the four material appropriation-aggregates (<s>upādānaskandha</s>s) — that is '<s>nāma</s>' (name). Having taken up those, form (<s>rūpa</s>) is produced.
Compressing both together, '#<s>nāmarūpa</s>#' (name-and-form) is defined — the stages of the body itself such as the embryonic mass (<s>kalala</s>), the bubble (<s>budbuda</s>), and the like. The sense-organs mixed with name-and-form are '#<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>#' (the six sense-bases). The convergence (<s>saṃnipāta</s>) of the three — name, form, and the sense-organs — is '#<s>sparśa</s>#' (contact). From contact arises '#<s>vedanā</s>#' (feeling) — of pleasure and the like. When feeling obtains, the determination 'This pleasure must be [attained]; let it be mine again' becomes '#<s>tṛṣṇā</s>#' (craving).
From that comes '#<s>upādāna</s>#' (clinging) — the activity of speech and body.
From that comes '#<s>bhava</s>#' (becoming) — since birth [arises] from this, '<s>bhava</s>' [means] <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit). The manifestation of the aggregates caused by that is '#<s>jāti</s>#' (birth).
Subsequent to birth as its cause are '#old age, death#' (<s>jarāmaraṇa</s>), and the rest.
The ripening of the born aggregates is '#old age#' (<s>jarā</s>).
The destruction of the aggregates is '#death#' (<s>maraṇa</s>).
The inner burning of one who is dying, deluded, and attached [to things such as] sons, wife, and the like is '#grief#' (<s>śoka</s>).
The lamentation arising from that — 'Alas, mother! Alas, father! Alas, my sons and wife!' — is '#wailing#' (<s>paridevanā</s>).
The experience of what is undesirable, conjoined with the effects of the five [types of sense-]consciousness, is '#suffering#' (<s>duḥkha</s>).
Mental suffering is '#dejection#' (<s>daurmanasya</s>).
Afflictions of this kind and their means are grasped [as the twelvefold chain].
These are mutually causal: <s>avidyā</s> and the rest are caused by birth and the rest, and birth and the rest are caused by <s>avidyā</s> and the rest — revolving ceaselessly like a water-wheel — thus 'by these — <s>avidyā</s> and the rest — the aggregate (#<s>saṃghāta</s>#) is projected.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes this: '##That is not so##.' Why? '##Because [the causes] are merely the occasions for origination##.'
The intent is this: An effect that is dependent on a [single] cause, requiring nothing else, since its origination depends on that cause alone — let it be produced.
But the aggregate of the five <s>skandha</s>s (aggregates) is dependent on conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>) — its origination does not depend on a single cause alone;
rather, it is born from the convergence of multiple causes.
And without a conscious [agent], no other [entity] can bring the causes into proximity — this has been stated.
Even the origination of a sprout from a seed, being dependent on conditions, is placed within the thesis [of the opponent] because it is the very subject of debate; and since raising a counter-example from the thesis itself, by over-application (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>), would lead to the destruction of all inference.
One might say this:
The [causes] such as earth and the like, having reached the final moment [of proximity] without depending on anything else, produce the sprout.
And their mutual convergence is due to the condition of approach (<s>upasarpaṇapratyaya</s>).
Nor should it be said: since the effect is accomplished from a single cause alone, what need is there for other causes?
For [the reply is:] since the effect arises immediately after the complete causal complex, this [objection] simply does not hold.
Nor is it reasonable [to say] that one [cause] alone is sufficient for that [effect], so the others stand aside.
For they are not intelligent beings who would deliberate: 'Since one among us is sufficient for the effect, we have no need to be present.'
Rather, since their mutual proximity arises under the control of the condition of approach, they can neither fail to arise nor fail to converge.
And since all [causes are present] without depending on anything [else], the effect too cannot fail to arise.
Nor can all [causes], even though each producing the effect by its own power, produce diverse effects — because of [each cause's] capacity being directed precisely there [toward the one effect].
Nor does the diversity of effects [arise] from the diversity of causes, since the causal complex (<s>sāmagrī</s>) is one.
And the diversity of that [complex] being the cause of the non-diversity of the effect, because it is so observed.
That is not so.
If [causes] that have reached the final moment, being independent, [produce] their own effect — well then, by this very reasoning, those prior to them, and those prior to those — all are equally independent in producing their respective effects. Thus, even when the seed is in the granary — there being no difference in its granary-status — the seed-moment that, through the chain of its own subsequent moments, is capable of producing a sprout, being independent, would produce a sprout in the granary itself. Likewise, all the infinitely succeeding seed-moments occurring between [the granary and the field] are independent [on this view]. Thus the farmer would have accomplished his purpose with the seed stored in the granary alone — what need has he for the laborious work of cultivation!
For that seed-moment whose chain of subsequent moments is to produce a sprout — that chain, being independent, will produce the sprout right there in the granary!
Therefore, it must be said that the moments — whether final, intermediate, or initial — are mutually dependent in producing the effect.
As they say: 'Nothing single [arises] from a single [cause]; everything arises from the totality [of conditions].'
And this convergence of causes is observed to be preceded by an intelligent being who knows the arrangement of [causes], their differences, and their purposes — hence it cannot arise from something insentient.
This is what was stated: '##The aggregate would be justified if some cause of the aggregate were apprehended.##
##Even if there is mutual causation##' — meaning: even if there is mutual causality.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>], unaware of the stated intent, raises an objection: '##But is it not the case that [the aggregate] is implicitly projected by <s>avidyā</s> and the rest?##'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] resolves: '##Here we say: If indeed##.'
Is the 'projection' origination, or notification?
To begin with, a cause does not produce an effect because [the effect would be] otherwise inexplicable, but rather through its own capacity.
Therefore, [projection is] notification.
And then, some other producer of what has been notified must be stated.
And that [other producer], even in the position [of the Buddhist] that [things are] permanent — and even when there is an experiencer — is not possible without a conscious controller; how much more so when entities are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>)!
The aggregate might be projected through the enjoyment of the experiencer, but [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] shows the far-removal [of even that possibility] by [stating]: that experiencer too does not exist: '##In [entities] devoid of an experiencer##.'
Moreover, many [causes], standing in the relation of helper and helped, produce an effect.
But in the momentarist position, the relation of helper and helped does not exist, because an entity has no scope for being helped.
Because a moment is indivisible, the impossibility of being helped or having been helped [arises].
Or, if that [relation] were justified through temporal difference, momentariness would be violated.
This is what is stated: '##In [entities] devoid of substrate and what depends on a substrate##.'
'##Now, this is the intent##' — [the opponent says:]
When dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) is dependent on conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>), then a conscious controller would also be required. But [our position involves] dependence not on conditions but on causes alone (<s>hetūpanibandha</s>).
And thus, a controller is unnecessary.
The cause, by its own nature alone, will produce the aggregate-effect — this is the purport.
Granting that an effect does not arise from a single cause alone — [the objection is:] in this position there is the fallacy of mutual dependence — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], with this intent, says: '##How then that very##.'
Now, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] raises an objection by adopting the position of condition-dependent origination: '##If you think that the aggregates themselves##.'
For even impermanent entities always arise and perish in aggregation.
They are not piled together from some other standing position by anyone.
And thus, a conscious assembler is unnecessary here — this is the purport.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] removes the mutual dependence [objection] by [the word] '##beginningless##.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] considers the alternatives and refutes: '##Even so, from the aggregate##.'
That disposition-continuum (<s>saṃskārasaṃtāna</s>) — called <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit) — pervading the aggregate-stream, producing pleasure and suffering as appropriate: would it produce [them] spontaneously without encountering any adventitious [cause], or by encountering one?
If it produces [them] without encountering [anything], it would always produce pleasure and suffering, since what is capable and independent cannot be delayed.
If it produces [them] by encountering [something], an intelligent being must be accepted as the cause of that encountering.
And thus, dependent origination is not dependent on conditions.
Therefore, by this [reasoning], one should accept that the aggregate-continuum — independent of any adventitious [cause] — has the nature either of producing similar [effects] or of producing dissimilar [effects].
And thus the refutation stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [stands].
'##Moreover, if the aggregate exists for the purpose of enjoyment##.'
For one who has not [yet] obtained enjoyment desires to obtain it and engages in the means for that — this is self-evident.
This engagement is conceived as existing in an experiencer who is permanent — other than enjoyment, and who pervades the time of enjoyment and its means — not in one who is impermanent.
Nor in one who is non-different from enjoyment.
For enjoyment does not serve enjoyment, nor does another [enjoyment serve] another's [enjoyment].
The same should be seen regarding liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>).
Therein, if one who desires enjoyment and one who desires liberation are accepted as permanent, that would contradict [the Buddhist's] own position; or [if they are impermanent], there is the consequence of [endless] engagement [without resolution] — this is the meaning.
'##But the aggregate cannot be established because of the absence of an experiencer##.'
Because of the impossibility of engagement in the absence of an experiencer, there is the absence of an agent.

#uttarotpāde ca pūrvanirodhāt# /
pūrvasūtreṇa saṃgatimasyāha-- #uktametaditi# /
hetūpanibandhanaṃ pratītyasamutpadamabhyupetya pratyayopanibandhanaḥ pratītyasamutpādo dūṣitaḥ /
saṃprati hetūpanibandhanamapi taṃ dūṣayatītyarthaḥ /
dūṣaṇamāha-- #idamidānīmiti /
nirudhyamānasyeti# /
na tāvadvaiśeṣikavannirodhakāraṇasāṃnidhyaṃ nirudhyamānatvaṃ vaktavyam /
niruddhatvaṃ ca ciraniruddhatvaṃ vivakṣitatvaṃ, tathā cobhayorapyabhāvagrastatvāddhetutvānupapattiḥ /
śaṅkate-- #atha bhāvabhūta iti# /
kāraṇasya hi kāryotpādāt prākkālasattār'thavatī na kāryakālā, tadā kāryasya siddhatvena tatsidydharthāyāḥ sattāyā anupayogāditi bhāvaḥ /
tadetallokadṛṣṭyā dūṣayati-- #bhāvabhūtasyeti# /
bhūtvā vyāpṛtya bhāvāḥ prayeṇa hi kāryaṃ kurvanto loke dṛśyante /
tathā ca sthiratvam, itarathā tu lokavirodha iti /
punaḥ śaṅkate-- #atha bhāva eveti# /
yathāhuḥ-- 'bhūtiryeṣāṃ kriyā saiva kārakaṃ saiva cocyate 'iti /
bhavatyevaṃ vyāpāravattā tathāpi kṣaṇikasya na kāraṇatvamityāha-- #tathāpi naivopapadyate#kṣaṇikasya kāraṇabhāvaḥ /
mṛtsuvarṇakāraṇā hi ghaṭādayaśca rūcakādaya mṛtsuvarṇātmāno 'nubhūyante /
yadi ca na kāryasamaye kāraṇaṃ sat kathaṃ teṣāṃ tadātmanānubhāvaḥ /
naca kāraṇasādṛśyaṃ kāryasya na tu tādātmyamiti vācyam /
asati kasyacidrūpasyānugame sādṛśyasyāpyanupapatteḥ /
anugame vā tadeva kāraṇaṃ, tathā ca tasya kāryatādātmyamiti siddhimakṣaṇikatvamityarthaḥ /
sarvathā vailakṣaṇye tu hetuphalabhāvastantughaṭādāvapi prāptaṃ ityatiprasaṅga ityāha-- #vinaiva veti# /
naca tadbhāvabhāvo niyāmakaḥ, tasyaikasmin kṣaṇe 'śakyagrahatvāt, sāmānyasya cākāraṇatvāt /
kāraṇatve vā kṣaṇikatvahānerasmatpakṣapātaprasaṅgacceti bhāvaḥ /
api ca cotpādanirodhayorvikalpatraye 'pi vastunaḥ śāśvatatvaprasaṅga ityāha-- #api cotpādanirodhau nāmeti# /
paryāyatvāpādane 'pi nityatvāpādanaṃ mantavyam /

children.translated_text: '##The thing being unconnected with origination and cessation — there is the consequence of the entity being eternal##.'
Because contact with the non-existent is impossible, even in the case of association,
if existence is accepted, then permanence would follow — this should be understood.
The remainder is explained by mere recitation. //20//

body.translated_text:
'##And because upon the arising of the later, there is the cessation of the earlier##.'
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the connection of this [<s>sūtra</s>] with the previous one: '##This has been stated##.'
Having accepted cause-dependent (<s>hetūpanibandhana</s>) dependent origination, condition-dependent (<s>pratyayopanibandhana</s>) dependent origination was refuted.
Now, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes even the cause-dependent [version] — this is the meaning.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states the refutation: '##Now then##.' '##Of that which is ceasing##.'
To begin with, the cessation-state is not to be stated, as the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>s do, as being in the presence of a cause of destruction.
And the 'having ceased' state means having ceased long ago.
And since both [the ceasing and the ceased] are consumed by non-existence, causality is impossible [for either].
[The Buddhist] raises a doubt: '##If it is an existent entity##.'
For the reality of a cause is meaningful before the production of the effect, not at the time of the effect — since at that time, the effect being already accomplished, the reality [of the cause] is of no use for accomplishing it — this is the purport.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] refutes this from the standpoint of common observation: '##Of an entity that has existed##.'
For entities are generally observed in the world to act after having existed and functioned.
And thus [they are] permanent; otherwise there would be contradiction with common experience.
[The Buddhist] raises a further doubt: '##If it is just the existing entity itself [that acts]##.'
As they say: 'The coming into being of [entities] is their very activity, and that itself is called their causal efficacy (<s>kāraka</s>).'
Even if this is so, still the causality of a momentary [entity] is not possible — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '##Even so, it is not at all possible##' — the causality of a momentary [entity].
For pots and the like, whose causes are clay, gold, and the like, and necklaces and the like, are experienced as being of the nature of clay and gold.
And if the cause does not exist at the time of the effect, how can they be experienced as having that [causal] nature?
Nor should it be said: the effect has similarity to the cause, but not identity — for in the absence of the continuity of any form [between cause and effect], even similarity is impossible.
Or, if there is continuity, that itself is the cause, and thus the cause is identical with the effect — hence non-momentariness is established — this is the meaning.
But if [cause and effect] are entirely dissimilar, then the cause-effect relationship would apply even between thread and pot — hence the absurd consequence [of anything causing anything] — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '##Or, even without##.'
Nor is the relation of 'when that exists, this exists' (<s>tadbhāvabhāva</s>) the determining factor, since it cannot be grasped in a single moment, and since a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is not a cause.
Or, if [the universal] were a cause, momentariness would be abandoned, falling into our position — this is the purport.
Moreover, in all three alternatives regarding origination and cessation, there is the consequence of the entity being eternal — thus [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '##Moreover, origination and cessation indeed##.'
Even when [origination and cessation are posited as] alternating, the consequence of eternality should be understood.
