#asati pratijñoparodho yaugapadyamanyathā# /
nīlābhāsasya hi cittasya nīlādālambanapratyayānnīlākāratā /
samanantarapratyayātpūrvavijñānādbodharūpatā /
body.translated_text: "In the absence [of external objects], there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, simultaneity [would result]." For a cognition that has a blue appearance, the blue form arises from the objective condition (<s>ālambana-pratyaya</s>) of blue; the nature of awareness arises from the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantara-pratyaya</s>), i.e., the prior cognition;

body.text:
cakṣuṣo 'dhipatipratyayādrūpagrahaṇapratiniyamaḥ /
ālokātsahakāripratyayādhetoḥ spaṣṭārthatā /

children.text: evaṃ sukhādīnāmapi caittānāṃ cittābhinnahetujānāṃ catvāryotānyeva kāraṇāni /
children.translated_text: Likewise, for pleasure and other mental factors (<s>caitta</s>), which arise from causes not different from the mind (<s>citta</s>), these same four types of causes apply.

children.text: seyaṃ pratijñā caturvidhān hetūn pratītya cittacaittā utpadyanta ityabhāvakāraṇatva uparudhyeta /
children.translated_text: This thesis — that mind and mental factors arise depending on four types of causes — would be contradicted if non-existence were held to be a cause.
"It persists until the arising of the next moment" —
origination is not different from the entity that is originating, and thus there would be abandonment of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), which means abandonment of the thesis. //21//

body.translated_text: the restriction to apprehending visible form arises from the dominant condition (<s>adhipati-pratyaya</s>) of the eye; and clarity of the object arises from the cooperative condition (<s>sahakāri-pratyaya</s>), namely light.

body.text:
#pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhāprāptiravicchedāt# /
bhāvapratīpā saṃkhyā buddhiḥ pratisaṃkhyā , tayā nirodhaḥ pratisaṃkhyānirodhaḥ /
santamimamasantaṃ karomītyevamākāratā ca buddherbhāvapratīpatvam /
body.translated_text: "Cessation through deliberation (<s>pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>) and cessation without deliberation (<s>apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>) cannot be established, because of non-interruption." The cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) that is opposed to existence is <s>pratisaṃkhyā</s> (deliberation); cessation through that is <s>pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>. The form of cognition that takes the shape 'I make this existent thing non-existent' constitutes its opposition to existence.

body.text:
etenāpratisaṃkhyānirodho 'pi vyākhyātaḥ /
saṃtānagocaro vā nirodhaḥ, saṃtānikṣaṇagocaro vā /
na tāvatsaṃtānasya nirodhaḥ saṃbhavati /
hetuphalabhāvena hi vyavasthitāḥ saṃtānina evodayavyayadharmāṇaḥ saṃtānāḥ /
tatra yo 'sāvantyaḥ saṃtānī, yannirodhātsaṃtānocchedena bhavitavyam, sa kiṃ phalaṃ kiñcidārabhate na vā /
ārabhate cet, nāntyaḥ /
tathā ca na saṃtānocchedaḥ /
anārambhe tu bhavedantyaḥ saḥ, kintu syādasan, arthakriyākāritāyāḥ sattālakṣaṇasya virahāt /
tadasatve tajjanakamapyasajjanakatvenāsadityanena krameṇāsantaḥ sarva eva saṃtānina iti tatsaṃtāno nitarāmasanniti kasya pratisaṃkhyayā nirodha- /
naca sabhāgānāṃ saṃtānināṃ hetuphalabhāvaḥ saṃtānaḥ, tasya visabhāgotpādo nirodhaḥ, visabhāgotpādaka eva cakṣaṇaḥ saṃtānasyāntyaḥ /
tathāsati rūpavijñānapravāhe rasādivijñānotpattau saṃtānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ /
kathañcitsārūpye vā visabhāge 'pyantataḥ sattayā tadastīti na saṃtānocchedaḥ /
tadanenābhisaṃdhināha-- #sarveṣvapi saṃtāneṣu saṃtānināmavicchinnenahetuphalabhāvena saṃtānavicchedasyāsaṃbhavāditi /
nāpi bhāvagocarau saṃbhavataḥ#pratisaṃkhyāpratisaṃkhyānirodhau /
atra tāvadutpannamātrāpravṛttasya bhāvasya na pratisaṃkhyānirodhaḥ saṃbhavati, tasya puruṣaprayatnāpekṣābhāvādityastyeva dūṣaṇaṃ, tathāpi doṣāntaramubhayasminnapi nirodho brūte-- #na hi bhāvānāmiti# /
yato niranvayo vināśo na saṃbhavatyato nirūpākhyo 'pi na saṃbhavati, tenaivānvayinā rūpeṇa bhāvasya naṣṭasyāpyupākhyeyatvāt /
niranvayavināśābhāve hetumāha-- #sarvāsvapyavasthāsviti# /
yadyadanvayirūpaṃ tattatparamārthasadbhāvaḥ /
avasthāstu viśeṣākhyā upajanāpāyadharmāṇaḥ, tāsāṃ sarvasāmanirvacanīyatayā svato na paramārthasattvam /
anvayyeva tu rūpaṃ tāsāṃ tattvam /
tasya ca sarvatra pratyabhijñāyamānatvānna vināśa ityavasthāvato 'vināśānnāvasthānāṃ niranvayo vināśa iti /
tāsāṃ tattvasyānvayinaḥ sarvatrāvicchedāt /
syādetat /
mṛtpiṇḍamṛdghaṭamṛtkapālādiṣu sarvatra mṛttattvapratyabhijñānādbhavatvevam /

children.text: taptopalatalapatitanaṣṭasya tūdabindoḥ kimasti rūpamanvayi pratyabhijñāyamānaṃ, yenāsya na niranvayo nāśaḥ syādityata āha-- #aspaṣṭapratyabhijñānāsvapīti# /
children.translated_text: But for a water-drop that is destroyed upon falling on the surface of a heated stone — what persisting form is there that is recognized, so that its destruction would not be traceless? To this he says: "Even in cases where recognition is unclear ..."

children.text: atrāpi tattoyaṃ tejasā mārtaṇḍamaṇḍalamambudatvāya nīyata ityanumeyaṃ, mṛdādīnīmanvayināmavicchedadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: Even here, it is to be inferred that this water is being transformed by heat into the disc of the sun and into the state of clouds, based on the observation of the unbroken continuity of persisting substances like clay.

children.text: śakyaṃ tatra vaktum'udambindau ca sindhau ca toyabhāvona bhidyate /
children.translated_text: It is possible to say in this regard: 'The nature of water in a water-drop and in the ocean does not differ;
Even when the drop is destroyed, its continuity persists in the ocean.'

body.translated_text: By this, cessation without deliberation (<s>apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha</s>) is also explained. Cessation may pertain either to the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>) or to a momentary member of the continuum. First, cessation of the continuum is not possible. For the members of the continuum, established in the relation of cause and effect, are themselves subject to arising and passing away, and they alone constitute the continua. Among them, the final member of the continuum — upon whose cessation the continuum would be cut off — does it produce some effect or not? If it does produce an effect, it is not the final member, and thus there is no cutting off of the continuum. If it does not produce, it would indeed be the final member, but it would be non-existent, since it lacks the defining characteristic of existence, namely causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritā</s>). If that is non-existent, its producer too would be non-existent as the producer of a non-existent thing — and by this progression all members of the continuum would be non-existent, so the continuum itself would be entirely non-existent. Then whose cessation through deliberation could there be? Nor can the continuum be the cause-effect relation among homogeneous members, with its cessation being the arising of a heterogeneous member, and the moment that produces the heterogeneous arising being the final member of the continuum. For if so, in the stream of visual cognition of form, when a cognition of taste arises, there would be the absurd consequence of the continuum being cut off. Or, if there is some similarity, even in the heterogeneous case there would ultimately be existence by virtue of mere being, so there would be no cutting off of the continuum. With this intent he says: "In all continua, because of the unbroken cause-effect relation among the members of the continuum, the interruption of the continuum is impossible." "Nor are the two — cessation through deliberation and cessation without deliberation — possible with respect to individual entities." Here, cessation through deliberation is not possible for an entity that, having just arisen, has not yet engaged in activity, since it does not depend on human effort — this criticism certainly stands. Nevertheless, he states a further defect applying to both types of cessation: "For entities [that are momentary] ..." Since traceless destruction is not possible, formless destruction is also not possible, because even a destroyed entity must be describable by that very persisting form. He states the reason for the impossibility of traceless destruction: "In all states ..." Whatever persisting form there is, that constitutes ultimate reality. States, however, are modifications characterized by arising and passing away; since all of them are indescribable in themselves, they do not have ultimate reality of their own. Rather, the persisting form alone is their true nature. Since that is recognized everywhere through recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), there is no destruction — and because the substrate of the states is not destroyed, there is no traceless destruction of the states. Because the persisting nature, which is their reality, is uninterrupted everywhere. One might object: let it be so in cases like clay-lump, clay-pot, and clay-sherd, where clay-nature is recognized everywhere through recognition.

body.text: 'tasmānna kaścidapi niranvayo nāśa iti siddham //22 //
body.translated_text: Therefore it is established that there is no traceless destruction whatsoever. //22//

children.translated_text: "And there is a defect in both cases."

The preparatory equipment (<s>parikara</s>) refers to the aggregate (<s>sāmagrī</s>) of means for right knowledge, such as <s>yama</s>, <s>niyama</s>, and the like, as well as hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and so forth.
The paths (<s>mārga</s>) are the meditations on momentariness, non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>), and the like.
The rest is self-evident. //23//

body.text:
#ākāśo cāviśeṣāt# /
etadvyācaṣṭe-- #yacca teṣāmiti# /
vedaprāmāṇye vipratipannānapi pratiśabdaguṇānumeyatvamākāśasya vaktavyam /
tathāhi-- jātimattvena sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyebhyo vibhaktasya śabdasyāsparśatve sati bāhyaikendriyagrāhyatvena gandhādivadguṇatvamanumitam /
nāyamātmaguṇo bāhyendrigocaratvāt /
ata eva na manoguṇaḥ, tadguṇānāmapratyakṣatvāt /
na pṛthivyādiguṇaḥ, tadguṇagandhādisāhacaryānupalabdheḥ /
tasmādguṇo bhūtvā gandhādivadasādhāraṇendriyagrāhyo yadravyamanumāpayati tadākāśaṃ pañcamaṃ bhūtaṃ vastviti /

children.translated_text: "Moreover, for those who hold <s>ākāśa</s> to be the absence of obstruction ..."
Negation, whose determination depends on the determination of the locus of what is negated and what negates, cannot be determined without the determination of a real locus.
And that locus of the absence of obstruction is <s>ākāśa</s>, a real entity.
The rest is self-evident in meaning. //24//

body.translated_text: "And <s>ākāśa</s> (space), because of non-distinction." This he explains: "And what they ..." Even for those who disagree about the authority of the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>ākāśa</s> should be acknowledged as inferable from the quality of sound. Thus: sound, being distinct from universals (<s>sāmānya</s>), particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) by virtue of possessing a class-nature (<s>jātimatva</s>), and being intangible yet apprehensible by a single external sense-organ, is inferred to be a quality like smell and the rest. It is not a quality of the self (<s>ātman</s>), because it is apprehensible by an external sense-organ. For the same reason, it is not a quality of <s>manas</s> (mind), since the qualities of mind are imperceptible. It is not a quality of earth and the like, because the co-occurrence with smell and other qualities of those elements is not observed. Therefore, being a quality and being apprehensible by a distinctive sense-organ like smell, the substance it leads one to infer is <s>ākāśa</s>, the fifth element.

body.text:
#anusmṛteśca# /
vibhajate-- #api vaināśikaḥ sarvasya vastuna iti# /
yastu satyapyetasminnupalabdhṛsmartroranyatve 'pi samānāyāṃ saṃtatau kāryakāraṇabhāvāt smṛtirupapatsyata iti manyamāno na parituṣyati taṃ prati pratyabhijñāsamājñātapratyakṣavirodhamāha-- #api ca darśanasmaraṇayoḥ kartarīti# /
tato 'hamadrākṣīditi pratīyāt,ahaṃ smarāmyanyastvadrākṣīdityarthaḥ /
pratyabhijñāpratyakṣavirodhaprapañcastūttaraḥ /
#ā janmanaḥ ā cottamāducchvāsāt# /
āmaraṇādityartha- /
naca sādṛśyanibandhanaṃ pratyabhijñānaṃ, pūrvāparakṣaṇadarśina ekasyābhāve tadanupapatteḥ /
śaṅkate-- #temedaṃ sadṛśamiti# /

tatkathamekasyānekadarśinaḥ sthirasya prasaṅga iti /

na caikasya jñānasya nānākāratvaṃ saṃbhavati, ekatvavirodhāt /
naca tāvantyeva jñānānīti yuktaṃ, tathāsati pratyākāraṃ jñānānāṃ samāptesteṣāṃ ca parasparavārtājñānābhāvānnānetyeva na syāt /
tasmāt pūrvāparakṣaṇatatsādṛśyagocaratvaṃ jñānasya vaktavyam /

yadyucyeta astytasmin vikalpe tenedaṃ sadṛśamiti padadvayaprayogo na tviha tattedantāspadau padārthau tayośca sādṛśyamiti vivakṣitam, api tvevamākāratā jñānasya kalpiteti, tatrāha-- #yadā hi lokaprasiddhaḥ padārtha iti# /
ekādhikaraṇavipratiṣiddhadharmadvayābhyupagamo vivādaḥ /
tatraikaḥ svapakṣaṃ sādhayatyanyaśca tatsādhanaṃ dūṣayati /
na caitatsarvamasati vikalpānāṃ bāhyālambanatve 'sati ca lokaprasiddhapadārthakatve bhavitumarhati /
jñānākāratve hi vikalpapratibhāsināṃ nityatvānityatvādīnāmekārthaviṣayatvābhāvāt jñānānāṃ ca dharmiṇāṃ bhedānna virodhaḥ /

tasmādanena svapakṣaṃ pratitiṣṭhāpayiṣatā parapakṣasādhanaṃ ca nirācikīrṣatā vikalpānāṃ lokasiddhapadārthakatā bāhyalambanatā ca vaktavyā /

ayamabhisaṃdhiḥ-- keyamadhyavaseyatā bāhyasya /
yadi grāhyatā na dvaividhyam /
athānyā socyatāṃ, nanūktā taireva svapratibhāse 'narther'thādhyavasāyena pravṛttiriti /

kiṃ karaṇamāho yojanamutāropa iti /
na tāvat karaṇam /
nahyanyadanyat kartu śakyam /
nahi jātu sahasramapi śilpino ghaṭaṃ paṭayitumīśate /
na cāntaraṃ bāhyena yojayitum /
api ca tathāsati yukta iti pratyayaḥ syāt /
na cāsti /
āropo 'pi kiṃ gṛhyamāṇe bāhye utāgṛhyamāṇe /

children.text: yadi gṛhyamāṇe tadā kiṃ vikalpenāho tatsamayajenāvikalpakena /
children.translated_text: If upon one that is apprehended, then is it apprehended by a conceptual cognition or by a non-conceptual cognition arising at the same time?

A conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>), whose domain is suited for association with verbal expression, cannot have as its object a unique particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that is inexpressible and not shared across place and time.
As they say: 'The essential nature of pleasures and the like, which cannot be conventionally expressed, belongs exclusively [to them];
Therefore their self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvitti</s>) is not accompanied by verbal elaboration.'

body.translated_text: "And from memory (<s>anusmṛti</s>)." He analyzes: "Moreover, the follower of destruction (<s>vaināśika</s>) holds that all entities ..." But for one who is not satisfied, thinking that even though there is difference between the perceiver and the rememberer, memory would be explicable in the same continuum through the cause-effect relation, he states the contradiction with direct perception as established by recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>): "Moreover, the agent of seeing and remembering ..." Otherwise, one would cognize 'another saw,' while 'I remember' — meaning that the one who remembers is different from the one who saw. The elaboration of the contradiction with the direct perception of recognition will come later. "From birth, and from the last breath" — meaning until death. And recognition is not based on mere similarity, because in the absence of a single entity that perceives both the earlier and later moments, recognition would be impossible. He raises an objection: "'This is similar to that' ..." The meaning is this: this is a conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>), and <s>vikalpa</s> superimposes its own form as external, but does not truly apprehend the earlier and later moments or similarity between them. How then would the consequence of a single, stable perceiver of multiple things follow? He refutes: "No, because there is the use of words referring to distinct objects in 'this is that' ..." This conceptual cognition manifestly appears as having a meaning composed of multiple objects — to say that these multiple objects do not appear therein would contradict self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>). Nor is it possible for a single cognition to have multiple forms, since that would contradict its unity. Nor is it proper to hold that there are just as many cognitions as forms, for then, with cognitions complete for each form, and each being unaware of the others, the cognition 'this is that' would never arise. Therefore, cognition must be said to have as its object the earlier and later moments and their similarity. And this is not possible without a single knower who persists across the earlier and later moments — hence the consequence of the collapse of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>). If it be said that in that conceptual cognition, the use of the two words 'this' and 'that' is present, but the objects denoted by 'that' and 'this' and their similarity are not intended — rather, this is merely a constructed form of cognition — to that he says: "For when a well-known real object ..." A dispute is the acceptance of two contradictory properties in the same locus. In that, one party establishes his own position and the other refutes that proof. But all this cannot occur if conceptual cognitions do not have external objects and if well-known real objects are not their content. For if the contents of conceptual appearance were merely cognition-forms, there would be no single-object reference for permanence, impermanence and the like, and since the cognitions as substrata are different, there would be no contradiction. Indeed, one who asserts the permanence of the self and another who asserts the impermanence of intellect do not contradict each other. Nor does one who, using the word 'impermanent' in a non-ordinary sense, intends pervasiveness for the self, contradict one who uses the word 'permanent' in its ordinary sense for the self. Therefore, one who wishes to establish his own position and refute the proof of the opponent's position must accept that conceptual cognitions have well-known real objects as their content and have external referents. If it be said: conceptual cognitions have two kinds of objects — apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and determined (<s>adhyavaseya</s>); the apprehended is one's own form, while the determined is external; and thus disputation characterized by acceptance of thesis and antithesis, as well as having well-known real objects as content, would both be explained — to that he says: "Whatever is thus ascertained as the meaning, that alone should be stated; saying something other than that would merely proclaim one's own garrulousness." The intent is this: what is this 'determination' of the external? If it is apprehension, there is no duality. If it is something else, let it be stated. But it has already been stated by those very [Buddhists] that there is activity through the determination of a real object in what is actually an unreal appearance. Now, what is this 'determination' of the conceptual form? Is it an action, a connection, or a superimposition? It is not an action, for one thing cannot be made into another. Indeed, even a thousand craftsmen cannot make a pot into a cloth. Nor can the internal be connected with the external. Moreover, in that case there would be a cognition 'it is fitting,' but there is none. As for superimposition — is it upon an external that is apprehended, or upon one that is not apprehended?

'iti /
na ca tatsamayabhāvinā nirvikalpakena gṛhyamāṇe bāhye vikalpenāgṛhīte tatra vikalpaḥ svākāramāropayitumarhati. /

children.translated_text: Therefore it is well said: 'Saying something other than that would merely proclaim one's own garrulousness.'

children.translated_text: Moreover, practical activity based on similarity is grounded in a cognition of the form 'this is similar to that,' not in a cognition of the form 'this is that itself.' He says: "Nor is this practical activity based on similarity."

body.translated_text: Nor can conceptual cognition superimpose its own form upon an external object apprehended by a non-conceptual cognition arising at the same time while it itself has not apprehended it. For it is not possible for a cognition of silver to superimpose silver upon an object before one in which the cognition of silver does not appear. And if the external is not apprehended, it would simply be one's own form, not an external — and thus there is no superimposition. Moreover, does this conceptual cognition, having through self-awareness apprehended the concept as truly existing, first grasp its own form and then superimpose the external? Or does it superimpose at the very moment it grasps its own form? A cognition that is momentary and therefore devoid of sequence cannot have the sequential acts of grasping and superimposing. Therefore, it must be said that at the very moment it grasps its own form — which is not a real object — it superimposses a real object. But this is untenable. For with respect to its own form, it is exceedingly vivid through the directness of self-awareness. And the external being superimposed would be indistinct — being essentially different from the vivid, it would be something other than one's own form superimposed. Nor is superimposition merely the non-apprehension of difference, since the apprehension of difference has been stated through the distinction of vividness and non-vividness. Moreover, if, when the external is not apprehended, there is activity directed toward it through non-apprehension of difference from one's own particular — then, since difference from the entire triple world would also not be apprehended, one should engage with anything whatsoever, without distinction. By this, the superimposition of externality even upon the form of cognition, like light, is also refuted.

body.translated_text: "Not from non-existence, because it is not observed." "And for this further reason, the doctrine of the destructionists (<s>vaināśika</s>) is untenable." The <s>vaināśikas</s>, who hold that effects arise from what is unstable, in effect assert that entities arise from non-existence itself. This has been stated earlier. If effects arise from something independent [of auxiliary causes], human effort would be purposeless. And if there is dependence, since a moment cannot be modified, there is the impossibility of being assisted; and when there is no assistance, the absence of dependence would lead to the absurd consequence of non-momentariness. Since the negation of one of the two — dependence and independence — necessarily entails the establishment of the other, and there is no third alternative, origination of an entity from an unstable entity is impossible; therefore, in the momentarist position, origination of existence from non-existence remains as the only conclusion. Not only does it follow implicitly, but they also explicitly teach: "Because there is no manifestation without first destroying ..." This is analyzed: "For indeed, from what is destroyed ..." The particle 'kila' expresses reluctance. "If the effect were to arise from an immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) cause, then everything would arise from everything." The intent is this: an immutable entity either has the nature of producing effects or does not. If it has the nature of producing effects, then whatever it must produce, it would produce all at once, since a capable entity cannot be delayed. If it does not have that nature, it would never produce anything. If one says: even though capable, it produces effects sequentially through the sequential association of auxiliary causes — that is untenable, because it cannot withstand analysis. Do these auxiliaries confer some benefit upon it or not? If they confer no benefit, they would not be depended upon, as they would be unhelpful. If they do confer benefit, the benefit would be either identical or different [from the cause].

body.translated_text: Thus, if an effect were to arise even from an immutable entity that does nothing, then everything would arise from everything — this is well stated. He summarizes: "Therefore, from those consumed by non-existence ..." "Here it is said: 'Not from non-existence, because it is not observed.'" Effects do not arise from non-existence. Why? Because it is not observed. For the arising of effects like sprouts from a hare's horn is not observed. If entities were to arise from non-existence, then, since there is no distinction in non-existence, sprouts should arise from hare's horns too. For non-existence is not differentiated. Or if it were qualified, it too would be an existent entity, not something indeterminate — this is the meaning. Assuming that non-existence does possess qualification, he says: "Nor is non-existence the cause of the origination of anything." Moreover, whatever is not pervaded by something is not a modification of that thing — just as pots, troughs, and waterpots, not being pervaded by gold, are not modifications of gold. And these modifications are not pervaded by non-existence. Therefore they are not modifications of non-existence. But they are modifications of existence, since existence pervades them — thus he says: "And if entities were to arise from non-existence ..." Having paraphrased the statement of the advocate of non-existence as cause, he refutes it: "But what was said ..." Even a stable entity produces effects sequentially through the sequential co-presence of auxiliary causes. And the auxiliaries are not unhelpful. The benefit conferred upon it by the auxiliaries is neither different nor identical, but rather indescribable (<s>anirvācya</s>). And from the indescribable, the effect too arises as indescribable. Nor does this make the stable entity a non-cause, for the effect has it as its material cause (<s>upādāna</s>), just as the snake has the rope as its material cause — this has been stated. And thus the <s>śruti</s> declares: 'Clay alone is real.' Furthermore, even for those who maintain that unique particulars (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that are entirely distinct from everything are real entities — for them too, why do effects of the sprout-class arise only from causes of the seed-class and not of the camel-class? For between a seed and another seed, or between a seed and a camel, when there is absolute dissimilarity, there is no distinction. Nor does the universal 'seed-sprout-ness' ultimately exist, by which there could be a natural cause-effect relation between them.

children.translated_text: "And even for those who are neutral, the same conclusion holds."

body.translated_text: "Non-existence is not [established], because of perception (<s>upalabdhi</s>)." He states the connection with the preceding topic: "Thus ..." He indicates the distinctive position of the consciousness-only advocates (<s>vijñānamātravādin</s>) as intended by the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), as distinguished from the external-object realists: "For some, indeed ..." Now, the totality of reality is exhausted in the four categories: the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>), the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>), and the resultant cognition (<s>pramiti</s>); even if the most general category is absent, reality cannot be established. Therefore, one who establishes consciousness-aggregate (<s>vijñāna-skandha</s>) alone as reality must account for these four categories — and thus consciousness-aggregate alone cannot be reality. For it is not possible that there be consciousness alone and also the four categories. Therefore he says: "And in that consciousness-doctrine, through a form mounted upon cognition ..." Although experience, the experienced, the experiencer, and the experiencing are not different from one another, nevertheless, through a form mounted upon — that is, constructed by — cognition, this practical usage of means of knowledge, object of knowledge, and result, as well as the practical usage of the knower, pertains to what is actually other — this too should be understood. It is not ultimate — this is the meaning. And thus it amounts to proving what is already established. For the <s>Brahman</s>-theorists do not accept that cognition has the form of blue and such; rather, blue and the like are indescribable (<s>anirvācanīya</s>). Thus: the intrinsic nature of cognition, endowed with an unreal form, is the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>); its illumination of the object is the result of the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa-phala</s>); and its power to illuminate is the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). children.translated_text: Therefore, let grossness not be a property of individual atoms, like blue-ness, since it is absent in each atom individually.

children.text: pratibhāsadaśāpannānāṃ tu teṣāṃ bhaviṣyati bahutvādivatsāṃvṛtaṃ sthaulyam /
children.translated_text: But for those [atoms] in the state of appearing, there will be a conventional (<s>sāṃvṛta</s>) grossness, like multiplicity.
As they say: 'When many are apprehended by one, some form is grasped;
that is conventional, residing in appearance, being impossible in a single atom. //1//

body.translated_text: is it understood?" For the external object, which is supposed to be the basis of cognition according to consciousness-only doctrine, cannot first of all be an atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>). For cognition appears as a single gross blue, not as an extremely subtle atom. And something that appears as one thing cannot have another as its object, for by over-extension, everything would be the object of everything and everyone would be omniscient. Nor is it proper to say that grossness is a property of the appearance. For this cannot withstand analysis. Is this grossness a property of the appearance, i.e., of cognition, or a property of the object at the time of appearing? If the first alternative, then in that case cognition would be accepted as having its own aspect as its object — and then who opposes this and who agrees? [It would already concede the consciousness-only position.] If the second alternative: thus — atoms of form, arising without interval, mounting upon a single cognition, constitute grossness. And there is no error here. For they are indeed atoms of form, and they do indeed arise without interval, and they do mount upon a single cognition.

children.translated_text: And that perception is not erroneous, because it is the apprehension of multiple real things;

children.text: sāṃvṛtaṃ grahaṇaṃ nānyatra ca vastugraho bhramaḥ //2 //

children.translated_text: For difference is pervaded by the non-invariance of co-perception — just as the two <s>Aśvins</s>, being distinct, are not necessarily perceived together, since sometimes, when one is covered by clouds, only one is perceived.

children.translated_text: Here, this invariance [of co-perception], being observed as contradicting the non-invariance that pervades difference, negates the difference that is pervaded by it.
As it has been said: 'From the invariable rule of co-perception, blue and the cognition of blue are non-different;
and difference is perceived [only] through erroneous cognitions, like duality in the case of the moon.'

body.translated_text: This is not so. The appearance of contiguity is erroneous. For those atoms of form are interspersed with atoms of smell, taste, and touch, and are therefore not contiguous. Hence, just as the cognition of a single dense forest in the case of trees that are actually spaced apart [is erroneous], so too this cognition of grossness with respect to atoms that have gaps between them is seen to be erroneous. Therefore, even if the cognition of a pot and the like is free from conceptual construction (<s>kalpanāpoḍha</s>), it is not perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) because of its erroneousness — like the cognition of a yellow conch shell — if atoms are accepted as the objects. This has been stated: "First, atoms cannot be the objects delimited by the cognition of pillars and the like. Nor are the aggregates of atoms, namely pillars and the like, wholes (<s>avayavin</s>). If they are non-different from the atoms, they are just atoms — and the refutation stated there applies. If different, then, like a cow and a horse, there would be absolute dissimilarity, and hence no identity. And inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) has been rejected." Thus, through the analysis of difference and non-difference, one should also reject universals (<s>jāti</s>), qualities (<s>guṇa</s>), actions (<s>karma</s>), and the rest. Therefore, since everything that appears cannot withstand analysis, and since there is no means of knowledge for the existence of what does not appear, cognitions do not have external objects. Moreover, cognition cannot, like a sense-organ, make a hidden object directly perceptible. For cognition cannot produce another cognition having an object in the way a sense-organ produces a cognition having an object. Since the same question would apply equally there too, there would be an infinite regress. Nor can one maintain that the result — characterized as manifestation — resides in the object. For this is impossible with respect to past and future [objects]. For it is not possible that the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) be non-present while its properties (<s>dharma</s>) are present. Therefore, the direct perceptibility of the intrinsic nature of cognition itself must be accepted as the perceptibility of the object. And if cognition, being formless, is always of the nature of mere awareness, then, because of the absence of differentiation, how could it establish the differentiation of objects? Therefore, differentiation of forms must be posited for it in order to establish the differentiation of objects. As it has been said: 'The mere existence of awareness is not properly its apprehension of that [object], since that is undifferentiated everywhere. But conformity entering into it makes it conform and thus connects it [with the object].' And this form is experienced as unitary. If it belongs to cognition and not to the object, there is no means of knowledge for the existence of the external — thus he says: "Moreover, from experience alone, cognition being of a common nature ..." "And because of the invariable rule of co-perception (<s>sahopalambha-niyama</s>)." Whatever is invariably co-perceived with something is not different from it, just as a second moon [is not different] from the one moon. And the object is invariably co-perceived with cognition — this is a proof by the apprehension of what contradicts the pervader (<s>vyāpaka-viruddha-upalabdhi</s>).

body.translated_text: "This should be viewed like dreams and the like." Every cognition is without an external object, just like the cognitions of dreams, illusions, and the like; and so too is this cognition under dispute — this is a proof from essential nature (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>). For the absence of an external object invariably accompanies the mere nature of being a cognition, just as being a <s>śiṃśapā</s> tree invariably accompanies being a tree. When the absence of external reference is to be proved as invariably accompanying mere cognition-hood, cognition-hood becomes a proof from essential nature. At this point, the <s>Sautrāntika</s> raises an objection: "How then, if there is no external object," can the variety of cognitions such as 'this is blue,' 'this is yellow' "be explained?" For he held that whatever is occasional even in the presence of something else, all of those require a cause beyond that [constant factor];

body.translated_text: just as cognitions appearing as speech and movement, when I do not wish to speak or go, require a different mental continuum [as cause]. And so too the cognitions under dispute — even when the <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> (store-consciousness) continuum exists, the six types of active cognitions (<s>pravṛtti-vijñāna</s>) [are occasional] — this is a proof from essential nature. And that cause beyond the <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> continuum, which accounts for the occasional differentiation of active cognitions, is the external object. If [the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> says] the occasionality is due to the ripening of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) as a condition — well, the latent impressions are the capacity of <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>s falling within a single continuum to generate their respective active cognitions; their ripening is the coming to fruition in producing their own effects; and the condition for that ripening is a prior moment within one's own continuum, since dependence on another continuum is not accepted. And thus all moments falling within the <s>ālaya</s> continuum would be causes of ripening — or none at all, since there is no distinction in belonging to the <s>ālaya</s> continuum. If [one says] that difference of moments entails difference of capacities, and the occasionality of capacities entails the occasionality of effects — well then, a single moment would have only the capacity to generate blue cognition, and its capacity to awaken that [cognition]; a different moment would not have this. And if it did, how could difference of moments entail difference of capacities? Thus all moments within the <s>ālaya</s> continuum would be equally capable — and when a competent cause exists, the postponement of the effect is untenable. If [the occasionality of] what is to be negated depends solely on one's own continuum, the omnipresence contradicting that occasionality, being apprehended, negates the occasionality and establishes dependence on something else — this is the proof of the invariable connection. And not all active cognitions are accepted even by the <s>Vijñānavādins</s> as caused by another mental continuum; only certain active cognitions, those appearing as interrupted speech and movement, [are so accepted]. Moreover, even if caused by another being's continuum, since that too is always present, there would be no occasionality. For there is no possibility of spatial or temporal remoteness of another being's continuum. In the consciousness-only doctrine, since no space apart from consciousness is accepted, and since cognitions, being immaterial, have no spatial nature, and since there is no acceptance of new beings appearing — given that <s>saṃsāra</s> is beginningless — there is no possibility of temporal remoteness either. Therefore, since the variety of cognitions cannot be explained without an external object, the external object is to be inferred — thus the <s>Sautrāntikas</s> concluded. He refutes them: "From the variety of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), he says" — the <s>Vijñānavādin</s>. The idea here is: even if cognitions arise solely from one's own continuum, since the occasionality of cognitions can be explained [by <s>vāsanā</s>-variety], the argument has uncertain exclusion of the counter-position and is therefore inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). Thus: even if external objects are the cause, how is it that sometimes there is blue-sensation and sometimes yellow-sensation? Because of the presence and absence of external blue and yellow, one might say. But why, even in the presence of yellow, does blue cognition not arise, while yellow cognition does? Because of the capacity and incapacity of each for that, one might say. But whence this difference of capacity and incapacity? From the difference of causes, one might say. In that case, differences in moments too will have differences in capacity based on their own distinct causes. For the moments within a continuum are causes of different effects, and they differ with respect to each effect. And the continuum is not some single entity that produces moments, whose non-difference would entail the non-difference of moments. But it was said that neither from the difference nor from the non-difference of moments do the difference and non-difference of capacities follow, since even different moments are observed to have a single capacity. Otherwise, only a single moment would have the capacity to generate blue cognition, and blue cognitions would not arise again, since that capable moment has passed, and other moments lack the capacity. Therefore, even when moments differ, there is no difference in capacity; but when continua differ, capacity does differ. This is not so. If different continua do not have a single capacity, then even different blue-continua, being mutually distinct, would not have a single capacity for producing blue form — and thus even in the presence of another blue-continuum, blue cognition would not arise. Therefore, just as for different continua, so too for different moments — since they arise dependent on their own distinct causes — it must be said that some have the difference of capacity and some do not. And thus, among cognition-moments falling within a single <s>ālaya</s> continuum, only a particular cognition-moment has that particular excellence of capacity called <s>vāsanā</s>, acquired from its own condition, from which an active cognition of blue form arises and not of yellow form; and another has that sort [of <s>vāsanā</s>] from which yellow cognition arises and not blue. Thus, from the variety of <s>vāsanā</s> alone — acquired from one's own conditions — the variety of cognitions is established, and there is no means of knowledge whatsoever for the existence of an object beyond that. The <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> cognition falling within the continuum that is itself unperceived is the <s>vāsanā</s>; from its variety comes the variety of experience of blue and the like; and from the prior variety of experience of blue and the like comes the variety of <s>vāsanā</s> — thus this [relation] of cognition and <s>vāsanā</s> is beginningless. Therefore there is no possibility of the defect of mutual dependence, like the [beginningless] continuum of seed and sprout. And by positive and negative concomitance too, it is the variety of <s>vāsanā</s> alone that is the cause of the variety of cognition, not the variety of objects — thus he says: "And also by positive and negative concomitance ..." Having thus presented [the <s>Vijñānavāda</s> position], we say: 'Non-existence [of the external] is not [established], because of perception.'" The non-existence of the external object cannot be established. For it would be established either from the complete absence of apprehension, or — even when there is apprehension — from cognition not having external objects, or — even when it does have external objects — from the existence of a means of knowledge that sublates the external object. First, there is no complete absence of apprehension — introducing this with a question, he says: "Why? Because of perception." For when there is a most vivid, universal apprehension, its absence cannot be asserted — this is the meaning. He takes up the second alternative: "But I do not say this ..." He refutes: "Indeed you do say this." For perception, apprehended by the witness-consciousness (<s>sākṣin</s>) that grasps apprehension, is grasped specifically as having an external object — not as mere apprehension. This is the meaning. "And therefore" — this is a reference to the arguments to be stated [subsequently]. He takes up the third alternative: "But

children.translated_text: Nor is it tenable that a single gross conceptual cognition (<s>sthūla-vikalpa</s>), which is a composite of all cognitive forms, arises as a subsequent entity.
Because even that [composite cognition], being possessed of form (<s>sākāra</s>), cannot be gross.

children.translated_text: As <s>Dharmakīrti</s> states: 'Therefore, neither in the object nor in cognition does a gross appearance belonging to that nature [exist];

body.translated_text: the external object is impossible." He refutes: "This is not a sound determination." The idea here is: pots, cloths, and the like appear as gross, not as extremely subtle. Now, this grossness, characterized by extension across multiple directions, even if combined with the form of cognition through the association of contradictory properties — namely obstruction and non-obstruction — since the substratum of cognition is by nature unobstructed, nevertheless its manifoldness — entailed by the association of contradictory properties characterized as being in this place and not in that place, being rigid and red and non-rigid and non-red — cannot be prevented even by <s>Śakra</s> (Indra) himself, even on the view that [grossness] is a form of cognition. The alternatives of being co-extensive or not co-extensive [with the pervaded], and the partedness of the atom, have been demonstrated in the examination of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> [system]. Therefore, just as grossness is impossible in an external object [composed of atoms], so too is it impossible in cognition. Moreover, a single cognition cannot have atomic appearance, since a single entity cannot have a manifold nature. Or, if the forms are identical with cognition, there would be the absurd consequence of [all forms collapsing into] unity. Nor can there be as many cognitions as there are forms, for since that many cognitions would be mutually unaware, there would be the absurd consequence of the absence of gross experience.

yathā hi sarvaṃ cākṣuṣaṃ prabhārūpānuviddhaṃ buddhibodhyaṃ niyamena manujairupalabhyate, na caitāvatā ghaṭādirūpaṃ prabhātmakaṃ bhavati,kintu prabhopāyatvānniyamaḥ, evamihāpyātmasākṣikānubhavopāyatvādarthasyaikopalambhaniyama iti /
api ca yatraikavijñānagocarau ghaṭapaṭau tatrārthabhedaṃ vijñānabhedaṃ cādyavasyanti pratipattāraḥ /
na caitadekātmye 'vakalpata ityāha-- #tathā ghaṭadarśanaṃ paṭajñānamiti# /
tathārthābhede 'pi vijñānabhedadarśanānna vijñānātmakatvamarthasyetyāha-- #tathā ghaṭadarśanaṃ ghaṭasmaraṇamiti# /
api ca svarūpamātraparyavasitaṃ jñānaṃ jñānāntaravārtānabhijñamiti yayorbhedaste dve na gṛhīte iti bhedo 'pi tadgato na gṛhīta iti /
evaṃ kṣaṇikaśūnyānātmatvādayo 'pyanekapratijñāhetudṛṣṭāntajñānabhedasādhyāḥ /
evaṃ svamasādhāraṇamanyato vyāvṛtaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ yasya tadapi yadvyāvartate yataśca vyāvartate tadanekajñānasādhyam /
evaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇamapi vidhirūpamanyāpoharūpaṃ vānekajñānagamyam /
evaṃ vāsyavāsakabhāvo 'nekajñānasādhyaḥ /
evamavidyopaplavavaśena yatsadasaddharmatvaṃ yathā nīlamiti saddharmaḥ, naraviṣāṇāmityasaddharmaḥ, amūrtamiti sadasaddharmaḥ /

children.translated_text: For it is possible to say that a hare's horn is formless,
and it is possible to say that consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is formless.
As stated: 'Established through conceptual construction born of beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>),
the word-referent is of three kinds, based on existence, non-existence, and both.'

body.translated_text: Thus it is established. Therefore, even you [the Buddhist], when attempting to justify the grossness of the cognitive form, must rely on the possibility and impossibility that presuppose the operation and non-operation of valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). And if so, it is impossible to deny the external [object] which is distinct from cognition and which serves as the basis for this [grossness]. And as for the conformity of cognition to the object (<s>viṣaya-sārūpya</s>) that was posited for the determination of cognition with respect to each object — the object cannot be denied thereby, since without a real object, neither that conformity nor that determination would be possible. This is stated: 'Nor [can it be denied] because of the conformity of cognition to the object.' And the rule of co-apprehension (<s>sahopalambha-niyama</s>) that was stated also does not withstand analysis. If the apprehension of cognition and object occurs together, then [co-apprehension] is a contradictory reason (<s>viruddha-hetu</s>) and cannot establish non-difference, since togetherness is pervaded by difference which contradicts [non-difference], and in the case of non-difference, togetherness would be impossible. If, however, the rule is one of single apprehension — no, the word 'together' (<s>saha</s>) does not denote oneness. Moreover, is there apprehension as one, or is there one apprehension of cognition and object? It is not apprehension as one — this is stated: 'And because of the external apprehension of the object.' If [you mean] a rule of single apprehension, to that he says: 'Therefore, the rule of co-apprehension too pertains to the content of cognition and is caused by the means-and-end relationship, not by non-difference — this should be understood.' Just as all visual [perception] is invariably apprehended by humans as pervaded by the form of light and knowable by the intellect, yet the form of a pot and so on does not thereby become identical with light — rather, the invariable rule is due to light being the means — so too here, the rule of single apprehension of the object is due to the witness-self (<s>ātma-sākṣin</s>) being the means of experience. Moreover, where a pot and a cloth are objects of a single cognition, the cognizers ascertain both a difference of objects and a difference of cognitions. And this cannot be accounted for if they are identical in nature — this is stated: 'Thus, the seeing of the pot and the cognition of the cloth.' Likewise, even when the objects are non-different, since a difference of cognitions is observed, the object is not of the nature of cognition — this is stated: 'Thus, the seeing of the pot and the remembering of the pot.' Moreover, cognition, being confined to its own essential nature alone and unaware of the content of other cognitions — since those two [cognitions] whose difference [exists] are not grasped [as one], the difference pertaining to them is also not grasped. Similarly, momentariness, emptiness, non-self and so on are also to be established through multiple cognitions of thesis, reason, example, and the differences among them. Likewise, one's own unique characteristic (<s>sva-lakṣaṇa</s>), which is differentiated from others, and that from which it is differentiated and that by which it is differentiated — all require multiple cognitions. Similarly, the universal characteristic (<s>sāmānya-lakṣaṇa</s>), whether in the form of positive entity or in the form of exclusion of the other (<s>anyāpoha</s>), is cognizable through multiple cognitions. Likewise, the relationship of container and contained (<s>vāsya-vāsaka</s>) requires multiple cognitions. Similarly, through the influence of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the property of being existent-and-non-existent: 'blue' is an existent property, 'the horn of a man' is a non-existent property, 'formless' is an existent-and-non-existent property.

no khalu chidā chidyate kintu dāru /
nāpi pākaḥ pacyate 'pi tu taṇḍulāḥ /

ayamarthaḥ-- svarūpādatiriktamarthaṃ cedvijñānaṃ gṛhṇāti tatastadapratyakṣaṃ sannarthaṃ pratyakṣayitumarhati /
na hi cakṣuriva tannilīnamarthe kañcanātiśayamādhatte, yenārthamapratyakṣaṃ satpratyakṣayet /
apitu tatpratyakṣataivārthapratyakṣatā /
yathāhuḥ-- 'apratyakṣopalambhasya nārthadṛṣṭiḥ prasidhyati'iti /
taccet jñānāntareṇa pratīyeta tadapratītaṃ nārthaviṣayaṃ jñānamaparokṣayitumarhati /
evaṃ tattadityanavasthā tasmādanavasthāyā bibhyatā varaṃ svātmani vṛttirāsthitā /
apica yathā pradīpo na dīpāntaramapekṣate, evaṃ jñānamapi na jñānāntaramapekṣitumarhati samatvāditi /
body.translated_text: Thus, the thesis of liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) too — who is liberated, from what one is liberated, and by what one is liberated — requires multiple cognitions to be established. Similarly, the thesis that demonstrates the disputed point — what is demonstrated, by what it is demonstrated, and who [demonstrates] — all require multiple cognitions. Therefore, without a single [consciousness] that synthesizes the cognitions of multiple objects, none of this is possible. All of this is untenable if cognition apprehends only its own aspect — this is stated: 'Moreover, of two cognitions, earlier and later in time.' Furthermore, the relationship of action and result (<s>karma-phala</s>), which depends on difference, cannot obtain in a non-different cognition. Indeed, it is not the cutting that is cut, but the wood; nor is it the cooking that is cooked, but the rice. So too here, cognition does not, by its own aspect, operate upon the knowable, due to the contradiction of being both agent and object of the same action — rather, the object is distinct from it, just as the rice to be cooked is distinct from the cooking. Introducing a new topic, he says: 'Moreover, something else: one would accept that cognition cognizes cognition.' He raises an objection: 'But surely cognition does not apprehend anything beyond its own nature.' The meaning is this: if cognition apprehends an object not distinct from its own nature, then, being itself not directly perceived, it cannot render the object directly perceptible. For it does not, like the eye, impart any special quality to the object latent in it, by which it could make the non-perceived object perceived. Rather, the direct perceptibility of cognition itself is the direct perceptibility of the object. As they say: 'For one whose apprehension is not directly perceived, the vision of the object is not established.' If [cognition] were cognized by another cognition, then that [first cognition], being itself uncognized, would not be able to render the object directly perceptible. Thus, [cognition upon cognition] and so on — there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, those who fear the infinite regress should rather accept self-operation [of cognition]. Moreover, just as a lamp does not require another lamp, so too cognition should not require another cognition, because of their similarity.

tadetatpariharati-- #tadubhayamapyasat /
vijñānagrahaṇamātra eva vijñānasākṣiṇo grahaṇākāṅkṣānutpādādanavasthāśaṅkānupapatteḥ# /

artho hi nilīnasvabhāvaḥ pramātāraṃ prati svapratyakṣatvāyāntaḥkaraṇavikārabhedamanubhavamapekṣate, anubhavastu jaḍo 'pi svacchatayā caitanyūbimbodgrahaṇāya nānubhavāntaramapekṣate, yenānavasthā bhavet /
nahyasti saṃbhavo 'nubhava utpannaśca,na ca pramātuḥ pratyakṣo bhavati, yathā nīlādiḥ /
tasmādyathā chettā chidayā chedyaṃ vṛkṣādi vyāpnoti, na tu chidā chidāntareṇa, nāpi chidaiva chetrī, kintu svata eva devadattādiḥ, yathā vā paktā pākyaṃ pākena vyāpnoti nanu pākaṃ pākāntareṇa, nāpi pāka eva paktā kintu svata eva devadettādiḥ, evaṃ pramātā prameyaṃ nīlādi pramayā vyāpnoti na tu pramāṃ pramāntareṇa, nāpi pramaiva pramātrī, kintu svata eva pramāyāḥ pramātā vyāpakaḥ /
na ca pramātari kūṭasthanityacaitanye pramāpekṣāsaṃbhavo yataḥ pramātuḥ pramāyāḥ pramātrantarāpekṣāyāmanavasthā bhavet /

tatrāha- #sākṣipratyayayośca svabhāvavaiṣamyādupalabdhrupalabhyabhāvopapatteḥ# /
mā bhūt jñānayoḥ sāmyena grāhyagrāhakabhāvaḥ /
jñātṛjñānayostu vaiṣamyādupapadyata eva /
grāhyatvaṃ ca jñānasya na grāhakakriyājanitaphalaśālitayā yathā bāhyārthasya, phale phalāntarānupapatteḥ. yathāhuḥ-- 'na saṃvidaryate phalatvāt' iti /

children.text: nanu sākṣisthāne 'stvasmadabhimatameva vijñānaṃ tathā ca nāmnyeva vipratipattirnārthā iti śaṅkate-- #sākṣiṇo 'vagantuḥ svayaṃsiddhatāmupakṣipatā#abhipreya #tā svayaṃ prathate vijñānamityeṣa eveti# /
children.translated_text: One might object: 'Let our own accepted cognition occupy the position of the witness; and thus the disagreement is merely nominal, not substantive.' He raises this objection with the words: 'By one who implies the self-established nature of the knower, the witness,' intending [the Buddhist position that] 'cognition shines by itself — this is just that [witness].'
He refutes this: 'No.'

children.text: bhavanti hi vijñānasyotpādādayo dharmā abhyupetāstathā cāsya phalatayā nāvagantṛtvaṃ, kartṛphalabhāvasyaikatra virodhāt /
children.translated_text: For cognition is admitted to have properties such as origination and so forth; and thus, being a result, it cannot be the knower, since the roles of agent and result are contradictory in a single entity.
Rather, it is merely similar to a lamp and so on — this is the meaning. //28//

body.translated_text: He refutes both [objections]: 'Both of these are untenable. Since, upon the mere apprehension by cognition, no desire for [further] apprehension arises in the witness of cognition, the apprehension of an infinite regress is impossible.' The meaning is this: it is true that for one whose apprehension is not directly perceived, the vision of the object is not established; however, for the apprehender, another apprehension is not required for the direct perceptibility of that [cognition]. Rather, when, through the contact of sense and object, a modification of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) has arisen, the luminous [consciousness] and the object and the apprehension all become directly perceived simultaneously. For the object, whose nature is concealed, requires a modification of the internal organ — namely, experience (<s>anubhava</s>) — for its direct perceptibility to the knower. But experience, though inert, due to its transparency does not require another experience for receiving the reflection of consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>), and therefore no infinite regress arises. For there is no possibility that an experience has arisen and yet is not directly perceived by the knower, as [happens with objects like] blue and so on. Therefore, just as the cutter pervades the object to be cut (such as a tree) through the cutting instrument, but the cutting instrument is not [pervaded] by another cutting instrument, nor is the cutting instrument itself the cutter — rather, <s>Devadatta</s> and so on are the cutter by their own nature; and just as the cooker pervades the cookable through cooking, but cooking is not [pervaded] by another cooking, nor is cooking itself the cooker — rather, <s>Devadatta</s> and so on are the cooker by their own nature; so too, the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) pervades the knowable such as blue through the means of valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), but the means of cognition is not [pervaded] by another means, nor is the means of cognition itself the knower — rather, the knower is by its own nature the pervader of the means of cognition. And since the knower is an immutable, eternal consciousness (<s>kūṭastha-nitya-caitanya</s>), there is no possibility of it requiring a means of cognition, which would [otherwise] lead to an infinite regress if the knower required another knower for the means of cognition. Therefore, it is well said: 'Upon the mere apprehension by cognition, no desire for [further] apprehension arises in the witness of cognition — the knower who is immutable, eternal consciousness.' As for what was stated — 'Because of similarity, the relationship of illuminated and illuminator is impossible' — to that he says: 'And because of the essential dissimilarity between the witness and the cognition, the relationship of apprehender and apprehended is established.' Let there not be a grasper-grasped relationship between two cognitions due to their similarity; but between the knower and cognition, due to their dissimilarity, it is indeed established. And the graspability of cognition is not in the manner of producing a result through the action of grasping, as with an external object, since a result cannot produce another result. As they say: 'Awareness is not the object [of another awareness], because it is a result.' Rather, [it is grasped] through its self-established manifestness to the knower. The object too, though grasped, is manifest to the knower only when awareness exists; and awareness too is manifest. As others say: 'There is no objecthood of this [awareness].' One might say: 'Whatever is illuminated is illuminated by something else, just as cognition and object are; and so too the witness — therefore there is no dissimilarity between the cognition and the witness.' To this he says: 'And because the self-established witness cannot be rejected.' For this witness, being always undoubted and unerring, its nature of eternal direct perception and non-adventitious luminosity is established. Thus, the knower, even when doubting, is himself undoubted; even when erring, is himself unerring; even when conjecturing about a remote object, is himself not remote; even when remembering, is himself an experiencer — for every living being. And this cannot be established if awareness depends on something else. The absurdity of infinite regress has been stated. Therefore, the self-established nature [of the witness] is irrefutable even by one who does not wish it, because it is established by the path of valid knowledge. Moreover, since cognition by the method described above lacks the capacity of being a self-knower, if one who does not accept the knower says 'cognition, like a lamp, shines by itself without depending on another illuminator' — then one would be saying that cognition is beyond the reach of valid means of knowledge and has no knower, like the shining of a thousand lamps inside a solid rock. And if it is not manifest to any knower at all, then what use is self-luminosity? To one who holds that cognition itself is the knower, he raises an objection: 'Very well, so be it — because [cognition] is of the nature of experience.' A result cannot be the agent or the object — and therefore, just as with a lamp, a separate agent must be posited; and thus this is not a case of proving what is already established. He refutes: 'No — because of another knower.'

jāgratpratyayasya tu bādhyatve svapnapratyayasyāsau na bādhako bhavet /
nahi bādhyameva bādhakaṃ bhavitumarhati /
tathā ca na svapnapratyayo mithyeti sādhyavikalo dṛṣṭāntaḥ syāt svapnavaditi /
tasmādbādhābādhābhyāṃ vaidharmyānna svapnapratyayadṛṣṭāntena jāgratpratyayasya śakyaṃ nirālambanatvamadhyavasātum /
#nidrāglānamiti# /
karaṇadoṣābhidānam /
mithyātvāya vaidharmyāntaramāha- #- api ca smṛtireveti# /
saṃskāramātrajaṃ hi vijñānaṃ smṛtiḥ /
pratyutpannendriyasaṃprayogaliṅgaśabdasārūpyānyathānupapadyamānayogyapramāṇānutpattilakṣaṇasāmagrīprabhavaṃ tu jñānamupalabghiḥ /
tadiha nidrāṇasyasāmagryantaravirahātsaṃskāraḥ pariśiṣyate, tena saṃskārajatvātsmṛtiḥ, sāpi ca nidrādoṣādviparītāvartamānamapi pitrādi vartamānatayā bhāsayati /
tena smṛtereva tāvadupalabdherviśeṣastasyāśca smṛtervaiparītyamiti /

children.text: api ca svataḥprāmāṇye siddhe jāgratpratyayānāṃ yathārthatvamanubhavasiddhaṃ nānumānenānyathayituṃ śakyam, anubhavavirodhena tadanutpādāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, when self-validity (<s>svataḥ prāmāṇya</s>) is established, the veridicality of waking cognitions is established through experience itself and cannot be overturned by inference, since [such inference] cannot arise due to its contradiction with experience.
The fact of having an unsublated object is also a valid means of knowledge, insofar as it is graspable by the causal complex that produces inference.
And an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause — with this intent he says: 'Moreover, because there would be the absurdity of contradiction with experience.'

body.translated_text: 'And because of dissimilarity, [waking experience] is not like dream and so on.' The dissimilarity consists in being sublated and unsublated. Dream cognition is sublated, while waking cognition is unsublated. Even you [the Buddhist] must accept the unsublated nature of waking cognition, for it is by waking cognition that dream cognition is sublated and known to be false. If waking cognition were also sublatable, then it could not serve as the sublator of dream cognition. For indeed, what is itself sublatable cannot be a sublator. And thus, dream cognition would not be false, and the example 'like a dream' would lack the property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>). Therefore, due to the dissimilarity of being sublated and unsublated, one cannot determine the contentlessness of waking cognition by the example of dream cognition. 'Drowsiness and fatigue' — this indicates a defect in the cognitive instrument (<s>karaṇa-doṣa</s>). He states another point of dissimilarity regarding falsity: 'Moreover, [dream cognition] is merely memory (<s>smṛti</s>).' For cognition born solely from latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is memory. Cognition that arises from the capacity of a causal complex characterized by present sense-contact, inferential marks, words, similarity, or the non-arising of otherwise-inexplicable valid means — that is apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>). Here, for one who is asleep, since other causal complexes are absent, only latent impressions remain; therefore, being born from impressions, it is memory. And that [memory] too, due to the defect of sleep, is distorted — it presents as present things like a father and so on that are not actually present. Thus, the distinction from apprehension belongs to memory itself, and that memory is distorted. Therefore the difference [between dream and waking] is great — this is the meaning.

body.text:
na bhāvo 'nupalabdheḥ# /
yathālokadarśanaṃ cānvayavyatirekāvanuśriyamāṇāvartha evopalabdherbhavato nārthānapekṣāyāṃ vāsanāyām /
vāsanāya apyarthopalabdhyadhīnatvadarśanādityarthaḥ /
api cāśrayābhāvādapi na laukikī vāsanopapadyate /

children.translated_text: And a momentary store-consciousness (<s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>) cannot serve as the substratum of latent impressions.
For two things arising simultaneously cannot have the relationship of support and supported, just like the left and right horns [of an animal].

children.text: prāgutpannasya cādheyotpādasamaye 'sataḥ kṣaṇikatvavyāghāta ityāśayavānāha-- #api ca vāsanā nāmeti# /
children.translated_text: And for what arose previously, at the time of the arising of the supported, it would be non-existent [due to momentariness], which contradicts momentariness — with this intent he says: 'Moreover, [what is called] latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>)...'
The rest is self-evident in meaning. //30//

body.translated_text: 'The [external] object does not exist, because of non-apprehension' — [this Buddhist thesis is refuted as follows.] Just as the perception of light, when examined through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), pertains to the object alone, apprehension belongs to you not through object-independent latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>). For latent impression too is seen to depend on the apprehension of an object — this is the meaning. Moreover, worldly latent impression is impossible even because of the absence of a substratum (<s>āśraya</s>).

children.translated_text: Moreover, what is to be negated must be something superimposed (<s>āropita</s>).

children.text: āropaśca tattvādhiṣṭhāno dṛṣṭo yathā śuktikādiṣu rajatādeḥ /
children.translated_text: And superimposition is observed to rest upon a real substrate (<s>tattva</s>), as silver upon mother-of-pearl and so on.

children.text: na cet kiñcidasti tattvaṃ kasya kasminnāropaḥ /
children.translated_text: If there is no reality whatsoever, what is superimposed upon what?

children.text: tasmānniṣprapañcaṃ paramārthasabrahmānirvācyaprapañcātmanāropyate, tacca tattvaṃ vyavasthāpyātāttvikatvena sāṃvyavahārikaṃ pramāṇānāṃ bādhakenopapadyata iti yuktamutpaśyāmaḥ //31 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the unmanifest ultimate reality — <s>Brahman</s> — is superimposed upon by the inexpressible (<s>anirvācya</s>) phenomenal world; and it is proper, we see, that by establishing that reality and then sublating [the phenomenal world] as non-ultimate, the conventional validity of the means of knowledge is [appropriately] accounted for through the sublating cognition. //31//

body.translated_text: The meaning is: they do not stand firm in any position whatsoever. Wishing to refute this, he says: 'But the position of the <s>Śūnyavādin</s> (emptiness-advocate) is contradicted by all valid means of knowledge, and therefore no effort is made to refute it.' For worldly valid means of knowledge deal with existence and non-existence. When something existent is grasped as existent, veridical and non-erroneous reality is established thereby. When something non-existent is grasped as non-existent, veridical and non-erroneous reality is established thereby. But one who establishes the inability of both existence and non-existence to withstand analysis thereby establishes something contradicted by all valid means of knowledge. And thus, because of contradicting all valid means, this position is untenable. If it be said that this analysis overturns the ultimate validity of the means of knowledge but not their conventional (<s>sāṃvyavahārika</s>) validity, and that therefore, since they pertain to different domains, there is no contradiction with all valid means — to this he says: 'For this [empirical] world-transaction, established by all valid means of knowledge, cannot be denied without arriving at another reality.' For valid means of knowledge, operating within their own domain, operate precisely [with the understanding] that 'this is reality.' Their non-ultimacy, however, must be understood from a separate sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka</s>) regarding their domain. They do not operate [with the understanding] 'our validity is merely conventional, not ultimate.' And the sublating cognition should demonstrate their non-ultimacy by revealing a reality contrary to the object of the entire range of valid means, just as [one says] 'this is mother-of-pearl, not silver,' 'these are mirages, not water,' 'there is one moon, not two' — similarly here too, one should demonstrate the non-ultimacy of the means of knowledge through a sublating cognition that establishes a reality contrary to the object of all means of knowledge; but without establishing such an alternative reality, the means of knowledge cannot be sublated. If it be said that by establishing the inability of things to withstand analysis as their true nature, the sublating cognition demonstrates the non-ultimacy of the means of knowledge — then, what exactly is this 'inability to withstand analysis'? Is it a real entity that is held to be the true nature? Is it ultimately one of the [four alternatives] — existent and so on — that merely does not withstand analysis? Or is it, by virtue of its inability to withstand analysis, devoid of any nature whatsoever? In the first case, [to say] it is ultimately one of the [alternatives] — existent and so on — and yet does not withstand analysis is self-contradictory. If it does not withstand [analysis], then it is not any one of [the alternatives] — existent and so on. But if it is one of them, how can it not withstand analysis? And if it is devoid of any nature — how can one say this without establishing [some] alternative nature? Nor is the very absence of nature the nature of things. For in that case, there would be an absence of nature. And that [absence] too, you have said, does not withstand analysis.

children.translated_text: He elaborates: 'In brief' — both textually and in meaning — 'this is the Buddhist (<s>Vaināśika</s>) doctrine.'
Textually, [the Buddhist scriptures contain] incorrect word-usages such as 'paśyanātiṣṭhāna,' 'middha,' 'poṣadha,' and so forth.

And in meaning, having accepted non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>), [the Buddhist] who then posits a store-consciousness (<s>ālaya-vijñāna</s>) as the substratum of all latent impressions tacitly accepts an imperishable self (<s>ātman</s>).

body.translated_text: 'Not in a single [entity], because of impossibility.' Thus the doctrine of the <s>Sugatās</s> (Buddhists), who are unclad [in consistent logic], has been refuted. Now the doctrine of the unclad ones (<s>Vivasanās</s>, i.e., Jainas) is refuted. He states their doctrine in both summary and detail. 'And these seven categories (<s>padārthas</s>) are accepted by them.' There he states the summary: 'In brief, there are just two categories.' The conscious soul (<s>jīva</s>) and the insentient class is the non-soul (<s>ajīva</s>). The further elaboration of these two — <s>jīva</s> and <s>ajīva</s> — is stated as appropriate. He says: 'The five extended substances (<s>astikāyas</s>) are named thus. And the sub-divisions of all these...' The soul-substance (<s>jīvāstikāya</s>) is threefold: bound (<s>baddha</s>), liberated (<s>mukta</s>), and eternally accomplished (<s>nitya-siddha</s>). The matter-substance (<s>pudgalāstikāya</s>) is sixfold: the four elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) beginning with earth, and the stationary (<s>sthāra</s>) and the mobile (<s>jaṅgama</s>). The principle-of-motion substance (<s>dharmāstikāya</s>) is inferred from activity; the principle-of-rest substance (<s>adharmāstikāya</s>) is inferred from rest. The space-substance (<s>ākāśāstikāya</s>) is twofold: occupied space (<s>lokākāśa</s>) and unoccupied space (<s>alokākāśa</s>). Of these, the occupied space exists between the worlds situated one above another; above them, the place of liberation is the unoccupied space, for there are no worlds there. Thus the two categories of <s>jīva</s> and <s>ajīva</s> have been elaborated fivefold. The three categories — influx (<s>āsrava</s>), restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>), and dissipation (<s>nirjarā</s>) — characterized by activity, are elaborated [as follows]. Activity is twofold: right and wrong. Wrong activity is influx (<s>āsrava</s>). Right activity is restraint and dissipation. <s>Āsrava</s> is the activity of the senses that causes the person to flow towards sense-objects; for through the doors of the senses, the luminous essence of the person is transformed in the form of cognition of objects such as form and so on. Others, however, call <s>karmas</s> the influx, for they pervade and follow the agent, flowing [with him] — hence <s>āsrava</s>. This wrong activity is the cause of harm. Restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>) and dissipation (<s>nirjarā</s>) are right activity. Of these, activity in the form of tranquility (<s>śama</s>), self-control (<s>dama</s>), and so on is restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>); for it closes the door of the stream of influx, hence it is called <s>saṃvara</s>.

children.text: tatra #sarvatra cemaṃ saptabhaṅgīnayaṃ nāma nyāyamavatārayanti, syādasti, syānnāsti, syādasti ca nāsti ca, syādavaktavyaḥ, syādasti cāvaktavyaśca, syānnāsti cāvaktavyaśca, syādasti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaśceti# /
children.translated_text: Among these, 'they introduce everywhere this method called the seven-fold predication (<s>saptabhaṅgī-naya</s>): (1) perhaps it exists (<s>syād asti</s>), (2) perhaps it does not exist (<s>syān nāsti</s>), (3) perhaps it both exists and does not exist (<s>syād asti ca nāsti ca</s>), (4) perhaps it is inexpressible (<s>syād avaktavyaḥ</s>), (5) perhaps it exists and is inexpressible (<s>syād asti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>), (6) perhaps it does not exist and is inexpressible (<s>syān nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>), (7) perhaps it exists and does not exist and is inexpressible (<s>syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca</s>).'
The word <s>syāt</s> is indeed a particle resembling a finite verb form, indicating non-absoluteness (<s>anekānta</s>).
As they say: 'In sentences, the particle <s>syāt</s> shines forth as indicating non-absoluteness, serving as a qualifier of the meaning to be understood,
because of its connection with meaning, being a particle resembling a finite verb form.'

body.translated_text: Dissipation (<s>nirjarā</s>) is [the practice] such as ascending heated rocks, which is the cause of eliminating the merit and demerit that have been sullied by the afflictions (<s>kaṣāya</s>) accumulated since beginningless time. For it completely wears away (<s>jarayati</s>) merit and demerit through the experience of pleasure and pain — hence <s>nirjarā</s>. Bondage (<s>bandha</s>) is eightfold <s>karma</s>. Of these, obstructive <s>karma</s> (<s>ghātikarma</s>) is fourfold, namely: knowledge-obscuring (<s>jñānāvaraṇīya</s>), perception-obscuring (<s>darśanāvaraṇīya</s>), deluding (<s>mohanīya</s>), and obstructive (<s>antarāya</s>). Likewise, the four non-obstructive <s>karmas</s> (<s>aghātikarma</s>) are: feeling-producing (<s>vedanīya</s>), name-determining (<s>nāmika</s>), status-determining (<s>gotrika</s>), and life-span-determining (<s>āyuṣka</s>). Of these, right knowledge is not the means of liberation — for the establishment of a real entity does not follow from knowledge, lest there be an absurd over-extension — hence the opposite view is called knowledge-obscuring <s>karma</s>. The cognition 'liberation does not come from mere seeing and practice' is perception-obscuring <s>karma</s>. Among the many mutually contradictory paths to liberation taught by the <s>Tīrthaṅkaras</s>, the inability to determine their specific [validity] is deluding <s>karma</s>. The cognition that creates obstacles for those engaged in the path of liberation is obstructive <s>karma</s>. These are called obstructive <s>karmas</s> because they destroy spiritual welfare. The non-obstructive <s>karmas</s> are: feeling-producing <s>karma</s> is the cause of the fruition of luminous matter (<s>śukla-pudgala</s>); for even though it is bondage, it does not obstruct the highest good, since it does not obstruct the knowledge of reality. Name-determining <s>karma</s> accords with the feeling-producing <s>karma</s> that initiates luminous matter; for it brings about the initial stage of luminous matter — the embryonic form (<s>kalala-budbudādi</s>). Status-determining [<s>karma</s>] is indeterminate and exists in a prior, latent form (<s>śakti-rūpeṇa</s>). Life-span-determining (<s>āyuṣka</s>) is so called because it 'tells' (<s>kāyati</s>) or declares the lifespan through the door of production. These are non-obstructive <s>karmas</s> because they depend on luminous matter and so on. This eightfold <s>karma</s> binds the person — hence bondage (<s>bandha</s>). Liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), according to some, is the abiding of the self — from whom all afflictions and their impressions have fallen away, who possesses unobstructed knowledge and the nature of bliss — in the uppermost region. Others say: the soul, whose nature is to move upward, being bound by the principle-of-motion-and-rest substance (<s>dharmādharmāstikāya</s>), upon release from that [bondage], goes upward — that alone is liberation. These are the seven categories beginning with <s>jīva</s>, along with their sub-divisions, as presented.

body.text: 'iti //
body.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: yadi punarayamanekāntadyotakaḥ syācchabdo na bhavet syādastītivākye syātpadamanarthakaṃ syāt tadidamuktam-- 'arthayogitvāt'iti /
children.translated_text: If, however, this word <s>syāt</s> were not an indicator of non-absoluteness, then in the sentence '<s>syād asti</s>' (perhaps it exists), the word <s>syāt</s> would be meaningless. This is [addressed by] the statement 'because of its connection with meaning.'

children.text: anaikāntadyotakatve tu syādasti kathañcidastīti syātpadātkathañcidartho 'stītyanenānuktaḥ pratīyata iti nānarthakyam /
children.translated_text: But if [<s>syāt</s>] does not indicate non-absoluteness, then from the word <s>syāt</s> in '<s>syād asti</s>' the meaning 'it exists in some respect' — the sense of 'in some respect' (<s>kathañcit</s>), which is not explicitly stated by '<s>asti</s>' alone — is understood [implicitly], and therefore it is not meaningless.
And thus: '<s>Syādvāda</s> (the doctrine of conditional predication), by abandoning absolutism in every respect, through the operation of a certain rule,
with reference to the seven-fold predication method, distinguishes what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.'

yattu kvacit kathañcit kadācit kenacidātmanāstītyucyate, yathā prapañcaḥ, tadvyavahārato na tu paramārthataḥ, tasya vicārāsahatvāt /
