children.translated_text: And an alternative cannot obtain in a [single] real entity.

children.text: tasmāt sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti jñānavat saptatvapañcatvanirdhāraṇasya phalasya nirdhārayituśca pramātustatkaraṇasya pramāṇasya ca tatprameyasya ca saptatvapañcatvasya sadasattvasaṃśaye sādhu samarthitaṃ tīrthakaratvabhṛṣebheṇātmanaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as in the cognition 'is it a post or a person?', the result of determining whether there are seven or five [categories], the knower who determines, the means of knowledge that is the instrument of determination, and the object of knowledge that is the [nature of] seven-ness or five-ness — in the doubt between existence and non-existence of all these, the <s>Tīrthaṅkara</s> has well established his own [claim to] authority!

children.text: nirdhāraṇasya caikāntasattve sarvatra nānekāntavāda ityāha-- #ya ete sapta padārthā iti# /
children.translated_text: And if determination [itself] were absolutely existent, then the non-absolutist doctrine would not apply anywhere — this he says: 'These seven categories...'
The rest is self-evident in meaning. //33//

body.translated_text: In the operation of a cognition, by the rule of the particle 'cit' (indicating 'a certain'), through the abandonment of absolutism in every respect, the <s>syādvāda</s> is established with reference to the analysis (<s>bhaṅga</s>) within each of the seven [absolute] positions, for the purpose of distinguishing what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. For if a thing existed absolutely — that is, in every way, at all times, in all places, in all aspects — it would simply exist, and then no one would ever engage in or withdraw from it through desire or aversion in any respect, at any time, or in any manner, since it would be beyond attainment or avoidance, and since abandonment of the undesirable would be impossible. But in the non-absolutist position, since [a thing] exists for someone, at some time, in some place, in some respect, engagement and disengagement become possible for the discerning. He refutes this seven-fold predication method: 'Not in a single [entity], because of impossibility.' He elaborates: 'For in a single substrate' — which is ultimately real — 'the simultaneous co-presence of properties such as existence and so on' — which are mutually exclusive by nature — 'is not possible.' What is said amounts to this: what truly exists, exists in every way, at all times, in all places, in all aspects, in an inexpressible manner — it simply exists and is not non-existent, like the inner self (<s>pratyag-ātman</s>). But that which is said to exist for someone, in some respect, at some time, in some aspect — like the phenomenal world (<s>prapañca</s>) — that is [so] conventionally, not ultimately, because it cannot withstand analysis. Nor does mere cognition establish reality, since in [cases like] mother-of-pearl and mirages, there would be the absurd consequence of the reality of silver and water as well. If [reality were established] by the non-sublation of ordinary [cognition], then since the identification of the body with the self is also unsublated [for the ordinary person], if that were taken as ultimate, the materialist (<s>Lokāyata</s>) view would follow and there would be the absurd consequence of nihilism. But for those of discerning intellect, the sublation through analysis of the body-self identification is the same as [the sublation] of the phenomenal world's non-absoluteness. Moreover, since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, their combination is impossible; [only] an alternative [between them is possible].

children.translated_text: A lamp, to begin with, cannot serve as an illustration here, because of the absurd consequence of impermanence.

children.text: viśarāravo hi pradīpāvayavaḥ #,#pradīpaścāvayavī pratikṣaṇamutpattinirodhadharmā, tasmādanityatvāttasya nāsthiro jīvastadavayavāścābyupetavyāḥ /
children.translated_text: For the parts of a lamp are perishable, and the lamp as a composite entity (<s>avayavin</s>) is subject to origination and destruction at every moment; therefore, because of its impermanence, the soul and its parts should not be modeled on it as something stable.
And thus the refutation stated under both alternatives applies.
And the infinity of the soul's parts that was proposed is even more untenable — this he says: 'Moreover, [the soul would be] mere body.' //34//

body.translated_text: 'And thus the incompleteness of the self (<s>ātma-akārtsnya</s>).' The word 'and thus' (<s>evaṃ ca</s>) indicates a cumulative [argument] by the particle 'ca.' For if the self were co-extensive with the body, there would be incompleteness, that is, limitedness. And consequently, impermanence — for all that is limited is impermanent, like a pot and so on; and so too the self. This is stated: 'Just as in a single substrate.' And this further [point of] incompleteness is formulated by the <s>sūtra</s>: 'And because bodies are of unstable size.' For a soul that has the size of a human body cannot pervade the entire body of an elephant, being too small — thus, because the self does not pervade the entire body, there is incompleteness; and therefore, the [Jaina theory that the] self has the size of the body is untenable. And when [the soul], leaving the elephant's body, becomes embodied in an ant, it does not fit entirely into the ant's body — thus the self is incomplete. The rest is easy [to understand]. He raises an objection: 'One might say: [the soul] has infinite parts.' Just as a lamp, being inside a pot or the interior of a great mansion, contracts and expands, so too the soul in the bodies of an ant and an elephant — this is the meaning. Having considered this alternative, he refutes it: 'But of those infinite [parts]...'

śaṅkāpūrvaṃ sūtrāntaramavatārayati- #atha paryāyeṇeti# /
tatrāpyucyate-- #na ca paryāyādapyavirodho vikārādibhyaḥ /
karmāṣṭaka#muktaṃ jñānāvaraṇīyādi /
kiṃ cātmano nityatvābhyupagame āgacchatāmapagacchatāṃ cāvayavānāmiyattānirūpeṇena cātmajñānābhāvānnāpavarga iti bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: Because of defects such as transformation and so on.
If the continuum is real, [there would be] transformation, and from that, the absurd consequence of impermanence like leather and so on.
And if it is unreal, the defect of the absurd consequence of the absence of self (<s>nairātmya</s>), indicated by the word 'and so on' (<s>ādi</s>), would follow.
The unclad ones (<s>Vivasanās</s>, Jainas) are [thus] refuted. //35//

body.translated_text: He introduces the next <s>sūtra</s> with a preliminary objection: 'Now, if [one proposes change] in succession...' To that too he responds: 'And there is no non-contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and other [defects]. The eightfold <s>karma</s>' — the knowledge-obscuring and so on, as stated. Moreover, if permanence of the self is accepted, since the number of parts that come and go cannot be determined, knowledge of the self would be impossible, and therefore there would be no liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) — this is the purport. 'Therefore, because of the absurdity of such and other defects.' The word 'and so on' (<s>ādi</s>) indicates [further] defects that we shall state. Moreover, do these parts of the soul each individually possess consciousness, or does the aggregate? If each individually possesses consciousness, then since many conscious entities cannot be determined to have a single purpose, the body would sometimes be torn apart by activities in contradictory directions. But if the aggregate possesses consciousness, then when the elephant's body becomes that of an ant, the soul — reduced to a remainder of two or three parts — would not be conscious, since the aggregate, having lost the majority [of its parts], would cease to exist in the ant's body. 'Or alternatively' — this [second interpretation applies as follows]: given the impermanence of the soul implied by the previous <s>sūtra</s>, one might suspect a continuity-based impermanence like the Buddhist [view], and hence this <s>sūtra</s>: 'And there is no non-contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and other [defects].' Even through succession — that is, even by accepting continuity despite the instability of size — there is no non-contradiction regarding bondage and liberation, since the self is [in fact] permanent. Why?

#antyāvasthiteścobhayanityatvādaviśeṣaḥ# /

abhūtvā bhāvināmantyatvāddhaṭadīnām /
kathaṃ cābhūtvā na bhavedyadi prāgapyāsīt /

children.translated_text: And here, the construction is: because both sizes would entail permanence.
And [the statement] that there would be only the size of a single body is to be understood [as the implication].
But in the second interpretation, the construction is: of both states.

children.text: ekaśarīraparimāṇatā na dīpyā, kintvekaparimāṇatāmātramaṇurmahān veti vivekaḥ //36 //
children.translated_text: The [consequence of] having the size of a single body need not be stated explicitly; rather, the mere point is of a single size — the distinction being whether [it is] atomic or large. //36//

body.translated_text: 'And because both [sizes] in the final state would be permanent, there is no distinction.' For the size of the soul that would obtain in the state of liberation would be permanent, if it did not previously fail to exist [i.e., if it existed all along]. The final state [shares the character of impermanence] with pots and so on, which come into being having not existed before. And how could it not have existed before, if it existed previously as well? Nor can it be unprecedented when confined to a different size. Therefore, the very final size existed previously too — hence there is no difference. And thus, the self would have only the size of a single body, and there would be no attainment of bodies of increased or decreased size, which contradicts the assumption that the self has the size of the body.

children.text: kāruṇye hi satyasya duḥkhaṃ bhavati tena tatprahāṇāya pravartata iti kāruṇikā api svārthaprayuktā eva pravartanta iti /
children.translated_text: For when compassion exists, one's own suffering arises, and therefore one acts to remove that; thus even compassionate persons act only when impelled by self-interest.

children.text: nanu svārthaprayukta eva pravartatāmevamapi ko doṣa ityata āha-- #svārthavatvādīsvarasyeti# /
children.translated_text: Objection: let him act impelled by self-interest alone — even so, what is the fault? To this he says — 'Because <s>Īśvara</s> would have self-interest.'
The meaning is: because he would be one who desires something.
'And because of the accepted indifference of <s>Puruṣa</s>' — there is no real activity. //37//

body.translated_text: To explain the purpose of removing the misconception that the general doctrine of <s>Īśvara</s> (God) as cause is refuted by this [<s>sūtra</s>], he says — 'only' etc. Those who rely on <s>Sāṅkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s> are <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>, <s>Patañjali</s>, and others. '<s>Pradhāna</s>' — this has been explained. The power of seeing is '<s>Puruṣa</s>' — the witness of cognitions. And the special <s>Puruṣa</s> untouched by the various <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karmas</s> (actions), <s>vipākas</s> (results), and <s>āśayas</s> (latent impressions) is <s>Īśvara</s>, who is different from <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>. The <s>Māheśvaras</s> are four — the <s>Śaivas</s>, the <s>Pāśupatas</s>, the <s>Kāruṇikasiddhāntins</s>, and the <s>Kāpālikas</s>. All four of these are called <s>Māheśvaras</s> because they follow the doctrines promulgated by <s>Maheśvara</s>. The cause is <s>Īśvara</s>. The effect is the <s>Pradhāna</s>-based <s>Mahat</s> and so forth. <s>Yoga</s> also consists of meditation on <s>Oṃkāra</s>, <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), and the like. The prescribed practice begins with bathing three times a day and ends with secret conduct; liberation is the cessation of suffering. The <s>paśus</s> (bound souls) are the <s>ātmans</s> (selves); their <s>pāśa</s> (bondage) is bondage, and release from that is the cessation of suffering. This is their position — since it is contradictory for a conscious superintendent like a potter to be merely the efficient cause of effects like a pot, it follows [that the objection is raised]. When this is thus set forth, it is stated — 'Because of the inconsistency of the Lord.' The intention here is this — it has been stated repeatedly that [these doctrines] are devoted solely to establishing that <s>Īśvara</s> is merely the efficient cause. Therefore, another means of valid knowledge must be relied upon in this matter. In that regard, inference is not possible to begin with, for it operates by following what is observed, and following that leads to inconsistency. This he states — 'inferior, middling' etc. What is said amounts to this — when <s>Īśvara</s> is established through scripture, observation should not be followed. For regarding heaven, <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit), deities, and such things known through scripture, there is nothing observed [to correspond]. Scripture does not proceed from similarity with the observed. Therefore, even though very many unobserved things of a nature contrary to observation are postulated for the purpose of establishing what is heard, they do not incur the taint of fallacy, because they are based on valid means of knowledge. Whatever conformity to observation is attempted there is merely out of friendliness. But inference independent of scripture, proceeding by similarity to the observed, is all the more afraid even of chaff when it contradicts observation. 'If it be said that there is no fault because [<s>Īśvara</s>'s activity] depends on the <s>karma</s> of living beings' — No. Why? 'Because of the defect of mutual dependence between <s>karma</s> and <s>Īśvara</s> as that which is to be set in motion and the mover respectively.' The meaning is this — if <s>Īśvara</s> is free from passion and subject to compassion, then he would not impel beings toward evil <s>karma</s>, nor would he superintend such <s>karma</s> even when it has arisen, and to that extent alone suffering would not arise for beings. For people dependent on <s>Īśvara</s> cannot independently perform evil <s>karma</s>. Or evil <s>karma</s> not superintended by him cannot be capable of producing its result. Therefore, even though <s>Īśvara</s> is independent, it must be supposed — contrary to observation — that he is set in motion by <s>karmas</s>. And thus this would be another boil upon a boil — the defect of mutual dependence would arise: <s>Īśvara</s> is to be set in motion by <s>karma</s>, and <s>karma</s> by <s>Īśvara</s>. He raises an objection — 'Because of beginninglessness.' <s>Īśvara</s> is set in motion by prior <s>karma</s> with respect to present <s>karma</s>, and by that <s>Īśvara</s> the present <s>karma</s> would be set in motion toward its own effect. He refutes this — 'Not as in the case of the present time.' But how does prior <s>karma</s>, not set in motion by <s>Īśvara</s>, produce the effect characterized as being set in motion by <s>Īśvara</s>? Even there, [the prior <s>karma</s>] was set in motion by <s>Īśvara</s> who was set in motion by still prior <s>karma</s> — thus the defect of blind leading the blind applies. For a blind person is led by a sighted person, not by another blind person. Similarly here too, both being things to be set in motion, who would set whom in motion? — this is the meaning. Moreover, that <s>Īśvara</s> according to the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> is without faults contradicts their own doctrine, he says — 'moreover' etc. But this is not our position — this is the purport. Objection: a person is seen to act even out of compassion, and compassion is not a fault. To this he says — 'One acts only when impelled by self-interest.'

body.text:
aparamapi dṛṣṭānusāreṇa dūṣaṇamāha-- #saṃbandhānupapatteśca# /
dṛṣṭo hi sāvayavānāmasarvagatānāṃ ca saṃyogaḥ /
aprāptipūrvikā hi prāptiḥ saṃyogo na sarvagatānāṃ saṃbhavatyaprāpterabhāvānniravayavatvācca /
avyāpyavṛttitā hi saṃyogasya svabhāvaḥ /
na ca niravayaveṣvavyāpyavṛttitā saṃyogasya saṃbhavatītyuktam /
tasmādavyāpyavṛttitāyāḥ saṃyogasya vyāpikāyā nivṛttestadvyāpyasya saṃyogasya vinivṛttiriti bhāvaḥ /
nāpi samavāyalakṣaṇaḥ /
sa hyayutasiddhānāmādhārādheyabhūtānāmihapratyayahetuḥ saṃbandha ityabhyupeyate /
na ca pradhānapuruṣeśvarāṇāṃ mitho 'styādhārādheyabhāva ityarthaḥ /
nāpi yogyatālakṣaṇaḥ kāryagamyasaṃbandha ityāha-- #nāpyanya iti# /
nahi pradhānasya mahadahaṅkārādikāraṇatvamadyāpi siddhamiti /
śaṅkate-- #brahmavādina iti# /
nirākaroti- #na# /
kutaḥ /
#tasya#mate 'nirvacanīya #tādātmyalakṣaṇasaṃbandhopapatteḥ /
apiceti# /
āgamo hi pravṛttiṃ prati na dṛṣṭāntamapekṣata ityadṛṣṭapūrve tadviruddhe ca pravartituṃ samarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: But inference, which follows observation, is not capable of operating regarding such matters.
He raises an objection — 'Even for the other [<s>Vedāntic</s> view].'
He resolves it — 'No.'

children.text: asmākaṃ tvīśvarāgamayoranāditvādīśvarayonitve 'pyāgamasya na virodha iti bhāvaḥ //38 //
children.translated_text: But for us, since both <s>Īśvara</s> and scripture are beginningless, even though scripture has <s>Īśvara</s> as its source, there is no contradiction — this is the purport. //38//

body.translated_text: He states yet another refutation following observation — 'And because of the impossibility of relation.' For conjunction is observed among things that have parts and are not omnipresent. For contact, which is preceded by non-contact, is not possible for omnipresent entities, since there is no non-contact and because they are without parts. For the nature of conjunction is non-pervasive occurrence. And it has been said that non-pervasive occurrence of conjunction is not possible in partless entities. Therefore, since the non-pervasive occurrence that pervades conjunction ceases, conjunction which is pervaded by it also ceases — this is the purport. Nor is there a relation of the nature of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). For inherence is accepted as the relation between inseparably connected entities standing as substrate and superstratum, which is the cause of the cognition 'here.' And there is no substrate-superstratum relationship among <s>Pradhāna</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s>, and <s>Īśvara</s> — this is the meaning. Nor is there any other relation of the nature of fitness, a relation inferred from effect, he says — 'nor any other.' For the causal status of <s>Pradhāna</s> with respect to <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, etc. has not been established even to this day. He raises an objection — 'the <s>Brahmavādin</s>.' He refutes — 'No.' Why? 'Because in that [<s>Vedāntic</s>] view, the relation characterized as indescribable identity is possible. Moreover' etc. — For scripture does not require an observed example for activity, and therefore it is capable of operating regarding what is unprecedented and even what is contrary to observation.

children.translated_text: 'And because of the impossibility of a substratum [for <s>Īśvara</s>'s activity].'
Here too it should not be forgotten that inference operates according to what is observed and does not pertain to extraordinary objects.
The rest is easy to understand. //39//

body.text:
#karaṇavaccenna bhogādibhyaḥ /
rūpādihīnamiti# /
anudbhūtarūpamityarthaḥ. rūpādihīnakaraṇādhiṣṭhānaṃ hi puruṣasya svabhogādāveva dṛṣṭaṃ nānyatra /
nahi bāhyaṃ kuṭhārādyaparidṛṣṭaṃ vyāpārayan kaścidupalabhyate /
tasmādrūpādihīnaṃ karaṇaṃ vyāpārayata īsvarasya bhogādiprasaktiḥ tathā cānīśvaratvamiti bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: He states an alternative interpretation — 'otherwise' etc.
Previously, 'superintendence' meant the act of controlling; now, however, 'substratum' means the body as the seat of enjoyment.
Previously, non-sovereignty was established through the consequence of enjoyment and the like.
But now non-sovereignty is stated through the consequence of enjoyment and the like by virtue of having a body — this is the distinction. //40//

body.translated_text: 'If [it be said that <s>Īśvara</s> acts] like the sense organs, [we say] no, because of enjoyment and so forth. Being devoid of form and the like' — the meaning is: having unmanifested form. For the superintendence of instruments devoid of form and the like by <s>Puruṣa</s> is observed only in the case of his own enjoyment, not elsewhere. For no one is seen operating an external [instrument] like an axe that is not perceived. Therefore, if <s>Īśvara</s> operates instruments devoid of form and the like, there follows involvement in enjoyment and so forth, and consequently the state of being non-sovereign — this is the purport.

body.text:
#antavatvamasarvajñatā vā# /
api ca sarvatrānumānaṃ pramāṇayataḥ pradhānapuruṣeśvarāṇāmapi saṃkhyābedavattvamantavattvaṃ ca dravyatvāt saṃkhyānyatve sati prameyatvādvānumātavyaṃ, tataścāntavattvamasarvajñatā vā /
asmākaṃ tvāgamagamyer'the tadbādhitaviṣayatayā nānumānaṃ prabhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
#svarūpaparimāṇamapi#yasya yādṛśamaṇu mahat paramamahaddīrghaṃ hrasvaṃ ceti /
#atha mā bhūdeṣa doṣa ityuttaro vikalpaḥ# /
yasyānto 'sti tasyāntavattvāgrahaṇamasarvajñatāmāpādayet /

children.text: yasya tvanta eva nāsti tasya tadagrahaṇaṃ nāsarvajñatāmāvahati /
children.translated_text: But for that which has no limit at all, the non-apprehension of its limit does not entail non-omniscience.
For one does not become ignorant from not knowing the horns of a hare and such things — this is the purport.
He resolves — 'from that' etc.
It has been said that inference, independent of scripture, establishes the finitude of these. //41//

body.translated_text: 'Finitude or non-omniscience.' Moreover, for one who validates inference everywhere, finitude and the possession of numerical distinction among <s>Pradhāna</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s>, and <s>Īśvara</s> must be inferred — because they are substances, or because they are knowable while being other than number — and from that follows either finitude or non-omniscience. But for us, since the object [established by] scripture is contradicted by inference operating in a domain already overridden [by scripture], inference does not prevail — this is the purport. 'Its own intrinsic magnitude also' — of whatever kind: atomic, great, supremely great, long, short, etc. 'Now, lest this fault apply — the latter alternative:' — the non-apprehension of the limit of that which has a limit would entail non-omniscience.

body.text: #utpattyasaṃbhavāt# /

children.translated_text: Where the <s>Veda</s> is non-contradicted, that portion where there is contradiction is rejected.
He states that portion — 'And what is said, that from <s>Vāsudeva</s> [arises] <s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s>' — the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul).

If the <s>jīva</s> has a cause, it would be non-eternal; and if non-eternal, there would be no future-world being, hence no future world; and from that, since the non-existence of heaven, hell, and liberation would follow, [the doctrine would amount to] nihilism — this is the meaning.
And the origination of the <s>jīva</s> is untenable, he says — 'And it will be refuted.' //42//

body.translated_text: 'Because origination is impossible.'

children.translated_text: 'Nor can the agent [produce] an instrument.'

children.text: yadyapyanekaśilpaparyavadātaḥ paraśuṃ kṛtvā tena palāśaṃ chinatti,yadyapi ca prayatnenendriyārthātmamanaḥ saṃnikarṣalakṣaṇaṃ jñānakaraṇamupādāyātmārthaṃ vijānāti, tathāpi saṃkarṣaṇo 'karaṇaḥ kathaṃ pradyumnākhyaṃ manaḥ karaṇaṃ kuryāt /
children.translated_text: Although one skilled in many crafts, having made an axe, cuts a <s>palāśa</s> (leaf/tree) with it, and although through effort one knows an object of the self by means of the instrument of cognition characterized by the contact of sense organ, object, self, and mind — nevertheless, how can <s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s>, who is without instruments, produce the instrument called mind (<s>Pradyumna</s>)?
Or if one without instruments has the power to create instruments, then what need is there for creating instruments at all?
All effects could be accomplished without instruments — this is the purport. //43//

body.text: #vijñānādibhāve vā tadapratiṣedhaḥ# /
body.translated_text: 'Or, if [they are said to be] in the state of <s>vijñāna</s> (pure knowledge) and so forth, that does not prevent [the refutation].'

body.text:
#vāsudevā evaite#saṃkarṣamādayo #nirdeṣā#avidyādidoṣarahitāḥ /
#niradhiṣṭhānā#nirūpādānāḥ /
ata eva #niravadyā#anityatvādidoṣarahitāḥ /
tasmādutpattyasaṃbhavo 'nuguṇatvānna doṣa ityarthaḥ /
#atrocyate-- evamapīti# /
mā bhūdabyupagamena doṣaḥ, prakārāntareṇa tvayameva doṣaḥ /
praśnapūrvaṃ prakārāntaramāha- #katham /
yadi tāvaditi# /
na tāvadete parasparaṃ bhinnā īśvarāḥ parasparavyāhatecchā bhavitumarhanti /
vyāhatakāmatve ca kāryānutpādāt /
avyāhatakāmatve vā pratyekamīśvaratve ekenaiveśanāyāḥ kṛtatvādānarthakyamitareṣām /
saṃbhūya ceśanāyāṃ pariśuddho na kaściddīśvaraḥ syāt, siddhāntahāniśca /

children.translated_text: Because it is accepted that the blessed <s>Vāsudeva</s> alone is the ultimate reality.
Therefore, an alternative interpretation must be adopted.

And in that case, having presented the alternative interpretation with the intention that the impossibility of origination is the defect, he refutes it through the impossibility of origination — 'But this is the intention' etc.
The rest is easy to understand. //44//

body.translated_text: 'These — <s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s> and the others — are indeed <s>Vāsudevas</s> themselves,' 'without faults' — free from defects such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the like. 'Without substratum' — without material cause. Hence 'blameless' — free from defects such as non-eternality. Therefore, the impossibility of origination is not a fault because it is consistent — this is the meaning. 'To this it is said — even so' etc. Let there be no fault by [your] admission; but by another means, this very fault [remains]. He states the other means, preceded by a question — 'How? If indeed' etc. These [<s>Vyūhas</s>] cannot be mutually distinct lords with mutually contradictory desires, for if their desires were contradictory, effects would not be produced. Or if their desires were non-contradictory, then since sovereignty by each one alone would suffice, the others would be purposeless. And if they were to rule jointly, none would be a pure sovereign, and the established doctrine would be undermined.

children.translated_text: 'And because of contradiction.'

children.text: guṇibhyaḥ khalvātmabhyo jñānādīn guṇān bhedenoktvā punarabhedaṃ brūte-- #ātmāna evaite bhagavanto vāsudevā iti# /
children.translated_text: Having described knowledge and other qualities as distinct from the selves who possess them, he again asserts non-difference — 'These blessed <s>Vāsudevas</s> are the selves themselves.'

children.text: ādigrahaṇena pradyumnāniruddhayormano 'haṅkāralakṣaṇatayātmano bhedamabhidhāyātmana evaita iti tadviruddhābhedābhidhānamaparaṃ saṃgṛhītam /
children.translated_text: By the word 'and so forth,' the statement of the difference of <s>Pradyumna</s> and <s>Aniruddha</s> from the self in the form of mind and ego respectively, followed by the contradictory statement of their non-difference — 'these are the selves themselves' — is also included.
The contradiction within the <s>Veda</s> [of the <s>Pāñcarātra</s>] has been explained. //45//

body.text: iti śrīvācaspatimiśraviracite śārīrakabhagavatpādabhāṣyavibhāge bhāmatyāṃ dvitīyādhyāyasya dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ //2 //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the second <s>pāda</s> of the second <s>adhyāya</s> in the <s>Bhāmatī</s>, the exposition of the commentary of the blessed <s>Śārīraka</s> [<s>Brahmasūtra</s>], composed by the revered <s>Vācaspati Miśra</s>. //2//

body.text: #iti dvitīyādhyāyasya sāṃkhyādimatānāṃ duṣṭatvapradarśanaṃ nāma dvitīyaḥpādaḥ#
body.translated_text: Thus ends the second <s>pāda</s> of the second <s>adhyāya</s>, entitled 'Demonstration of the defectiveness of the doctrines of <s>Sāṅkhya</s> and others.'

body.text: #dvidīyādhyāye tṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ# /
body.translated_text: Third <s>pāda</s> of the second <s>adhyāya</s>.

body.text:
#na viyadaśruteḥ# /
pūrvaṃ pramāṇāntaravirodhaḥ śruternirākṛtaḥ /
saṃprati tu śrutīnāmeva parasparavirodho nirākriyate /
tatra sṛṣṭiśrutīnāṃ parasparavirodhamāha- #vedānteṣu tatra tatreti# /
śrutivipratiṣedhācca parapakṣāṇāmanapekṣitatvaṃ sthāpitaṃ tadvatsvapakṣasya śrutivipratiṣedhāditi /
#tadarthanirmalatvamar#thābhāsavinivṛttyārthatattvapratipādanam /
tasya phalaṃ svapakṣasya jagato brahmakāraṇatvasyānapekṣatvāśaṅkānivṛttiḥ /
iha hi pūrvapakṣe śrutīnāṃ mitho virodhaḥ pratipādyate, siddhānte tvavirodhaḥ /
tatra siddhāntyekadeśinovacanaṃ 'na viyadaśruteḥ' iti /
tasyābhisaṃdhiḥ-yadyapi taittirīyake viyadutpattiśrutirasti tathāpi tasyāḥ pramāṇāntaravirodhādbahuśrutivirodhācca gauṇatvam /

children.text: tathāca viyato nityatvāttejaḥpramukha eva sargaḥ, tathāca na virodhaḥ śrutīnāmiti /
children.translated_text: And thus, since <s>ākāśa</s> is eternal, creation begins only with <s>tejas</s> (fire/light) and what follows it, and thus there is no contradiction among the scriptural texts.
This is what is stated — 'First, with reference to <s>ākāśa</s>, it is considered: does this <s>ākāśa</s> have an origination or not?'
If it does not, there is no apprehension of contradiction among the scriptures.

children.text: athāsti tataḥ śrutivirodha iti tatparihārāya prayatnāntaramāstheyamityarthaḥ //1 //
children.translated_text: But if it does, then there is scriptural contradiction, and another effort must be made to resolve it — this is the meaning. //1//

body.translated_text: '<s>Ākāśa</s> (space) [does not originate] because there is no [such] scriptural statement.' Previously, the contradiction from other means of knowledge was refuted with regard to scripture. Now, however, the mutual contradiction among the scriptures themselves is being resolved. In that regard, he states the mutual contradiction among the creation-texts — 'In the <s>Vedāntas</s>, here and there' etc. And just as the <s>para-pakṣas</s> (opposing views) were established as not to be relied upon because of contradiction among scriptural texts, so too [it might be argued] of one's own view due to contradiction among scriptural texts. 'The purity of that meaning' is the establishment of the true meaning by removing semblances of meaning. Its fruit is the removal of the apprehension that one's own position — that <s>Brahman</s> is the cause of the world — is unreliable. For here in the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view), mutual contradiction among the scriptures is demonstrated, while in the <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion), non-contradiction [is shown]. There, the statement of a partial proponent of the <s>siddhānta</s> is: '<s>Ākāśa</s> [does not originate] because there is no [such] scriptural statement.' His intention is — although in the <s>Taittirīyaka</s> there is a scriptural statement about the origination of <s>ākāśa</s>, nevertheless, because of contradiction from other means of knowledge and because of contradiction with many other scriptural texts, that statement is figurative.

body.text:
tatra pūrvapakṣasūtram- #asti tu# /
taittirīye hi sargaprakaraṇe kevalasyākāśasyaiva prathamaḥ sargaḥ śrūyate /
chāndogye ca kevalasya tejasaḥ prathamaḥ sargaḥ /
naca śrutyantarānurodhenāsahāyasyādhigatasyāpi sasahāyatākalpanaṃ yuktamasāhatvāvagamavirodhāt /
śrutasiddhyarthaṃ khalvaśrutaṃ kalpyate na tu tadvidhātāya, vihanyate cāsahāyatvaṃ śrutaṃ kalpitena sasahāyatvena /
naca parasparānapekṣāṇāṃ vrīhiyavavadvikalpaḥ /
anuṣṭhānaṃ hi vikalpyate na vastu /

children.translated_text: For the alternative between a post and a person does not find a footing in reality.
Nor can a reconciliation be achieved by [positing] different creations, since a past creation too would be of the same nature as the present creation.

children.text: na khalviha sarge kṣīrāddadhi jāyate sargāntare ti dadhnaḥ kṣīramiti bhavati /
children.translated_text: For it is not the case that in this creation milk produces yogurt, while in another creation yogurt produces milk.

children.text: tasmātsargaśrutayaḥ parasparavirodhinyo nāsminnarthe pramāṇaṃ bhavitumarhantīti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ //2 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the creation-texts, being mutually contradictory, cannot be a valid means of knowledge in this matter — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s>. //2//

body.translated_text: The <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> <s>sūtra</s> is — 'But it exists.' For in the <s>Taittirīya</s>, in the context of creation, the first creation of <s>ākāśa</s> alone is heard. And in the <s>Chāndogya</s>, the first creation is of <s>tejas</s> alone. And it is not proper to suppose, on the basis of another scriptural text, that what has been understood as unaccompanied is actually accompanied, because this would contradict the understanding of its being unaccompanied. For the unheard is postulated for the sake of establishing what is heard, not for undermining it; and the heard status of being unaccompanied is undermined by the postulated status of being accompanied. Nor is there an option between them like [the option between] rice and barley as mutually independent [alternatives]. For it is performance that admits of alternatives, not a matter of fact.

body.text:
siddhāntyekadeśī sūtreṇa svābhiprāyamāviṣkaroti- #gauṇyasaṃbhavāt# /
pramāṇāntaravirodhena bahuśrutyantaravirodhena cākāśotpattyasaṃbhavādgauṇyeṣākāśotpattiśrutirityavirodha ityarthaḥ /
pramāṇāntaravirodhamāha- #na hyākāśasyeti# /
samavāṭyasamavāyinimittakāraṇebhyo hi kāryasyotpattirniyatā tadabhāve na bhavitumarhati dhūma iva dhūmadhvajābhāve /
body.translated_text: The partial proponent of the <s>siddhānta</s> reveals his view through the <s>sūtra</s> — 'Because of the possibility of figurative usage.' Because the origination of <s>ākāśa</s> is impossible due to contradiction from other means of knowledge and from many other scriptural texts, this scriptural statement about the origination of <s>ākāśa</s> is figurative — and thus there is no contradiction, this is the meaning. He states the contradiction from other means of knowledge — 'For <s>ākāśa</s> does not [have]' etc. For the origination of an effect from material, co-inherent, and efficient causes is invariable; in their absence, it cannot occur, just as smoke [cannot occur] in the absence of fire.

body.text:
tasmātsadakāraṇamākāśaṃ nityamiti /
apica ya utpadyante teṣāṃ prāgutpatteranubhavārthakriye nopalabhyte utpannasya ca dṛśyete, yathā tejaḥprabhṛtīnām /
na cākāśasya tādṛśo viśeṣa utpādānutpādayorasti, tasmānnotpadyata ityāha- #utpattimatāṃ ceti# /
prakāśanaṃ prakāśo ghaṭapaṭādigocaraḥ /

children.translated_text: 'And because of the dissimilarity from earth and the rest.'
By the word 'and so forth,' it is understood that <s>ākāśa</s>, being a substance yet possessing the quality of being intangible, is eternal like the <s>ātman</s>.
'In the forest [passages and other passages about] <s>ākāśas</s>' etc.
Even in the <s>Veda</s>, the multiplicity of the one <s>ākāśa</s> is due to limiting adjuncts. //3//

body.translated_text: Therefore, <s>ākāśa</s>, being without a cause, is eternal. Moreover, of things that originate, the capacity for experience and purposeful action is not observed before their origination but is seen after they have originated — as in the case of <s>tejas</s> and the rest. But there is no such distinction in <s>ākāśa</s> between the states of having originated and not having originated; therefore it does not originate — he says, 'And of things that have originated' etc. '<s>Prakāśana</s>' (illumination) means the manifestation that has pots, cloths, and such things as its objects.

children.translated_text: Having thus stated figurativeness on the basis of contradiction from other means of knowledge, he now states figurativeness also on the basis of contradiction from other scriptural texts — 'And from the [scriptural] word.'
Easy to understand. //4//

body.text:
syāccaikasya brahmaśabdavat /
padasyānuṣaṅgo na padārthasya /
taddhi kkacinmukhyaṃ kkacidaupacārikaṃ saṃbhavāsaṃbhavābhyāmityavirodhaḥ /
codyadvayaṃ karoti- #kathamiti# /
prathamaṃ codyaṃ pariharati- #ekameveti tāvaditi /
kulaṅ#gṛham /
#amatrāṇi# /
pātrāṇi ghaṭaśarāvādīni /
āpekṣikamavadhāraṇaṃ na sarvaviṣayamityarthaḥ /
upapattyantaramāha- #naca nabhasāpīti# /
apirabhyupagame /
yadi sarvāpekṣaṃ tathāpyadoṣa ityarthaḥ /
#naca prāgutpatteḥ# /

children.translated_text: — of the world, is to be supplied.
He removes the second objection — 'For this very reason, through the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>' etc.
Because there is no otherness of defining characteristics, <s>ākāśa</s> is non-different from <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: api cāvyatiriktadeśakālamākāśaṃ brahmaṇā ca brahmakāryaiśca tadabhinnasvabhāvairataḥ kṣīrakumbhaprakṣiptakatipayapayobinduvadbrahmaṇi tatkārye ca vijñāte nabho viditaṃ bhavatītyāha- #api ca sarvaṃ kāryamutpadyamānamiti# //5 //
children.translated_text: Moreover, <s>ākāśa</s>, whose space and time are not distinct [from <s>Brahman</s>], being of a nature non-different from <s>Brahman</s> and its effects — therefore, like a few drops of water thrown into a pot of milk, when <s>Brahman</s> and its effect are known, <s>ākāśa</s> too becomes known — he says, 'Moreover, every effect, when it originates' etc. //5//

body.translated_text: It might be that, like the word '<s>Brahman</s>,' the connection of one word [carries over but] not the connection of the referent. For that [word] is sometimes primary and sometimes figurative, depending on possibility and impossibility — thus there is no contradiction. He raises a twofold objection — 'How?' etc. He resolves the first objection — 'One only, indeed' etc. '<s>Kulaṅ</s>' means house. '<s>Amatrāṇi</s>' means vessels such as pots, saucers, and the like. The restrictive assertion is relative, not universal in scope — this is the meaning. He states another resolution — 'And not even with <s>ākāśa</s>' etc. The word 'even' indicates concessive acceptance. Even if [the restriction] applies to everything, still there is no fault — this is the meaning. 'And not before the origination'

body.text:
evaṃ siddhāntaikadeśamite prāpta idamāha- #pratijñāhāniravyatirekacchabdebhyaḥ# /
brahmavivartātmatayājagatastadvikārasya vastuto brahmaṇābhede brahmaṇi jñāte jñānamupapadyate /
nahi jagattattvaṃ brahmaṇo 'nyat /
tasmādākāśamapi tadvivartatayā tadvikāraḥ sattajjñānena jñātaṃ bhavati nānyathā /
avikāratve tu tatastattvāntaraṃ na brahmaṇi vidite viditaṃ bhavati /
bhinnayostu lakṣaṇānyatvābhāve 'pi deśakālābhede 'pi nānyatarajñānenānyatarajñānaṃ bhavati /
nahi kṣīrasya pūrṇakumbhe kṣīre gṛhyamāṇe satsvapi pāthobinduṣu pāthastattvaṃ prati jñātatvamasti vijñāne /
tasmānna te kṣīre vidite viditā iti pratijñādṛṣṭāntapracayānuparodhāya viyata utpattirakāmenābhyupeyeti /
tadevaṃ siddhāntaikadeśini dūṣitepūrvapakṣī svapakṣe viśeṣamāha- #satyaṃ darśitam# /
ata eva #viruddhaṃ tu taditi# /
siddhāntasāramāha- #naiṣa doṣaḥ# /
#tejaḥ#- #sargasya taittirīyaka iti# /
śrutyoranyathopapadyamānānyathānupapadyamānayoranyathānupapadyamānā balavatī taittirīyakaśrutiḥ /
chāndogyaśrutiścānyathopapadyamānā durbalā /
nanvasahāyaṃ tejaḥ prathamamavagamyamānaṃ sasahāyatvena virudhyata ityuktamata āha- #nahīyaṃ śrutistejojanipradhāneti# /
sargasaṃsargaḥ śrauto bhedastvārthaḥ /
sa ca śrutyantareṇa virodhinā bādhyate, jaghanyatvāt /
naca tejaḥ pramukhasargasaṃsargavadasahāyatvamapyasya śrautaṃ, kintu vyatirekalabhyam /
naca śrutena tadavādabādhane śrutasya tejaḥsargasyānupapattiḥ, tadidamuktam-'tejojanipradhānā' iti /
syādetat /
yadyekaṃ vākyamanekārtha na bhavatyekasya vyāpāradvāsaṃbhavāt, hanta bhoḥ kathamekasya sraṣṭuranekavyāpāratvamaviruddhamityata āha- #sraṣṭā tveko 'pīti# /
vṛddaprayogādhīnāvadhāraṇaṃ śabdasāmarthyam /
nacānāvṛttasya śabdasya kramākramābhyāmanekatrārthe vyāpāro dṛṣṭaḥ /
dṛṣṭaṃ tu kramākramābhyāmekasyāpi karturanekavyāpāratvamityarthaḥ /
nacāsminnartha ekasya vākyasya vyāpāro 'pi tu bhinnānāṃ vākyānāmityāha- #nacāsmābhiriti# /
sugamam /
codayati- #nanu śamavidhānārthamiti# /
yatparaḥ śabdaḥ sa śabdārthaḥ /
na caiṣa sṛṣṭiparo 'pi tu śamapara ityarthaḥ /
paraharati- #nahi tejaḥprāthamyānurodheneti# /
guṇatvādārthatvācca kramasya śrutapradhānapadārthavirodhāttattyāgo 'yukta ityarthaḥ /
siṃhāvalokitanyāyena viyadanutpattivādinaṃ pratyāha- #apica chāndogya iti# /
yatpunanyathā pratijñopapādanaṃ kṛtaṃ, taddūṣayati- #yaccoktamiti# /
body.translated_text: When the partial view of the <s>siddhānta</s> has thus been obtained, this is stated — 'The abandonment of the proposition [would follow], from the [scriptural] words indicating non-difference.' Since the world, as a transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>, is in reality non-different from <s>Brahman</s> as its modification, when <s>Brahman</s> is known, knowledge [of all] is justified. For the reality of the world is not other than <s>Brahman</s>. Therefore, <s>ākāśa</s> too, being a transformation of that, is its modification, and is known through the knowledge of that — not otherwise. But if [<s>ākāśa</s>] were not a modification, then, being a different reality, it would not be known when <s>Brahman</s> is known. Even between things that are distinct, though there is no difference in defining characteristics and no difference in space and time, the knowledge of one does not produce the knowledge of the other. For in a pot full of milk, even when the milk is apprehended and water-drops are present, there is no knowledge of the water in that cognition. Therefore, they are not known when milk is known — and so, in order not to undermine the proposition, examples, and reasoning, the origination of <s>ākāśa</s> must be accepted even by one who does not wish to. When the partial view of the <s>siddhānta</s> has thus been refuted, the <s>pūrvapakṣin</s> states a special point in favor of his own view — 'True, it has been shown.' Hence, 'but that is contradictory.' He states the essence of the <s>siddhānta</s> — 'This is not a fault.' '<s>Tejas</s>' — 'the creation [beginning with <s>tejas</s>] in the <s>Taittirīyaka</s>' etc. Between two scriptural texts, one of which can be explained otherwise and the other which cannot, the one that cannot be explained otherwise is stronger — the <s>Taittirīyaka</s> text. And the <s>Chāndogya</s> text, which can be explained otherwise, is weaker. Objection: <s>tejas</s>, initially understood as unaccompanied, is contradicted by [supposing it to be] accompanied — this has been said. To this he replies — 'For this scriptural text does not primarily concern the origination of <s>tejas</s>' etc. The association of creation [elements] is scriptural; the distinction, however, is derived [from reasoning]. And that is overridden by the contradicting scriptural text of the other, because it is of lesser force. And the unaccompanied nature [of <s>tejas</s>] is not directly stated in scripture like the association of the creation beginning with <s>tejas</s>, but is rather obtained through exclusion. And the overriding of what is obtained through exclusion by what is directly stated does not make the directly stated creation of <s>tejas</s> untenable — this is what is stated: 'primarily concerns the origination of <s>tejas</s>.' One might say: if one sentence cannot convey multiple meanings because a single [sentence] cannot function twice, then how is it not contradictory for a single creator to have multiple functions? To this he says — 'But a single creator also' etc. Determination dependent on the usage of the learned is the capacity of a word. And no function of a word not [previously] employed is seen — whether sequential or simultaneous — with respect to multiple meanings. But it is observed that even a single agent has multiple functions — whether sequential or simultaneous — this is the meaning. And in this matter it is not one sentence that functions but rather different sentences, he says — 'And we do not' etc. Easy to understand. He objects — 'But it is for the purpose of teaching quiescence' etc. The meaning of a word is that which the word aims at. And this [text] does not aim at creation but at quiescence — this is the meaning. He resolves — 'For it is not [the case that] in accordance with the primacy of <s>tejas</s>' etc. Because the sequence is secondary and purposive, and because it contradicts the primary referent established by scripture, its abandonment is not improper — this is the meaning. By the method of the lion's backward glance, he addresses the proponent of the non-origination of <s>ākāśa</s> — 'Moreover, in the <s>Chāndogya</s>' etc. And what was said by way of justifying the proposition differently, that he refutes — 'And what was said' etc.

body.text:
dṛṣṭāntānurūpatvāddārṣṭāntikasya, tasya ca prakṛtivikārarūpatvāddārṣṭāntikasyāpi tathābhāvaḥ /
apica bhrāntimūlaṃ caitadvacanam 'ekamevādvitīyam' iti toye kṣīrabuddhivat /
aupacārikaṃ vā siṃho māṇavaka itivat /
tatra na tāvadbhrāntamityāha- #kṣīrodakanyāyeneti# /
bhrāntervipralambhābhiprāyasya ca puruṣadharmatvādapauruṣeye tadasaṃbhava ityarthaḥ /
nāpyaupacārikamityāha- #sāvadhāraṇā ceyamiti# /
kāmamupacārādastvekatvam, avadhāraṇādvitīyapade nopapadyete /
nahi māṇavake siṃhatvamupacarya na siṃhādanyo 'sti manāgapi māṇavaka iti vadanti laukikāḥ /

children.text: tasmādbrahmatvamaikāntikaṃ jagato vivakṣitaṃ śrutyā na tvaupacārikam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the absolute <s>Brahman</s>-hood of the world is what scripture intends to convey, not something figurative.

children.text: abhyāse hi bhūyastvamarthasya ūvati natvaspatvamapi prāgevaupacārikamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For repetition conveys the emphasis of meaning, not its absence; still less is what precedes figurative — this is the meaning.
'And not with reference to its own effects' etc.

children.text: niḥśeṣavacanaḥ svarasataḥ sarvaśabdo nāsati śrutyantaravirodhe ekadeśavaviṣayo yujyata ityarthaḥ //6 //
children.translated_text: The word 'all,' which in its natural sense encompasses everything without remainder, cannot, in the absence of contradiction from another scriptural text, be restricted to a partial referent — this is the meaning. //6//

body.translated_text: Because the illustrandum conforms to the illustration, and because the illustration has the nature of a transformation of <s>prakṛti</s> (material cause), the illustrandum too is of the same nature. Moreover, this statement — 'One only, without a second' — is rooted in error, like the cognition of milk in water, or is figurative, like 'The boy is a lion.' In that regard, it is not erroneous — he says, 'by the analogy of milk and water.' Since error and the intention to deceive are properties of persons, they are impossible in the impersonal [<s>Veda</s>] — this is the meaning. Nor is it figurative — he says, 'And this [statement] has a restrictive [particle].' Granted, there might be unity through figurative usage; but the second word, being restrictive, would be unjustified. For when lionhood is figuratively attributed to a boy, people do not say 'there is nothing whatsoever other than a lion in the least, i.e., a boy.'

body.text:
ākāśasyotpattau pramāṇāntaravirodhamuktamanubhāṣya tasya pramāṇāntarasya pramāṇāntaravirodhenāpramāṇabhūtasya na gauṇatvāpādanasāmarthyamata āha- #yāvadvikāraṃ tu vibhāgo lokavat# /
so 'yaṃ prayogaḥ-ākāśadikklāmanaḥramāṇavo vikārāḥ, ātmanyatve sati vibhaktatvāt, ghaṭaśarāvodañcanādivaditi /
#sarvaṃ kāryaṃ nirātmakamiti# /
nirūpādānaṃ syādityarthaḥ /
śūnyavādaśca nirākṛtaḥ svayameva śrutyopanyasya 'kathamasataḥ sajjāyeta' iti /
upapāditaṃ ca tannirākaraṇamadhastāditi /
ātmatvādevātmanaḥ pratyagātmano #nirākaṇāśaṅkānupapattiḥ# /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-sopādānaṃ cetkāryaṃ tata ātmaivopānatvena śruterupādānāntarakalpanānupapatteriti /
syādetat /
astvātmopādānamasya jagataḥ, tasya tūpādānāntaramaśrūyamāṇamapyanyadbhaviṣyatītyata āha- #nahyātmāgantukaḥ kasyacit#upādānāntarasyopādeyaḥ /
kutaḥ /
#svayaṃsiddhatvāt# /
sattā vā prakāśo vāsya svayaṃsiddhī /
tatra prakāśātmikāyāḥ siddhestāvadanāgantukatvamāha- #nahyātmātmana iti# /
upapāditametadyathā saṃśayaviparyāsapārokṣyānāspadatvātkadāpi nātmā parādhīnaprakāśaḥ, tadadhīnaprakāśāstu pramāṇādayaḥ /
ata eva śrutiḥ-'tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti' iti /
#nacedṛśasya narikāraṇaṃ saṃbhavatīti# /
nirākaraṇamapi hi tadadhīnātmalābhaṃ tadviruddhaṃ nodetumarhatītyarthaḥ /
sattāyā anāgantukatvamasyāha-tathāhamevedānīṃ jānāmīti /
pramāpramāṇaprameyāṇāṃ vartamānātītānāgatatve 'pi pramātuḥ sadā vartamānatvenānubhavādapracyutasvabhāvasya nāgantukaṃ sattvam /
traikālyāvacchedena hyāgantukatvaṃ vyāptaṃ, tatpramātuḥ sadāvartamānādvyavartamānamāgantukatvaṃ svavyāpyamādāya nivartata iti /
#anyathābhavatyapi jñātavya iti# /
prakṛtipratyayābhyāṃ jñānajñeyayoranyathābhāvo darśitaḥ /
nanu jīvataḥ pramāturmā bhūdanyathābhāvo mṛtasya tu bhaviṣyatītyata āha- #tathā bhasmībhavasyapīti# /
yatkhalu satsvabhāvamanubhavasiddhaṃ tasyānirvacanīyatvamanyato bādhakādavasātavyam /
bādhakaṃ ca ghaṭādīnāṃ svabhāvādvicalanaṃ pramāṇopanītam /
yasya tu na tadasyātmano na tasya tatkalpanaṃ yuktam, abādhitānubhavasiddhasya satsvabhāvasyānirvacanīyatvakalpanāpramāṇābhāvāt /
tadidamuktam- #na saṃbhāvayituṃ śakyamiti# /
tadanena prabandhena pratyanumānenākāśānutpattyanumānaṃ tūṣayitvānaikāntikatvenāpi dūṣayati-yattūkaṃ samānajātīyamiti /

children.translated_text: 'Nor does a single material cause produce a single effect.'

children.text: yatra hi kṣīraṃ dadhibhāvena pariṇamate tatra nāvayavānāmanekeṣāmupādanatvamabhyupagantavyaṃ kintūpāttameva kṣīramekamupādeyadadhibhāvena pariṇamate /
children.translated_text: For where milk transforms into the state of curds, one should not accept that the many parts serve as the material cause; rather, the single milk that has been taken up transforms into the state of curds as the single effect.
Just as, for those who hold the doctrine of partless atoms, a milk-atom transforms into the state of a curd-atom.
The rest is of evident meaning. //7//

body.translated_text: Having stated in the sub-commentary the absence of conflict with other means of knowledge regarding the origination of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), since that other means of knowledge, being rendered non-authoritative by conflict with yet another means of knowledge, does not have the capacity to establish secondary meaning, he says: 'The division extends as far as the modifications, just as in the world.' The argument is as follows: space, direction, time, mind, and atoms are modifications; because they are differentiated while being other than the self, like a pot, an arrow, or a pulley-bucket, etc. 'All effects would be without a self' — the meaning is that they would be without a material cause. And the doctrine of the void has been refuted by scripture itself having presented it thus: 'How could being arise from non-being?' And the refutation of that has been established below. Due to being the self itself, there is no possibility of suspecting the negation of the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>). What is said here amounts to this: if the effect has a material cause, then the self alone is the material cause, since scripture declares it so and it is impossible to postulate any other material cause. One might object: let the self be the material cause of this world, but perhaps it has some other material cause, unheard in scripture, that will serve as an additional material cause — to this he says: 'For the self is not something adventitious, to be taken up by any other material cause.' Why? 'Because it is self-established.' Either its existence or its luminosity is self-established. Regarding luminosity, he first states the non-adventitious nature of luminous self-establishment: 'For the self is not of the self' and so on. This has been demonstrated — that since the self is never the ground of doubt, error, or mediacy, the self never has its luminosity dependent on another; but the means of knowledge and the like have their luminosity dependent on that. Hence the scripture: 'Everything shines after that which shines; by its light all this is illuminated.' 'And for such a one, negation is impossible' — the meaning is that negation too, having its very existence dependent on that, cannot arise contrary to it. Regarding the non-adventitious nature of existence, he says: 'Thus I know now.' Though the cognition, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge exist as present, past, and future, for the knower who is always experienced as present, whose nature never lapses, existence is not adventitious. For adventitiousness is pervaded by temporal limitation to the three times; since adventitiousness withdraws from the knower who is always present, it departs taking its own concomitant with it. 'Even though it becomes otherwise, as something to be known' — by the root and the suffix, the becoming-otherwise of both knowledge and the knowable has been shown. But one might say: let there be no becoming-otherwise for a living knower, but there will be for a dead one — to this he says: 'Even when one is reduced to ashes.' Indeed, that whose nature as being is established through experience — its being called indeterminable must be forced upon it by some contradicting factor from elsewhere. And the contradicting factor is the deviation from their own nature of pots and the like, brought by the means of knowledge. But for that which has no such deviation — namely the self — it is not proper to postulate such, because there is no means of knowledge for postulating the indeterminability of the nature of being that is established through uncontradicted experience. This is what is stated: 'It cannot be imagined.' Thus, by this sequence of reasoning, having silenced the inference against the non-origination of <s>ākāśa</s> through a counter-inference, he also refutes it as inconclusive: 'As for what was said about being of the same class' —

body.text:
#etena mātariśvā vyākhyātaḥ# /
yadyabhyāse bhūyastvamarthasya bhavati nālpatvaṃ dūrata evopacaritatvaṃ, hanta bhoḥ pavanasya nityatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
'vāyuścāntarikṣametadamṛtam' iti dvayoramṛtatvamuktvā punaḥ pavanasya viśeṣeṇāha- #saiṣānastamitā devatā yadvāyuriti# /
tasmādabhyāsānnāpekṣikaṃ vāyoramṛtatvamapi tvautpattikameveti prāptam /
tadidamuktaṃ bhāṣyakṛtā- #astamayapratiṣedhādamṛtatvādiśravaṇācceti# /
cena samuccayārthenābhyāso darśitaḥ /
evaṃ prāpta ucyate-ekavijñānena sarvavijñānapratijñānāt, pratijñāvākyārthasya prādhānyāt, tadupapadanārthatvācca vākyāntarāṇāṃ, teṣāmapi cādvaitapratipādakānāṃ mātariśvotpattikramapratipādakānāṃ bahulamupalabdheḥ,
body.translated_text: By this, <s>Mātariśvan</s> (wind) is explained. If repeated mention (<s>abhyāsa</s>) establishes the preponderance of a meaning and not its lesser significance, then from a distance itself its figurative nature is determined — well then, there would be the unwanted consequence that wind is eternal. Having stated the immortality of both in 'Wind and the atmosphere — this is immortal,' he then says specifically about wind: 'This is the unperished deity, namely <s>Vāyu</s> (wind).' Therefore, due to repeated mention, the immortality of wind is not merely relative but is indeed intrinsic — such is the prima facie view. This is what the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> has stated: 'Because of the denial of setting and the mention of immortality, etc.' But the repetition has been shown to serve the purpose of aggregation. When this prima facie view has been stated, the conclusion is: since the promise that through knowing one thing everything becomes known, since the meaning of the promise-statement is primary, since other statements serve to support that, and since among those too there is abundant evidence of statements establishing non-duality and statements indicating the order of origination of <s>Mātariśvan</s>,

children.translated_text: due to the greater strength of those scriptures through both directness and preponderance, in accordance with these, the immortality and the denial of setting must be understood in a relative sense.

children.text: bhūyasīḥ śrutīrapekṣya dve api śrutī śabdamātramukte //8 //
children.translated_text: In view of the more numerous scriptures, both scriptures merely express the word. //8//

body.text:
#esaṃbhavastu sato 'nupapatteḥ# /
nanu 'na cāsya kaścijjanitā' ityātmanaḥ sato 'kāraṇatvaśruteḥ kathamutpattyāśaṅkā /
naca vacanamadṛṣṭvā pūrvaḥ pakṣa iti yuktam, adhītavedasya brahmajijñāsādhikārādarśanānupapatterata āha- #viyatpavanayoriti# /
yathāhi viyatpavanayoramṛtatvānastamayatvaśrutī śrutyantaravirodhādāpekṣikatvena nīte /
evamakāraṇatvaśrutirātmano 'gnivisphuliṅgadṛṣṭāntaśrutivirodhātpramāṇāntaravirodhāccāpekṣikatvena vyākhyātavyā /
na cātmanaḥ kāraṇavattve 'navasthā lohagandhitāmāvahatyanāditvāt kāryakāraṇaparamparāyā iti bhāvaḥ /
#tathā vikārebhya iti# /
body.translated_text: The impossibility, however, is due to the unfeasibility of that which exists. Now, since there is a scriptural statement declaring the causelessness of the self that exists — 'And none is its progenitor' — how can origination be suspected? And it is not proper to say that the prima facie view exists without seeing the statement, because one who has studied the <s>Veda</s> would not be seen to have the qualification for the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s> — therefore he says: 'Regarding space and wind.' Just as the scriptural statements about the immortality and non-setting of space and wind have been interpreted in a relative sense due to conflict with other scriptures, so too the scriptural statement about the causelessness of the self must be explained in a relative sense due to conflict with the scriptural illustration of fire and sparks and conflict with other means of knowledge. And in the self having a cause, there is no infinite regress, because the chain of cause and effect is beginningless, which leads to the defect of contamination — such is the import. 'Likewise from the modifications' —

body.text:
pramāṇāntaravirodho darśitaḥ /
evaṃ prāpta ucyate-sadekatvabhāvasyotpattyasaṃbhavaḥ /
kutaḥ #anupapatteḥ# /
sadekasvabhāvaṃ hi brahma śrūyate tadasati bādhake nānyathayitavyam /
uktametadvikārāḥ sattvenānubhūtā api katipayakālakalātikrame vinaśyanto dṛśyanta ityanirvacanīyāstraikālyāvacchedāditi /
na cātmā tādṛśastasya śruteranubhāvādvā vartamānaikasvabhāvatvaina prasiddhestadidamāha- #sanmātraṃ hi brahmeti# /
etaduktaṃ bhavati-yatsvabhāvādvicalati tadanirvacanīyaṃ nirvacanīyopādānaṃ yuktaṃ, na tu viparyayaḥ /
yathā rajjūpādānaḥ sarpo na tu sarpopādānā rajjuriti /
yayostu svabhāvādapracyutistayornirvacanīyayornopādeyopādānabhāvaḥ, yathā rajjuśuktikayoriti /
naca niradhiṣṭhāno vibhrama ityāha- #nāpyasata iti# /
naca niradhiṣṭhānabhramaparaṃparānāditetyāha- #mūlaprakṛtyanabhyupagame 'navasthāprasaṅgāditi# /
pāramārthiko hi kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'nādirnānavasthāyā duṣyati. samāropastu vikārasya na samāropitopādāna ityupapāditaṃ mādhyamikamataniṣedhādhikāre, tadatra na prasmartavyam /
tasmānnāsadadhiṣṭhānavibhramasamarthanānāditvenocitetyarthaḥ /
agnivisphuliṅgaśrutiścaupādikarūpāpekṣayā netavyā /
śeṣamatirohitārtham /

children.text: ye tu guṇadikkālotpattiviṣayamidamadhikaraṇaṃ varṇayāñcakrustaiḥ 'sato 'nupapatteḥ' iti kleśena vyākhyeyam /
children.translated_text: Those who describe this section (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>) as concerning the origination of qualities, direction, and time would have to explain 'due to the unfeasibility of that which exists' with great difficulty.
And its connection would have to be stated in the context of demonstrating non-contradiction.
Because of the non-comprehension of a statement establishing the origination of direction, time, and the like.
Let that be set aside for now. //9//

body.translated_text: the conflict with other means of knowledge has been shown. When this prima facie view has been stated, the conclusion is: the impossibility of origination of that which has the nature of being and oneness. Why? 'Due to unfeasibility.' For <s>Brahman</s> is heard in scripture as having the sole nature of being; in the absence of a contradicting factor, it should not be interpreted otherwise. This has been stated — that modifications, even though experienced as existent, are seen to perish after the passage of some time and duration, and hence are indeterminable due to temporal limitation. But the self is not like that, since from scripture, from experience, and from its well-known nature of being ever-present, this is what he states: 'For <s>Brahman</s> is mere being.' What is said here amounts to this: that which deviates from its own nature is indeterminable and it is proper for it to have an indeterminable material cause, but not the reverse — just as a snake has a rope as its material cause, but a rope does not have a snake as its material cause. And for two things that do not lapse from their own nature, there is no relation of effect and material cause between those two indeterminables, just as between a rope and a mother-of-pearl. And it is not the case that error is without a substratum — to this he says: 'Nor from non-being.' And it is not the case that there is a beginningless chain of errors without a substratum — to this he says: 'In the absence of accepting a root <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), there would be the unwanted consequence of infinite regress.' For the real cause-effect relation, being beginningless, is not vitiated by infinite regress. But the superimposition of a modification is not a superimposed material cause — this has been established in the section refuting the <s>Mādhyamika</s> view, and should not be forgotten here. Therefore the meaning is that non-being cannot serve as a substratum for error by establishing its beginninglessness. And the scriptural statement about fire and sparks must be interpreted with reference to the form of the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>). The rest is of evident meaning.

body.text:
#tejo 'tastathāhyāha# /
yadyapi 'vāyoragniḥ' ityapādānapañcamī 'kārakavibhaktirupapadavibhakterbalīyasī' iti neyamānantaryaparā yuktā, tathāpi bahuśrutivirodhena durbalāpyupapadavibhaktirevātrocitā /
tataścānantaryadarśanapareyaṃ vāyoragniriti śrutiḥ /
naca sākṣādbrahmajatvasaṃbhave tadvaṃśyatvena tajjatvaṃ paraṃparayāśrayituṃ yuktam /
vājapeyasya paśuyūpavaditi prāptam /
evaṃ prāpte ucyate-yuktaṃ paśuyāgavājapeyoraṅgāṅginornānātvattatra sākṣādvājapeyāsaṃbandhe kleśena paraṃparāśrayaṇam /
iha tu vāyorbrahmavikārasyāpi brahmaṇo vastuto 'nanyatvādvayūpādānatve sākṣādeva brahmopādānatvopapatteḥ kārakavibhakterbalīyastvānurodhenobhayathopapadyamānāḥ śrutayaḥ kāṃsyabhojinyāyena niyamyanta iti yuktamiti rāddhāntaḥ /
#'pāramparyajatve 'pi'#iti bhedakalpanābhiprāyaṃ yataḥla pāramārthikābhedamāha- #vāyubhāvāpannaṃ#
body.translated_text: 'Fire, in the same manner, for thus it declares.' Although the ablative fifth case-ending in '<s>Vāyu</s> produced fire' can properly be taken as denoting immediate succession — since 'a case-ending denoting a verbal relation is stronger than a case-ending dependent on a nominal stem' — still, even the weak case-ending dependent on a nominal stem is appropriate here due to conflict with numerous scriptures. Thus this scripture 'fire from wind' is to be understood as showing immediate succession. And when direct origination from <s>Brahman</s> is possible, it is not proper to resort to origination from it through lineage, indirectly. This is like the sacrificial post for animals in relation to the <s>Vājapeya</s> sacrifice — such is the prima facie view. When this has been stated, the conclusion is: the analogy of the <s>Vājapeya</s> and the animal sacrifice is fitting because the subsidiary and principal rites are different; there, since there is no direct connection with the <s>Vājapeya</s>, resorting to indirect succession involves difficulty. But here, since wind, which is itself a modification of <s>Brahman</s>, is in reality non-different from <s>Brahman</s>, when wind is accepted as the material cause, the origination directly from <s>Brahman</s> itself is feasible; therefore, following the principle that a case-ending denoting a verbal relation is stronger, scriptures that are explicable both ways are determined by the principle of the bronze-eating (<s>kāṃsyabhojin</s>) maxim — this is the established conclusion. 'Even if the origination is through succession' — this is said with the intention of postulating difference; hence, stating the ultimate non-difference, he says: 'That which has entered the state of <s>Vāyu</s> (wind)'

children.translated_text: 'is <s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text: yathā tasyāḥ śṛtam#iti tu dṛṣṭāntaḥ paramparāmātrasāmyena na tu sarvathāṃ sāmyeneti sarvamavadātam //10 //
children.translated_text: 'Just as the cooked preparation of that' — this illustration is given only for the similarity of succession, not for similarity in all respects — thus everything is clear. //10//
'Water.'
It is explained by the commentary that is explained through recitation (<s>nigada</s>). //11//

body.text:
#pṛthivyadhikārarūpaśabdāntarebhyaḥ# /
annaśabdo 'yaṃ vyutpattyā ca prasiddhyā ca vrīhiyavādau tadvikāre caudane pravartate /
śrutiśca prakaraṇādbalīyasī, sā ca vākyaśeṣeṇopodbalitā 'yatra kkacana varṣati' ityetena tasmādabhyavahārthaṃ vrīhiyavādyevātrādbhyo jāyata iti vivakṣitam /
kārṣṇyamapi hi saṃbhavati kasyacidadanīsya /

children.text: nahi pṛthivyapi kṛṣṇā, lohitādirūpāyā api darśanāt /
children.translated_text: For earth too is not always black, since it is also seen to have red and other colors.

children.text: tataśca śrutyantareṇa 'adbhyaḥ pṛthivī pṛthivyā oṣadhayaḥ' ityādinā virodha iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus there is conflict with other scriptures such as 'From water, earth; from earth, herbs' — this is the prima facie view.
When there is conflict between two scriptures regarding a matter, since alternation is unfeasible, one must be interpreted in conformity with the other.

children.text: tatra kim 'adbhyaḥ pṛthivī' iti pṛthivīśabdo 'nnaparatayā nīyatāmuta 'annamasṛjata' ityannaśabdaḥ pṛthivīparatayeti viśaye, mahābhūtādhikārānurodhātprāyikakṛṣṇarūpānurodhācca 'tadyadupāṃ śara āsīt' iti ca punaḥ śrutyanurodhācca vākyaśeṣasya cānyathāpyupapatterannaśabdo 'nnakāraṇe pṛthivyāmiti rāddhāntaḥ //12 //
children.translated_text: In this regard, the question is whether the word 'earth' in 'from water, earth' should be taken as meaning food, or the word 'food' in 'he created food' should be taken as meaning earth. In this matter, considering the context of the great elements, considering the predominantly black color, considering also the further scriptural corroboration 'that which was the essence of water,' and considering that the remainder of the passage can be explained otherwise as well, the established conclusion is that the word 'food' refers to earth, which is the cause of food. //12//

body.translated_text: The section on earth: from other words denoting form. The word 'food' (<s>anna</s>), by both etymology and common usage, applies to rice, barley, and the like, as well as to their preparation such as cooked rice. And scripture is stronger than context; and that scripture is corroborated by the remainder of the passage 'wherever it rains' — therefore what is intended is that rice, barley, and the like, meant for consumption, are born from water. For blackness too is possible for something edible.

body.text:
#tadabhidhyānādeva tu talliṅgātsaḥ# /
sṛṣṭikrame bhūtānāmavirodha uktaḥ /
idānīmākāśādibhūtādhiṣṭhātryo devatāḥ kiṃ svatantrā evottarottarabhūtasarge pravartanta uta parameśvarāpekṣāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāt, prastāvasya ca liṅgasya ca pāramparyeṇāpi mūlākāraṇasya brahmaṇa upapatte-, svatantrāṇāmevākāśādīnāṃ vāṭvādikāraṇatvamiti jagato brahmayonitvavyāghāta iti prāptam /
evaṃ prāpte 'bhidhīyate- #ākāśādvāyuḥ'#ityādaya ākāśādīnāṃ kevalamupādānabhāvamācakṣate, na punaḥ svātantryeṇādhiṣṭhātṛtvam /
naca cetanānāṃ svakāryasvātantryamityetadapyaikāntikaṃ paratantrāṇāmapi teṣāṃ bahulamupalabdherbhṛtyāntevāsyādivat /
tasmālliṅgaprastāvasāmañjasyāya sa īśvara eva tena tenākāśādibhāvenopādānabhāvenāvatiṣṭhamānaḥ svayamadhiṣṭhāya nimittakāraṇabhūtastaṃ taṃ vikāraṃ vāṭvādikaṃ sṛjatīti yuktam /
itarathā liṅgaprastāvau kleśitau syātāmiti /
body.translated_text: 'But it is through his meditation alone, as indicated by the marks, that he is so.' The non-contradiction in the order of creation of the elements has been stated. Now the question arises: do the deities presiding over the elements beginning with <s>ākāśa</s> (space) engage independently in the creation of successive elements, or is there no evidence for their dependence on the supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>)? Since even through the succession of the context and the marks, the feasibility of <s>Brahman</s> as the root cause is established, the independence of space and the like as causes like a barren woman's son would contradict the doctrine that <s>Brahman</s> is the source of the universe — such is the prima facie view. When this has been stated, the conclusion is: scriptures such as 'From <s>ākāśa</s>, <s>Vāyu</s>' and the like declare only the material cause status of space and the like, but not their independent presiding status. And it is not conclusively established that conscious beings are independent in their own effects, since such beings are also abundantly seen to be dependent on others, like servants and pupils. Therefore, for the consistency of the marks and the context, that very Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), remaining in the form of the material cause as space and the like, himself presiding as the efficient cause, creates each modification such as barren women's sons and the like — this is proper. Otherwise, the marks and the context would be strained.

children.translated_text: 'Due to the possession by the supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>).'

children.text: parameśvara evāntaryamibhāvenāviṣṭa īkṣitā, tasmātsarvasya kāryajātasya sākṣātparameśvara evādhiṣṭhātā nimittakāraṇaṃ na tvākāśādibhāvamāpannaḥ /
children.translated_text: The supreme Lord himself, having entered as the inner controller (<s>antaryāmin</s>), is the seer; therefore, for the entire class of effects, the supreme Lord himself is directly the presiding efficient cause, not one who has merely assumed the form of space and the like.
But the one who has assumed the form of space and the like is the material cause — thus it is established. //13//

body.text:
#viparyayeṇa tu kramo 'ta upapadyate ca# /
utpattau mahābhūtānāṃ kramaḥ śruto nāpyaye 'pyayamātrasya śrutatvāt /
tatrava niyame saṃbhavati nāniyamaḥ /
vyavasthārahito hi saḥ /
naca vyavasthāyāṃ satyāmavyavasthā yujyate /
tatra kramabhedāpekṣāyāṃ kiṃ dṛṣṭo 'pyayakramo ghaṭādīnāṃ mahābhūtāpyayakramaniyāmako 'stvāho śrauta utpattikrama iti viśaye śrautasya śrautāntaramabhyarhitaṃ samānajātīyatayā tasyaiva buddhisāṃnidhyāt /
na dṛṣṭaṃ, viruddhajātīyatvāt /
tasmācchrautenaivotpattikrameṇāpyayakramo niyamyata iti prāpta ucyate-apyayasya kramāpekṣāyāṃ khalūtpattikramo niyāmako bhavet, na tvastyapyayasya kramāpekṣā, dṛṣṭānumānopanītena kramabhedena śrutyanusāriṇo 'pyayakramasya bādhyamānatvāt /
tasmin hi satyupādānoparame 'pyupādeyamastīti syāt /
na caitadasti /
tasmāt /

children.translated_text: due to the constraint of the observed order which is contrary to that, there is no expectation at all, since that other order is unfit.
This is what the author of the <s>sūtra</s> has stated: 'And it is feasible.'
The author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> also says: 'And that is not desired by dissolution, due to its unfitness.'
Therefore, the order is the reverse of the order of origination — and the <s>smṛti</s> (traditional text) based on this principle has also been cited. //14//

body.translated_text: 'But the order is in reverse, and it is feasible.' An order of the great elements has been heard in origination, but not in dissolution, since only dissolution in general has been mentioned. Where a fixed order is possible, there should be no absence of fixed order, for the absence of a fixed order is devoid of systematic arrangement. And when there is a systematic arrangement, disorder is not appropriate. Regarding the expectation of a difference in order: should the observed order of dissolution of pots and the like determine the order of dissolution of the great elements, or should the scriptural order of origination? In this matter, a scriptural authority is more worthy of determining another scriptural matter, due to being of the same class and due to its being present in the mind. Not the observed, because it is of a contrary class. Therefore, when it is prima facie established that the order of dissolution is determined by the scriptural order of origination itself, the conclusion is stated: if the order of origination were to determine the order of dissolution, it could do so only when dissolution requires an order; but there is no such requirement of order for dissolution, since the order of dissolution that follows scripture is contradicted by the order established through observation and inference that differs from it. For if that were the case, even when the material cause ceases, the effect would still exist — but this is not so. Therefore:

body.text:
#antarāvijñānamanasī krameṇa talliṅgāditi cennāviśeṣāt# /
tadevaṃ bhāvanopayoginau bhūtānāmutpattipralayau vicārya buddhīndriyamanasāṃ kramaṃ vicārayati /
atra ca vijñāyate 'neneti vyutpattyā vijñānaśabdenendriyāṇi ca buddhiṃ ca brūte /
tatraiteṣāṃ kramāpekṣāyāmātmānaṃ ca bhūtāni cāntarā samāmnānāttenaiva pāṭhena kramo niyamyate /
tasmāt pūrvotpattikramabhaṅgaprasaṅgaḥ /
yata ātmanaḥ karaṇāni karaṇebhyaśca bhūtānīti pratīyate, tasmādātmana ākāśa iti bhajyate /
annamayamiti ca mayaḍānandamaya itivat na vikārārtha iti prāpte 'bhidhīyate-vibhaktatvāttāvanmanaḥprabhṛtīnāṃ kāraṇāpekṣāyāmannamayaṃ mana ityādiliṅgaśravaṇādapekṣitārthakathanāya vikārārthatvameva mayaṭo yuktam, itarathā tvanapekṣitamuktaṃ bhavet /
naca tadapi ghaṭate /
nahyannamayo yajña itivadannaprācuryaṃ manasaḥ saṃbhavati /
evaṃ codbhūtavikārā mana ādayo bhūtānāṃ parastādutpadyanta iti yuktam /
prauḍhavāditayābhyupetyāha- #atha tvabhautikānīti# /

children.text: bhavatvātmana eva karaṇānāmutpattiḥ, na khalvetāvatā bhūtairātmano notpattavyam /
children.translated_text: Granted that the instruments originate from the self alone; but this alone does not establish that the elements should not originate from the self.
And thus there is no unwanted consequence of disrupting the stated order.
'Is distinguished' — means is divided.
That is to say, is separated. //15//

body.translated_text: 'In between, the intellect and the mind, in order, as indicated by the marks — if this be said, no, because of the absence of distinction.' Having thus examined the origination and dissolution of the elements, which are useful for meditation, he now examines the order of the intellect, sense organs, and mind. Here, by the etymology 'that by which one knows,' the word <s>vijñāna</s> denotes both the sense organs and the intellect. Regarding the expectation of their order: since they are enumerated between the self and the elements, their order is determined by that very textual sequence. Therefore, there would be the unwanted consequence of disrupting the previously established order of origination, since it would be understood that from the self come the instruments and from the instruments come the elements, and thus 'from the self, space' would be disrupted. And the suffix <s>mayaṭ</s> in '<s>annamaya</s>' (made of food), as in '<s>ānandamaya</s>' (made of bliss), does not mean modification — such is the prima facie view. The conclusion is stated: since the mind and the rest are differentiated, in expecting their cause, the hearing of marks such as 'the mind is made of food' and the like, in order to convey the required meaning, it is proper to take the suffix <s>mayaṭ</s> in the sense of modification; otherwise, something unrequired would have been stated. And that too does not work, for it is not possible that the mind has an abundance of food in the way that 'a sacrifice is made of food' means abundance of food. And thus it is proper that the mind and the rest, being fully evolved modifications, originate after the elements. Adopting the position of a strong debater, he says: 'But if they are non-elemental' —

body.text:
#carācaravyapāśrayastu syāttadvyapadeśo bhāktastadbhāvabhāvitvāt# /
devadattādināmadheyaṃ tāvajjīvātmano na śarīrasya, tannāmne śarīrasya śrāddhadikaraṇānupapatteḥ /
tanmṛto devadatto jāto devadatta iti vyapadeśasya mukhyatvaṃ manvānasya pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ, mukhyatve śāstroktāmuṣmikasvargādiphalasaṃbandhānupapteḥ śāstravirodhāllaukikavyapadeśo bhākto vyākhyeyaḥ /
bhaktiśca śarīrasyotpādavināśau tatastatsaṃyoga iti /
jātakarmādi ca garbhabījasamudbhavajīvapāpaprakṣayārthaṃ, na tu jīvajanmajapāpakṣayārtham /

children.text: ata eva smaranti 'evamenaḥ śamaṃ yāti bījagarbhasamudbhavam' iti /
children.translated_text: Hence they remember: 'Thus the sin arising from the seed and the womb is pacified.'
Therefore, it is established that the birth and death of the individual soul do not occur through the origination and destruction of the body.
And this section (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>) is based on the assumption that the worldly designation has a non-erroneous basis.
But in the preamble on superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>), it has been stated that its basis is error. //16//

body.translated_text: 'The designation of moving and non-moving beings is figurative, because of the nature of being dependent on that.' A name such as <s>Devadatta</s> belongs to the individual soul (<s>jīvātman</s>), not to the body, since rituals like the funeral offering (<s>śrāddha</s>) performed in the name of the deceased would be impossible otherwise. The prima facie view holds the designation 'so-and-so has died, so-and-so is born' to be primary; if it were primary, there would be the impossibility of connection with fruits such as heaven and the like pertaining to the other world as stated in scripture, and hence there would be conflict with scripture; therefore the worldly designation must be explained as figurative (<s>bhākta</s>). And the figurative usage consists in: the body undergoes origination and destruction, and hence the connection with it. And the birth rites (<s>jātakarma</s>) and the like are for the purpose of destroying the sins arising from the seed and the womb of the individual soul, not for destroying the sins arising from the birth of the soul itself.

body.text:
mā bhūtāmasya śarīrodayavyayābhyāṃ sthūlāvutpattivināśau, ākāśāderiva tu mahāsargādau tadante cotpattivināśau jīvasya bhaviṣyata iti śaṅkāntaramapanetumidamārabhyate /
#nātmāśruternityatvācca tābhyaḥ# /
vicāramūlasaṃśayasya bījamāha- #śrutivipratipatteriti# /
tāmeva darśayati- #kāsucicchutiṣviti# /
pūrvapakṣaṃ gṛhṇāti- #tatra prāptamiti# /
paramātmanastāvadviruddhadharmasaṃsargādapahatānapahatapāpmatvādilakṣaṇājjīvānāmanyatvam /
te cenna vikārāstatastattvāntaratve bahutarādvaitaśrutivirodhaḥ /
brahmavijñānena sarvavijñānapratijñāvirodhaśca /
tasmācchutibharanujñāyate vikāratvam /
pramāṇāntaraṃ cātroktam-vibhaktatvādākāśādivaditi /
'yathāgneḥ śrudrā visphaliṅgaḥ' iti ca śrutiḥ sākṣādeva brahmavikāratvaṃ jīvānāṃ darśayati /
'yathā sūdīptāt pāvakāt' iti ca brahmaṇo jīvānāmutpattiṃ ca tatrāpyayaṃ ca sākṣāddarśayati /
nanvakṣarādbhāvānāmutpattipralayāvavagamyete /
na jīvānāmityata āha- #jīvātmanāmiti# /
syādetat /
sṛṣṭiśrutiṣvākāśādyutpattiriva kasmājjīvotpattirnāmnāyate /
tasmādāmnānayogyasyānāmnānāttasyotpattyabhāvaṃ pratīma ityata āha- #naca kkacidaśravaṇamiti# /
evaṃ hi kasyāñcicchākhyāyāmāmnātasya katipāyāṅgasahitasya karmaṇaḥ śākhāntarīyāṅgopasaṃhāro na bhavet /
tasmādbahutaraśrutivirodhādanupraveśaśrutirvikārabhāvātpattyā vyākhyeyā /
