Because of the absence of a basis for [choosing one meaning over the other as] determinative.
And because the <s>gaṇakāra</s>'s (the grammatical grouper's) indication of meaning — even as a mere representative example (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) — is seen there [in the sense of abandonment].
Therefore, [the word] here has the meaning of abandonment alone — this is fitting. //26//

body.translated_text:
'#But when there is abandonment, because of being a remainder of the word <s>upāyana</s> (transference), it is as stated — like <s>kuśa</s>-grass, meter, praise, and <s>upagāna</s> (auxiliary chanting)#.'
Where both abandonment (<s>hāna</s>) and transference (<s>upāyana</s>) are heard, there is no dispute — there is conjunction.
Where only transference is heard, there too — since abandonment is implied as its necessary concomitant — there is conjunction.
But where only the abandonment of merit (<s>sukṛta</s>) and demerit (<s>duṣkṛta</s>) is heard, and transference is not heard — there the doubt is: does transference, [i.e.,] the taking up [by another], conjoin [with the abandonment] or not?
Herein, [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] takes up the prima facie view: '#There is no conjunction#' — thus.
One might say: just as a subsidiary of a meditation heard in one <s>śākhā</s> is incorporated into that very meditation [as taught] in another <s>śākhā</s>,
so too the transference heard in another <s>śākhā</s> will be incorporated — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Because of pertaining to a different <s>vidyā</s>#' — thus.
For when the meditations are one, the conjunction of what is heard in one place with what is stated in another place is fitting.
But here the meditations are not one, because of the difference between <s>saguṇa</s> (qualified) and <s>nirguṇa</s> (unqualified) [<s>Brahman</s>] — this is the meaning.
But [one might object:] just as the hearing of transference presents abandonment [as implied], so too the hearing of abandonment [should present] transference — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Moreover, the self is the agent#' — thus.
For acquisition (<s>grahaṇa</s>) does not occur without the departure of the owner — hence from acquisition, the establishment of departure is inevitable.
But departure is seen even without acquisition by another — as in the case of the departure of sin through <s>prāyaścitta</s> (expiation).
The statement of the difference of agents is for the purpose of corroboration, not [to establish] inevitability, because of the non-invariability of transference — thus.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] commences the established conclusion: '#When this [prima facie view] has been arrived at#' — thus.
The meaning of this is: what is prescribed in one ritual (<s>karma</s>) is not incorporated into another ritual, because of the absence of a valid means [of knowledge for doing so].
But what is not prescribed but is mentioned in its accomplished form for the purpose of praise — that, in the absence of a sublating [cognition], cannot be abandoned from the meaning understood from the word, by the principle of the <s>devatādhikaraṇa</s> (topic of deities).
And thus, when merit and demerit have been shaken off in the <s>nirguṇa</s> (unqualified) <s>vidyā</s>, the question arises — like the [analogies of] horse-hair, <s>Rāhu</s>, and the like — what happens [to them]?
To begin with, it is not possible that they dissolve [into nothing], as in the case of expiation — because then the analogies of the horse-hair and <s>Rāhu</s> would be inapplicable.
For horse-hair and the face of <s>Rāhu</s> never dissolve.
Rather, there is separation from the horse and the moon [respectively].
Nor is the purpose of shaking off or releasing possible when [the thing] has been destroyed.
Therefore, when the <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) has an expectation, the specific [element of] transference — even though brought about by textual proximity — is capable of presenting transference to the mind and fulfilling the expectation.
Even the <s>nirguṇa</s> <s>vidyā</s> is to be praised through [the mention of] abandonment and transference.
But the excellence of praise is the purpose, not a [new] means of valid knowledge.
Because praise is tenable even without excellence.
Nor is it the case that <s>arthavāda</s>s that require [supplementation from] other <s>arthavāda</s>s are not seen.
Nor is it the case that they cannot be fulfilled by those [other <s>arthavāda</s>s] — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#And it is well known#' — thus. '#And because the statement about transference is for the purpose of praising the <s>vidyā</s>#' — thus.
Even though the merit and demerit belonging to another give fruit to yet another — as the <s>Śrāddha</s> rite of a son [gives] satisfaction to the father, and the <s>Vaiśvānarīyeṣṭi</s> (offering to <s>Vaiśvānara</s>) of a father [gives fruit to] the son,
and the wife's drinking of wine [leads to] the husband's hell —
nevertheless, the merit and demerit belonging to another cannot directly [go] to another — this is the intent of the doubt.
The resolution is: [the transference occurs only] through the fruit.
'#When the intention is the incorporation of attributes#' — this too is not with the intent that there is an actual transfer of merit and demerit in their own form.
But [one might object:] in a section (<s>adhikāra</s>) on the incorporation of attributes of <s>vidyā</s>, what is this out-of-place investigation of praise? [<s>Śaṅkara</s>], while raising this doubt, also removes it: '#Therefore, in connection with the investigation of the incorporation of attributes#' — thus.
In connection with the incorporation of <s>vidyā</s>-attributes, the incorporation of praise-attributes was investigated.
And the purpose is that the practitioner should cultivate friendliness — not his own friendliness [toward himself] — as in the <s>chandas</s> (meter): [the word] '<s>chanda</s>' (pleasing) derives from '<s>ācchādana</s>' (covering/pleasing).
'#And just as the non-specific <s>upagāna</s> (auxiliary chanting)#' — thus.
The priests (<s>ṛtvij</s>s) chant the <s>upagāna</s> — this is the non-specific <s>upagāna</s> of the priests.
But the <s>Bhāllavin</s>s [have the specific rule:] 'The <s>Adhvaryu</s> does not chant the <s>upagāna</s>.'
Therefore, the statement of the <s>Bhāllavin</s>s — being the remainder of [the general statement] 'the priests chant the <s>upagāna</s>' — is understood [as specifying an exception].
What is thus stated amounts to this: the priests, excluding the <s>Adhvaryu</s>, chant the <s>upagāna</s>.
Why is it explained thus?
[One might say:] let them be independent statements — to this [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#Because it is brought about by another <s>Śruti</s>#' — thus.
Out of fear of the eightfold defect of optionality, the venerable <s>Jaimini</s> too accepts that one statement is a remainder of another statement — [<s>Śaṅkara</s>] says: '#That has been stated in the <s>Dvādaśalakṣaṇī</s>#' — thus.
The <s>sūtra</s> — 'But it should be a <s>vākyaśeṣa</s> (sentence-remainder), because of the irregularity of optionality; it should be a part of the injunctions' — is recited through the medium of its meaning: '#But because of being a <s>vākyaśeṣa</s>, it is the exclusion of the other; in the case of prohibition, optionality#' — the remainder being: '#would be [irregular]#.'
This is how it is heard: 'This indeed is the seventeen-fold <s>Prajāpati</s>, connected with every sacrifice.' Thereafter, in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s (after-offerings), the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> formula is performed.
Therein, the instruction of performing the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> formula in [all] sacrifices is given without commencing any particular sacrifice.
Having instructed that, it is recited: 'not in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s.'
Therein the doubt is: is there an optionality between the injunction and the prohibition, or is there an exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) [meaning] the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> is to be performed in sacrifices excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s?
Let there not be optionality when the prohibition is of what is [already] established by [another valid] means — for thus, what is seen as producing its beauty [in the present moment] does not negate its defectiveness in the long run.
Because of its indifference toward that [long-term effect].
But the prohibitive scripture, while not overriding the present beauty, redirects the person inclined toward action by making him understand that it will result in suffering in the future.
As it is said: 'What is not to be done is that which results in suffering.'
Therefore, the scriptural prohibition — being able to redirect even one who has been prompted by desire, since he fears suffering in the future — is stronger than the desire-prompted inclination, and hence does not deserve to be made optional with it.
But when both the injunction and the prohibition are scriptural, they are postulated as optional — like the [case of] taking the <s>Ṣoḍaśi</s> cup.
For there, from seeing the injunction, the [overall] benefit of the principal [rite] is postulated as preponderant.
And from seeing the prohibition, the accomplishment of the fruit even in the absence [of the <s>Ṣoḍaśi</s>] is understood.
As it is said: 'If one says it is [merely] established by [other] means — no, because of the equal status [of both], both being characterized by words [i.e., scriptural authority].'
Nor should one say: the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> performance in all <s>yajati</s>-sacrifices — by the general rule about all <s>yajati</s>s — approaches the specific <s>yajati</s> called <s>Anuyāja</s>, and there it is prohibited by the prohibition pertaining to the <s>Anuyāja</s>; hence the specific prohibition overrides the general rule — [this is not valid] because of the swift application [of the general rule].
For let this be so in injunctions like 'curds should be given to <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s; buttermilk to <s>Kauṇḍinya</s>'
There, [the specific statement] requires the injunction of curds for the purpose of obtaining the prohibition of buttermilk. But here, since the prohibition presupposes something [already] established, and since the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> is not otherwise established [in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s], the injunction must be expected for the purpose of the prohibition's obtaining [its object].
Nor is it correct [to say] that since the prohibition depends [on the injunction], the injunction is stronger [and so] there is no optionality but only the overriding of the prohibition — because [they are] equally undetermined in that regard, [and] in that case, the prohibitive scripture would be like a madman's song.
Nor is [the objection] valid, for what is equally traditional is of equal force.
Nor is there [the possibility of treating it as] an <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) — as in 'he does not perform [the offering] in the case of the animal [sacrifice]' — because of the absence of connected meaning.
For in the animal sacrifice, the absence of the <s>ājyabhāga</s>s (ghee-portions) is tenable [on other grounds].
But here, the absence of the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> [in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s] is not [tenable on other grounds], since the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> is prescribed in [all] <s>yajati</s>-sacrifices.
And the <s>Anuyāja</s>s possess that character [of being <s>yajati</s>-sacrifices].
Nor is this an exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) [meaning 'not in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s'] — because, by <s>Kātyāyana</s>'s view, there would be the applicability of a restriction (<s>niyama</s>).
Therefore, when the [prima facie] conclusion is that there is optionality between the enjoined and the prohibited, [the reply is given:]
Having thus arrived at [the prima facie view], the reply is stated: It has been said that in the case of [taking or not taking] the <s>Ṣoḍaśi</s> cup, there is optionality.
But there, there is no other recourse.
Therefore, even though tainted with the eightfold defect, optionality is resorted to; and because even such a position has [a claim to] validity, let there not be [the charge of] a madman's song.
But here, when the possibility of exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) is available, resorting to optionality — which is irregular (<s>anyāṭya</s>) — is inappropriate.
For thus, the connection of the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) is [as follows:] 'not in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s' — [meaning] in the <s>yajati</s>-sacrifices excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s, the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> is to be performed.
What follows from this? This follows from this:
The statement 'not in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s' — being incomplete and having an expectation — is joined with a portion of the preceding statement, namely 'he performs the <s>yeyajāmaha</s>' — [so that the meaning is:] this [<s>yeyajāmaha</s>] is not in the <s>Anuyāja</s>s — [and this] amounts to saying: [it is to be performed] in [sacrifices] excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s.
And thus, since [the negative] serves to qualify the <s>yajati</s>s [by excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s], this is an injunction for [the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> in sacrifices] excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s — and because of the absence of a prohibition, there is no optionality.
Nor is it possible that, despite the conflict with the more authoritative <s>Pāṇini</s>, <s>Kātyāyana</s> — who holds the doctrine of eternal compounds — could be speaking falsely.
For he teaches compounds in the domain of optionality.
Therefore, it is established that the <s>yeyajāmaha</s> is prescribed in [sacrifices] excluding the <s>Anuyāja</s>s.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] states another interpretation: '#Or, in these#' — thus.
For just as the postulation of the [transfer of] merit and demerit — which are formless — is not straightforward, since [their] movement follows that of the <s>Śruti</s>,
so too the transfer of what belongs to another to another is untenable, precisely because of formlessness.
Therefore, where only the shaking off (<s>vidhūnana</s>) is heard, there — by [interpreting it as] trembling [i.e., mere agitation from one's own effect] — let merely the dislodgement from its own effect be indicated, not departure from [the self] and transfer to another — because of the heaviness of such a postulation.
Therefore, when the [prima facie view that] shaking off means merely dislodgement from its own effect has been arrived at, the reply is given: Where transference is heard in the <s>Śruti</s>, there — inevitably — the shaking off must be explained as abandonment (<s>tyāga</s>).
And where shaking off is used in the sense of abandonment, there it deserves to be used in the same sense elsewhere [too].
For thus: it would not [be used in the same sense] only if shaking off obtained its primary meaning here [i.e., if mere agitation were the primary meaning].
But this is not the case.
Because even there [where transference is heard], the indicated meaning of dislodgement from one's own effect [is what is taken].
Nor does the heaviness of postulation become a valid authority, producing [the defect of] 'iron-smell' [i.e., an unwanted taint of spurious reasoning].
Moreover, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, '<s>vidhūyate</s>' (is shaken off) will be primary even in the sense of abandonment (<s>tyāga</s>),

children.translated_text: That is unreasonable — here, mere proximity in thought is what is useful, nothing else; and that [proximity] applies to <s>vidyā</s> too, since [<s>vidyā</s>] is the immediately preceding topic — hence the <s>Śruti</s> is equally [applicable] in both cases.
The meaning and the textual order remain [as the two candidates] — and between them, the meaning is stronger.
Nor is there a contradiction with the <s>Tāṇḍya</s> and other <s>Śruti</s>s in the prima facie view.

children.translated_text: 'Shaking off like a horse [shakes off] its hairs' — for this speaks of the activity of an independent person, and a deceased person has no independence; therefore, there is a contradiction [with the midway-shedding view]. //27//

body.translated_text:
'#At the time of departure, there is nothing to be crossed, for thus [declare] others#.'
Objection: from the order of the text, the crossing over of merit and demerit is understood [to occur] midway [on the path].
And from the power of <s>vidyā</s>, [the shedding of merit and demerit] is understood to occur even earlier.
Similarly, from the <s>Śruti</s> of the <s>Śāṭhyāyanin</s>s and the <s>Tāṇḍin</s>s.
And the <s>Śruti</s> and the meaning are stronger than the textual order, as in 'he offers the <s>Agnihotra</s>, he cooks the gruel.'
Therefore, since there is no prima facie objection, this [<s>sūtra</s>] need not be commenced.
To this it is said:
This is not merely the textual order, but rather a <s>Śruti</s> — 'that one shakes off merit and demerit.'
For 'that' (<s>tad</s>) is a pronoun, and therefore, in the sense of referring to what is proximate, it indicates the causal relationship thereof.
And what is proximate is what is heard immediately after.
And that is situated midway — the approaching of the river <s>Virajā</s> in the mind — hence the relinquishing of merit and demerit is midway on the path.
Nor is there a contradiction with other <s>Śruti</s>s.
Because the shaking off of sin even midway is tenable as occurring at a time prior to the attainment of <s>Brahmaloka</s>.
Similarly, there is no contradiction with the <s>Śāṭhyāyanin</s>s' [<s>Śruti</s>] either.
For neither 'while living' (<s>jīvan</s>) nor 'while alive' (<s>jīvataḥ</s>) is heard there.
And thus the release from merit and demerit is indeed midway on the path.
And thus [the release] is not from the <s>Paryaṅka-vidyā</s> [alone], and hence the destruction thereof [is midway] — this is the prima facie view.
But the established view is: for the knower whose impurities have been shaken off by the power of <s>vidyā</s>, the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> [occurs] while traveling by the northern path; and the journey on the northern path is not possible for one whose impurities have not been destroyed.
Just as the <s>Agnihotra</s> [is performed] before cooking the gruel.
Because it is heard that <s>vidyā</s>, accompanied by the practice of <s>yama</s>, <s>niyama</s>, and the like, is the means for attaining <s>Brahman</s> who is seated on the couch [in <s>Brahmaloka</s>] via the northern path.
And because this is untenable for one whose sins have not been destroyed.
<s>Vidyā</s> itself of that kind destroys impurity, and having destroyed the impurity, leads [the soul] to the northern path — so how [can there be] destruction of impurity midway?
Therefore, overriding the textual order, the logical order must be followed.
Objection: this is not merely the textual order — it has been stated that through the <s>Śruti</s> of the pronoun 'that,' there is a reference to what is proximate.

'#At will (<s>chandataḥ</s>), because of the non-contradiction of both#.'
This <s>sūtra</s> [is derived] from certain words.
Objection: just as the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> by the northern path for the deceased is the fruit of <s>vidyā</s>, so too the shedding of merit and demerit midway will also be [the fruit of <s>vidyā</s>] — the <s>sūtra</s> is a response to [the words that give rise to] this doubt.
[<s>Śaṅkara</s>] explains: '#If, after separating from the body#.'
The attainment of <s>Brahman</s> too, which is the fruit of <s>vidyā</s>, is not tenable for the deceased — because of [the words that generate] doubt.
As they say: 'Those who are not born there do not go there.'

'At will' means 'by intention' — [they explain it as] non-contradiction of <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>.
